units.la: AN alteri ἀντεξηγήσει Gronovii de Fœnore Vnciaro respondere deberem, diu mecum deliberavi, licet admodum in proclivi esset. Dissuadebant amici, & quidem multis de causis. Primo meam sententi-amam omnibus, quibus modò judicii mica est, placituram esse, qvum in adversarii opinionem conveniat illud Augusti-ni contra duas Epistolas Pelagii lib. 3. in Fine: Qvisqvis de qvacunq; re obscura id astruit, unde hoc, quod verisi-mum, fundatissimum notissimum est, destru-at; aut corrigendus est aut cavendus. Deinde hoc addebant, mores meos à tot annis omnibus bonis exploratos, homini maledico abundè prostituendo suffice-re. Tertiò haud decorum mihi fore, si, tantus natu, congrediar cum homine ejusmodi, qui dum aquilas meras somniat, vultures mortici-nos captat, nihil non ele-gan-
units.tr: For a long time I weighed in my own mind whether I ought to answer Gronovius's counter-explanation [ἀντεξήγησις] concerning the Vuncarian usury, although the task was very easy. My friends advised against it, and for many reasons. First, my opinion would please all those whose judgment is at all sound, since it agrees with the adversary's view that Augustine's statement in the third book against the two letters of Pelagius, at the end, holds: whoever asserts anything about an obscure matter by which what is most true, most well founded and most widely known is overturned must be corrected or avoided. Next, they added that my character, proven good over so many years, would be enough to refute a slanderer who is so lavishly abusive. Thirdly, it would not be fitting for me, at my age, to engage with a man of this kind, who, while he dreams of pure eagles, hunts for carrion vultures and leaves no elegant insult unsaid.

units.la: gantiarum jactare soli- tus apud stolidos adole- scentes, modò apud illos consequatur famam vir- tutis. Hæc sententia adhuc animo fixa sederet, nisi invidia & malevo- lentia, quæ ubique ter- rarum me persequutæ fuerunt, in hanc Mar- chiam usque penetras- sent, & male quidam fe- riatus, meam ignorantiam lingvæ Latinæ, produćto Gronovii libello, traduxisset. Eoqve consilium mutavi, cogitando illud Vespasiani: Non oportere, maledici senatoribus: remaledici civile fasqve esse. Atqve licet morbus vetare videretur & aurem velleret Celsus lib. 3. cap. 5. monens: ægros securos agere debere, ut, si corpore, non etiam tiam animo laborent: nihilominus tamen pauca homini, ex maledictis confuto, reposui, attendens illud, quod sapiēter non orator tantum, sed &Philosophus Romanus Cicero inquit: Dissenti-entium inter sereprehen-siones non sunt vitupe-randæ. Maledicta, contumeliæ, tum iracundiæ, contentionesque in dis-putanputando pertinaces, indignæ Philosophia mihi videri solent &c. Fateor, me, & hominem, & asperiùs sæpe verbum aspersum esse, sed cogita, mi lector, illud Ovidii:
units.tr: This opinion would have remained fixed in my mind, had not envy and ill will, which have pursued me throughout the whole world, reached even this March, and had not a certain ill-advised fellow, using the pamphlet of Gronovius, cast my ignorance of the Latin tongue in my face. So I changed my mind, reflecting on the saying of Vespasian: that one ought not to be slandered by senators, and that it is right and lawful to slander them in return. And although illness seemed to forbid it, and Celsus in the third book, chapter five, warned that the sick ought to be left undisturbed, so that they labour in body rather than also in mind, nevertheless I have replied briefly to the man with a few slanders of my own, bearing in mind what Cicero, the Roman orator and also philosopher, wisely said: that the reproofs of those who disagree are not to be condemned. Abuse, insults, and angry and obstinate contentions in disputing seem to me unworthy of philosophy, and so on. I confess that I myself, being human, have often spoken more harshly than I should, but consider, my reader, that saying of Ovid:

units.la: Mihi crede, Verba movent iras non circumspecta Deorum. Cur non scripta incircumspecta hominum, qui ordinis sui obliviscuntur? Si aliqvid qvoq; occurrat;qvod aptum sit, risum movere, cogitari velim illud Platonis in Sympos. Non reformido, ut aliqvid, qvod risum moveat, in medium afferam (hoc enim Musae nostrae proprium est & peculiare emolumentum, & qvasi gentile) sed ne ridicula dicam. Tibi, lector, extra livo-rem rem & animi fcabitudi- nrm pofite,cum plurimo tuæ falutis voto, meafi placuerint,tuàqve faven- tia potiar, omnium mali. volentium hirritus & la- tratus facilè patiar.
units.tr: "Believe me, the thoughtless words of men stir the anger of the gods." Why, then, should not thoughtless writings be judged likewise, written by men who forget their own station? If anything also occurs that is apt to raise a laugh, I would have you recall that saying of Plato in the Symposium: I do not shrink from bringing into the midst something that raises a laugh (for this is a peculiar and, as it were, native advantage of our Muse), but I do so lest I speak mere trifles. Reader, put aside all envy and bitterness of mind, and, with my most earnest wish for your welfare, if my writings please you and you favour them, I will readily bear the empty barking of all who wish me ill.

units.la: QUadriennium est, quod Exercitationes sacras de quæstionibus quibusdam Theologico-Practicis, inter ipsos Orthodoxos Theologos quàm controversis, evulgaverim. Placuerunt illæ multis viris doctis, sapientibus, pacisq; Ecclesiæ studiosis. Displicuerunt solis illis ex ordine sacro, qui à singularitate gloriam aucupantur: qui quum soli sapere videantur, femur non modo ferire solent, sed maledicentiæ pelves profundere, si quis sua placita aliquanto liberius examinare instituerit. Cum quibus quòd à plurimis annis noluerim novam in Ecclesia reformationem moliri, dura multa perpeti debui. Deus tamen indignissimum suum servum non deseruit, sed animum & vires concessit, ut non modo potuerim ex Verbo suo placita magnorum Theologorum tueri, verum etiam factionis illius primipilos ad incitas adigere, ut ipsi pertinaci silentio coacti fuerunt fateri. Vltima harum Exercitationum agebat de Fœnore Trapezitico, adeoque arrisit viro Philosopho, sani præ aliis sensus & subactissimi judicii in Academia Lugduno-Batava, ut ea honorifice ad suffragium vocata, publicam Disputationem instituerit, qua causam solide agebat gebat illorum, quos vulgus per Belgium probrosó vocabulo Lombardos vocat: quod ad rem faceret, obiter deflexeram ad Fœnus unciarium, inter viros eruditos quam controversum, ac veniam (quod tamen non oportuit) præfatus, libere inquirere coepi in sententiam Salmasii & Gronovii, ea modestia, ut cum forte hunc liberius notare potuissem, quod ex protrito magno illo Salmasio, quo vivo in scriptis dissensum vix profiteri sustinuerat, tropeum famæ erigere moliretur; contentus tamen fui hoc obiter solum innuisse, licet interim non dissimularem, omnia Gronoviana Phidiæ operibus nequaquam adæquanda esse. Pupugisse sic videor hominem, qui cum se & sua duntaxat admiretur, seseque ab excessu Salmasii (sed hactenus absque populi suffragio) pro Reip. literariæ dictatore gerat, copias non tam eruditionis, quam maledicentiæ conduxit, ut, si fieri posset, orbi literario me non modo misericordiæ, sed sui quoque nasi victimam exhiberet. Quærat forte aliquis, nec absque causa, cur vir, minime scil. ambitiosus, tot per annos silentium sibi imperare potuerit? Sed idem quærat, cur ante annum folium & amplius libelli sui, typis quoque expressum, amicis interioris admissionis oftentarit, &c, adulto demum mense Martio hujus anni, eundem vulgarit. In arenam protractum credo à quibusdam, in sua quoque urbe, qui cum videant suam sententiam de iis, qui exercent mensam fœnebrem, quod ab omni charitate tate & ratione aliena fit , displicere coepisse non modo Synodis Belgicis , sed supremis quoque Patriæ Patribus , & per totum foederatum Belgium, illos , quos ut Lombardos traducere solent , ad mensam Domini admitti , inclementer & dicunt, & male volunt omnibus , per quos norunt sententiam suam protritam esse. Gronovium siquidem , qui pag. 8. asserit Lombardos prædam sperare , ab hostibus eorundem de mensarum fœnebrium conditione edoctum fuisse , evincit narratio, quæ ibid. occurrit: quare , ut iis placeret , mihi quoque insultat pag. 42. quod alibi innuerim , quos ipse contumeliose Lombardos vocat , legi posse in Consistorium, & fieri Presbyteros ac Diaconos. Viderit verò , an bene componi possit cum iis , quibus probare se voluit. Hoc scio, quod si iis ( rigidi gratiæ Dei sunt patroni , nec quicquam naturæ tribuunt ) sisteretur ut Catechumenus, forte ob moderationem, & ignorantiam fallaciarum Pelagianarum, commendandum esse diligenti Catechistæ. Prodigiosum censet, si Trapezita,cœtera pius & honestus, in Consistorium adoptetur : sed multos eorum novi , qui licet bonis ipsius libris præferant unum solum librum, eumque optimum , adversariis religionis felicius resistere possint , quam ipse, & constantissime aut Romæ,aut Coloniæ,aut Antverpiæ, aut etiam alibi , existimationem Ecclesiæ tuituri sint. Quum Lipsius Lcidæ minus diligenter exploratus esset, admissus est in Consistorium: sed quod nimis quam asiduus fuisset in libris, quos solos Gronovius bonos censet, prostituit non tam Ecclesiam, à qua recessit, quam se probavit esse hypocritam. Gronovius dum præ iisdem libris alios non æstimat, viderit, ne, dum unius libri quam securus est, Vno quoque illo excidat, quod solum cognovisse & in hac & altera vita prodest. Duƈtor factionis Antitrapeziticæ, ne nimium diligat suos bonos libros, commendaret libellum, habentem hunc titulum: F. Gabrielis Putherbei Theotimus, sive de tollendis & expungendis malis libris, libri tres. Prævideo facile, contemneret, si offerretur: quod sui boni libri, ibi probentur esse pessimi. Sed, ut spero, si scopum Censoris attende-ret, inciperet suspectare thesauros, quos sui libri promittunt, nec carbones margaritis diutius præ-ferret. Vlterius de his viderint Theologi. Ad me accedo & heroëm nostrum: par, ut ipse profitetur, non bene compositum. Illi sum Thersites pag. 85. ipse Hector, pag. 88. Si quæras, unde hoc sciat? ipse respondebit pag. 2 quod fatis sit consisus suis moribus. Hoc scil. didicit ex bonis suis libris. Dei Codicem si æque diligenter evolveret, hos bonos suos mores suspectaret, & expavesceret ad cor su-um, fraudulentum super omnia. Nam nec ipse, nec quisquam mortalium, sed solus Deus, hoc per-scrutari potest. An ego vero merear cum homine in caustris Græcorum monstroso comparari, arbitren-turtur,qui me norunt, & scripta legerunt. Qui perso- nam hominibus, publice histrioniam facientibus detrahit; & alios monet, ne patiantur se decipi ab iis, quorum mores fucati sunt, de publico bene me- retur. Aliud à me factum fuisse, ipsa calumnia non probaverit. Nec moror, quod, qui me plus ode- runt, quam Vatinius posset, hactenus hominibus videantur satisfacere, & magni æstimentur. Recor- dor, quod Christus olim Pharisæis dixerit: Vos ii estis, qui justificatis vos ipsos in hominum con- spectu: Deus autem novit corda vestra: quia quod apud homines sublime est, abominatio est in conspectu Dei. Quicunque hæc legent, judi- cent, uter nostrum Thersites an Hector haberi me- reatur. Egone? qui ne viderer inquietare voluisse unius Salmasii Manes, in arenam pariter Heroëm nostrum protraxi, innuendo, dum ingratum ani- mum arguebam, volupe mihi non esse cum Larvis luctari. An vero is? qui audire vult rei numma- riæ oraculum, & temperare sibi non potuit, in ipsa maledici sui libelli Mantissa, quin quatuor Semo- nes, Josephum Scaligerum, Salmasium, Pancirol- lum, & Jacobum Capellum, è quorum sepulchris à tot annis rosæ natæ sunt, Pædagogi instar flagella- ret, quòd sententiam à sua opinione alienam, sed aliis quoque quàm putidæ Grammaticæ fulcris suf- fultam, in scriptis cedro dignis proposuerint. Di- ligens aliquis Homeri lector, si cum Pythagora animæ recidivatum agnosceret, juraret non Hectoris animam in Gronovio stabulari, sed ignavi illius Græculi, qui, cum fortissimus Trojanorum ab Achille esset occisus, non dubitavit mortuum procaci hac oratione incessere:
units.tr: It is four years since I published my Sacred Exercitations on certain theological and practical questions, questions on which the orthodox theologians themselves disagree very much. They pleased many learned and wise men who are zealous for the peace of the Church. They displeased only those from the sacred order who hunt for glory through singularity: since they alone seem to be wise, they are accustomed not only to beat their thigh but to pour out a flood of slander if anyone sets about examining their opinions somewhat more freely. Because I have for many years been unwilling to undertake any new reformation in the Church, I have been obliged to suffer many harsh things at their hands. Yet God has not deserted his most unworthy servant, but has granted me the spirit and the strength not only to defend the opinions of the great theologians from his Word, but also to drive the chieftains of that faction to the walls, so that, forced into stubborn silence, they were obliged to confess. The last of these Exercitations dealt with the interest of the money-changer's table, and it so pleased a philosopher of sound judgement and very sharp sense, in the Academy of Leiden, that, having been honourably called to give his opinion on it, he held a public disputation in which he argued solidly the cause of those whom the common people in Belgium call by the shameful name of Lombards. In doing so I had digressed briefly to the unciary interest, a question much disputed among learned men. I prefaced it with an apology (which, however, I ought not to have needed), and began to examine freely the opinion of Salmasius and Gronovius, with such moderation that, when I could perhaps have noted the latter more freely, I only hinted in passing that, while Gronovius was trying to raise a trophy of fame from the worn-out and great Salmasius, whom in his lifetime he scarcely dared to disagree with in print, nevertheless all Gronovius's writings were by no means to be compared with the works of Phidias. I seem to have pricked the man who, while he admires himself and his own things alone, and, since the death of Salmasius (but so far without the vote of the people), sets himself up as dictator of the literary commonwealth, has hired troops not so much of learning as of slander, so that, if it were possible, he might offer me to the literary world as a victim not only of his pity but also of his nose. Perhaps someone will ask, not without reason, how a man who is by no means ambitious could for so many years impose silence on himself. But let the same person ask why, more than a year and a half ago, he showed his pamphlet, already printed, to his intimate friends, and then, only in the full month of March of this year, published it. I believe he was dragged into the arena by certain persons, even in his own city, who, seeing that his opinion about those who keep the money-lending table, which is wholly alien to all charity and reason, has begun to displease not only the Belgian Synods but also the supreme Fathers of the Fatherland, and that throughout the whole united Belgium those whom they are accustomed to malign as Lombards are admitted to the table of the Lord, speak harshly and wish ill to all by whom they know his opinion has been worn out. For the account given in the same place proves that Gronovius, who on page 8 asserts that the Lombards hope for plunder, was informed about the conditions of the money-tables by their enemies; therefore, to please them, he also insults me on page 42, because I have elsewhere hinted that those whom he himself insultingly calls Lombards may be admitted into the Consistory and made Elders and Deacons. Let him see whether that can be reconciled with those whom he wished to prove. This I know: if they (who are strict defenders of the grace of God and attribute nothing to nature) were presented as catechumens, perhaps they would have to be commended to a diligent catechist on account of their moderation and their ignorance of Pelagian deceits. He considers it monstrous if a money-changer, otherwise pious and honest, is admitted to the Consistory; but I know many of them who, although they prefer to all his books one single book, and that the best, are able to resist the enemies of religion more successfully than he does, and who would most steadfastly defend the reputation of the Church either at Rome, or at Cologne, or at Antwerp, or indeed elsewhere. When Lipsius was less carefully examined at Leiden, he was admitted to the Consistory; but because he was far too devoted to those books which Gronovius alone considers good, he prostituted not so much the Church from which he withdrew as showed himself to be a hypocrite. While Gronovius does not value other books in comparison with these, let him see that, in his zeal for that one book he is so sure of, he does not lose the one thing which alone it is profitable to have known in this life and in the next. The leader of the Anti-Trapezitic faction, lest he love his good books too much, might commend a little book bearing this title: F. Gabriel Putherbeus's Theotimus, or On Removing and Expunging Bad Books, in three books. I foresee that he would despise it if it were offered to him, because his own good books are there shown to be the worst. But, as I hope, if he were to attend to the aim of the Censor, he would begin to suspect the treasures which his own books promise, and would no longer prefer coals to pearls. Let the theologians look further into these matters. I come to myself and to our hero, who, as he himself professes, is not well matched with me. To him I am Thersites, on page 85; he himself is Hector, on page 88. If you ask how he knows this, he himself will answer on page 2 that he is sufficiently confident of his own character. He learned this, of course, from his good books. If he unrolled the Codex of God as diligently, he would suspect this good character of his, and would be terrified at the heart of himself, deceitful above all things. For neither he nor any mortal, but God alone, can search this out. Let those who know me and have read my writings judge whether I deserve to be compared with a man who, among the Greek camps, is a monster. He who tears the mask from men who publicly play the actor, and warns others not to allow themselves to be deceived by those whose characters are painted over, deserves well of the public. That I have done anything else, even slander itself will not prove. Nor do I dwell on the fact that men who hate me more than Vatinius could are so far able to satisfy people, and are esteemed highly. I remember what Christ once said to the Pharisees: You are they who justify yourselves before men: but God knows your hearts: for what is lofty among men is an abomination in the sight of God. Let whoever reads these things judge which of us ought to be held Thersites and which Hector. Am I the one who, so as not to seem to have wished to disturb the ghost of Salmasius alone, dragged our hero into the arena as well, insinuating, while I charged him with an ungrateful mind, that it is no pleasure to me to wrestle with shades? Or is it he who wants to hear the oracle of the money business, and who could not restrain himself, in the very appendix of his slanderous pamphlet, from flogging, like a schoolmaster, the four Semones, Joseph Scaliger, Salmasius, Pancirollus, and Jacob Capellus, from whose tombs roses have sprung up for so many years, because they proposed in writings worthy of cedar an opinion alien to his own, but supported by other props than those of rotten grammar? Any careful reader of Homer, if he recognised that the soul of Pythagoras had returned in him, would swear that the soul of Hector does not stable in Gronovius, but that of that cowardly little Greek who, when the bravest of the Trojans had been killed by Achilles, did not hesitate to assail the dead man with this insolent speech:

units.la: Ὀπόποι, ἢ μάλα δὴ μαλακώτερος ἀμφαφά-ξλωξ, ἢ ὅτε γῆας ἐνέπτησεν πυρὶ κηλέῳ (ad ἀν)

units.tr: "He pierced the sinews behind both his feet, from ankle to heel, and fastened on thongs of ox-hide." [Ἀμφοτέρων μετόπισθε ποδῶν τέτρηνε τένοντε ἐς σφυρὸν ἐν πλέφνης, βοέας δ' ἐξῆπτεν ἱμάντας.]

units.la: Eoque fero, quòd in ipso titulo saluter Theologisto-ricophilosopholo-gus. Si pariter his chartis præscri-psissem titulum Grammaticalogocriticojurisconsulti, & narrassem quendam Senatus Critici principem, sordido lucello suadente, consuevisse Collegia, à tantis viris negligi solita, instituere, exteris visus fuissem æquè monstra narrare; atq; Hectorem literarium, domi è sublimi Cathedra, (ne videatur, quando à ferula recentes adolescentes instituit, inferioris subsellii esse) quoscunque Latinæ linguæ authores (quos olim pueri duodecennes intelligere solent in inferioribus Gymnasiis) Ascensianū in morem interpretari, observatiuncularm quamq; classici alicujus authoris dicto illustratam, non quidem numo sestertio, (famam licet pro fato seculi procurarit) sed contra auream imaginem vendere; simul hunc ipsum, omnium aliarum Academiarum rum Profeffores Philologos, (forte solis discipulis, quos promovit, exceptis) notare,traducere,ridere, ut reales doctores & commentatores, fi, aut quando docent, aut quando scribunt, Politicas disfertationes instituant,aut narrationem aliquam historicam, singulareve dictum, convenientibus exemplis ac sententiis illustrent, nam fi in hoc aliquid situm foret, æquè sibi in proclivi fore, ac quando vulpes pyrum comest. Verum bonæ caufiæ fiducia, talibus præsidiis haut opus esse, me monuit. Posthac fi irriter, forte aureæ institutionis exempla publicè exhibebo : diu est, quòd,quæ discipuli grandi pretio emerunt, (dubito,an faciat ad commendandum præceptorem) ausint vendere. Mererne haberi Theologus & Philosophus, testentur scripta, testentur discipuli. Noster Hector saltem, non potest hic judex sedere. Nec ausurum confido,
units.tr: And I bear it badly, because the very title is "Theologisto-ricophilosopholo-gus." If in these pages I had likewise prefixed the title "Grammaticalogocriticojurisconsultus," and had told of some leader of the Critical Senate who, urged on by a filthy little profit, was in the habit of setting up lectures, the sort of thing neglected by such great men, I would seem to be recounting monsters to outsiders just as much. And a literary Hector, sitting aloft in his lofty chair at home (lest he seem to belong to the lower bench when he teaches young boys from the ferule), interprets whatever Latin authors (whom boys of twelve usually understand in the lower schools) in the manner of Ascensius, and sells a little observation illustrated by a saying of some classical author, not indeed for a sestertius (though he may have procured fame in exchange for the fate of his age), but for a golden image. At the same time he marks, traduces and laughs at the professors of philology in all other academies (perhaps excepting only the pupils he has promoted), calling them real doctors and commentators, if, whether when they teach or when they write, they set up political dissertations, or illustrate some historical narrative or a single saying with suitable examples and opinions. For if there were anything in this, it would be just as easy for him as when the fox eats a pear. But the confidence of a good cause has reminded me that such props are not needed. Hereafter, if I am provoked, I may perhaps publicly exhibit examples of a golden training. It is a long time since pupils, who bought them at a great price (I doubt whether this helps to recommend the teacher), dared to sell them. Whether he deserves to be considered a theologian and philosopher, his writings bear witness, and his pupils bear witness. Our Hector, at least, cannot sit as judge here. Nor do I trust that he will dare:

units.la: Abrotanum agro Non audet, nisi qui didicit, dare.
units.tr: Only one who has learned how dares to give southernwood to a field.

units.la: Historici & Philologi existimationem an decoxerim, ex sequentibus judicent, quibus datum est sapere. Ad rem accedo. Quid fit fœnus unciarium, inter me & Gronovium controvertitur. Ipsi videtur illud esse, pag. 5. ubi mensibus singulis centesi-ma partis uncia seu duodecima pars, omni anno una pars centesima integra, seu nummus in centenos nummos collocatæ pecuniæ fructus est. Ego vero, ut ipsius verba non mutem, putarim uncias uncias usuras, vel unciarium fœnus prorsus i-dem esse, quod usuras centesimas, seu duodecim annuos in centenos. Vtri nostrum hic debeatur triumphus, postea liquebit: at viderit Gronovius, ne eum ante victoriam proclamaverit, & nimis festinarit in tropæo erigendo. Persuasum quidem cupit, sibi præ aliis fidem deberi, quod nemo ea dili-gentia de re nummaria scripserit, quo ipse conatus fuit,pag. 4. eoque,quæ hac de re Jos. Scaliger, & tot alii posteritati reliquerunt,ipsi sunt festinata nimis. Sed hæc parum me movent. Sufficit mihi, ab iis, qui hæc discutere possunt, rationes cum rationibus contendi. Erat hæc prima ratio,quam ne quidem Achilles, nedum Hector noster de statu deturbaverit.
units.tr: Let those who can judge historians and philologists see from what follows whether I have ruined my reputation; to them it has been given to be wise. I come to the matter. What a fœnus unciarium is, is in dispute between me and Gronovius. He thinks it is what he states on p. 5: where in each month the hundredth part of a pound, or the twelfth part of a unit, and in each year one hundredth part whole, or a coin, is the yield on a hundred coins lent. I, however, without changing his words, would think that uncial interest and the unciarium fenus are exactly the same as hundredths of interest, or twelve per cent a year on a hundred. Which of us deserves the triumph here will become clear later. But let Gronovius see to it that he does not proclaim victory beforehand, and that he does not hurry too much in raising his trophy. He very much wants it believed that more trust is due to him than to others, because no one has written about monetary matters with the care that he himself attempted (p. 4). And so what Joseph Scaliger and so many others have left to posterity on this subject is, in his view, too hastily done. But these things move me little. It is enough for me that the arguments have been weighed against arguments by those who are able to examine these things. This was my first argument, which not even Achilles, let alone our Hector, could have overthrown from its position.

units.la: Quum apud omnes sanæ mentis homines, in confesso sit, in ea repub. quæ subditos habet pauperes, & æris indigos, usuras esse grandiores, quam ubi subditi opibus & pecunia abundant, quis persuasum habeat, eo tempore, quo Roma circa matrem suam adhuc luctabatur, (ut cum Floro loquar) atque fasces suos ultra Italiam nondum extenderat, annuatim modo unam centesimam sortis partem, modo iterum unam ducentesimâ sortis partem solutam nomine usuræ fuisse; atque, cum ea ipsa Romuli urbs ferme ὅλης τῆς οἰκουμένης opes mœnibus suis completeretur, centesimam usuram fuisse ordinariam, atque atque duodenas centesimas partes fortis citra querelam quoque anno pensas fuisse.
units.tr: Since it is agreed among all sane men that in a commonwealth whose subjects are poor and in need of money, interest is higher than where the subjects abound in wealth and money, who would believe that at the time when Rome was still struggling about her mother (to use Florus' words), and had not yet extended her fasces beyond Italy, only one hundredth part of the principal was paid annually as interest, or again one two-hundredth part of the principal; and that, when that very city of Romulus was filling her walls with the riches of almost the whole world, the ordinary interest was one hundredth, and twelve hundredths of the principal were paid each year without complaint?

units.la: Multa adversus haec accumulantur, nam com-plentur paginę sedecim. Nihil vero quod faciat πρὸς τὸ ἐπῳ, (provoco ad quoscunque) respon-detur. Aut dissimulavit Noster, quod argumen-tum intelligeret. Aut noluit intelligere. Aut non potuit intelligere. Ridet me ut Dialecticum pag. 20. alibi Dialecticam Sophisticæ exæquat; at, si a li-mine salutasset Divam hanc, monente suo Cicero-ne, sciret dijudicare qua ratione verum falsumve sit, quid efficiatur e quoque: quod cui conse-quens sit, quodque contrarium. Putat pag. 6. & seqq. se pulchre contudisse hunc meum Achillem, quod ostendere possit, publicam & communem paupertatem non esse crescentis pecuniæ potissi-mam cau�am: atque, ut hoc astruat, (securus vinculorum, quibus postea constringendus erit) quo non divagatur? Sed non fuit hoc meum argumen-tum. Comparative procedit, & componit Roma-ni Imperii infantiam, cum virili ætate: quod si non intelligat, consulat Philosophos in sua Academia: vel si supercilium ipsius eousque se submittere non possit, consulat saltem Serviurs ad verf. 69. Eclog. 8. Virg. nisi forte & hic malus Author sit. Mihi cer-te est Grammaticus ἀντιξι decem Gronovio-rum. Confido vero nullum præter ipsum, nisi forte ἀρρωστίας διανοίας laboraverit, aliter conclusu-rum rum esse, quam certo credi debere, in ea Repub. cum egen i & impotens adhuc esset, minimum usu-ras Centesimas per leges receptas fuisse ;, quod tantæ, eadem Republ. quam locupletata & potenti, jure probatæ fuerint. Attendatur Batavorum Resp. quum Albanus eam exerceret, supremi illius moderatores, iis, qui pecunia sua laboranti rei communi succurrebant, aliquando usuras centesimas, sæpius dextantes, & dodrantes promiserunt, nec vitio datum fuit privatis eo tempore, si tantundem exigerent. Anno trigesimo sexto hujus seculi, reip. ejusdem nomine quotannis adhuc solvebantur usuræ semisses, quæ ab illo tempore, cæperunt redigi ad quincunces: nunc vero conversæ sunt in trientales, & forte brevi redigentur ad quadrantes: quod debetur solummodo Dei benedictioni, quæ reipubl. isti tantum incrementum contulit. At fingE,hodie Præpotentes Batavie Ordines, adhuc centesimis usuris pecuniam mutuam accipere, an cuiquam, præter Gronovium, tam male cum ratione conveniet, ut exiltimet illorum majores anno sep-tuagesimo, aut octuagesimo superioris seculi, reipubl. creditoribus usuras duntaxat trientales solvisse? Applicentur hæc ad rem Romanam, & argumentum meum nondum solutum esse patebit. Do lubens, acri adversarie sententiæ patrono, (hoc contendit pag. 6.) rempub subsistere posse absque fœnore, nec barbatos Romanos, pauperes licet, celeres Calendas metuisse; adhoc, neque lo-cuplecupletes, neque extreme pauperes, sed τὰς τὴν ἀντιξηκείαν ἀναιχυνομένας (ut ex Plutarcho pag. 6. docet) foeneratoribus maxime obnoxios esse; praeterea, Romae foeneratorum crudeles rapinas & fraudes vix ullis legibus coerceri potuisse. postremum hoc necessum non fuisset, pag. 11. 12. 13. tam prolixe deduxisse; ut neque pag. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. quibus legibus grassanti malo obviam itum fuerit. Nihil horum inter nos controvertebatur, sed quis usurarum modus, per leges, maxime xii. tabularum, definitus fuerit. Foeneratores Protei instar, vincula aut effugere, aut perrumpere omni evo scieverunt. Apposite ad Trapezitam Plautinus Curculio, Act. 4. sc. 2.
units.tr: Many objections are heaped against this, for the pages run to sixteen. Yet nothing is answered that bears on the point (I challenge anyone). Either our author concealed that he understood the argument, or he was unwilling to understand it, or he could not understand it. He laughs at me as a dialectician (p. 20), and elsewhere he equates dialectic with sophistry. But if he had greeted this goddess from the threshold, as his own Cicero advises, he would know how to judge by what reasoning a thing is true or false, what follows from each, and what is consequent upon what and what is contrary to it. On p. 6 and following he thinks he has neatly crushed my Achilles, because he can show that public and common poverty is not the chief cause of growing money. And to establish this (careless of the chains with which he will afterwards be bound), where does he not wander? But this was not my argument. It proceeds by comparison, and sets the infancy of the Roman Empire beside its manly age. If he does not understand this, let him consult the philosophers in his own academy; or if his haughtiness cannot stoop so far, let him at least consult Servius on verse 69 of Virgil's Eclogue 8, unless perhaps this too is a bad author. For my part he is surely a grammarian worth ten Gronovii. I trust, however, that no one but himself, unless he suffers from some weakness of mind, will conclude otherwise than that it must be taken as certain that in that commonwealth, while it was still needy and powerless, the lowest interest allowed by the accepted laws was one hundredth, a rate that was approved by law for the same republic once it had grown rich and powerful. Consider the Batavian Republic: when the Duke of Alva governed it, its supreme rulers sometimes promised interest of one hundredth, and more often nine-twelfths and ten-twelfths, to those who came to the aid of the common cause with their money in its need, and it was not held against private lenders at that time if they demanded as much. In the thirty-sixth year of this century, the interest paid on the same republic's behalf every year was still semisses, which from that time began to be reduced to quincunces; now indeed they have been changed to trientes, and perhaps soon will be reduced to quadrantes. This is owed solely to God's blessing, which has conferred such growth on that commonwealth. But imagine: do the most powerful Dutch States today still borrow money at one hundredth interest? Would anyone, other than Gronovius, be so badly reconciled with reason as to think that their ancestors in the seventieth or eightieth year of the last century paid their creditors only trientes of interest? Apply these things to the Roman case, and it will be clear that my argument has not yet been answered. I gladly grant to this keen defender of the opposing view (he contends on p. 6) that the commonwealth can subsist without interest, and that the bearded Romans, though poor, did not fear the swift Kalends; further, that neither the rich nor the extremely poor, but those who were ashamed of their poverty (as Plutarch teaches on p. 6), were especially liable to moneylenders. Besides, the cruel robberies and frauds of Roman moneylenders could scarcely be restrained by any laws. This last point would not have been necessary to develop at such length on pp. 11, 12, 13, nor on pp. 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, to show by what laws the spreading evil was met. None of this was in dispute between us; what was in dispute was what limit on interest was fixed by law, especially by the Twelve Tables. Moneylenders, like Proteus, have always known how to escape or break through the bonds. Plautus' Curculio, Act 4, scene 2, fits the money-changer well:

units.la: Rogationes plurimas propter vos populus scivit, Quasrogatas rumpitis: aliquâ reperitis rimâ, Quasi aquam ferventem frigidam esse, ita vos putatis leges.
units.tr: The people have passed many measures on your account, and you break the measures once passed; you find some crack, as if you thought the laws were boiling water that is cold.

units.la: Quasi diceret, ubi primum leges latae fuerint, & quasi ferventes, tunc illas metuitis: postquam paulum obsoleverint, & frigent, negligitis. Nec dubium est, florente Roma, ultra centesimam hos ipsos progressos fuisse, & non modo afflixisse ambitiosorum fortunas, qui eos sectabantur, ut favente nummo consequi possent, quod de virtute desperabant: sed & dissolutorum juvenum, ganeonumque, quorum libidini satisfieri non poterat, absque praesenti pecunia. Interim omnibus his, non tam fœnus,quam singulares fœneratorum artes exitium accelerare solent. Pulchre Ambrosius libel. de Tobia. Nihil nequius fœneratoribus,qui lucra sua aliena damna arbitrantur? aucupantur hæredes novos ,adolescentulos divites explorant per suos, adjungunt fe, simulantes paternam & avitam amicitiam , volunt domesticas eorum cognoscere necefitates. Si quam caussam invenerint, accusant verecundiam , pudorem arguunt, quod non ante de fe speratum atque præsumptum. sin vero nullos laqueos alicujus necessitudinis offenderint, intexunt tabulas, ajunt nobile prædium esse venale, amplam domum, accumulant proventus fructuum , annuos reditus exaggerant, hoc tantum ut coëmant. Similiter faciunt, preciofas vestes & monilia nobilia prædicantes. Negant fe habere pecuniam, ingerunt suam , utere ut tua: de fructibus emptę possessionis precium multiplicabis, debitum reddes. Prætendunt alienos fundos adolescenti , ut eum suis expolient , tendunt retia. Simul,ut indagine cincta, septa fuerit ingressus , cogunt eum in retia cautionum, laqueos usurarum, petunt sibi obligari avitum prædium , paternum sepulchrum , præstituitur dies solutioni, dissimulatur conventio, quando potest solutio sustineri ; ubi satis securum reddiderint, repente ,ingruunt , & instant vehementius, causanti incumbunt, dicentes : Tu possides tua prædia, nos nostram pecuniam non habemus , aurum dedimus , lignum tenemus, tibi fructuum emolumenta procedunt, cedunt, nobis nihil accrescit pecunię: Ociosa cau-satio est, saltem renovetur chirographum. Itaque dum primum putat adolescens nihil de vestibus suis, aut possessionibus esse vendendum, ad hęc facienda poscit dilationem. Vsurę applicantur ad fortem, aceumulantur centesimę. Jam suspirare incipit, jam malum suum agnoscit, die ac nocte usuram cogitat: quicquid occurrit, fœneratorem putat: quicquid crepuerit, vocé sibi videtur fœneratoris audire, &c.
units.tr: He means that as long as laws are newly passed and still "boiling hot," you fear them; once they have grown stale and gone cold, you neglect them. There is no doubt that in flourishing Rome these same laws were carried beyond the hundredth, and they not only ruined the fortunes of ambitious men who pursued them so that, with money in their favour, they might obtain what they despaired of gaining by merit, but also those of dissolute young men and spendthrifts whose lust could not be satisfied without ready cash. Meanwhile, for all these people it is not so much the interest as the particular tricks of the moneylenders that usually hasten their ruin. Ambrose writes admirably in his book On Tobias: "Nothing is more wicked than moneylenders, who count their gains as other people's losses. They hunt for new heirs and seek out rich young men through their agents. They attach themselves to them, pretending a paternal and ancestral friendship, and wish to learn their domestic necessities. If they find some cause, they accuse the young man's modesty and rebuke his shame, because he has not come to them earlier, as they had hoped and presumed. But if they find no snare in any kind of need, they weave their schemes: they say that a noble estate is for sale, a spacious house; they magnify the yearly yield of the crops and the annual income, all so that he will buy. They do the same by praising costly clothes and noble jewels. They deny that they have money, and they press theirs on him: 'Use it as your own; from the fruits of the land you have bought you will multiply the price, and you will repay the debt.' They put out other people's estates as bait for the young man, so that they may strip him, and they spread their nets. And at once, once the entrance has been fenced in as if by a hunting-net, they drive him into the nets of guarantees and the snares of interest. They demand that his ancestral estate and his father's tomb be pledged to them. A day is set for payment; the agreement is kept quiet while payment can still be made. But when they have made him sufficiently secure, they suddenly rush in and press harder, attacking his excuses: 'You possess your estates, but we do not have our money. We gave gold and hold wood. The profits of the fruits come to you; nothing accrues to us from the money. The excuse is idle; at least let the bond be renewed.' So while the young man at first thinks nothing of his clothes or his properties has to be sold, he asks for a delay to do these things. Interest is added to the principal, and the hundredths pile up. Now he begins to sigh; now he recognises his evil; day and night he thinks of the interest. Whatever happens, he thinks it is the moneylender; whatever rattles, he seems to hear the moneylender's voice, and so on."

units.la: Hactenus Ambrosius. En! ut arguat fœneratores, non quod centesimas acciperent, sed quod accumularent. Scaptius quaternas exigebat à Salaminiis, ut ipse Cicero testatur lib. 5. ad Att. ep-ult. Fide minus bonaagit Adversarius, quando quę à fœneratoribus facta sunt, confundit cum illis,quę jure licebant: ideo,ut evincatRomanos,antequam egressi essent Italiam, fœnerantibus quidem sol-visse centesimas, sed legibus solum jussum fuisse fœnus unciarium, pag. 20. quod ipsi duodecima centesimę pars. At discat ab ipso Justiniano, usu-ras majores centesimis jam olim permissas fuisse,leg. 26. §. 6. Cod. de Vsuris, expresse sic loquitur Imperator: In trajectitiis autem contractibus, vel specierum fœnori dationibus, usque ad centesimam tantummodo licere stipulari, nec eum excedere, licet Veteribus Legibus hoc erat concessum. Paraphraftes commodus hujus legis est Harmenopylus libr. 3. tit. 7. §. 25. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ναυτικῶν χῶν δανείων, καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τῶν δανειζομένων ἐ-δῶν, ἐφ' ὧν τὸ ΠΑΛΑΙΟΝ ἐξὴν πλείονα τόκον λαμβάνειν, μόνον μένοι ἕως ἑκατοστῆς, καὶ μὴ περαιτέρω. In nauticis autem fœnoribus, aut speciebus, quæ fœnori dantur, in quibus V E-TERI JURE licebat graviores vsuras exigere, centesima duntaxat & non ultra exigatur. Quid vetus Jus, quid veteres leges, nisi quę Roma in cunis adhuc vagiente, vigebant, & præ-senti pauperis reipub. conditioni serviebant? non ignoro, vetus jus in Jure Romano aliquando cen-seri, quodcunque novam legem præcessit. Sed hoc quoque scio, l. 1. ff. de Or. I. per leges vetustas, & §. 5. Instit de Exhær. liber. per leges antiquas jus xii. Tab. intelligi: quod & legis antiquæ nomen fert l. 1. Cod. de Except. item jus antiquum vocatur l. 7. ff. de cap. min. Jus vetus l. 1. ff. de hæred. petit. & alibi sæpe. Jus priscum l. ult. Cod. Theod. de ufur. rei judic. Si non ostenderit Adversarius legem sub Principibus latam, quam Justinianus respexerit, concludam per xii. Tab. in casibus, quos tangit Imperator, licuisse usuram Centesimam excedere. Neque enim Tacitus Annali 6. totum legis carmen exhibet, cum dicit, Neque unciario fœnore amplius exerceret. Vnciarium fœnus, quod mihi coincidit (imo, ut clarissimè liquebit, coincidere debet) cum Centesima, potuit æque ordinarium fœnus fuisse, juxta xii. ratione omnium contractuum ;atque ratione cujuscunque licitæ negotiationis d.l.Imp. Justinianus usuras bes- ses permisit. Et ut Imp.in trajestitiis contrac̃ti- bus & specierum fœnori dationibus, centesimam concessit, licuerit quoque per xii. Tab. in simili- bus casibusCentesimam excedere. Fatcor lubens, me hæc probare non posse, per ipsas leges vetustas ; (quod solummodo rudera earum nobis supersint) confido tamen conjecturas has omni ratione non destitui. Interim seponere tuto mihi licet hasce conjecturas, quum audax Adversarii assertio, per ipsas leges (Jurisconsultus est, præ me has nosse debuis- set) & confundatur, & prostituatur : ex quibus mihi sufficit probasse, jam olim Jure licuisse centesi- mam excedere. Forte exceperit contra Justinia- num, & aliquid in Adversariis invenerit, quod Grammatico colore inficere possit. Eoque pro asse- rendo argumento meo, testem assiduum magis lau- do : Ipsum Hectorem nostrum. si aliquem grandi quoque ære voluissem conducere, æque commo- dum (sed & verum) testimonium non potuisset di- cere. Omnes credent, modo audiatur. Ita ergo pag. 72.vaticinatur : Fœnoris modus crescit minuitur- ve,partim pro tempore proq. modo pecunia, qua inter homines Versatur, partim pro fide illorum, qui mutuum petunt. Qui ergo ibat in creditum adpendendo centum aut mille libras æris, stipu-
units.tr: So far Ambrose. See! He attacks the moneylenders not because they took a hundredth, but because they piled it up. Scaptius demanded fourfold from the Salaminians, as Cicero himself testifies in book 5 to Atticus, last letter. The adversary acts with little good faith when he confuses what the moneylenders did with what was lawfully allowed. Therefore, to prove that the Romans, before they left Italy, had indeed paid a hundredth to moneylenders, but that only the unciary interest had been ordered by law, p. 20, which he calls the twelfth part of a hundredth. But let him learn from Justinian himself that higher interest than a hundredth was permitted long ago: Cod. de Usuris, law 26, §6. The Emperor speaks plainly thus: In maritime contracts, or in loans of goods given at interest, it is permitted to stipulate only up to a hundredth, and not to exceed it, although under the old laws this had been allowed. The paraphrast most suited to this law is Harmenopoulos, book 3, title 7, §25. [ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ναυτικῶν χρεῶν δανείων, καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τῶν δανειζομένων ἐδῶν, ἐφ' ὧν τὸ ΠΑΛΑΙΟΝ ἐξῆν πλείονα τόκον λαμβάνειν, μόνον μένοι ἕως ἑκατοστῆς, καὶ μὴ περαιτέρω.] In maritime loans, or in goods given as loans, in which under the OLD LAW it was permitted to exact a higher interest, let only a hundredth be exacted, and no more. What is the old law, what are the old laws, except those that held force while Rome was still in its cradle and crying, and served the present condition of the poor commonwealth? I am not unaware that the old law in Roman law is sometimes taken to mean whatever preceded a new law. But I also know that by old laws (law 1, Dig. de Orig. Iuris) and by ancient laws (§5, Inst. de Exheredatione Libera) is meant the Law of the Twelve Tables; and the name ancient law is found in law 1, Cod. de Exceptionibus; ancient law is also called such in law 7, Dig. de Capitis Minutione; old law in law 1, Dig. de Hereditatis Petitione, and often elsewhere; primitive law in the last law, Cod. Theod. de Usuris Rei Iudicatae. If the adversary does not show a law passed under the princes which Justinian had in view, I will conclude that by the Twelve Tables it was permitted, in the cases the Emperor touches upon, to exceed the hundredth interest. For Tacitus, in Annals 6, does not set out the whole text of the law when he says: nor was he to practise lending at more than unciary interest. The unciary interest, which I take to coincide (indeed, as will be most clearly shown, it must coincide) with the hundredth, could just as well have been the ordinary interest, according to the Twelve Tables, in regard to all contracts and every lawful business; and Justinian's law permitted interest of this kind. And just as the Emperor granted a hundredth in maritime contracts and in loans of goods given at interest, so it would also have been allowed under the Twelve Tables to exceed the hundredth in similar cases. I gladly confess that I cannot prove this from the old laws themselves, since only their ruins survive for us; yet I trust these conjectures are in no way unfounded. Meanwhile I may safely set these conjectures aside, since the bold assertion of the adversary, which is supported by the laws themselves (he is a jurist and ought to have known these better than I), is both confused and falsified. From these points it is enough for me to have shown that long ago it was lawful by right to exceed the hundredth. Perhaps he will object against Justinian and find something in our opponents that he can colour with grammatical pretence. For proving my argument, I praise a witness who is more constant still: our Hector himself. Even if I had wished to hire some witness at a great price, I could not have named a more convenient (and also a truthful) one. All will believe him, provided he is heard. So, on p. 72, he prophesies thus: The rate of interest rises or falls, partly according to the time and the state of money circulating among men, partly according to the credit of those who ask for a loan. So whoever lent a hundred or a thousand pounds of money on credit, stipulated

units.la: B labalabatur mercedem usus pecunia sua, quam alte-ri concedebat, menstruam vel centesimam partem crediti, ut de mille libris decem, de centenis unam, vel plus minusve: prout erant tempora & fides necessitasque mutuantis: quoties fides erat angustior & rei nummariæ difficultas, multum; quoties abundabat pecunia & bonum nomen creditor, minus. Quid eque appositè pro statuminando meo argumento (circa quod Adversarius frustra lacertos fatigavit) dici posset? Hoc ipsum volo, hoc ipsum contendo. Romæ, cum pecuniæ esset sterilitas, & populus egenus, Vnciarium fœnus, seu Centesima Legibus permissa fuit. Imo (licet ex Historiis, quæ interciderunt, probari non possit) ipso Justiniano teste, grandior quoque usura. De quo ne quis dubitet, cogitet, florente Roma, Centesimam per Leges (non ergo per solam fœneratorum libidinem) usuram ordinariam fuisse. Si ego tam turpiter me dedissem, quantum non pulveris Adversarius concitasset? Ipse forte eodem privilegio gaudet, quo olim Chii. At, si neque ratio neque Adversarius (sibi maxime adversus) faveret: Romanæ saltem reip. ratione, favere deberet Dion Cassius, apud quem lib. 51. postquam de Octavio Augusto Triumphatore egisset, hæc occurrunt:
units.tr: stipulated as the price for the use of his money, which he lent to another, a monthly or a hundredth part of the loan, as in ten pounds out of a thousand, one out of a hundred, or more or less, according to the times, the credit, and the need of the lender: whenever credit was tighter and money scarce, much; whenever money abounded and the creditor had a good name, less. What could be said more fittingly to establish my argument, on which the adversary has vainly exhausted his muscles? This very thing I maintain, this very thing I contend. At Rome, when money was scarce and the people poor, unciary interest, or the hundredth, was permitted by law. Indeed (although this cannot be proved from the histories that have perished), by the testimony of Justinian himself, a higher interest was also allowed. On this point let no one doubt or think: while Rome flourished, the hundredth was the ordinary interest by law (not therefore by the mere lust of the moneylenders). If I had disgraced myself so shamefully, how much dust would the adversary have raised? Perhaps he himself enjoys the same privilege the people of Chios once had. But if neither reason nor the adversary (least of all against himself) favoured it, then at least by the reasoning of the Roman commonwealth Dion Cassius should favour it, in whom, in book 51, after treating of Octavian Augustus the triumphant, the following occurs:

units.la: τοσοῦτον γὰρ ὁ πλῆθος τῶν χρημάτων ἀλλὰ πάσης ὁμοίως τῆς πόλεως ἐλώφησεν, ὥστε τὰ μὲν κτήματα ἐπιπρασθῆναι, τὰ δὲ δανείσματα, ἀγαπητῶς
units.tr: "For the abundance of money relieved the whole city alike, so that estates were sold off and loans [were called in], and [the debtors] gladly fell into bondage, until at last they were set free from it" [τοσοῦτον γὰρ ὁ πλῆθος τῶν χρημάτων ἀλλὰ πάσης ὁμοίως τῆς πόλεως ἐλώφησεν, ὥστε τὰ μὲν κτήματα ἐπιπρασθῆναι, τὰ δὲ δανείσματα, ἀγαπητῶς]

units.la: ἐπὶ δεσμὸν πεσεῖσθαι ἐν οὐλα, τότε ἐπὶ τῷ τελευτῶν ζῶν ἀυλῆς γενέσθαι.
units.tr: "to fall into bond, [and] then at last to become free" [ἐπὶ δεσμὸν πεσεῖσθαι ἐν οὐλα, τότε ἐπὶ τῷ τελευτῶν ζῶν ἀυλῆς γενέσθαι.]

units.la: Tantum enim pecuniæ per universam urbem ferebatur, ut & facultatum census auctus sit: & fœnus quod antea denario pendebatur, tum ad trientem ejus reciderit. Si aliud non haberem, solus hic locus (qui infra novum argumentum suggeret) Hectori nostro papyraceo æternum prostituendo sufficeret. Non accedo adhuc ad vindicandum secundum argumentum.
units.tr: So much money was circulating throughout the whole city that the assessed value of estates also rose, and the interest which had formerly been paid at a denarius per month was then reduced to a third of that. If I had nothing else, this passage alone (which suggests a new argument below) would be enough to expose our paper Hector to ridicule for all time. I do not yet come to defending the second argument.

units.la: Subsistere aliquantum oportet, circa fœnus improbum, quod contra leges, fœneratores jam olim Romæ exercuisse Noster concedit, ut ipsam quoque Centesimam excesserint. Quis fando unquam audivit, quod si in aliqua Republ. fœnus contra leges immodicum exercitum fuerit, leges, quæ ad illud coërcendum ferebantur, usuras minimas, & non potius mediocres definivisse. Prudentes Legislatores idem hic observare solent, quod circa valorem pecuniæ, qui si in immensum surrexit, ad justum reducunt. Sed ipsa florente Roma, justa & ordinaria Centesima fuit, quis ergo sibi non persuadeat, fœneratores Centesimam excedere solitos, ad eam, seu, unciarium fœnus, per jus antiquum revocatos fuisse: quum ridiculum fuisset, duodecimam illius usuræ partem, quæ ordinariò à fœneratoribus exigi solet, & à multis absque gemitu solvebatur, ordinarii fœnoris modum statuere. Tacitus in loco controverso, occasione mali fœnebris
units.tr: We must dwell a little on the wicked usury which, contrary to the laws, our author concedes the moneylenders had practised at Rome long ago, so that they even exceeded the Centesima. Who has ever heard, in any commonwealth, that when usury was practised immoderately and against the laws, the laws enacted to restrain it set the interest at the lowest rate instead of a moderate one? Wise lawgivers usually do here what they do with the value of money: when it has risen beyond measure, they bring it back to a just level. But while Rome was flourishing, the just and ordinary rate was the Centesima. Who, then, would not be persuaded that the moneylenders used to exceed the Centesima and were brought back to it, or to the unciary usury, by the ancient law? It would have been ridiculous to fix the ordinary rate of interest at a twelfth part of that usury, which the moneylenders usually exacted and which many paid without a groan. Tacitus, in the disputed passage, adds on the occasion of the evil of usury:

units.la: addit: Multisque plebiscitis obviam itum frau-dibus, quae toties repressa, miras per artes rur-sum oriebantur. Idem querentem audivimus Cur-culionem. Demus jam adversario, unciarium foe-nus, jure concessum, duodecimam Centesimae par-tem fuisse, quae impudentia foeneratorum fuerit, legitimas usuras in tantum multiplicasse, ut unde-cies excesserint, quod leges jusserant. Inaudita haec sunt & a ratione alienissima. Atque, si aliquis co-gitet, duplicasse eosdem Centesimas, magis adhuc obstupescet. Nemo repente fieri solet turpissimus: nec ab extremo ad extremum pervenitur, nisi per medium. Foenus unciarium si fuerit duodecima Centesimae pars, necessum fuerit, per deunces, tri-entes, semisses, dodrantes, & dextantes, foenera-tores ad Centesimas pervenerint. At, ut multae querelae (apud Ciceronem maxime, speciatim li-quet ex lib. 5. epist. ad Att. epist. ult. lib. 6. epist. 1. & 3.) jam olim Romae de foeneratoribus fuerunt; ita potissimum excessum Centesimae respexerunt. Quae cum fuerit concessa, quorsum unciarium foe-nus alio trahitur? Cum sub Tiberio populus de foe-noris incommodis queretur, teste Tacito, trepidi Patres (neque enim quisquam tali culpa vacu-us) veniam a Principe petivere. Quis dubitet, multis seculis ante, utrumque ordinem, Laticlavi-os & Angusticlavios, per foeneratores quoque, col-locasse suam pecuniam? At, quis exististimet eos po-pulo pulo tantum gratificari voluisse, ut duodecima centesimæ pars ordinarii foenoris regula esset? Ne ipse quidem Gronovius (qui hominem domi cognoverunt, affirmant) si jus habuisset sedendi in Orchestra, hoc concessisset. Ipsos Senatorii ordinis viros, quod pecunia abundare soliti essent, foeneratoribus clanculum favisse, quis dubitet? Iis enim olim omnis foeneratio interdicta fuit, ut viri docti jam olim observarunt ex hom. 57. Chrysost. in cap. 27. Matth. Vnde & Augustinus dicit in Quæst. Vet. Test. Senatoribus foenus dissamia fuit. Postea ei modus datus est, per Impp. Arcadium, Honorium, & Theodosium, qui leg. 4. Cod. Theod. de Vsur. sic rescripserunt Optato: Senatores sub medietate centesimæ usuræ, ad contractum creditæ pecuniæ censemus admitti. Quod Tiberius sciret Senatores pecunia affluere, & eam foeneratoribus credere, cum pauperibus foenore oppressis vellet succurrere, jussit διοχλίας μυριάδας ὑπ' ἀνδρῶν βασιλευῶν ἀποχεῖ τοῖς δεομένοις ἐς τέλα ἐπηνάδαν, ut loquitur Dion lib. 58. Dici posset, aliquando omne foenus legibus prohibitum fuisse; sed, modò ad illud respondebitur. Hoc interim auctarium accedat vindiciis primi argumenti. Secundum meum argumentum his verbis conceptum erat: Quis sibi persuadeat, plebem Romanam indignatam fuisse, quòd ex præscripto XII. tabularum, usuræ loco, quoque anno, unam cen-
units.tr: Many plebiscites were passed to meet the frauds, which, though so often suppressed, arose again by wonderful arts. We have heard the same complaint from Curculio. Let us now grant the opponent that the unciary usury, allowed by law, was a twelfth part of the Centesima. What shamelessness it was for the moneylenders to multiply their lawful interest so far that they exceeded it eleven times over, contrary to what the laws had ordered! These things are unheard of and wholly alien to reason. And if anyone considers that they doubled the same Centesimae, he will be even more astonished. No one is usually made utterly shameless all at once, nor does one pass from one extreme to the other except through the middle. If the unciary usury was a twelfth part of the Centesima, the moneylenders must have reached the Centesimae by way of the eleventh-parts, the thirds, the halves, the three-quarters and the five-sixths. But that there were many complaints against moneylenders at Rome long ago (especially in Cicero, as is clear from book 5, letter to Atticus, the last letter of book 6, and letters 1 and 3) shows that they were chiefly aimed at the excess over the Centesima. Since that was conceded, why is the unciary usury dragged in elsewhere? When under Tiberius the people complained of the troubles caused by usury, as Tacitus witnesses, the anxious Fathers (for none was free of such fault) sought pardon from the Prince. Who doubts that many centuries earlier both orders, the Laticlavii and the Angusticlavii, also placed their money with moneylenders? But who would think they wished to gratify the people so far that the twelfth part of the Centesima became the rule of ordinary interest? Not even Gronovius himself (whom those who knew him at home affirm) would have conceded this, had he had the right to sit in the orchestra. Who doubts that the senators themselves, because they were accustomed to abound in money, secretly favoured the moneylenders? For all lending at interest was once forbidden to them, as learned men long ago observed from Chrysostom's homily 57 on chapter 27 of Matthew. Hence Augustine also says in the Quaestiones Veteris Testamenti: Usury was a disgrace for senators. Afterwards a limit was set on it by the emperors Arcadius, Honorius and Theodosius, who, in law 4 of the Theodosian Code, De Usuris, rescripted thus to Optatus: We decree that senators may be admitted to contracts for money lent at half the centesimal interest. Because Tiberius knew that senators had money in abundance and lent it to moneylenders, he wished to help the poor who were oppressed by interest, and so ordered that ten thousand myriads [διοχλίας μυριάδας ὑπ' ἀνδρῶν βασιλευῶν ἀποχεῖ τοῖς δεομένοις ἐς τέλα ἐπηνάδαν] be paid out by the royal men to those in need, as Dion says in book 58. It might be said that all usury was once forbidden by law, but this will be answered presently. Meanwhile let this addition accompany the defence of my first argument. My second argument was framed in these words: Who can believe that the Roman plebs was indignant that, by the prescription of the Twelve Tables, one hundredth part of the principal had to be paid each year as interest, and that ten years later, in the consulship of Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gnaeus Plautius, the semi-unciary interest was to be made out of the unciary, since this would have been too heavy for the plebs, seeing that Livy, book 7, chapter 16, refers the unciary usury to the proposal of M. Duillius (which had been passed only ten years before) after the Twelve Tables. The words are these: In the consulship of Gaius Marcius and Gnaeus Manlius, a proposal about unciary interest was brought forward by M. Duilius the tribune of the plebs; the plebs voted for it rather eagerly and accepted it. If an example could be given of any nation so poor in silver and so impatient of usury that it could receive the principal on condition of paying only a hundredth part of it each year, and yet regarded that interest as a notable burden, I would gladly confess that these arguments have no weight. The opponent, as men of his profession do, need not seek many knots in a bulrush (p. 24 and following), as if he had achieved something great by rearranging the chronological points, which in my argument hang together well. It matters little whether Manlius's praenomen was Gaius or Gnaeus, since the printed books show both. So that I may press my argument harder, before I meet the objections, I will tie it with yet another knot, one firmer than the Gordian. The opponent admits that the Romans had monthly interest and that it was usually paid off each month.

units.la: {B 3} — centesimam sortis partem solvere debuerit, atq; T. Manlio Torquato & Cn. Plautio Coff. decen-nio post, semunciarium fœnus ex unciario fieri debuerit, quod hoc plebi nimis grave foret, si-quidem Liv. lib. 7. cap. 16. unciarium fœnus ad M. Duillii rogationem (quæ decennio solum ante lata erat) post XII. tabulas refert. Verba hæc sunt: C. Marcio, Cn. Manlio Coss. de unciario fœnore à M. Duilio Tribunopl. rogatio est perlata: & plebs aliquanto cupidius eam scivit, accepitque. Si possit exemplum dari ullius nationis, quæ adeo & argenti fuerit inops, & usurarum impatiens, ut potuerit sortem accipere, sub conditione solvendi annuatim centesimam duntaxat istius partem, eaque usura insignis adhuc oneris rationem habuerit, lubens fatebor, hisce rationibus nihil momenti ineste. Non est, quod Adversarius, more hominum suæ professionis, pag. 24. & seq. multos nodos in scirpo quærat, ut videatur grande quid præstitisse, secundum temporis articulos illa quasi reformando, quæ in Argumento meo probe cohærent. Parum quoque refert, Manlio, Cajo an Cnæo prænomen fuerit, quum utrumque libri editi exhibeant: Ut argumentum meum magis stringat, priusquam occurro illis, quæ opponuntur, alio adhuc nodo, eoque plus quam Gordio id firmatum ibo. Fatetur Adversarius, usuras fuisse menstruas apud Romanos, quoque etiam mense exsolvi con-
units.tr: {B 3} — a hundredth part of the principal to be paid, and that in the tenth year after, under Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gnaeus Plautius, consuls, the semi-unciary interest was to be made out of the unciary, since this would have been too heavy for the plebs, seeing that Livy, book 7, chapter 16, refers the unciary usury to the proposal of M. Duillius (which had been passed only ten years before) after the Twelve Tables. The words are these: In the consulship of Gaius Marcius and Gnaeus Manlius, a proposal about unciary interest was brought forward by M. Duilius the tribune; the plebs voted for it rather eagerly and accepted it. If an example could be given of any nation so poor in silver and so impatient of usury that it could receive the principal on condition of paying only a hundredth part of it each year, and yet regarded that interest as a notable burden, I would gladly confess that these arguments have no weight. The opponent, as men of his profession do, need not seek many knots in a bulrush (p. 24 and following), as if he had achieved something great by rearranging the chronological points, which in my argument hang together well. It matters little whether Manlius's praenomen was Gaius or Gnaeus, since the printed books show both. So that I may press my argument harder, before I meet the objections, I will tie it with yet another knot, one firmer than the Gordian. The opponent admits that the Romans had monthly interest and that it was usually paid off each month.

units.la: Liv. lib. 7. consuevisse. Fingamus ergo, Titium accepisse à Cajo quinquaginta numos sestertios, & pro usu promisisse foenus semunciarium, quod annuo spatio, quartam sestertii partem conficiet: Cajus autem mensibus singulis usuras, solvere voluerit,quis tam peritus fuerit Calculator, qui ad pecuniam Romanam tantillum reducere possit, aut, quis dixerit exili illi foenori numum quoque respondisse? Sed demus respondisse, quis voluerit tantillo vel pecuniam suam collocare, periculum sustinere, simul & tabulas conscribere, aliasque molestias devorare.
units.tr: Let us therefore suppose that Titius received fifty sesterces from Gaius and promised semi-ounce interest in return, which over a year would make a quarter of a sestertius; and that Gaius wished to pay the interest every month. Who would be so skilled a calculator as to reduce Roman money to so small a sum, or who would say that even a coin would correspond to such trifling interest? But grant that someone was willing to lay out his money for such a trifle, to undertake the risk, to draw up the documents at the same time, and to endure the other troubles.

units.la: Acceperim à Dn. Adversario, jam Posidonio, moribus Romanis quinquaginta florenos nostrates, & promiserim foenus semunciarium, ea lege, ut quoque mense sortem cum foenore restituere possim. Redeam autem primo mense, & exhibeam tres deutas nostrates cum quadrante, an propterea voluerit Calendarium suum conscribillare, metuere perintegrum mensem ne malum nomen sim, tabulas simul conficere & abolere? Haud equidem credederim, si audierit quoque ex Plauti sui Mostellaria Misargyrides. Magistratus quando leges de foenore ferunt, non modo conditionem suorum subditorum attendere solent, verum etiam iis, qui pecuniæ suæ usum, stipulando usuras, aliis concedere possunt, sic succurrunt, ut semper inveniantur, qui in illa mutuo danda nolint esse difficiles. Neutiquam vero hoc circa foenus semuncia-rium, ex Adversariorum mente si explicetur, subsistere potest. Nec est, quod aliquis odiose Lombardos nostros objiciat, quod exile foenusculum sæpe ingentes iis labores creet. Hoc enim pensatur aliis emolumentis, longe majoribus. præterea, ob pignus semper iis licet esse securis & sortis & fœnoris. Sed quis idem dixerit de Roma, si ibi foenus semunciarium, ex Adversariorum mente intelligendum, aliquando solummodo exigere licuerit? Hæc πώςεςγα. Quid vero præcedenti argumento, prout primò propositum erat, Adversarius opponit? Varia accumulavit, sed plane ἀπεῤῥσδιόνυσα. Pag. 21. hæc offendo: Respondeo, &c. An non planis verbis Liv. lib. 7. Etsi unciario foenore levata usura erat, sorte ipsa obruebantur inopes, nexumque inibant. Si fortem ipsam solvere grave erat, si forte sola sine ullo augmento obruebantur, quidni grave erat, quantillum supra sortem accedebat? Si Noster consuluisset eundem illum, virum forte Reverendum, à quo de Lombardis se edoctum fatetur pag. 7. non ignoraret, ex infima quoque plebe homines, qui vestes & necessaria vasa oppignerata habent, usuras, quotiescunque pignorum instat distractio, ad assem exhibere, sortem vero ne post plures quidem annos, quibus foenus solverint, pro pignoribus suis recuperandis, solvere posse. Ponderis aliquid responsioni huic inesset, nisi foenus ex consuetudine Romana, ante sortem exsolvi debuisset. Si ignoret Noster, discat ex Plauti tiMostellaria. Cum Tranio diceret: Sortem accipe. Danista respondit: Immo fœnus: id primum volo. Fœnoris solutio, pauperiores quoque minus gravare solet, quam fortis. Eoque vere testatur Livius, populum Romanum forte fuisse obrutum, postquam scil. fœnus, ex consuetudine prius solvisset. Proxime pag. 22. & 23. sic ex Livio instat: Caeterum in hoc Livii loco notanda etiam illa verborum consecutio: etsi unciario fœnore, tamen sorte ipsa. Quis hic tam subitus saltus ab unciario fœnore ad nudam sortem: si unciarium fœnus tam longe a nuda sorte distabat, ut genus usuræ esset maxime maleficum? Cur idem hiatus apud Tacitum: sanctum, ne quis unciario, &c. dein rogatione tribunicia ad semuncias redacta, postremo vetita versura. Cur post semuncias vetita? Si semunciæ sunt semisses, & hæ quoque onerosæ, saltem quincunces, trientes, quadrantes, sextantes, & quas quo nomine appellem, ignoro. Sed cur hic factus fuerit saltus, a semisse, seu semuncia, non ad trientes, quadrantes, & sextantes; sed fœnus omne fuerit abrogatum, supra, post Curculionem Tacitus nos docuit. Verba Scriptoris iterum exhibeo: Multisque plebis scitis obviam itum fraudibus, quæ toties repressæ, miras per artes rursum oriebantur. Ne autem fœnerari liceret, Romæ multis annis, post T. Manlium um Torquatum, & C. Plautium Coff. effecit L.Genutius Trib. Pl. Ita enim Livius lib. 7. cap. 42. Praeter hac (inquit) invenio apud quosdam L. Genutium Trib. Plebis, tulisse ad populum ne fenerari liceret. Quaeret iterum Adversarius, cur non usurae sextantes, quadrantes, aut trientes jure receptae fuerint? Sed si semunciarium foenus, ex suo sensu Centesimae vigesima quarta pars, oneris singularis rationem habuerit, caussa non est, cur de sextantibus, quadrantibus, aut trientibus quaeramus? Cum vero fallatur toto coelo, in explicando unciario & semunciario foenore, rationem dicam, cur lege sextantes, quadrantes, aut trientes usurae receptae non fuerint. Locupletiores, ex ipso Senatorio quoque ordine (ad hoc probandum supra adductus fuit Tacitus) apud foeneratores levioribus usuris pecuniam suam collocare solent, quam illi grandioribus dein mutuo dabant. Vlpianus leg. 7. §. 2. ff. Depositi: Quoties foro cedunt nummularii, solet primo loco ratio haberi depositariorum: hoc est, eorum, qui depositas pecunias habuerunt, non quas foenore apud nummularios, vel cum nummulariis, vel per ipsos exercebant. Suet. lib. 2. cap. 39. de Octavio Augusto: Notavit aliquos, quod pecunias levioribus mutuati, graviore foenore collocassent. Quod ergo locupletiores minus quam semisse, cum argentariis (qui pro arbitratu suo, in fraudem legum, foenus exercere solent) transfigere nollent, passi fuerunt per Plebisci-tum omni foenore interdiceretur. Priusquam per-go in examinandis Adversarii responsionibus, no-vum argumentum, ex iis, quae observata sunt, se sistit. Quum locupletiores (patet quoque ex Plau-ti Mostellaria) foeneratoribus pecunias suas, cer-tam usuram stipulando, ut ea foenerarentur, crede-re consueverint, quantillum locupletiores acce-perint, si Jure foeneratores; non nisi duodecimam centesimae partem, & alias, non nisi vigesimam quartam stipulari potuerint? Necesse um ergo, unci-arium & semunciarium foenus, ex nostro sensu ex-plicentur. Porro, ut & Manutio viro doctissimo, & mihi testatum faciat, unciarium & semunciari-um foenus, ex sua mente intelligendum, Romae onus grande censeri debuisse; pag. 25. ita profatur e sua Cathedra, non vero Tripode: Sed & prae-sto sunt exempla omnium civitatum, quae tabu-las poposcerunt novas, quae quadrante aut besse deciderunt, quae omne foenus vetuerunt. Prae-terea centesima sortis annua pars fortasse ita gravis non sit, si sors ipsa non excedat centenos. Sed raro intra eum numerum sistitur. Quan-tum colligo, quadruplex accumulatur responsio. Sed omnis aeque inconveniens. Quid (primo) ad calculos & tabulas hominis nostri tabulae novae fa-ciunt? Proponere & promittere eas solent?qui eodem quo Catilina sunt ingenio. Livius lib. 32. de Nabi Lacedæmoniorum præfecto: Concione deinde advocata rogationem promulgavit, unam de tabulis novis, alteram de agro viritim dividendo, duas faces novantibus res, ad plebem in Optimates accendendam. Et lib. 42. de altero quodam: Confudit & miscuit omnia in Thessalia Perrhabiaque ipse, novarum tabularum, ut manu debitorum obnoxia sibi, Optimates opprimeret. Nec male judicat de Tabulis novis Cicero lib. 2. de Offic. Tabulæ novæ (inquit) quid habent argumenti, nisi ut emas mea pecunia fundum: eum tu habeas, ego non habeam pecuniam. Ab iis tamen Adversarius argumentatur, ut videatur potuisse respondere. Qui largius suo non modo, sed & alieno usi, debita expungere non possunt, execrari ordinario quidem solent, & creditores, & leges de foenore: sed, ut juxta Senecam Consol. ad Marciam cap. 1. Pessimi est debitoris, creditori facere convitium; ita male sani est Grammatici, ut sententiam solo tibicine Grammatico suffultam tutari queat, à seditiosis decoctoribus argumentum petere ad illa improbanda, quæ publice visa fuerunt utilia. Deinde, quid ad rem, si aliquæ civitates vel esse vel quadrante deciderint? earum rectores, quantum oneris pro pecuniæ usu subditis suis imponi posset, prudenter expenderunt. Romæ idem factum fuisse jam dixi, atque ideo mea de foenore unciario sententia vincere debet. Ne quis vero existimet, à me præter rationem in rep. paupere, unciarium foenus Centesimæ adæquari, cogitet, ibidem prærogativam non fuisse debitoris, cujus fortunas tristis aliquis casus perdiderat, præ decoctore. Senec. lib. 7. de Benef. c. 16. Quid tu tam imprudentes judicas majores nostros fuisse, ut non intelligerent, iniquissimum esse, eodem loco haberi eum, qui pecuniam, quam à creditore acceperat, libidine an alea abfumfit, & eum, qui incendio, aut latrocinio, aut aliquo casu triftiore, aliena cum suis perdidit? Nullam excusationem recepe-runt: ut homines scirent fidem utique præstandam. Satius enim erat, à paucis etiam justam excusationem non accipi, quam ab omnibus aliquam tentari. Quis credat, rigidos hos justi antistites, audire voluisse illos, qui foenoris unciarii, centesimæ æquivalentis, iniquitatem incusatum veniebant? Nec unciarium foenus ad semunciarium redactum fuisset, nisi spes fuisset, foeneratores, qui mille artes norant illudendi legibus, ultra unciarium progressuros non esse. Quod vero tum quoque excederent, usura omnis Plebiscito est prohibita. Sed quid inde tertio Noster evicerit? aut quid cum ratione concludet, quod alicubi foenoris nomen ignotum fuerit? Haud equidem ubi foenufcu-lum legibus est permissum, (hoc est τὸ κεχνόμενον) mox redditur grande onus. Nam ideo foenus alicubi fuit vetitum, quod aut resp. absque eo posset subsistere: aut quod eo admisso, absque modo metueretur esse exercendum: aut quod civibus, qui ex lege deberent esse distincti à peregrinis, interdicta fuerit mercatura: ut docet Spartana resp. aut denique, quod de foenoris ratione homines probe non fuerint edocti. Vbicunque vero foenus unquam Jure permissum fuit, illi, penes quos fuit potestas ferendi leges, attenderunt regulam initio à nobis vindicatam, & assertam calculo ipsius Joh. Frederici Gronovii. Quarto & postremo Thesi non servit, quod garrit de onere semunciarii foenoris, aggravati quasi, quod sors potuerit surgere ad multa nummorum millia. Ipse, vir scil. Illustris insultat mihi pag. 26. ut Scholastico: sed, si voluisset per hunc Scholasticum erudiri de justitia Vsuræ, quam multi Theologi quoque in universum injustitiæ arguunt, didicisset usuras ad modum compensationis admitti & solvi, quod, qui accepit sortem, eam honeste præsumatur collocaturus esse, & tantum lucraturus, ut usuræ graves nullo modo sint futuræ: Etenim juxta Paulum leg. 16. ff. de Vsur. Iniquum est usuras ab eo exigi, qui fructus non percepit. Ganeones, similesqve, qui & ipsius fortis, sive grandis, sive exiguæ sunt decoctores, hic attendi non debent, atque per errorem summum ab illo, qui & Jurisconsultus est, producuntur, Transfirem firem ad tertium meum argumentum, nisi manum injiceret lepida atque simul homine Nostro dignissima fabula. Pag. 16. ita lego: At in vicina Frisiæ Saxonia novimus possessores, qui à viginti annis & foenus & sortem debent, quibus non dico semunciam,ne scriptulum quidem centesimæ annuum extorqueant creditores. Ad prætorem ibis? hypothecas dices commissas? Recte: addicetur tibi ager, sedita gravatus censu, ut, nisi parcissime ac durissime, non alat exercentem, & gravandus magis, si domino locupleti cessisse intelligant regnantes.
units.tr: I may have received from my opponent, now Posidonius, fifty of our florins on the Roman custom, and promised interest of a semuncia, on the condition that I could return the principal with the interest each month. But if I returned it in the first month and paid over three deutas and a quadrans of ours, would he have wanted to scribble his calendar, fearing that for a whole month I would be a bad debtor, and to draw up and cancel the accounts at the same time? I would scarcely believe so, even if he had also heard from his own Plautus, in the Mostellaria, Misargyrides. When magistrates pass laws on interest, they are accustomed to consider not only the condition of their subjects, but also those who, by stipulating interest, can grant the use of their money to others. They so provide that there are always people who are not difficult about lending money in that way. Yet by my opponent's understanding of the semuncia, this can in no way stand. Nor is there any reason for someone to object spitefully to our Lombards that such a small interest payment often creates great labours for them. For this is balanced by other profits, far greater. Moreover, they can always be secure about both principal and interest because of the pledge. But who would say the same of Rome, if the semuncia were to be understood in my opponent's sense, and it were only sometimes lawful to exact it? Such is the state of things [πώς ἔχει]. But what does my opponent set against the preceding argument, as I first proposed it? He has piled up various points, but they are plainly thoughtless [ἀπερίσκεπτα]. On page 21 I come across this: I reply, etc. Does not Livy, Book 7, say in plain words "Although the debt was lightened by the unciarium interest, the poor were overwhelmed by the principal itself, and they entered into bondage"? "If it was hard to pay the principal itself, if they were overwhelmed by the principal alone without any addition," why should it not be hard when a small amount was added above the principal? If our author had consulted that same man, the reverend one from whom he confesses on page 7 that he was taught about the Lombards, he would not be ignorant that even people from the lowest plebs, who have garments and necessary vessels pawned, pay the interest down to the last as-penny whenever the sale of their pledges is imminent, but cannot pay the principal, even after many years in which they have paid interest, in order to recover their pledges. There might be some weight in this reply, if by Roman custom the interest had to be paid before the principal. If our author does not know this, let him learn it from Plautus's Mostellaria. When Tranio said, "Take the principal," the moneylender replied, "No, the interest: that is what I want first." The payment of interest is usually a lighter burden even for the poorer sort than the payment of principal. Hence Livy truly attests that the Roman people were overwhelmed by the principal after, that is, they had first paid the interest by custom. On pages 22 and 23 he presses further from Livy in this way: Moreover, in this passage of Livy one must also note the sequence of words: "although by unciarium interest, yet by the principal itself." What is this sudden leap from unciarium interest to the bare principal? If the unciarium interest was so far from the bare principal that it was the most harmful kind of usury? Why is the same gap found in Tacitus: "it was sanctioned that no one should [lend at] unciarium..., then by a tribunician proposal it was reduced to semunciae, and finally borrowing to pay off debts was forbidden"?
