Why forbidden after the semunciae? If semunciae are semisses, and these too are burdensome, then at least quincunces, trientes, quadrantes, sextantes, and whatever else I should call them, I do not know. But why, after Curculio, a leap was made from the semis or semuncia, not to trientes, quadrantes and sextantes, but all interest was abrogated, Tacitus has already taught us above. I present the writer's words again: And the frauds were countered by many plebiscites, which, though often repressed, arose again by remarkable arts. That interest might not be lent at all in Rome, for many years after Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gaius Plautius, consuls, Lucius Genucius, tribune of the plebs, brought it about. For so Livy, Book 7, chapter 42: "Besides these things," he says, "I find in some authors that Lucius Genucius, tribune of the plebs, proposed to the people that lending at interest should not be allowed." The opponent will again ask why sextantes, quadrantes or trientes were not admitted as lawful interest. But if the semuncia interest, in his own sense, is the one-twenty-fourth part of a hundred, and is a special burden, there is no reason why we should inquire about sextantes, quadrantes or trientes. But since he is utterly mistaken in explaining the unciarium and semunciarium interest, I shall say why sextantes, quadrantes or trientes were not admitted as lawful interest. Wealthier men, even from the senatorial order itself (Tacitus was cited above to prove this), are accustomed to place their money with moneylenders at lower interest, which those moneylenders then lent out at higher rates. Ulpian, Digest 16.3, law 7, §2, On Deposit: "Whenever bankers fail, regard is usually first given to the depositors, that is, to those who had deposited money, not to those who were carrying on lending at interest with the bankers, or through them." Suetonius, Book 2, chapter 39, on Octavius Augustus: "He noted some who, having borrowed money at lower rates, had lent it out at higher interest." Therefore, since the wealthier would not transact with bankers (who, at their own discretion and in fraud of the laws, usually lend at interest) at less than a semis, they allowed a plebiscite to forbid all interest. Before I go on to examine my opponent's replies, a new argument presents itself from what has been noted. Since the wealthier (it is clear also from Plautus's Mostellaria) were accustomed to entrust their money to moneylenders, stipulating a fixed interest so that it might be lent out at interest, how much would the wealthier have received if the moneylenders could lawfully stipulate only a twelfth part of a hundred, and otherwise only a twenty-fourth? It is necessary, therefore, that the unciarium and semunciarium interest be explained in our sense. Further, so that both the most learned Manutius and I may have it attested that the unciarium and semunciarium interest, understood in his own sense, ought to have been considered a great burden at Rome, he speaks from his own chair, not from the tripod, on page 25: "But there are also examples of all the states which demanded new account-books, which were reduced by a quadrans or a sixth, which forbade all interest. Besides, the annual hundredth part of the principal is perhaps not so heavy, if the principal does not exceed a hundred." But rarely is it kept within that number. As far as I can gather, a fourfold argument is piled up, but all equally inconsistent. What (first) do the new account-books have to do with our man's calculations and tables? They usually propose and promise them, being of the same temper as Catiline. Livy, Book 32, on Nabis, prefect of the Lacedaemonians: "Then, calling an assembly, he promulgated a bill, one about new account-books, another about dividing the land among individuals, two torches to inflame matters for the new men, and to stir the plebs against the optimates." And Book 42, on another man: "He himself threw everything into confusion and mixed it up in Thessaly and Perrhaebia, so that by the hand of debtors bound to him he might crush the optimates." Cicero, in Book 2 of On Duties, judges not badly about new account-books: "What have new account-books to do with the matter, except that you buy an estate with my money, which you have and I do not?" Yet my opponent argues from these as if he could have replied to them. Those who, having spent more than they had, and even others' money, cannot wipe out their debts, usually curse both their creditors and the laws on interest. But, as Seneca says in the Consolation to Marcia, chapter 1, "It is the worst kind of debtor to revile his creditor"; so it is the mark of a half-sane grammarian, propped up only by a grammatical flute-player's opinion, to take from seditious bankrupts an argument for condemning what has been publicly seen as useful. Next, what does it matter to the question whether some states have either lost a sixth or a quarter? Their rulers prudently weighed how great a burden could be laid on their subjects for the use of money. I have already said that this was done at Rome, and therefore my opinion about the unciarium interest ought to prevail. But lest anyone think that I, against reason, equate the unciarium interest with the hundredth in a poor state, let him consider that there was no privilege there for a debtor whose fortunes some sad accident had destroyed, over a bankrupt. Seneca, Book 7 of On Benefits, chapter 16: "Do you think our ancestors were so foolish that they did not understand it to be most unjust to treat alike the man who has spent the money he received from a creditor on lust or gambling, and the man who has lost it with his own property through fire, robbery or some other sadder chance? They accepted no excuse, so that men would know that good faith must be kept in every case. For it was better that a just excuse should not be accepted from a few, than that some pretext should be tried by all." Who would believe that these stern guardians of justice were willing to listen to those who came forward to complain of the injustice of unciarium interest, which is equal to the hundredth? Nor would the unciarium interest have been reduced to the semunciarium, unless there had been hope that the moneylenders, who knew a thousand arts of deceiving the laws, would not go beyond the unciarium. But that they went beyond it even then, all interest was forbidden by plebiscite. But what does my opponent prove by this third point, or what does he conclude rationally, from the fact that the word for interest was unknown somewhere? Certainly, wherever a little interest has been permitted by law (that is, what is customary [τὸ κεχρημένον]), it does not at once become a great burden. For interest was forbidden somewhere either because the state could subsist without it, or because, once admitted, it would be practised without limit and was feared on that account, or because trade was forbidden to citizens who by law ought to be distinct from foreigners, as the Spartan state shows, or finally because men had not been properly instructed about the principle of interest. But wherever interest has ever been permitted by law, those in whose power it lay to enact laws have observed the rule, asserted at the beginning by us and vindicated by the calculation of Johann Friedrich Gronovius himself. Fourth and last, what he chatters about the burden of the semunciarium interest, as if it were aggravated because the principal could rise to many thousands of coins, does not serve his thesis. He himself, that is the illustrious man, mocks me on page 26 as a Scholastic. But if he had wished to be instructed by this Scholastic about the justice of usury, which many theologians also condemn as unjust in general, he would have learned that interest is admitted and paid by way of compensation, and that whoever has received the principal is presumed honestly about to invest it, and to gain so much that heavy interest will in no way follow. For according to Paul, Digest 22.1, law 16, "It is unjust that interest should be exacted from one who has not received the fruits." Gamblers and the like, who are bankrupts of their principal, whether large or small, ought not to be considered here, and are brought forward through the great error of one who is also a jurist. I would pass on to my third argument, had not a witty fable, and one most worthy of our man, intervened. On page 16 I read it thus: "But in neighbouring Saxony in Friesland we know of owners who for twenty years have owed both interest and principal, from whom creditors do not extort, I do not say a semuncia, but not even a scruple of the yearly hundredth." Will you go to the praetor? Will you say the mortgages have been surrendered? Rightly: the field will be awarded to you, but burdened with a tax so heavy that it cannot feed its cultivator unless he is most sparing and hardest working, and it will be burdened all the more if the rulers understand that it has passed to a rich lord.

units.la: Explicit narratio. Credo quod in animo habuerit avitum in Chaucis agellum, hoc tempore Suecis vectigalem. Si fabella hæc à garrula anu narraretur, risu expianda esset. Quid ei decernas,quum à Dictatore literariæ reip. serio non modo narretur, sed & inculcetur? Quando secundum leges aliquis foenus stipulatur, præsentem conditionem illius attendit, cui pecuniam suam credit: quem si belli calamitas, aut alia vis major afflixerit, creditor ad tempus & sorte & usuris carere quidem cogitur, debitum tamen non expungitur. Et, ut juxta Ciceronem lib. 2. de Off. nulla res vehementius Remp. continet, quam fides, quæ esse nulla potest, nisi erit necessaria solutio rerum creditarum; ita, simul ac afflictus debitor respirare cœperit, compellari potest & de usura & sorte. Creditor,si aut negligens gens fuerit, aut sumptus facere noluerit, ut suum consequatur, sibi imputari debet. Probandum alias, quod habet Seneca lib. 4. de Benef. cap 39. Pecunia etiam male credita exactio est. Et appellare ad debitorem ad diem possum, & si foro cesserit, portionem feram. Pergo ad vindicandum tertium meum argumentum. Illud hisce verbis proposueram. Testatur Capitolinus de Antonino Pio, tanquam aliquid singulare & sine exemplo, quod fœnus trientarium exercuerit, ut patrimonio suo plurimos adjuvaret. Quod Pii exemplum, teste Ælio Lampridio, non modo secutus fuit, verum etiam superavit optimus Imp. Alexander Severus. Nam & ille fœnus trientarium, sed ita exercuit, ut pauperibus plerisque, sine usuris pecunias ad agros emendos dederit, reddendas de fructibus. At, quorsum ut singulare quid notatum fuisset, ab utroque Principe exercitum fuisse foenus trientarium, si unciarium & semunciarium foenus, à primis ferme reip. incunabulis legibus definitum, ita accipi debeat, ut unciarium foenus fit duodecima pars centesimae, semunciarium vero duntaxat vigesima quarta. Certe, si centum denarii ad foenus trientarium dati annuatim quaternos denarios pariant, & usurariae clementiae documentum singulare exhibeant, nae multo majorem clementiam evincere debebit foenus unciarium, ad quod, (modo credamus viris eximiis) miis. ) si crediti fuerint eidem centum denarii, annuatim singulos solummodo denarios profundent creditori. Quis vero credat, ratione trientarii fœnoris, tum Antonini Pii, tum etiam Alexandri Severi moderationem laudaturos fuisse Capitolinum & Lampridium, si fœnus unciarium, acceptum è mente virorum doctorum, jam olim ipsis xii. Tabulis definitum fuerit. Hæc ego, Quibus Adversarius pag, 26. & 27. opponit, quæ sequuntur: Quærit, quorsum ut singulare quid notent historici, à Pio & Alexandro Cæsaribus exercitum fuisse fœnus trientarium, si major clementia fuisset unciario gaudere? Quærat igitur etiam cur laudetur Augustus, quod non regno, neque dictatura compositus fuerit rempublicam, quam fuisset nobilius reddere Senatui & populo. Discat ab Hieronymo, de gratuito non judicare, & equi dentes non inspicere donati. Ea tum erant tempora & ita grassabatur fœnus, ut illa modestia ævi à nemine esset postulanda, & valde civiliter ageret, siquis trientibus contentus esset. Non magnum erat trientes usuras pati, quum pius ille bonusque Theodosius simul cum Gratiano & Valentiniano judicatos post alterum mensem binas centesimas æris debiti solvere jusserit? quod si contractus ex stipulatione descendat, & usuræ per annorum curricula casu summam fortis æquaverint, post sententiam insontem duplam centesimam, in usuras tanquam no-vam vam fortem, simplam praestari? Cognoscat hoc ex l. un. Cod. Theod. de usuris rei judicatae. Hæc & Adversarius. Verum cogor hæc vocare κωφὰ βέλη, siquidem non feriunt. Ex mente Adversarii, Lex xii. Tabularum gravissimum fœnus voluerit esse Vnciarium, hoc est 12. Centesimæ partem. De Jure autem xii. Tabularum non modo Cicero dicit lib. 1. de Orar. Fremant omnes licet, dicam quod sentio, Bibliothecas me Hercule omnium Philosophorum, unus mihi videtur xii. Tabularum libellus, si quis legum fontes & capita viderit, & auctoritatis pondere & utilitatis superare. Sed Justiniani quoque hoc est elogium leg. pen. Cod. de legit. hæred. Lege xii. Tabularum bene humano generi prospectum. Cur non ergo optimi Principes, ut Populo gratificarentur, jusserint potius fœneratores attendere ad xii. si, ut ipse contendit, tam exile fuerit fœnus unciarium? Quæ ex Hieronymo addit, illis quoque nota, qui nondum ære lavantur. Sed probare debuisset, ea fuisse tempora, & ita grassatos fœneratores, ut modestia veteris ævi a nemine esset postulanda. Vt gratis hæc finguntur, in gratiam fœnoris Vnciarii, velut duodecimæ partis Centesimæ; ita gratis à nobis rejiciuntur. Corruptissima necessum est fuerint tempora, quibus, cum domi pax esset & provinciæ pacatæ, optimi & prudentissimi Principes, fœneratores in ordinem redigere. gere non potuerit. Et tamen coërcendis iis par fuit Tiberius, Dione teste lib. 58. item Claudius, fidem faciente Tacito lib. 11. c. 13. Non video, unde Antonino Pio, & Severo Principi major difficultas objici potuerit, quam Diocletiano & Maximiano Impp. quorum hæc est constitutio leg. 20. Cod. ex quib. cauff. infam. irrog. Improbum fœnus exercentibus, & usuras usurarum illicite exigentibus, infamia nota irroganda est. Principes, aliive Magistratus, quibus modo Jurisdictio competit, legibus fœnus circumscribant, & noti erunt fœneratores. qui quamvis, ut jam observatum: artibus sine numero instructi sint, quibus Juri fraudem faciant, compesci tamen poterunt, si deprehensi, infames habeantur. Fœneratores autem secundum sequiorem sensum, omnes illos habeo, qui usuræ modum, Jure definitum, excedunt. Noster ignorare non deberet: quod sui Jcc. hoc vulgò, sed interim recte, colligant ex leg. 28. Cod. de Vsur. Sed ideo Principes optimi Fœnus trientarium exercuerunt, quod Vnciarium, publice receptum, Centesimæ æquivaleret. Illud si levius Centesima fuisset, profitentur fe, trientarium exercendo. Fatuus est ille Princeps, qui gloriam captat ex fœnore per suam aut constitutionem, aut singulare beneficium diminuto, si Jus ordinarium quod publice receptum est, & quo omnes tenentur, multo minus definiverit. Postremo, ne tertium hoc argumentum, hactenus inconcussum, valeat; leat; trahor obtorto quasi collo ad leg. unic. Cod. Theod. de usur. rei judic. legem ipsam adducere debuisset Adversarius. Ea ita habet: Impp. Gratianus, Valentinianus, & Theodosius, AAA. Eutropio. Pf. P. Qui post judicii finem, exceptis duobus mensibus, quibus per legis solutionem non-nunquam est concessa dilatio, moram afferent solutioni, à die patrati judicii, quo obnoxii redditi sunt, in duplicium centesimarum conveniantur usuras, extrinsecus scilicet mediocratem debiti de quo litigatum est, sicut prius constitutum est, inferentes usque in id tempus, quo debitum solutione diluerint. Quod à nobis exemplo æquabili ex juris prisci est formulis introductum, ut quia malæ fidei possessores in fructus duplos conveniuntur, æque malæ fidei debitores simile damni periculum persequantur. Sed tamen creditor ternis interjectis mensibus post sententiam, contestari moram debebit adhibitæ tarditatis, ut ei centesimarum duplicium fructus possit acquiri. Cavendum quippe ex diverso est, etiam contra illam malitiam creditorum, ne judicatis ad solutionem cunctantibus, incipiant spe dupli fœnoris imminere, quidquid judicatum, si hanc pœnam à se removere festinent, contractam pecuniam vel apud judices obsignatam locare, vel judicio conveniat offerre, ut periculum duplicium usurarum incurrere ex ea die, qua obnoxius esse coeperit, desistat. Distinguendum vero hoc quoque arbitrati sumus, ut si contractus debiti biti ex stipulatione descendit, & casu usurae per annorum curricula summam capitis impleverint, scilicet ut quantitas fortis, quantitati foenoris adaequetur, post sententiam usurae duplicis non utriusque debiti currant, sed capitis quidem duplae, usurarum vero simplae. Dat. xv. Kal. Jun. Thessal. Gratiano V. & Theodosio I. AA. CONSS: Hucusque Imperatores, at quomodo hi prodesse possunt, quum loquantur de Usuris punitoriis, quae ut dicit Paulus IC. leg. 17. §. 3. ff. de Usuris, non propter lucrum petentium, sed propter moram solventium infliguntur? Hae usurae modum accipiunt per judicem arbitrantem. Nos vero hic disputamus de Usuris, quae ex contractu descendunt. Sed viderit Adversarius, quid prosit digitum in hanc legem intendisse. Impp. testantur se progredi ex prisci juris formulis; hoc est, juxta Duodecim Tabulas: ut antea evicimus, hoc intelligendum esse. Sed xii. Tabulae non meminerunt Centesimae, verum foenoris unciarii: necessum ergo est, ipse Adversarius fateatur, (nisi conscientiae suae vim facere voluerit) illud, quod in xii. Tabulis, seu jure prisco, foenus unciarium vocatur, idem per omnia esse cum Centesima. Et hae quidem hactenus sunt vindiciae meorum Argumentorum, quae arrodere potuit Adversarius, non tamen evertere. Dum ea vindicavi ab ipsius ineptiis, multiplicata sunt. Tres Velites (ipsi tamen inexpugnabiles) antehac praemisi, ut exexplorarem quid aceti homini in pectore effet. Illis quinque Triarios succenturio. contra quos quæ directurus sit tela, patienter expecto. Primo resumo locum Dionis Cassii lib. 51. supra adductum. Testatur Historicus usque ad Augusti triumphum Romæ δανεισμα fuisse επι τη δεφγμη, quæ scil. quoque mense solvebatur, & ratione duodecim mensium Centesimam explebat. Hæc enim erat ordinaria Vsura: quam ad Trientem redegerunt nummorum acervi, Romam deportati. Non puto adeo impudentem fore Adversarium, ut Centesimam dicat fuisse Vsuram ordinariam illis, qui in foro mensas habebant. Dion de ea loquitur ut legitima & jure concessa. Quæ aliæ vero hic leges occurrunt, quam xii. Tabularum, in quibus fœnus unciarium vocatur, quod postea usitatius præeuntibus Jcc. ( quidquid Noster quoque censeat ) Centesima dici cœpit. Si possit vel aliam Legem, vel aliud Senatusconsultum, vel Plebiscitum adducere, quo Centesima oppositæ ad fœnus unciarium, quod secundum ipsum duodecima Centesimæ pars, permissa in Vrbe fuerit ut ordinaria Vsura, manus dabo, & publice errorem profitebor. Interim dum per Vtopiæ tabularia Legem hanc investigat, hæc mea ratio stabit inconcussa. Secundo, consideramus quid obvenerit Ciceroni Oratorum Principi, cui inter alia carcinomata summas molestias æs alienum exhibuit. Lib. 5. Famil. Epist. per jocum licet, ad Sextium scribit: Itaque nunc me scito tantantum habere aris alieni,ut cupiam conjurare, si quis me recipiat, &c. Laboravit hic non suo solum nomine, sed & alieno. Cum Ciliciæ Proconsul esset, Salaminii à Bruti familiaribus pecunias acceperant, per imprudentiam in Syngrapha quaternas Centesimas promittentes: sed,cum Bruti familiares,viderent sibi obstare Legem Gabiniam, cujus duo erant capita: Vnum, ne cuiquam in provinciis dare accipereve pecuniam in versuram liceret: Alterum, ne gravior usura per provincias quam Centesima foret; confugerunt ad duo Senatusconsulta de illa Syngrapha facta, Hæsit vero hic Cicero, ( videatur ep. ult. lib. 6:) veritus ne ex S. C. cogeretur jus dicere de quaternis Centesimis. Sed postea animadvertit illud S. C. non de quaternis exigendis cavere, sed ne fœneratores fortem ipsam amitterent, quia contra legem Gabiniam dedissent, neve Salaminii multarentur,qui contra eandem Legem accepissent. Remedio autem fuit alterum S. C. iisdem Coff. nempe, Lentulo Philippoque conditum, quo statuebatur, ut jus diceretur ex illa Syngrapha, qua Salaminii Scaptio debebant, cui singulas solum Centesimas promiserant: quanquam hic ( quæ erat hominis impudentia) ex altera Syngrapha quaternas exigeret. His præmissis, attendamus ad sequentia. 1. Lege Gabinia licitum fuit per provincas Centesimis contrahere. 2. Has Senatus in Contractu Salaminiorum ut justas probavit. 3. De iis ut justis Cicero jus dixit. Quæ vero iniquitas fuisset, si Romæ per leges xii. Tabularum, 12. solum Centesimæ pars (hoc Adversario est fœnus unciarium) maxima usura fuisset, & tamen promiscue omnibus, lege quoque lata, Centesimis in Provinciis fœnerari licuisset? Næ fœnus hoc injustissimum fuerit juxta Arnob. lib. 2. contra Gent. Ego aliud mihi persuadeo de justitia Romanorum. Cicero de se & æqualibus dicit lib. 1. de Orat. sub persona Marci: Discebamus nos pueri xii. ut carmen necessarium, respicit vero xii. Tabulas, quæ Livio lib. 3. teste, immensō quoque aliarum super alias acervatarum legum cumulo, fons omnis publici privatique fuerunt juris. Quis ergo certò non credat, Patres conscripptos xii respexisse, cum per provincias fœnus ordinarent. Alii, aliud existiment, putem ab iis non recedere legem Gabiniam, atque easdem in animo habuisse Lucullum, cum (teste Plutarcho in Lucul.) per Asiam omnes majores usuras rescinderet, atq; permitteret fœnoris nomine non amplius exigi quam Centesimam. Secus qui statuunt, viderint quomodo Senatum Romanum ab iniquitate & injustitia immunem præstent. Tertium Argumentum fit hoc: Quanquam Centesima (ut ipse Adversarius testatur) Romæ usura maxima, & As quasi usurarius fuerit, non semper tamen argentarii Centesimis suam pecuniam mutuare potuerunt, tempore Ciceronis quoque: sive, quod publice pecuniacuniarum abunde effet, five, quod locupletiores præ-senti pecunia non indigerent. Inde hæc querela Danifte apud Plautum:
units.tr: Explicit narratio. Here the story ends. I believe he had in mind a small ancestral field in the Chauci country, now subject to tax by the Swedes. If this little tale were told by a chattering old woman, it would be laughed off. But what should one decide about it, when it is related and pressed seriously by the Dictator of the literary commonwealth? When someone stipulates interest according to the laws, he takes account of the present condition of the man to whom he lends his money. If the calamity of war or some other greater force afflicts that man, the creditor is indeed compelled to go without both principal and interest for a time, but the debt is not wiped out. And, as Cicero says in book 2 of De Officiis, no thing holds the commonwealth together more strongly than good faith, which cannot exist unless there is a necessary payment of what has been lent. So, as soon as the afflicted debtor begins to get his breath back, he can be pressed both for the interest and for the principal. If the creditor has been careless, or has been unwilling to incur expense in order to get what is his, he must blame himself. There is another point to be proved, which Seneca has in book 4 of De Beneficiis, chapter 39: Even money lent badly is still something to be collected. I can appeal to the debtor on the day, and if he has gone to court, I will bear my share of the loss. I now proceed to defend my third argument. I had put it in these words. Capitolinus records of Antoninus Pius, as something singular and without precedent, that he practised lending at a third (trientarium), so that he might help very many people from his own estate. According to Aelius Lampridius, the excellent emperor Alexander Severus not only followed this example of Pius but even surpassed it. For he too practised lending at a third, but in such a way that he gave money without interest to many of the poor, to buy fields, to be repaid from the produce. But why would it have been noted as something singular that both princes practised lending at a third, if the lending at a twelfth (unciarium) and at a twenty-fourth (semunciarium), which were fixed by law almost from the earliest beginnings of the state, were to be understood so that unciarium lending is a twelfth part of the hundred, and semunciarium only a twenty-fourth? Surely, if a hundred denarii lent at a third yield four denarii a year and show a singular proof of usurious mercy, then lending at a twelfth ought to demonstrate a much greater mercy, since (if we believe these eminent men) if the same hundred denarii had been lent at that rate they would pay the creditor only one denarius a year. Who would believe that Capitolinus and Lampridius would have praised the moderation of Antoninus Pius and Alexander Severus in lending at a third, if lending at a twelfth had already been fixed by the Twelve Tables, as learned men have received it? These are my words, to which the Adversary objects on pages 26 and 27, and what follows: He asks why the historians note as something singular that the Caesars Pius and Alexander practised lending at a third, if a greater mercy had been enjoyed by lending at a twelfth? Then let him ask also why Augustus is praised for having set the commonwealth in order without royal power or dictatorship, which would have been nobler to restore to the Senate and people. Let him learn from Jerome not to judge a gift and not to inspect the teeth of a gift horse. Those were the times, and usury was so rampant that the moderation of the old age could be demanded from no one, and a man would be acting very decently if he were content with a third. Was it not a great thing to bear interest at a third, when that pious and good Theodosius, together with Gratian and Valentinian, ordered that those condemned should pay double the hundredth of the sum owed after one further month? But if the contract arises from a stipulation, and the interest over the course of the years by chance equals the amount of the principal, then after sentence should not double the hundredth be paid on the innocent party as a new principal, and simple interest be paid? Let him learn this from the single law in the Theodosian Code, On Interest on Adjudged Debts. These are the Adversary's words. But I am forced to call these dumb missiles [κωφὰ βέλη], since they do not strike. According to the Adversary's view, the law of the Twelve Tables meant the most serious interest to be unciarium, that is, a twelfth part of the hundredth. But of the law of the Twelve Tables Cicero not only says, in book 1 of De Oratore: Let all men rage as they will; I will say what I think. By Hercules, a single little book of the Twelve Tables seems to me to surpass the libraries of all the philosophers, if one has looked at the sources and heads of the laws, both in weight of authority and in usefulness. But also Justinian's words, in the last law of the Code, On Legitimate Heirs: By the law of the Twelve Tables, provision has been made well for the human race. Why then, to please the People, did the best princes not order the moneylenders to attend to the Twelve Tables, if, as he himself contends, unciarium interest was so trifling? What he adds from Jerome, that these things are known even to those who are not yet bathed in bronze, is also familiar to them. But he ought to have proved that those were the times, and that the moneylenders were so rampant that the moderation of the old age could be demanded from no one. As these things are invented without ground, for the sake of unciarium interest, as a twelfth part of the hundredth, so they are rejected by us without ground. The times must have been very corrupt, when, although there was domestic peace and the provinces were pacified, the best and most prudent princes could not bring the moneylenders into order. And yet Tiberius was obliged to restrain them, as Dio testifies in book 58, and likewise Claudius, as Tacitus attests in book 11, chapter 13. I do not see from where a greater difficulty could be objected to Antoninus Pius and Severus the Prince than to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, whose constitution in law 20 of the Code, On the Causes for Which Infamy Is Imposed, reads: Infamy with its mark must be imposed on those who practise wicked lending and who unlawfully exact usury upon usury. Princes, or other magistrates who have jurisdiction, may restrain lending by laws, and moneylenders will be known. Although, as has already been observed, they are equipped with countless arts by which they may defraud the law, yet they can be checked if, when caught, they are held infamous. By moneylenders, in the looser sense, I mean all those who exceed the rate of interest fixed by law. Our man ought not to be ignorant of what the jurists commonly, but rightly for the time, infer from law 28 of the Code, On Usury. But the best princes practised lending at a third for this reason, that the unciarium rate, publicly accepted, was equal to a hundredth. If that had been lighter than a hundredth, they would have declared themselves, by practising lending at a third. That prince is foolish who seeks glory from lending by a reduction made through his own constitution or a special favour, if the ordinary law, which is publicly accepted and binds everyone, had defined it far less. Lastly, so that this third argument, hitherto unshaken, may not be weakened, I am dragged, as it were by the neck, to the one law of the Theodosian Code, On Interest on Adjudged Debts. The Adversary ought to have cited that law itself. It reads thus: The emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Eutropius, Praetorian Prefect. Those who, after the end of the trial, except for two months, during which a delay of payment is sometimes granted by the law, cause delay in payment, shall be bound, from the day of the judgment by which they were made liable, to pay the double hundredth of interest on the amount in dispute, as was laid down before, continuing until the time when they discharge the debt by payment. This was introduced by us from the earlier forms of law, by an equal example, so that since bad-faith possessors are sued for double the fruits, debtors in equal bad faith should undergo a similar risk of loss. But nevertheless the creditor, after three months have intervened following the sentence, must bear witness to the delay that has been caused, so that the double hundredth of the fruits may be acquired for him. For on the other side, one must also guard against that malice of creditors, lest, when those condemned hesitate to pay, they begin to hang over them in hope of double interest; and whatever has been judged, if they hasten to remove this penalty from themselves, they should either place the money borrowed, sealed up before the judges, or offer it in court, so that the danger of incurring double interest ceases from the day on which they began to be liable. We have also judged that this must be distinguished: if the contract of the debt arises from a stipulation, and by chance the interest over the course of the years has filled up the sum of the principal, so that the amount of the principal equals the amount of the interest, then after sentence the interest does not run double on each debt, but double on the principal and simple on the interest. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Gratian for the fifth time and Theodosius for the first time, Augusti. Thus far the emperors. But how can these help him, since they speak of penal interest, which, as the jurist Paul says in law 17, §3, of the Digest, On Usury, is imposed not on account of the profit of those demanding it, but on account of the delay of those paying? This interest receives its measure from the judge who assesses it. But we are here disputing about interest which arises from contract. But let the Adversary see what good it does him to have pointed his finger at this law. The emperors testify that they proceed from the forms of the ancient law; that is, in accordance with the Twelve Tables, as we have shown before, this must be understood. But the Twelve Tables make no mention of the hundredth, only of unciarium interest. It is therefore necessary that the Adversary himself admit (unless he is willing to do violence to his own conscience) that what in the Twelve Tables, or in the ancient law, is called unciarium interest, is in every respect the same as the hundredth. And these, so far, are the defences of my arguments, which the Adversary has been able to nibble at but not overthrow. While I have defended them against his silliness, they have multiplied. I first sent forward three light-armed skirmishers (which nevertheless are impregnable to him), so that I might find out what vinegar the man has in his breast. I now await patiently the weapons he will aim against these five veterans, my centurion's reinforcements. First, I take up again the passage of Dio Cassius in book 51 quoted above. The historian testifies that until Augustus's triumph at Rome, a loan was at the monthly rate [ἐπὶ τῇ μηνιαίᾳ], which was clearly paid each month, and over twelve months made up the hundredth. For this was the ordinary usury; the heaps of money carried to Rome reduced it to a third. I do not think the Adversary will be so shameless as to say that the hundredth was the ordinary interest for those who had tables in the forum. Dio speaks of it as lawful and granted by right. What other laws occur here, except the Twelve Tables, in which interest at a twelfth is called unciarium, which afterwards, by the usage of the jurists who went before (whatever our man also thinks), began to be called the hundredth? If he can bring forward either another law, or another decree of the Senate, or a plebiscite, by which the hundredth was set against unciarium interest, which, on his own showing, is the twelfth part of the hundredth, and was permitted in the City as ordinary usury, I will give in and publicly confess my error. Meanwhile, while he searches for this law in the archives of Utopia, my argument will stand unshaken. Secondly, let us consider what happened to Cicero, the prince of orators, whom debt, among other burdens, caused great trouble. In book 5 of the Epistulae ad Familiares, he writes to Sextius, though in jest: So know that I now have so much debt that I would like to conspire, if anyone would take me in, etc. He suffered here not only in his own name but also in another's. When he was proconsul of Cilicia, the Salaminians had received money from the friends of Brutus, having promised by carelessness in the bond four hundredths; but when Brutus's friends saw that the Gabinian law stood in their way, which had two heads: one, that no one might be allowed to give or receive money in the provinces by way of a loan; the other, that interest in the provinces should not be heavier than a hundredth. They fled to two decrees of the Senate passed concerning that bond. Cicero hesitated here (see the last letter of book 6), fearing that by the decree he would be compelled to pronounce judgment on the four hundredths. But afterwards he observed that that decree did not provide for collecting four hundredths, but only that the moneylenders should not lose the principal itself, because they had given it contrary to the Gabinian law, and that the Salaminians should not be fined, since they had received it contrary to the same law. The remedy, however, was the second decree of the Senate, made in the same consulship, namely that of Lentulus and Philippus, by which it was laid down that judgment should be given on that bond by which the Salaminians owed the sum, in which they had promised only a hundredth each; although this man (such was his impudence) was collecting four hundredths on another bond. With these things set out, let us attend to what follows. 1. By the Gabinian law it was lawful to lend at a hundredth in the provinces. 2. The Senate approved these as just in the contract of the Salaminians. 3. Cicero pronounced judgment on them as just. But what unfairness would there have been, if at Rome, by the laws of the Twelve Tables, only a twelfth part of the hundredth (which, for the Adversary, is unciarium interest) had been the greatest usury, and yet to everyone without distinction, even by a law passed, it had been lawful to lend at a hundredth in the provinces? Indeed, that lending would have been most unjust, according to Arnobius, book 2 against the Gentiles. I am persuaded of something else about the justice of the Romans. Cicero says of himself and his contemporaries, in book 1 of De Oratore, in the person of Marcus: We boys used to learn the Twelve by heart as a necessary song. He refers to the Twelve Tables, which, as Livy testifies in book 3, were, amid the immense heap of other laws piled one upon another, the source of all public and private law. Who then can certainly fail to believe that the Conscript Fathers had the Twelve in view when they regulated lending in the provinces? Others may think otherwise; I suppose the Gabinian law was not departed from by them, and that Lucullus had the same in mind when, as Plutarch testifies in the Life of Lucullus, he annulled all the higher interest throughout Asia and permitted that no more than a hundredth should be exacted under the name of interest. Those who think otherwise must see how they can show the Roman Senate free from iniquity and injustice. The third argument is this: although the hundredth (as the Adversary himself testifies) was the greatest usury at Rome, and the banker was, as it were, a usurer, nevertheless the bankers could not always lend their money at a hundredth, even in Cicero's time; either because there was an abundance of public money, or because the wealthier had no need of ready money. Hence that complaint of Danistes in Plautus:

units.la: Scelestiorem ego Annum locando argento fœnori Nunquam ullum vidi, quam hic mihi Annus obtigit:
units.tr: I have never seen a more wicked year for lending money at interest than the one that has fallen to me.

units.la: A mane ad noctem totum usque in Foro degó diem:
units.tr: From morning till night I spend the whole day in the Forum.

units.la: Locare Argenti nemini nummum queo.
units.tr: I cannot lend a single coin of silver to anyone.

units.la: Nullibi autem legitur, quod fœnus adeo leve fuerit, ut non surrexerit ultra duodecimam Centesimæ partem. quod factum tamen oportuisset, si ipsis LL. xii. Tabularum, hæc usura, ut maxima definita fuisset. Lego quidem apud Ciceronem lib. 4. ad Att. ep. 15. Fœnus ex triente Idibus factum erat Bessibus. Sed, quanta distantia non intercedit inter trientem & unciam unam? quodque tam repente à triente ad bessem fuerit deventum, imputari debet ambitiosissimæ Candidatorum nationi. Alias Centesimæ erant ordinariæ, nec eas argentarii solum stipulabantur, sed alii quilibet Romæ. Cicero lib. 1. ad Att. ep. 12. A Cæcilio (inquit) minore Centesimis nummum movere non possunt.
units.tr: Nowhere, however, do we read that interest was ever so low that it did not rise above a twelfth part of the hundred. Yet that would have had to happen if the Laws of the Twelve Tables had fixed this usury as the maximum. I do read in Cicero, Letters to Atticus, book 4, letter 15: "On the Ides interest had gone up from a third to two-thirds." But what a great distance there is between a third and a single ounce! That the rate rose so suddenly from a third to two-thirds should be charged to the most ambitious nation of candidates. Otherwise the centesimae were the ordinary rate, and not only bankers exacted them but anyone at all in Rome. Cicero, Letters to Atticus, book 1, letter 12: "From Caecilius the younger (he says) they cannot get a single coin lent at the centesimae rate."

units.la: Quis sibi vero persuadeat, Leges xii. Tabularum hoc seculo, & præcedentibus aliis dormivisse, & non puniisse illos, qui in tantum excederent usu-rariam formulam: maxime quòd parati essent
units.tr: Yet who could persuade himself that the Twelve Tables slept through this century and the ones before it, and did not punish those who went beyond the usury formula to such an extent, especially since there were ready

units.la: Quadruplatores, qui tales accusarent. Afconius ad Cicer. Divinat. Aly dicunt, Quadruplatores esse eorum reorum accusatores, qui convicti quadrupli damnari soleant, ut alea, aut pecunia gravioribus usuris fœnerata, quam pro consuetudine: aut ejusmodi aliorum criminum. Sed quod unciarium fœnus Centesimæ æquivaleret, qui Centesimis fœnerabantur, contra xii. Tab. non peccabant. Quartum Argumentum suppeditant ipsi Pandectæ, quorum non potest non callentissimus esse Gronovius, Jurium Doctor, Antiquarius, Historicus, &c. In iis sæpius non modo simpliciter mentio fit Centesimæ, verum etiam ut usuræ legitimæ. De quo ne quis dubitet, probatum ibo. Centesimę usurę, maximæ sæpius vocantur à Tryphonino l. 38. ff. de Neg. gest. ab Vlpiano l. 7. §. 4. ubi agens de tutoribus, qui in usus suos converterant pupillorum pecunias, dicit eos præstare legitimas usuras, intelligendo Centesimas, quas postea gravissimas vocat. quomodo & Tryphoninus easdem usuras intelligendo, dicit l. 54. ff. eod. tit. Non existimo maximis usuris subjiciendum eum, qui à contutoribus suis mutuam pecuniam pupilli accepit. Et Papinianus l. 1. §. 3. ff. de Pignor. & Hypoth. Pacto placuit, ut ad diem usuris non solutis fructus hypothecarum usuris compensarentur, fini legitimæ usuræ quamvis exordio minores instipulatu venerint, non non esse tamen irritam conventionem placuit: cum, ad diem minore fœnore non soluto, legitimæ majores usuræ stipulanti recte promitti potuerunt. Vbi legitimæ usuræ majores (Centesimæ maximæ erant) minori fœnori aperte opponuntur. Quæro, quare Centesimæ usuræ legitimæ vocentur? Notum est, apud Jcc. illud legitimum censeri, quod ex aliqua lege descendit. Vnde illud Pauli l. 6. ff. de Pactis: Legitima conventio est, quæ lege aliqua confirmatur. Eoque Centesimæ usuræ lege aliqua definitæ fuerunt. Sed quænam illa Lex fuerit? Doctissimus Brissonius, (eum sequitur Dionys. Godofredus in d. l. 1. de Pign) lib. 2. Antiq. Jur. Civil. cap. 1. putat intelligendam esse Legem Gabiniam, & quædam Senatusconsulta, eodem forte tempore cum lege Gabinia condita. Verum ex Cicerone, qui hic ad suffragium vocatur, nihil aliud eviceris, quam Legem Gabiniam (Cicero lib. 6. ad Att. ep. 2. Auli legem vocat, quod Gabinio Auli prænomen fuerit) per provincias fœnus ordinasse, & prohibuisse excedere Centesimas. Quando autem Jcc. Romani absolute aliquid pronunciant legitimum esse, quod Legi sit consentaneum, talem potissimum Legem respiciunt, quæ in ipsa Vrbe inter Quirites valuit. Necessum ergo est, præter legem Gabiniam alia Lex detur. Nulla vero præter eam, quæ in xii. occurrit, datur, in qua unciarium fœnus vocetur, quod subsequentibus seculis usitatius usura Centesima dici cœpit. Sic & legitimæ ma Tutela sunt, qua lege duodecim tabularum adgnatis delata sunt, & consanguineis, item patronis, ut loquitur Vlpianus l. 1. ff. de Legit. tutor. Superest Quintum Argumentum, quod instar omnium esse potest: cum solum negotium hoc conficiat. Cato in Præf. lib. de R. R. ita ad filium: Majores enim nostri sic habuerunt, & ita in Legibus posiverunt, furem dupli condemnari, fæneratorem quadrupli. Respicit leges xii. Tabularum: quas & Cicero, mentione Majorum facta, commendare solet. Lib. 1. Off. Hostis apud Majores nostros is dicebatur, quem nunc peregrinum dicimus. Indicant xii. Tabula. Ita & legas leg. 2. Cod. Theod. de liber. caussa: Libertati a Majoribus tantum impensum est, ut patribus, quibus jus vitæ in liberos necisque potestas permissa est, eripere libertatem non liceret, &c. Catonem aliter intelligendum non esse, fatetur ipse Incomparabilis Salmasius, qui occasione verborum modo adductorum; sic commentatur lib. de Vsuris pag. 542. non omnem fæneratorem lex duodecim tabularum quadruplo condemnabat, sed, qui vetitum Lege modum in fenerando excessisset. Duodecim quippe Tabulis interdictum fuit, ne qui unciario fœnore amplius exerceret, si quis contra faceret, quadruplione luito. Intra hunc mo-
units.tr: Quadruplatores, to bring such men to trial. Asconius, on Cicero's Divinatio: Others say that the quadruplatores are the accusers of those defendants who, when convicted, are usually condemned to pay fourfold, such as gamblers, or those who lent money at higher interest than the custom, or those guilty of similar crimes. But because the unciarium rate was equal to the hundredth, those who lent at one percent did not, contrary to the Twelve Tables, do wrong. The fourth argument is supplied by the Pandects themselves, whose author must be the most learned Gronovius, doctor of law, antiquary, historian, and so on. In them the hundredth is mentioned often, and not merely as a rate, but as lawful interest. Lest anyone doubt this, I shall prove it. The hundredth interest is often called maximum by Tryphoninus in law 38 of the Digest, De negotiis gestis; by Ulpian in law 7, §4, where, treating of guardians who had turned their wards' money to their own use, he says that they must pay lawful interest, meaning the hundredth, which he later calls very heavy. Tryphoninus, too, meaning the same interest, says in law 54 of the same title: I do not think that he who received a loan from his co-guardians on the ward's behalf should be made subject to the highest interest. And Papinian in law 1, §3, of the Digest, De pignoribus et hypothecis: It was agreed that, if interest was not paid on the day, the fruits of the pledges should be set off against the interest, and although the interest stipulated at the start was lower, it was held that the agreement was not void: since, if the lower interest was not paid on the day, the higher lawful interest could rightly be promised to the one stipulating. Here the higher lawful interest (the hundredth was the highest) is openly set against the lower interest. I ask, why is the hundredth called lawful interest? It is well known that among the jurists something is deemed lawful when it derives from some law. Hence the saying of Paul in law 6 of the Digest, De pactis: A lawful agreement is one confirmed by some law. So the hundredth was fixed by some law. But what law was that? The most learned Brisson (and Dionysius Godefridus follows him, on the same law 1, De pignoribus), in book 2 of the Antiquitates Iuris Civilis, chapter 1, thinks it must be the Gabinian law, and certain senatorial decrees perhaps passed at the same time as the Gabinian law. But from Cicero, whom he calls in as a witness here, you will prove nothing more than that the Gabinian law (Cicero, book 6 of the Letters to Atticus, letter 2, calls it the law of Aulus, since Gabinius' praenomen was Aulus) set the rate of interest in the provinces and forbade it to exceed the hundredth. But when the Roman jurists flatly declare something lawful because it agrees with the law, they have in mind chiefly that law which held force among the citizens in the City itself. So there must be some other law besides the Gabinian. Yet no other law is given besides the one found in the Twelve Tables, in which the unciarium rate is named, which in later centuries began to be called more commonly the hundredth. So too the lawful guardianships are those which by the law of the Twelve Tables were granted to agnates, and to relatives, and likewise to patrons, as Ulpian puts it in law 1 of the Digest, De legitimis tutoribus. There remains the fifth argument, which may stand for all, since it alone settles the matter. Cato, in the preface of his book De re rustica, writes thus to his son: For our ancestors held this view, and so they laid down in their laws that a thief should be condemned to pay double, and a usurer fourfold. He refers to the Twelve Tables, which Cicero, too, is wont to commend whenever he mentions the ancestors. Book 1 of De officiis: Among our ancestors, the one whom we now call a foreigner was called a hostis. The Twelve Tables show this. So too you may read in law 2 of the Theodosian Code, De libera causa: So much did our ancestors grant to liberty that it was not lawful to take away freedom from fathers, to whom the right of life and the power of death over their children had been granted, and so on. That Cato must be understood in no other way, the incomparable Salmasius himself admits; on the strength of the words just quoted, he comments thus in his book De usuris, page 542: The law of the Twelve Tables did not condemn every usurer to fourfold payment, but only the one who had exceeded the rate forbidden by law in lending. For the Twelve Tables forbade anyone to lend at more than the unciarium rate; if anyone acted against this, he was to pay fourfold. Within this limit

units.la: Ex Cornelia tabula cap. 6. Sic de figura modum igitur impunitus fœnerator, & fœnus exercere permissus. His prœstructis, Impp. Valentinianus, Theodosius, & Arcadius docebunt nos, quid in Jure xii. Tabularum fœnus unciarium fuerit. Cynegio leg. 2. Cod. de Vsur. ita rescripserunt: Quicunque ultra CENTESIMAM JURE PERMISSAM, quicquid sub occasione necessitatis eruerit, QUADRUPLI POENA & obligatione constrictus, sine cessatione, sine requie protinus ablata redhibebit. Quid clarius dici posset? Cum Imperatores & Juris (Veteris scil. quod jus xii. Tabularum) & pœnæ quadrupli mentionem faciant, illam ipsam legem, quam D. Salmasius bona fide modo adduxit, respiciunt: atque, cum pro fœnore unciario, substituunt Centesimam, hanc fœnori unciario æquivalere manifestò ostendunt. Quid ad hæc jam dicet Gronovius? Quid amici? qui cum maledicum ipsius libellum accepissent, idem se naƈtos putarunt, quod pueri in faba invenient: atque cum hoc Thesauro ad omnes cursitarunt, quos augurabantur conatibus nostris non bene velle: ut pluribus constaret, quam vapulassemus. Excutiant jam sua Adversaria, illa recondite eruditionis pretiosissima promptuaria, & viderint, quomodo Senatus Critici Principi, qui solus scil. novit quid boni libri compleƈtuntur, succurrant. Sed habere videtur caussæ suæ præsidia? Grammatici matica concedo. Antea illa excutiam, quam vindicem, quę Salmasii argumento oppositi. Interim ϰοϰϰύζει, & eadem Hottomanno, Manutio, Adr. Junio, Pichenę, & mihi occinit. Omnia ad haec redigi possunt. 1. Romanos in universum omnes, (pag. 72.) à Romulo usque, secundum usurarium assem, illiusque partes in mensis singulos, usuras stipulari consuevisse. 2. Hanc distributionem (p. 76.) neutiquam veteribus Icc. esse acceptam referendam: quod fit (pag. 77.) non veterum Jurisconsultorum inventum, sed patrum familias, sive qui fenerabantur, sive qui fenori accipiebant. 3. Eoque, unciarium foenus ab ipsis Reip. Romanae primordiis, velut duodecimam Centesimae usurae partem, æstimari debere. Haec usque adeo verbose, confidenter, & maledice proponit, ut ab Inferis rediisse videatur Heros Homericus, qui Φοῖζος ἐηνχεφαλὴν οξέα κεκληγώς λέγ' ὀνείδεα. Quicunque haec legent, putabunt me dissimulare, quae ex bonis suis Authoribus attulit. Sed perlustrentur omnes chartae, Author non occurrit, vel per indicem citatus: & tamen in his narrandis, repetendis, & inculcandis aeque sibi certus esse videtur, ac si Alphio à tabulis, & Macedonio à calculis fuisset. Fidem ne inveniat, nisi forte apud improvidos adolescentes, quos circumvenit, ξὺν Θεῷ curabo. Hoc solum meminisse velint Lectores, quaestionem esse, quantum valuerit Vnciarium foenus apud calcos Romanos, speciatim in xii. tabulis. Grammaticorum juxta Assem calculos attendi non debere, patebit, ubi ex bonis Authoribus probatum fuerit, consuetudinem loquendi, quoque seculo receptam, eum, qui audire vult Criticus Grammaticus, considerare magis debere, quam quae Grammatici suas juxta regulas ineptiunt, si non delirant. Ergoprimo observetur, quod quando de verbis explicandis sermo est, primas consuetudo ferre debeat, quum suffragante Quintiliano lib. i.cap. 5. Auctoritatem sermonis consuetudo superet: penes quam teste Flacco.
units.tr: From the Cornelian tablet, chapter 6, thus concerning the figure: therefore the usurer was unpunished within this limit, and was allowed to lend at interest. With these things laid down in advance, the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius will teach us what the unciarium rate was under the law of the Twelve Tables. In their rescript to Cynegius, law 2 of the Code, De usuris, they wrote: Whoever has extracted anything beyond the hundredth permitted by law, under pretext of necessity, shall be bound by the penalty and obligation of fourfold payment, and shall restore what was taken away at once, without delay or rest. What could be stated more clearly? Since the Emperors mention both the law (that is, the old law, the Twelve Tables) and the penalty of fourfold, they have in view that very law which Lord Salmasius quoted in good faith just now; and since they substitute the hundredth for the unciarium rate, they plainly show that the hundredth is equal to the unciarium rate. What will Gronovius now say to this? What will his friends say, who, when they received his scurrilous little book, thought they had found what boys find in a bean, and ran about with this treasure to everyone whom they thought ill-disposed to our efforts, so that more people would know how we were thrashed? Let them now search their notebooks, those most precious storehouses of recondite learning, and see how the Critic's senate can help its Prince, who alone knows what good books contain. But he seems to have defences for his cause? I grant the grammarians' point. Before defending these things, I shall first examine the argument opposed to Salmasius. Meanwhile he cackles [κοκκύζει], and sings the same tune to Hottoman, Manutius, Adrian Junius, Pichena and me. All of it can be reduced to these points. 1. The Romans in general, from Romulus onward, were accustomed to demand interest by the as and its parts, a unit per month for each. 2. This division (p. 76) should by no means be credited to the ancient jurists: which is (p. 77) not the invention of the ancient jurists, but of the heads of families, whether those who lent or those who borrowed. 3. Therefore the unciarium rate should be reckoned from the very beginnings of the Roman Republic as the twelfth part of the hundredth. He puts this forward so verbosely, confidently and scurrilously that the Homeric hero seems to have returned from the dead, who, shrieking shrilly and hurling insults [Φοῖζος ἐηνχεφαλὴν οξέα κεκληγώς λέγ' ὀνείδεα]. Whoever reads these things will think that I am hiding what he has brought forward from his own good authors. But let every page be searched: the author does not turn up, not even cited through an index; yet in narrating, repeating and inculcating these things he seems as certain of himself as if he had been Alphius with his account-books or Macedonius with his counters. Whether he will find belief, except perhaps among the unwary young men whom he has taken in, I shall see to with God's help [ξὺν Θεῷ]. Let the readers remember this one thing: the question is how much the unciarium rate was worth among the Roman calculators, specifically under the Twelve Tables. That the calculations of the grammarians by the as ought not to be heeded will be clear once it has been proved from good authors that the custom of speaking, received in each century, ought to be considered by one who wishes to hear a critic who is also a grammarian, more than what the grammarians trifle over by their own rules, if they are not raving. So, first, let it be observed that when the discussion is about explaining words, custom ought to carry the first place, since, with Quintilian's support in book 1, chapter 5, Custom should prevail over the authority of speech: with custom, as Flaccus attests, rests [context omitted]

units.la: Arbitrium est, & jus, & norma loquendi, quare etiam usus frequens, (quod Cicero dixit Orat. proRab. Post.) non tantum magister est artis: sed (ut idem testatur lib. 1. de Orat.) magistrorum quoque omnia praecepta superat. Praeterea secundo, Romani seu Latini sermonis ratio ad eandem hanc consuetudinem perpetuo fuit composita, usque adeo, ut qui posterioribus seculis vivebant, eos intelligere non quiverint, qui ad priora pertinebant. Ne jam sollicitem Victorinum Afrum, qui lib. de Orthographia dicebat: Antiquitatem posterior consuetudo vicit; quod intendo, uniusPolybij testimonio probari potest, qui lib. 3. foedus interRomanos & Carthaginenses, Coff. Junio Bruto & Marco Horatio percussum interpretans, tantum inter eam linguam, ab illa, quae suo tempore in usu erat, differentiam fuisse innuit,
units.tr: Use is the judge, the law and the rule of speaking. So also frequent usage, as Cicero said in the Pro Rabirio Postumo, is not merely the master of the art, but, as the same author attests in book 1 of De Oratore, it surpasses all the precepts of the masters. Moreover, secondly, the principle of the Roman or Latin language was always shaped by this same usage, to such an extent that those who lived in later ages could not understand those who belonged to earlier ones. Not to trouble you further with Victorinus Afer, who said in his book on orthography, later custom has overcome antiquity, what I mean can be proved by the testimony of Polybius alone. In book 3, when he interprets the treaty struck between the Romans and the Carthaginians in the consulship of Junius Brutus and Marcus Horatius, he hints that there was so great a difference between that language and the one in use in his own time,

units.la: ut non nisi à peritis difficulter intelligi posset: [illegible, ~12 letters] ἡ διαφορὰ γέγονε τῆς διαλέκ-τῳ, καὶ ῾Ρωμαίοις τῆς νῦν πρὸς τὴν ἀρχαί-αν. ὥστε τὰς συνετωδάς ἐνια, μόλισθ᾽ ἐπιστά-σεως διαχρῆσιν. Veteris sane linguae, etiam Latinae, tanta diversitas est ab illa, quà hodie utuntur, ut vel peritissimi nonnulla agre, ubi animum attenderint, explanare queant. Diligenter attendi velim haec verba: καὶ ῾Ρωμαίοις. Tertiò, quod ratione Latinae Linguae, in communi consideratae verum est (teste Scriptore gravissimo) speciatim ratione juris antiqui, quod in xii. exhibetur, certissimum est: Quotufquifq; Roma adhuc florente, aut illas, aut jus Aborigenum intelligere potuit? Formulae, quibus leges illae conceptae, ipsis antiquis Jcc. aenigmata fuerunt. Gell. lib. 16. cap. 12. Quaeri coeptum est (inquit) quid esset proletarius. Atque ego aspiciens quiempiam in eo circulo Jus civile callentem, rogabam ut id verbum nobis enarraret. Nam (inquam) Ennius verbum hoc ex xii. Tabulis vestris accepit. Ego vero, inquit ille, dicere atque interpretari hoc deberem, si jus Faunorum et Aborigenum didicissem. Senec. ep. 114. Multi ex alieno seculo petunt verba, xii. Tabulas loquuntur. Symmachus lib. 3. ep. 44.
units.tr: so that it could scarcely be understood except by experts: [illegible, ~12 letters] ἡ διαφορὰ γέγονε τῆς διαλέκτου, καὶ Ῥωμαίοις τῆς νῦν πρὸς τὴν ἀρχαίαν. ὥστε τὰς συνθήκας ἐνίοις μόλις ἐπιστάμενα διαλύεσθαι [the difference of the dialect, for the Romans too, between the present and the ancient one; so that the treaties are with difficulty understood by some, unless with close attention]. Indeed, there is so great a difference between the old language, even Latin, and that which is used today, that even the most expert can explain some parts only with difficulty, when they have applied their minds closely. I would have you attend carefully to these words: καὶ Ῥωμαίοις. Thirdly, what is true of the Latin language considered in general (as a most weighty writer attests) is most certain especially with regard to the ancient law, which is set out in the Twelve Tables. Who, while Rome was still flourishing, could understand either those tables or the law of the Aborigines? The formulas in which those laws were framed were enigmas even to the ancient jurists themselves. Gellius, book 16, chapter 12: It was asked (he says) what a proletarius was. And I, looking at a certain man in that circle who was skilled in civil law, asked him to explain that word to us. For (I said) Ennius took this word from your Twelve Tables. But he (that man replied) would have to say and interpret this, if he had learned the law of the Fauni and the Aborigines. Seneca, letter 114: Many seek words from a foreign age; they speak the Twelve Tables. Symmachus, book 3, letter 44:

units.la: Si tibi vetustatis tantus est amor, pari studio in verba prisca redeamus, quibus Salii canunt, & Augures avum consulunt, & Decemviri Tabulas condiderunt. Jamdudum bis renunciatum est, & successio temporum placita priora mutavit. Et tamen quarto, seculo Augusti quoque, plurimi, ut singulares viderentur, verbis antiquis, & non modo ex xii. Tabulis, verum & Saliorum axamentis petitis, loqui affectarunt. Horat. l. 2. ep. 1.
units.tr: If you have such a great love of antiquity, let us with equal zeal return to the ancient words in which the Salii sing, the augurs consult the grandfather, and the Decemvirs drew up the Tables. Long ago it was reported twice over, and the succession of times has changed the earlier things that were approved. And yet in the fourth century, even under Augustus, very many people, so that they might seem singular, affected to speak in old words, taken not only from the Twelve Tables but also from the hymns of the Salii. Horace, Epistles, book 2, letter 1.

units.la: Sic fautor Veterum, ut Tabulas peccare vetantes, Quas bis quinque viri sanxerunt, foedera Regum Vel Gabiis, vel cum rigidis aquata Sabinis, Pontificum libros, annosa volumina vatum Dictitet, Albano Musas in Monte locutas.
units.tr: So great a champion of the ancients is he that he maintains the tablets forbidding wrongdoing, which the ten men (the decemvirs) enacted, the treaties of kings, whether made at Gabii or made equal with the stern Sabines, the books of the pontiffs, and the aged volumes of the bards, which the Muses spoke on the Alban Mount.

units.la: Ad quae ita Porphyrion: Adeo Veteribus favet, ut etiam xii. Legum Tabula a Decemviris scripta, Latina esse videantur, ob austeram & rancidam vetustatem. Componantur haec, & prisci ævi vocabula atque formulas, rigide ad Grammaticorum Canones exigendas non esse, patebit; simul fœnus unciarium ipsis xii. Tabulis notum, haud æstimandum, ob rationes supra allatas, secundum recentiorem distinctionem fœnoris juxta Assis partes. Clamabit quidem adversarius, hæc non esse
units.tr: Porphyrion, on these words, says: "He so favours the ancients that even the Twelve Tables, written by the Decemvirs, seem to be Latin only because of their austere and musty antiquity." Let these things be compared, and it will be clear that the words and formulas of the early age are not to be rigidly measured by the canons of the grammarians. At the same time, the fenus unciarium is known from the Twelve Tables themselves, and is not to be assessed, for the reasons given above, according to the more recent distinction of interest by parts of the as. Our opponent will certainly cry out that these are not

units.la: D con-
units.tr: D con-

units.la: consentanea artis suæ ( Grammaticæ fcil. ) regulis, sed ex Lactantio lib. 2.cap. 7. audiat, in talibus (ab- fit, ut ulterius hoc extendi velim) majoribus no- ftris, etiam nulla ratione reddita, rationis esse credere. Nec hominum vulgo partes assis, usu- ras quasi definientes, Justiniani quoque ævo, liqui- dô notas fuisse, discat ex ipsius Novella xxxiv. ubi Imperator definiens modum usurarum, quas ab a- gricolis stipulari liceat, summatim hoc constituit, ut pro annua minutarum frugum usura, non am- plius octava modii parte in singulos modios exiga- tur: pro usura pecuniarum siliqua in solidos sin- gulos: Cur Imperator, usurarium hunc Canonem, juxta assis partes ,non definivisset potius, si omnes in Togata gente, omnesque in plebe Urbana & Ru- stica, aut, omnes qui Latine sciebant, eas in nume- rato habuissent? Sed, quia hic, ut sæpe alias, falli- tur Adversarius, Imperator alia formula uti voluit. Consequens ergo est, usum loquendi, quoque secu- lo receptum, in consilium admissa ratione, attendi magis debere, quam Grammaticorum aut Etymo- logias aut præcepta. Romanus populus cum à Ro- mulo in tres partes divisus esset,quæque pars,Gram- matica suffragante, Tribus dici cœpit, quod voca- bulum Romæ adhuc usitatum fuit, quum amplius quàm ttiginta tribus notarentur. Atrendantur quo- que anni Romani menses. Initio verum erat,quod Ovidius lib. 1. Fast. dicit:
units.tr: consistent with the rules of his art (that is, of grammar). But let him hear from Lactantius, book 2, chapter 7 (far be it that I should wish to extend this further), that in such matters to believe that reason is present even when no reason is given is to be attributed to our ancestors. Nor should he learn that the parts of the as, as if defining interest, were clearly known to the common people even in the age of Justinian, from that emperor's own Novella 34, where, defining the rate of interest which farmers may stipulate, he summarily establishes that for an annual interest on small crops, no more than the eighth part of a modius is to be exacted on each modius; for interest on money, a siliqua on each solidus. Why would the emperor not rather have defined this usury canon by parts of the as, if all in the toga-wearing nation, and all among the urban and rural plebs, or all who knew Latin, had those in ready reckoning? But, as often elsewhere, the opponent is mistaken here, and the emperor wished to use another formula. It follows, then, that the usage of speech received in each age, taking reason into account, ought to be attended to more than the etymologies or precepts of the grammarians. When the Roman people had been divided by Romulus into three parts, and each part, with grammar supporting it, began to be called a tribe, the word was still in use at Rome, although more than thirty tribes were noted. Let the Roman months also be considered. At first it was true what Ovid says in book 1 of the Fasti:

units.la: Tempora digereret cum conditor Urbis, in anno Constituit menses quinque bis esse suo.
units.tr: When the founder of the City was about to arrange the seasons, he fixed the months in his year at five pairs.

units.la: Non multis autem annis post, verum quoque fuit, quod mox subjicit:
units.tr: Not many years later, however, what he goes on to say was also true:

units.la: At Numa nec Janu, nec avitas praeterit umbras, Mensibus antiquis addidit ille duos.
units.tr: But Numa did not pass over Janus or the ancestral shades; to the old months he added two.

units.la: In usu tamen manserunt nomina antea receptaMensium, Septembris, Octobris, Novembris, Decembris. Quum September November, October December, November Vndecember, December Duodecember dici debuissent. Sed vulgus, vocibus pro suo arbitratu, subserviente consuetudine, significationes indere solet, Grammaticis, Analogiam & Etymologias suas urgentibus, laqueum mandando. Idem contendo ratione foenoris Vnciarii, pro usu Quiritium, & xii. Tabularum, maxime pro conditione Reip. Romanae, neutiquam vero secundum Canones Grammaticorum, & morosos eorundem calculos intelligendi. Nec inconveniens esse, ut usura Centesima, Vnciaria aut Vncia vocetur, liquido ostenderam, modo admittatur Synecdoche. Prolixe quidem a pag. 27. usque ad 59. contra ea, quae dixeram, Adversarius tumultuatur, aut verius κοχχύζει. sed tanti mihi non sunt haec χελιδόνων μύσσια, ut iis obstrepam. Non hoc meum argumentum fuit: Vnciarium foenus, Centesimae debere respondere, quod illud e principiis Salmasii & Gronovii elici posset; sed sententiam meam certissimis rationibus (quibus assentiri quilibet debet, cui mo-do do mensfana fuefit) confirmatam, modo Synec- doche admittatur, à principiis illorum non longe recedere. Non ego assem unciæ (ut calumniatur Adversarius) aut totum parti adæquavi; sed Cente- simam, ut assem Vsurarium, sic Synecdochice atten- di posse scripsi, ut duodena ipsius pars, ratione an- ni, quo solveretur, Vncia vocaretur, quæ duodeci- es soluta juxta duodecim menses, quibus annus con- stat, quum conficeret duodecies Centesimam men- struam, simul quoque mense, Centesimam sortis partem confecisse, eamque Vnciam, & Synecdo- chice, &c, maxime pro usu loquendi, vocari potuisse, quod Centesima, ut as Vsurarius, ratione anni, æque duodecim partibus, seu unciis, quoque mense debi- tis constaret, atque annus totidem mensibus, aut, ut Assi cuilibet duodenæ unciæ assignari solent. Quin- tilianus lib. 8. cap. 6. sic dicit: Quod aliquanto pene jam magis de Synecdoche dicam. Nam translatio promovendis animis plerumque & signandis rebus, ac sub oculos subjiciendis, reper- ta est. Hæc variare sermonem potest, ut ex u- no plures intelligamus, parte totum, specie ge- nus, præcedentibus sequentia, vel contra. Sed perierit mihi hæc Analogia? non tamen de gradu dejici possum. Argumenta supra vindicata, & de novo allata, nullus unquam Grammaticus evertet. Omnibus illis, quæ objici possent, jam præstruxi. Tria sua postulata, si, æque firmaverit Adversarius (ten(tentet, si ausit) ex bonis suis authoribus, cedam ultro. nec tantum cedam, sed herbam porrigam. Quæ mihi falso pag. 57. improperat, sibi vere dixisse putet: Hæc ei ratio explicanda erat, si quam noverat: non tantummodo dicendum, &c. Interim, priusquam pergo, quod ipse Adversarius eo nomine insultet, expendere convenit Plinii locum lib. 10. ep. 62. Ita Trajanum alloquitur: Pecuniæ publicæ, Domine, prudentia tua & ministerio nostro etiam exactæ sunt & exiguntur: quæ neque ne otiosæ jaceant. nam & prædiorum comparandorum, aut nulla, aut rarissima occasio est, nec inveniuntur, qui velint debere Reip. præsertim, duodenis assibus, quanti à privatis mutuantur. Illud duodenis assibus obesse sibi prævidebat, eoque p. 55. occurrit: Quod cum insolens sit, (inquit) & contra omnem usitati his in rebus sermonis analogiam, nec simile quidquam in tota antiquitate reperiatur, docte & ingeniose suspicatus est Salmasius, Plinium scripsisse, usuris assibus. Sed etiamsi vulgatum retineatur, nihil illum juvabit, qui vult idem nomen significare & menstruum & annuum: at duodeni hi asses quo pacto applicabuntur menstruo? Pensitare hæc convenit, & quidem exacte. 1. Docte & ingeniose Dn. Salmasii suspicioni partum tribuit, neque etiam niti audet. 2. Et tamen se præ tanto viro, suo promotore maximo, imprudentem esse prodit, quòd largiatur, vulgatam lectionem posse retineri, à qua, & quidem merito, suæ sententiæ periculum imminere Salmasius prævidebat. 3. More hominum suæ professionis, nimis quam liberaliter loquitur, quando dicit, simile quidquam in tota antiquitate non reperiri. A veri lineis non recessisset, si hæc verba adjecisset: Quantum mihi, secundum meum institutum & judicium antiquos Authores legenti, liquet. Atque, si scivisset rationes meas pro vera fœnoris unciarii significatione expendere, parcior fuisset. 4. Proba ergo Plinii lectio est, juxta quisquis debet duodenis assibus, simul Centesimis usuris debet. Sed Centesima, D. Salmasio teste, mensura reliquarum usurarum, & as quasi usurarius erat: eoque, qui debet duodenis assibus, usuram tantam debet, habita ratione anni. Finge jam Sejum cum Alphio in annum contraxisse usuris centesimis, & uniusque jusque mensis Calendis repræsentasse Vsuras, potueritne dicere V. C. Kal. Martii accipe assem usurarium, & iterum Cal. Aprilis, accipe assem &c. Sic enim jam duplicasset centesimas, si As proprie intelligendus fuisset. Sed, si acceperit V. C. centum denarios, ut quoque mense debuerit solvere singulos denarios, simul, assis hujus annui singulas Vncias quoque mense solvendo, fidem suam liberaverit. Et tamen Plinius dixit assibus duodenis, habita ratione assis ut usurarii per annum, sed per duodenos mens es distristribuendi ac solvendi- Atque, ut asses pro unciis dixit, quia distributive locutus fuit, ita unciæ assi usurario annuo respondentes, quoque mense duodecimam illius partem exhibent: duodecies vero multiplicatæ, Centesimam, seu assem usurarium. Aliud non contendo. Videbat summus Salmasius vulgatam Plinii lectionem hoc probare, eoque, ne obesset, eradendo illud duodenis, (securus interim Mnn. Codd.) Vsuris, pro libertate Critica substituit. Adversarius si dixerit, hæc Conjectu- ras esse; eas solidarum rationum loco mihi tantisper esse respondebo, quamdiu contrarium ex bonis su- is libris probaverit. Hactenus meæ Conjecturæ cum suis paria faciunt. Nec inficias tamen ivero, hic aliquos scrupulos superesse, & examussim omnia non convenire calculis, quos Adversarius attendi debere contendit. Sed Grammaticorum morosis præceptis opponere convenit usum loquendi, eruditis quoque probatum, quem secutum Plinium esse, cerro persuasum habeo. Utendum plane ser- mone ut nummo, cui publica forma est, monente Fabio lib. 1. cap. 6. Teste Plinio lib. 33. cap. 3.
units.tr: The months' names previously received nevertheless remained in use: September, October, November, December. Although they ought to have been called September November, October December, November Undecember, and December Duodecember. But the common people, obeying custom, are wont to give words whatever meanings they choose, thereby setting a snare for the grammarians, who press their analogy and etymologies. I maintain the same about the reckoning of the unciary interest, which must be understood according to the usage of the Quirites and the Twelve Tables, and especially according to the condition of the Roman commonwealth, and by no means according to the canons of the grammarians and their fussy calculations. I had made it clear that it is not inappropriate for a centesimal interest to be called unciary, or an uncia, provided that synecdoche is admitted. My opponent indeed storms at great length, from page 27 to 59, against what I had said, or rather he coughs [κοχχύζει]. But these swallows' droppings [χελιδόνων μύσσια] are not so important to me that I should shout them down. This was not my argument: that the unciary interest must correspond to the centesimal interest, which could be drawn from the principles of Salmasius and Gronovius. Rather, my view, confirmed by the most certain reasons (to which anyone must assent who has a sound mind), is that, provided synecdoche is admitted, it does not stray far from their principles. I did not equate the as of the uncia (as my opponent falsely charges) with the whole, or with the part. I wrote that the centesimal, like the usurer's as, can be regarded synecdochically, so that its twelfth part, reckoned by the year in which it was paid, is called an uncia. For this, paid twelve times according to the twelve months of the year, when it makes up the monthly centesimal twelve times, at the same time in one month completes a hundredth part of the principal, and that is called an uncia; and synecdochically, and so on, it could be called so especially according to the usage of speech, because the centesimal, like the usurer's as, is by the year's reckoning made up of twelve parts, or unciae, which are owed each month, just as the year consists of as many months, or as each as is usually assigned twelve unciae. Quintilian, book 8, chapter 6, says thus: Of synecdoche I shall now say something more than a little. For a figure of speech has been devised chiefly to advance the mind, to mark things, and to set them before the eyes. It can vary the discourse so that from one we understand several: the whole from the part, the genus from the species, the following from the preceding, or the reverse. But has my analogy perished? Still I cannot be dislodged from my position. No grammarian will ever overturn the arguments defended above and newly advanced. I have already prepared answers to all the objections that could be raised. If my opponent will establish his three postulates as firmly, from his own good authorities (let him try, if he dares), I will yield at once, and not only yield, but hold up the white flag. What he falsely reproaches me with on page 57, let him think truly said of himself: this reasoning should have been explained, if he knew it; it should not merely be said, and so on. Meanwhile, before I proceed, it is fitting to weigh the passage of Pliny, book 10, letter 62, which my opponent taunts me about. He addresses Trajan thus: Lord, the public money has been and is being collected by your prudence and our service, so that it may not lie idle; for there is either no opportunity, or a very rare one, of buying estates, and men are not found who are willing to owe it to the commonwealth, especially at twelve asses, the rate at which they borrow from private persons. He foresaw that the phrase at twelve asses would be a hindrance to him, and he meets it on page 55: Since this is unusual (he says), and contrary to the whole analogy of ordinary speech in these matters, and nothing similar is found in all antiquity, Salmasius learnedly and ingeniously suspected that Pliny wrote usuris assibus (at the rate of interest in asses). But even if the vulgar reading is kept, it will not help him who wants the same word to mean both monthly and yearly; for how will these twelve asses apply to the monthly sum? These points are worth weighing, and exactly so. (1) Dominus Salmasius learnedly and ingeniously attributes the reading to a conjecture, and does not dare to rest on it. (2) Yet in the presence of so great a man, his chief patron, he reveals himself as imprudent in granting that the vulgar reading can be kept, a reading by which, and rightly so, Salmasius foresaw danger to his own opinion. (3) In the manner of men of his profession, he speaks far too liberally when he says that nothing similar is found in all antiquity. He would not have strayed from the lines of truth had he added these words: so far as is clear to me, following my method and judgment in reading the ancient authors. And had he known that I weighed my reasons for the true sense of the unciary interest, he would have been more sparing. (4) The reading of Pliny is therefore sound: whoever owes at twelve asses owes at the same time at the centesimal rate of interest. But the centesimal, as Dominus Salmasius bears witness, is the measure of the other interest, and the as was, as it were, the usurer's as. So he who owes at twelve asses owes such interest, with the year taken into account. Now suppose that Seius contracted with Alphius for a year at centesimal interest, and at the calends of each month presented the interest: could he say, on the fifth of the calends of March, take the usurer's as, and again on the calends of April, take the as, and so on? For he would then have doubled the centesimals, if the as were to be taken in its proper sense. But if Seius received a hundred denarii, and was to pay a single denarius each month, paying also in that month one uncia of this yearly as, he would have discharged his obligation. And yet Pliny said at twelve asses, taking the as as the usurer's as for the year, but distributing and paying it over twelve months. And just as he said asses for unciae because he spoke distributively, so the unciae corresponding to the yearly usurer's as each yield a twelfth part of it each month; and multiplied twelve times, they yield the centesimal, or the usurer's as. I contend for nothing more. The most learned Salmasius saw that the vulgar reading of Pliny proved this, and therefore, lest it hinder him, he erased duodenis (meanwhile, securely, the manuscripts agreed) and, with critical freedom, substituted usuris. If my opponent says that these are conjectures, I will answer that, for the time being, they stand in the place of solid reasons, until he proves the contrary from his own good books. Thus far my conjectures and his are on a par.
