Nor, however, do I deny that some scruples remain here, and that not everything agrees exactly with the calculations which my opponent insists must be attended to. But it is fitting to set against the fussy precepts of the grammarians the usage of speech, which is also approved by the learned, and which I am firmly convinced Pliny followed. One must use speech plainly, as one uses coin that has public currency, as Fabius advises in book 1, chapter 6. Pliny also bears witness, book 33, chapter 3.

units.la: Olim placuit denarius pro decem libris æris: postea iterum placuit denarium XVI. assibus permutari: & tamen fremente Grammatica, publice denarii nomen frequentatum fuit. Hoc adjicere convenit: quamvis apud Romanos usuræ essent menstruæ, & ordinario singulis mensibus exigi solerent, lerent, fors quoque singulis mensibus (si ita conven- tum esset) repeti posset; usurarum tamen aliam quam fortis fuisse rationem. Illæ quoque mensæ exigebantur exacte, unde fœneratores ab Ambro- sio, cap. 3. de Tobia, menstrui exactores vocantur; quum ratione fortis observari deberet dies, in quem conventum esset. Verisimile autem est, quod, qui pecuniam fœnori dabant, in annum potius, quia singulos menses eam credere voluerint, singulis licet mensibus usuræ exigerentur: quæ nisi ad diem solverentur, ἀναλοχισμὸς (ut alibi ostendemus) attendi solet. Ita & Provinciarum tributa per annos singulos definiri solent, singulis licet mensibus exigerentur. Quæ occasio fuit, quod nequam ille Licinnius Galliæ præfectus, teste Dione Cassio lib. 54. Provincialibus persuadere voluerit, quatuordecim menses annum constituere. Circumspecte dixi, ordinario fœnus quoque mense solvi consuevisse: nam aliquando conveniebat inter contrahentes, ut fœnus esset perpetuum: quod ideo fiebat, ne locus daretur ἀναλομισμῶ. Patet ex Cicerone lib. 5 ad Att. ep. ult. ubi ipse optat, quo Salminiis consulli posset, ut Centesima perpetuo fœnore duceren-tur. Responsiones meas ad prius & D. Salmasii & Gronovii argumentum proxime tutari deberem; sed quum Adversarius eadem chorda oberret, & sua solum principia tueatur, non est necessum juxta lineas singulas vindicare. Quod dixi de Sextariis, jugeris, geris, &c. verissimum est, cum suo modo, seu, peculiari ratione sint mensurabilia, non possunt ita in duodenas partes distribui, ut duodena cujusque anni parte, pars pariter duodena exhibenda sit. Nec per somnium cogitavi (ut pag. 47. mihi affingit) quod centesima dispertita est in duodecim uncias, ejus rei rationem esse quaerendam in anno: sed quod duodecies, hoc est, uniuscujusque mensis Calendis, duodena assis annui pars exigi consueverit. Marcus Dama usuris centesimis à Fufidio centum florenos acceperit, Fufidius non expectaret, usque dum annus usurarius finitus esset; sed, cum sacco primi mensis Calendis accessisset, unum florenum accepturus, hoc est, duodecimam assis usurarii partem, sive unciam: quem assem plene, valentem duodecim florenis, alius aliquis humanior finito demum anno exegisset. Foeneratores autem mensibus singulis usuras solvi volebant, ut haberent occasionem exigendi ἀναπηισμόν, prout modo innui. Hoc fuit meum responsum, hoc etiam examinare debuisset Adversarius: qui licet pag. 49. jactet se in libera Rep. vivere; (ea nulli licentiam convitiandi concedit) volens nolens tamen (ut jam antea innui) idem fateri cogitur, & iterum cogetur. Annum contrahat ut libuerit, & vel annum Arcadum assumat. An non Vsura centesima, forti centesimo quoque mense adaequabitur? Et, ut haec ipsa est, &manere debet as usurarius cujuscunque seu menmensis, seu anni ratione habita, ita certum manet, à tempore Numæ Pompilii Romanum annum habuisse duodecim menses, atque qui fortem per annum retinebat, pro more Romano duodecies Centesimam sortis partem debuisse soluere. Quæ ratio ergo, cur, quod duodecies quoque anno solueba-tur (toto illo, quod ex duodenis partibus constitue-batur, assis usurarii nomen ferente) non potuerit, ratione singularum partium, unciæ nomen ferre? cumque semel tantum centesima posset sol-ui, altero scil. mense forte restituta: cur con ratione assis usurarii, qui ad duodecim menses continuatus duodecim unciis constitisset, fœnus illud men-struum, æque unciarium, ac Centesima dici potuerit? Aperte agat Adversarius; & voculas (ut in toto hoc discursu agit) non captet, quò cavillari possit. Quæ Salmasio respondi de Vsura semuncia, æquivalente Vsura semissi, nondum sunt eversa. Quando vero scripsi, cum duodena Tacito semuncia, quoque mense soluenda, conficiant semissem assis annui, siue Centesima; quisquis candorem non exuit, hæc ita non interpretabitur, quasi innuere voluerim, quoque mense duodenas semuncias soluendas fuisse; (ut hæc Adversarius explicat) quid enim à ratione æque alienum est? Sed duodenas semuncias per partes quoque mense soluendas fuisse, ita ut singulis mensibus, singulæ semunciæ solverentur: Verum quod inops rerum & rationum esset, talia aucupari debuit, ut suam ostentare posseт. posset loquentiam. Porro sic scripseram: Quod alia usura pariter secundum propriam denominationem non referantur, & ad singulos menses, & ad assem annalem, sive ad assem Centesimæ, ratio est, quod non occurrant æque commoda vocabula, atque se offerunt ratione centesimæ, secundum annum considerandæ, & unciarum semunciarumque ratione, secundum menses singulos, & tamen ad proportionem Centesimæ, sive assis usurarii, aptarum vulgo denominari. His aliud cum opponere non sciret, sua pag. 53. & seqq. repetit. Erit vero mihi Apollo usurarius, si æque commoda invenerit nomina usurarum quadrantium, trientium, quincuncium, &c. quibus exprimatur duodena earum pars, quæ quoque mense Romæ exigi poterat: atque unicia quoque mense solvenda, duodecimam partem Centesimæ, seu assis usurarii signabat. Misericordia viro dignissimus est, quando pag. 51. hunc producit Achillem: Firmissimum & invictum argumentum est, si Vnciarium fœnus & Centesima, semunciarium, & (ut nos loquimur) sex in centum idem essent, sextantarium fœnus vel sextantes usuras fore duas centesimas, seu XXIV. in centum; quadrantarium, ternas centesimas, sive XXXVI. in centum; trientes usuras, quaternas centesimas, XLVIII. in centum; quincunces usuras, quinas nas centesimas, LX. in centum; semisses usuras, senas centesimas, LXXII. in centum; septunces usuras, septenas centesimas, LXXXIV. in centum, &c. Probasse antea debuisset, Romae (neque enim extra illam divagari licet) & sextantibus, & trientibus, & quadrantibus anni partibus, Vsuras solvi consuevisse. Hae unoquoque mense solvebantur, nisi aliter, ut jam patuit, convenisset: eoque, ratione solutionis habita, ubi Centesima, ut As usurarius, secundum annum considerabatur; illud, quod quolibet mense solvebatur, uncia, seu duodecima pars Centesimae, ut annuae, erat. Alius jussus solidum argumentum adducere, si ita argumentaretur, firmissimis Hippocratis vinculis constringendus foret. Gronovius venia dignus est, quia Dialecticam non didicit, sua quoque, ut Grammatica, duntaxat vult agnosci. Hinc oratione ad me conversa pag. 53. dicit: Si meminisset, quid sit, quantumque valeat analogia, &c. Triplex Analogia (Grammatica scil.) hic notari potest, λογικὴ, ἄλογος, & Gronoviana; quae, an media inter illas intervenire debeat, an ad posteriorem referri, ambigo? Videri, ne Analogiae huic nimium tribuat. Ea ipsum Ciceronem aliquando decepit, ut fatetur lib. 6. Ep. ad Att. ep. 2. Quod mihi constet ratio, Analogiae Dialecticae, Arithmeticae, Politicae, & Historicae; Grammaticae securus sum, quodque meam sententiam (ut confido, hactenus auspicato) cum hac conciliaverim, ringente Grammatico, superpondii dunduntaxat loco haberi cupio. Etiam omnia sua non cohaerere fatetur. Inde illud pag. 79. Omne simile etiam dissimile est. quod tam mihi, quam ipsi favere debet. Æque securus sum Authorum meæ sententiæ faventium. Gloriatur Adversarius, se mihi subduxisse Sigonium, Manutium, Adr. Junium, Hottomannum, Pichenam. Ego enim tam liberalis sum, & suis fautoribus, quorum ductor Accursius, (bonus scil. Author) ultro adjiciam Budæos, Brissonios, & Dionysium Godofredum, (filius Jacobus hic mecum sapit) & forte quamplurimos alios, qui Jus Romanum more consueto interpretantur. Vni veritati sacrameutum dixi, cui multi an pauci faveant, digitum non vertero. Ipse sequentia legit apud Senecam de Vita beat. ad L. Gallion. Non est, quod mihi illud disces ionum more respondeas: hæc pars major esse videtur; ideo enim pejor est. Non tam bene cum rebus humanis geritur, ut meliora pluribus placeant. Argumentum pessimi, turba est: quaramus quid optime factum sit, non quid usitatissimum. Quæ hactenus in hac controversia scripsi, Nostr licet Hector haberi velit; ἥης ὀνόσσεʃαι, ὅσσοι Ἀχαιοί, ὣδὲ πάλιν ἐρέει.
units.tr: Once it was agreed that the denarius should be worth ten pounds of bronze, and later it was agreed that the denarius should be exchanged for sixteen asses. Yet, though Grammar protested, the word denarii was in common public use. To this I should add that although interest among the Romans was monthly and was ordinarily collected each month, the principal could perhaps also be repaid each month, if that had been agreed; still, the reckoning of interest was different from that of the principal. Interest was also demanded exactly at the set dates, which is why moneylenders are called menstrui exactores (monthly collectors) by Ambrose, chapter 3, On Tobit. The principal, by contrast, had to be observed on the day agreed upon. It is likely that those who lent money preferred to lend it for a year rather than for each month, though interest could be collected each month. If it was not paid on the due day, the anatocism (ἀναλογισμός, as I shall show elsewhere) was usually reckoned. In the same way, provincial taxes are usually fixed for single years, although they could be collected each month. This gave occasion for that worthless Licinius, prefect of Gaul, according to Dio Cassius, book 54, to try to persuade the provincials that the year should consist of fourteen months. I spoke with care when I said that interest was ordinarily paid monthly, for sometimes the contracting parties agreed that the interest should be perpetual, so that no room was left for anatocism. This is clear from Cicero, book 5 to Atticus, last letter, where he himself wishes, so that he might be able to consult Salminius, that the hundredths should be carried on as perpetual interest. I ought to defend my replies to the first argument of Salmasius and of Gronovius in the next place; but since my opponent keeps to the same string and defends only his own principles, it is not necessary to answer every line. What I said about sextarii, iugera, geres and so on is quite true: since they are measured in their own way, or by a particular reckoning, they cannot be divided into twelve parts in such a way that a twelfth of each year's part must likewise be paid as a twelfth. Nor did I ever dream (as he attributes to me on p. 47) that the hundredth is divided into twelve ounces, and the reason for this must be sought in the year; rather, a twelfth of the yearly as, that is, one twelfth of the sum, was customarily demanded twelve times, on the Calends of each month. Marcus Dama received a hundred florins from Fufidius at the rate of one per cent a month; Fufidius would not wait until the year of interest had ended, but on the Calends of the first month, when the bag had arrived, he would take one florin, that is, the twelfth part of the interest as, or one ounce. Another, more civil man would have collected the full as, worth twelve florins, only at the end of the year. Moneylenders, however, wanted interest paid each month, so that they would have the opportunity of demanding anatocism, as I have just hinted. This was my reply, and my opponent ought to have examined this very point. Although on p. 49 he boasts that he lives in a free republic (which grants no one license to hurl abuse), he is nonetheless compelled, willy-nilly, to concede the same thing, as I have already suggested, and will be compelled again. Let him contract a year as he pleases, or adopt even the Arcadian year. Will not the hundredth at one per cent a month be equal to the principal at the same rate? And as this is so, the usurious as of any interest must remain, whether reckoned by the month or by the year. It is therefore certain that from the time of Numa Pompilius the Roman year had twelve months, and that whoever kept the principal for a year, following Roman custom, owed twelve times the twelfth part of the principal. What reason, then, is there why the part paid twelve times a year (the whole of which was made up of twelve parts and bore the name of the usurious as) could not bear the name of an ounce by reckoning of its single parts? And since the hundredth could be paid only once, if the principal was restored at the other month, why, by reckoning of the usurious as, which over twelve months had amounted to twelve ounces, could that monthly interest not be called an ounce-interest equally well as the hundredth? Let my opponent speak plainly, and not catch at little words (as he does throughout this whole discourse), so that he may have something to cavil at. What I replied to Salmasius about the half-ounce interest, equivalent to the half-as interest, has not yet been overturned. But when I wrote that twelve half-ounces of interest by Tacitus, to be paid each month, make up half of the yearly as, or the hundredth, whoever has not lost his fairness will not interpret this as if I meant to suggest that twelve half-ounces were to be paid each month (as my opponent explains it); for what could be further from reason? Rather, I meant that twelve half-ounces were to be paid in parts each month, so that a single half-ounce was paid each month. But since he was poor in facts and reasons, he ought to have snatched at such things, so that he could show off his eloquence. Further, I had written thus: That other interest is likewise not referred to by its proper name, both to each month and to the yearly as, or the as of the hundredth, is because there do not occur equally convenient words, such as present themselves in the case of the hundredth, to be considered by the year, and in the case of ounces and half-ounces, by each single month; and yet they are commonly named in proportion to the hundredth, or the usurious as, as suited to them. Since he did not know what to set against this, on pp. 53 and following he repeats his own points. I shall be an Apollo of usury indeed if I find equally convenient names for the interest of quadrants, thirds, five-twelfths and so on, by which the twelfth part of them, which could be collected each month at Rome, might be expressed. And the ounce, to be paid each month, marked the twelfth part of the hundredth, or of the usurious as. He is worthy of pity when, on p. 51, he brings forward this Achilles: It is a most firm and invincible argument, that if ounce-interest and the hundredth, half-ounce-interest, and (as we say) six in the hundred were the same, then sixth-part interest, or sextant interest, would be two hundredths, or 24 in the hundred; quadrant interest, three hundredths, or 36 in the hundred; third-part interest, four hundredths, 48 in the hundred; five-twelfths interest, five hundredths, 60 in the hundred; half interest, six hundredths, 72 in the hundred; seven-twelfths interest, seven hundredths, 84 in the hundred, and so on. He should first have proved that at Rome (for it is not permitted to wander outside it) interest was customarily paid by sextant, third-part and quadrant parts of the year. These were paid each month, unless otherwise agreed, as has already been made clear; and so, with payment reckoned in this way, where the hundredth, like the usurious as, is considered by the year, the amount paid each month, the ounce or twelfth part of the hundredth as an annual sum, was the ounce. Anyone else ordered to bring a solid argument who argued in this way would have to be bound with the firmest bonds of Hippocrates. Gronovius deserves pardon, because he has not learned dialectic and wishes his own methods, like his grammar, alone to be recognised. Hence, turning his speech to me on p. 53, he says: If he had remembered what analogy is, and how much it is worth, and so on. Here three kinds of analogy may be noted: the logical, the illogical, and Gronovius's own (grammatical, that is); and I am uncertain whether this last ought to lie between the other two or be referred to the latter. It seems that he attributes too much to this analogy. It once deceived Cicero himself, as he confesses in book 6, letter 2 to Atticus. I know well the reasoning of dialectical, arithmetical, political and historical analogy; I am untroubled about grammatical analogy, and since I have reconciled my opinion (as I trust, auspiciously so far) with it, I wish it to be held of no more than superficial account, though the Grammarian grumbles. He himself admits that not all his own points cohere. Hence that line on p. 79: Everything like is also unlike, which ought to favour him as much as me. I am equally untroubled about the authors who favour my view. My opponent boasts that he has taken from me Sigonius, Manutius, Adrian Junius, Hotman and Pichena. For I am so generous to his supporters, whose leader is Accursius (a good author, that is), that I will readily add Budé, Brisson, and Dionysius Godefroy (his son James is wise here along with me), and perhaps very many others who interpret Roman law in the usual way. I have sworn an oath to one truth alone, and I shall not turn my finger to see whether many or few favour it. He himself reads what follows in Seneca, On the Happy Life, to Lucius Gallio: There is no reason why you should answer me in the manner of the schools: this side seems the larger, therefore it is the worse. Human affairs do not go so well that the better things please the many. The mark of the worse is the crowd: let us seek what has been done best, not what is most common. Though Hector would like our man to be thought of as such, let him be blamed as many as the Achaeans are, and so he will speak back again [ἠὲ ὀνόσσεται ὅσσοι Ἀχαιοί, ὣδὲ πάλιν ἐρέει].

units.la: Atque ita sententia mea hactenus vindicata, simul in integrum restitutis viris egregiis, quibus Hector, Achillis nescius, insultare ausus fuit; despicispiciendum, quomodo explicanda sit lex 47. §. 4. ff. de Adminiftr. & peric. tutorum, in qua sic loquitur JC. Scævola: Prafectus legionis ita testamento cavit: Volo, ut fit in arbitrio tutorum filii mei, fi voluerint hujus summæ uncias inferre, usurarum nomine: ita, ne nummi dispergantur: quæro, fi apparuerit, pecunia fœnerata à tutoribus, judicio tutela uncias usuras, an vero eas, quas stipulati sunt, præstare debeant? Respondi, Si fecundum voluntatem defuncti elegissent usurarum præstationem, neque pupilli nomine, in fœnus dedissent, id præstatur, quod testator voluisset. Hanc legem, non tanquam Legum Pater, (prout à Nostro, qui Albi Prætoris confultus, imo Jurium Doctor, publice traducor) sed ut æquus Veritatis Historicæ antistes his verbis illustraveram, Testator, qui pupillis suis per tutores confultum volebat, pecuniam collocarat commode, nempe ad usuram centesimam, five usuram unciariam, cujus pecunia usum cum ambiffent Tutores, offensi sunt onere usurarum, atque minores usuras stipulari voluerunt. Adversarius, postquam instar medicorum è Circo (credo ad modum præludii) multa jactassset, casum Legis refingendo, pag. 56. sic profatur; Testator (inquit) incertos casus prævidens, si pecunia, quam relinquebat filio impuberi, inter plures creditores dispergeretur, maluit maluit eam esse penes tutores, quos ei dederat bonos viros & explorate fidei. Non poterat hoc mandare: ideo arbitrium illorum fecit: ut tamen eos ad desiderium suum pelliceret, levis- simas, si feneratam velint habere, constituit illis usuras. Tutores eam pecuniam collocarint haud dubio majoribus. Quod quum emanasset, quaesitum est, uncias usuras ex testatoris ordina- tione, an quas ipsi stipulati essent, judicio tute- le pupillo deberent. Respondet Scævola, si illi accepissent conditionem a tutore (credo voluit scribere a testatore, alias inepte omnia procedunt) latam, deinde pecuniam suo, non pupilli nomi- ne atque periculo, in fenus dedissent, non de- bere nisi uncias usuras. Insultarat antea mihi, quod Testatorem vivum collocasse pecuniam dixis- sem, quod addidissem, Tutores ambiisse usum pe- cuniae, & offensos fuisse onere usurarum: si quidem nihil horum in Lege diceretur. Sed, ubi Lex dicit, quod Testator maluerit pecuniam esse penes Tuto- res, quam alios? quod illi fuerint boni viri & explo- ratae fidei? Quod acceptam pecuniam sub levisi- ma usura, majoribus potuerint credere? Hae sunt conjecturae, quibus hactenus meae aequivalent. De- spiciamus an meae praeferri non debeant? Quis Pa- ter non praesumitur optime suis liberis consulere? At quis simul praesumat de tali Patre, eum voluisse pecu-
units.tr: So my position has been defended up to this point, and at the same time the distinguished men whom Hector, ignorant of Achilles, dared to insult have been restored to their standing. Next we must consider how the law 47 §4 ff. de administratione et periculo tutorum is to be explained, in which the jurist Scaevola speaks as follows: The prefect of a legion made this provision in his will: I wish that it be at the discretion of my son's guardians, if they wish, to pay an ounce of this sum as interest, so that the money is not scattered; I ask, if it appears that the money was lent at interest by the guardians, whether by the guardianship judgment they ought to pay the ounce-interest, or rather those rates which they stipulated? I answered: If, in accordance with the dead man's wish, they had chosen to pay interest, and had not lent the money in the ward's name, then what the testator wished is paid. I did not explain this law as a Father of the Laws (as I am publicly misrepresented by our opponent, who is an adviser of the Praetor of Alba, or rather a Doctor of Law), but as a faithful servant of historical truth, I had illustrated it in these words: A testator who wished his guardians to act for his minor children had placed the money conveniently, namely at a hundred-per-cent rate, or an ounce-interest; when the guardians had come to enjoy the use of that money, they were burdened by the interest, and wished to stipulate smaller interest. My opponent, after he had boasted much, like doctors from the Circus (I think by way of a prelude), and by rewriting the case of the law, says on page 56: The testator, foreseeing uncertain chances (he says), preferred that the money he left to his underage son, if it were scattered among several creditors, should be in the hands of guardians whom he had given as good men of tried fidelity. He could not order this, so he left it to their discretion; yet, to entice them to his wish, he set the very lightest interest for them, if they wished to have it lent out. The guardians certainly lent that money at higher rates. When this had come about, the question was raised whether the guardians ought to pay the ounce-interest, according to the testator's ordinance, or the rates they themselves had stipulated, by the judgment of the guardianship to the ward. Scaevola answers: if they had accepted the condition set by the guardian (I think he meant to write by the testator, otherwise everything proceeds absurdly), and then had lent the money in their own name, and not in the ward's name and at his risk, they ought to pay only the ounce-interest. Earlier he had taunted me that I said the testator had placed the money while alive, and that I added that the guardians had enjoyed the use of the money and were burdened by the interest; yet none of these things is said in the law. But where does the law say that the testator preferred the money to be in the hands of the guardians rather than others? That they were good men of tried fidelity? That they could lend the money received at a very light rate to greater borrowers? These are the conjectures by which, so far, mine are matched. Let us see whether mine ought not to be preferred. What father is not presumed to provide the best for his children? But who would at the same time presume about such a father that he wished to entrust his money to guardians so that they would pay only a twelfth part of the hundred-per-cent interest? And would it be allowed for guardians to lend the same money at higher interest (which both at Rome and throughout the Roman Empire, as is now clear, was the ordinary hundred-per-cent rate), when they themselves could not be certain whether it would not be scattered?

units.la: Fragment of marginal notes at left is not transcribed. pecuniam suam credere Tutoribus, ut duodecimam solum usurae Centesimae partem solverent? licuerit vero, tutoribus, majoribus usuris (quae & Romae, & in toto Imperio Romano, ut jam patet, ordinario Centesimae erant) eandem pecuniam collocare, de qua ipsi certi esse non poterant, an non foret dispergenda? Tutores ipsi, pupillis ex Lege, ratione pecuniae quam apud se detinuerint, solvere debent Usuras vel quincunces, vel Trientes, leg.7. §. 9.ff. de Peric. & Administ. Tut. atque, si vel dolo, vel negligentia pecuniam pupillarem collocare negle-xerint, usuras maximas, sive Centesimas, juxta Tryphoninum l. 38. ff. de Neg. gest. debent. Quae ratio ergo, ut duodecimam solum usurae centesimae partem solvendo, fidem suam liberare potuerint, &, simul eandem illam pupillorum pecuniam grandibus usuris collocare? Vt hoc, quod vult Adversarius, licuerit tutoribus, intervenire debuit cognitio judicis? Sed, quomodo judex permittere potuerit, ut tam levibus usuris tutoribus pecunia crederetur: quum ejus officiū sit primo, exigere, ut profiteatur tutor, quae sit penes se summa, & commi-nari graviores ei usuras infligi ejus, quod su-pra professione apud eum fuerit comprehensum, juxta Ulpian. l. 3. §. 4. ff. Vbi pupill. educari. Vt clarius pateat, in hoc Testamento per Usuras intelligendas esse Centesimas, attendatur Testator. Miles fuit, qui forte & militare Testamentum (cujus multa privilegia esse solent) condidit. didit. Idem formulam usurae unciariae ( abolitam jam consuetudine ) inter testandum usurpavit, ὡσπερ νόμισμα ἀρχαῖον ἐκ Ϸησαυρῶν ποθὲν ἀ- δεσπότῳ, ut loquar cum Dione Chrysostomo in Olympiaca. Habuit quoque dubio procul, pecuniam suam depositam apud argentarios pro more, stipulatus ab iis usuras Centesimas , ( multos enim consuevisse apud argentarios pecuniam suam deponere, & usuras stipulari, docet Vlpianus l. 24. §. 2. ff. de reb. Auct. jud. poff.) permisit vero arbitrio Tutorum,pecuniam hanc accipere , & grandioribus usuris collocare , modo Centesimas , seu uncias ipsi referrent. Quum enim Argentarii ordinario binas aut ternas Centesimas ( supra Sceptius nos do- cuit , de Fusidio consulendus quoque Horat. lib. 1. Sat. 2.) acciperent, simplices facile promittebant. Et huc tendunt verba Legis : Volo , ut sit in arbitrio tutorum filii mei , si voluerint hujus summae uncias inferre usurarum nomine , &c. ergo pecuniae depositae nomine, Usurae jam solvebantur. Non parcit mihi Adversarius , non parcam quoque hoc tempore illi, quia afferendae veritati studeo. Attendatur ergo, quod Tutores jubeantur uncias inferre usurarum nomine. Notum illud Horatii lib: 1. Sat. 6. Ibant Octonis referentes Idibus aera. Quaero ergo ex illo, quando ordinario moribus Romanis Usurae inferri consueverint, anno finito, an cujuscunque mensis Kalendis ? Nisi secum com-
units.tr: Fragment of marginal notes at left is not transcribed. Should he have entrusted his money to the guardians so that they paid only a twelfth part of the centesimal interest? And if the guardians were permitted to invest the same money at higher interest (which, as is now clear, was the ordinary rate both at Rome and throughout the Roman Empire, namely the centesimal rate), would it not have had to be scattered, since they could not be certain of it? The guardians themselves, by law, must pay the pupils leg.7. §. 9.ff. de Peric. & Administ. Tut. interest of five or four percent on the money they have held in their own hands; and if they have neglected, through fraud or carelessness, to invest the pupil's money, they must pay the highest interest, that is, the centesimal rate, according to Tryphoninus, l. 38, ff. de Neg. gest. What reason, then, could there be for them to discharge their obligation by paying only a twelfth part of the centesimal interest, and at the same time to invest that same money of the pupils at high interest? For the Adversary's claim that the guardians were permitted to do this, the intervention of a judge would have been required. But how could a judge have allowed money to be lent to guardians at such low interest, since his duty is first to require that the guardian declare what sum he holds, and to threaten him with heavier interest to be exacted on whatever was included in that declaration above, according to Ulpian, l. 3, §. 4, ff. Vbi pupill. educari? To make it clearer that in this will "interest" must be understood as centesimal interest, let us consider the testator. He was a soldier, who perhaps also made a soldier's will, which usually enjoys many privileges. In making his will he also used the formula of the ounce-interest (now abolished by custom), like an ancient coin brought up from some treasure-house belonging to no master [ὥσπερ νόμισμα ἀρχαῖον ἐκ θησαυρῶν ποθὲν ἀδεσπότῳ], to use the words of Dio Chrysostom in the Olympiacus. Without doubt he also had his money deposited with bankers, as was the custom, and stipulated from them centesimal interest (for, as Ulpian teaches in l. 24, §. 2, ff. de reb. Auct. jud. poss., many people were accustomed to deposit their money with bankers and stipulate interest), but he left it to the discretion of the guardians to take this money and invest it at higher interest, provided they reported the centesimal or ounce rate to him. For since the bankers ordinarily received two or three centesimal rates (Sceptius has taught us above; for Fusidius see also Horace, Sat. 1.2), they easily promised the simple rate. And to this the words of the law point: I wish that it be at the discretion of my son's guardians, if they wish to pay ounces of this sum by way of interest, etc. So interest was already being paid on account of the deposited money. My opponent does not spare me, and I shall not spare him at this time, because I am eager to establish the truth. Let it be noted, then, that the guardians are ordered to pay ounces by way of interest. We know that line of Horace, Sat. 1.6: "They went, paying back the money on Octo's Ides." I ask, then: when, according to Roman custom, was interest ordinarily paid, at the end of the year or on the Kalends of any month? Unless he wishes to be sent away with a rebuke, he must answer for the Kalends.

units.la: E mitti voluerit, pro Kalendis respondere debet. Sed jam totum negotium est confectum. Tutores uncias usuras singulis mensibus inferre debent, atque similes uncias minimum cujusque mensis idibus referre: duodenæ antem unciæ, duodenis Kalendis seu Mensibus respondentes, absolvunt assem Vsurarium annuum, seu Centesimam. Hæc mea sententia est. Suam si tutari voluerit Adversarius, necessum est summam, apud tutores depositam, valde grandem, & Tribunum quam locupletem fiat. Modica si fuisset summa, quantillum quoque mense inferendum fuisset nomine usurarum, duodecimam centesimæ partem conficientium. Interim, per me pertinax erroneæ sententiæ patronus maneat cum Accursio, qui illi non modò jam bonus, sed & optimus Author est, quia favet. licet suffragium dicere non potuerit, nisi & vapularet. Sed pariter vapulat JC. Scævola: nam juxta suum illud Ure, seca, pro præstatur, in ipsa Lege pag. §8. substituit præstaturos. Superest Senecæ lib. 3. de Ira cap. 33. Itahabet: Quod si propter usuram haud millesimam valetudinarius fœnerator distortis pedibus & manibus, ad computandum modò relictis, clamat, ac per vadimonia asses suos in ipsis morbi accessionibus vindicat. An usura haud millesima fœnori unciario respondeat, prout Adversarius interpretatur, controvertitur. Voluit illud Lipsius, voluerunt SalSalmasius & Gronovius, Lipsium secuti. Breviter sic scripseram: Certe, hoc fidiculis non extorse-ris ipsis Senecæ verbis. Quod si, dicit Seneca, aperte innuendo, à se fingi casum hominis ad extremas sordes avari & iracundi. Nos Philosophi, Tyronibus artis Logicæ, inculcare quam diligenter solemus axioma in Scholis decantatissimum: Conditionalis propositio nihil in esse ponit. Secundum quod, si considerentur Senecæ verba, luce meridiana clarius patebit, usuram vix mellesimam, quæ ex mente Senecæ, non nisi Chimæra, aut eius rationes est, nihil commune habere cum usura unciaria, aut unciali. Multa adversus hæc corrasit Noster, quæ, an ab ipso vel interioris admissionis amici exspectaverint, ipsi judicent. Quod mihi necessitas incumbat, exhibere & examinare cogor. Pag. 81. sic lego: Nulla est tam beata civitas, in qua non inveniuntur Capitecensi & Proletarii, sordidi & triparci, qui & parum habent, & velint id occupare, & parum possunt, vel quia diffidunt, vel quia eorum, apud quos occupare possent, accessu arcentur: deinde quantulocunque à sui similibus expresso contentisunt. Suetonius Julium testatur omnes circa Pompejum, atque etiam magnam partem Senatus, gratuito aut levi fœnore obstrictos habuisse. Neminem inter hos fuisse putat. putat, qui unciis usuris teneretur? &c. Ergo hæc est conclusio, quod apud Senecam usura vix millesima, fit Vsura unciaria, intelligenda non fecundum nostra principia, sed erronea Accurfii? Quis non cum Horatio exclamet,
units.tr: But the whole matter has already been settled. Guardians ought to pay ounces of interest each month, and to pay back at least a similar ounce on the Ides of each month; and twelve ounces, corresponding to the twelve Kalends or months, make up the annual interest, the as of interest, or the centesimal rate. This is my opinion. If the Adversary wishes to defend his own, it is necessary that the sum deposited with the guardians be very large and that the guardian become very rich. If the sum had been modest, the small amount to be paid each month by way of interest, making up a twelfth part of the centesimal rate, would have been quite trivial. Meanwhile let him remain, so far as I am concerned, a stubborn defender of his mistaken opinion together with Accursius, who for him is now not only a good but the best author, because he favours him. He could not have given his vote, however, unless he were beaten too. But the jurist Scaevola is beaten in the same way: for, following his own phrase Burn, cut (Ure, seca), he has put praestaturos in place of praestatur in the Law itself, p. §8. There remains Seneca, On Anger, book 3, chapter 33. It reads thus: For if, on account of a interest of not one-thousandth, an invalid moneylender with twisted feet and hands, left only able to reckon, shouts and by summonses claims his asses even in the very fits of his illness. Whether interest of not one-thousandth corresponds to the ounce-rate, as the Adversary interprets it, is disputed. Lipsius wished it so, and Salmasius and Gronovius, following Lipsius, wished it too. I had written briefly: Certainly, you will not wring this out of the very words of Seneca by torture. For if, says Seneca, clearly hinting, that the case of a man reduced to the extreme squalor of a miser and a hothead is imagined by himself. We philosophers are accustomed to drum into the beginners of logic the most widely repeated axiom in the Schools: a conditional proposition posits nothing as existing. Accordingly, if the words of Seneca are considered, it will be clearer than noonday light that interest of scarcely one-thousandth, which, in Seneca's mind, is nothing but a chimera, or its reasons, has nothing in common with ounce-interest, or the ounce-rate. Our author has gathered many objections against this, whether they expected them from him or from some inner friend of his, let them judge themselves. Since necessity compels me, I am forced to set out and examine them. On page 81 I read thus: There is no city so happy that there are not found capite-censi and proletarians, squalid and niggardly, who both have little and want to take up more, and have little power, either because they distrust, or because they are shut off from access to those from whom they could borrow; and then they are content with whatever small amount is extorted from their like. Suetonius testifies that Julius had all those around Pompey, and also a large part of the Senate, bound by free or light interest. Does he think that none of these was bound by ounce-interest? etc. So is this the conclusion, that in Seneca interest of scarcely one-thousandth becomes ounce-interest, to be understood not according to our principles but according to the erroneous principles of Accursius? Who would not exclaim with Horace:

units.la: Nil intra est oleam, nil extra in nuce duri?
units.tr: Is there nothing hard inside the olive, nothing hard outside in the nut?

units.la: Singula pensitemus: 1. Euclio non tantum propinquos habet inter quintæ classis homines, sed assiduos quoque, qui in Orchestra & Quatuordecim sedent. Nec desunt ei cognati in ipso ordine Sacro, & Penulatorum magistrorum. Ego certe novi aliquos, qui avaras manus ad διδαχ]εσν extendunt, & quæ unciatim potuerunt comparcere, non levibus usuris, sed quam grandibus occupare student, licet postea, graves in speciem debitores versuram faciant. Quorsum ergo foli Capitecenfi avaritiæ notantur,qui juxta Chryfoftomum hom.2 3. in ep. 1. ad Cor. fi morbo hoc laborent, solent λιμῳ γαστρὸς ἐκ]είνειν? 2. Vt omnis avarus suspicax est, & omnia tuta timet; (ut Comicus Latinus, graphice,circa ollam Euclionis ostendit) ita præ aliis suspicaces esse solent homines, quos Adversarius notat, ubi divitiarum amore æstuare coeperint. Pecuniolæ quid fi collegerint, tantum abest, ut credant suæ fortis hominibus; fundos, Basilicas, & similia circumspiciunt, quò sibi & de forte & de Vsuris liceat esse securis. Atque, fi amicus quoque pecuniæ usum rogarit, & prædiolum aut domum non habuerit, numum exorare non potuerit. terit, Si dubitet Adversarius, hujus ordinis homines in sua urbe adeat, atque intelligere discet sequens Martialis Epigramma:
units.tr: Let us weigh the points one by one. (1) Euclio does not have relatives only among the men of the fifth class, but also regular attendants, who sit in the orchestra and the fourteen rows. Nor are there lacking to him kinsmen in the sacred order itself and among the magistrates in their gowns. I certainly know some men who stretch greedy hands out for gifts [δωρεάν], and who, having been able to save by the ounce, study to seize not small interest but large sums, and afterwards, though they seem to be serious debtors, make new loans to pay off old ones. Why, then, are only the citizens of the capital branded with avarice, when, according to Chrysostom (hom. 23 on 1 Cor.), men suffering from this disease are accustomed to pinch their bellies with hunger [λιμῷ γαστρὸς ἐκτείνειν]? (2) Just as every miser is suspicious and fears that everything is unsafe (as the Latin comic poet vividly shows around Euclio's pot), so those whom my opponent notes are usually more suspicious than others once they begin to seethe with love of riches. If they have collected a little money, they are so far from trusting it to men that they look about for estates, public buildings and the like, so that they may feel secure both about their capital and about the interest. And if a friend also asks for the use of money, and they have no little farm or house, they cannot be persuaded to part with a penny. If my opponent doubts this, let him go to these men in their own city and learn from the following epigram of Martial:

units.la: Cum rogo te numos sine pignore, non habeo, inquis:
units.tr: When I ask you for money without a pledge, you say, "I have none."

units.la: Idem, si pro me spondet agellus, habes.
units.tr: The same man, if my little farm stands surety for me, has it.

units.la: Quod mihi non credis veteri, Thelesine, sodali,
units.tr: Because you do not trust me, Thelesinus, your old comrade,

units.la: Credis colliculis, arboribusque meis.
units.tr: you trust my little hills and my trees.

units.la: 3. Quis credat hos ipsos, quos notat, quantulocunque contentos fore? Dubiae fidei (ipso Adversario teste) solent esse tribules, & ejusdem sortis homines. Audiat ergo seipsum: pag. 72. jam dixerat: Quoties fides erat angustior & rei nummariae difficultas, multum: scil. stipulabatur mutuans. 4. Quis ei quoque dixit tales potentiorum accessu arceri? Contrarium verissimum est, atque proh dolor! plurimi in ipso hoc Belgio inveniuntur, qui opes maximas corraserunt, quod à pauperioribus, & suis quoque ancillis, famulis, atque clientibus, pecuniam mutuam accipere solerent trientibus usuris, eamque apud alios occupare semissibus, imo bessibus. 5. Julius Caesar cur advocetur, nescio. Apud Suetonium lib. 1. cap. 27. haec lego: Omnibus vero circa eum, atque etiam parte magna Senatus, gratuito, aut levi faenore obstrictis, ex reliquo quoque ordinum genere vel invitatos, vel sponte ad se venientes, uberrimo congiario prosequebatur. Quae sequela: Julius quosdam dam levi fœnori obstrinxit, ergo fœnus illud fuerit usura vix millesima, sive boni Accursiii unciaria? Quum per hæc tempora ternæ quoque Centesimæ receptæ essent, Julius aliquos ex laticlaviis sibi & suis conatibus mancipare potuerit, pecuniam apud eos occupando, usuris bessibus aut semissibus. Hodie per Hollandiam ipsorum Illustrium Ordinum nomine solvuntur usuræ trientes, & levis fœnoris rationem habent, quod elapsis nondum xxv. annis, semisses per eosdem solvi solerent. Pergit Noster & Historicum agit: Scythas Asiam perdomitam tectigalem fecisse ait Justinus, modico tributo magis in titulum imperii quam in victoriæ præmium imposito. Nunquam putat simile quid fecisse privatos? At vidi novique parentes, dominos, heras, qui quæve liberorum, servorum, ancillarum, vidi cives, matronasque ornatas, qui quæve tenuiorum aut anicularum pecunias quum revera custodirent, sic tamen eis gratificarentur. Sed ἐmφυλίδες τωυτ' ἐστι γ στωμύλματα: & quem non pudeat, sic ineptire Gronovium? Equidem me pudet, quod hæc debeam examinare, & ligonem ligonem vocare. 1. Quare huc advocantur Scythæ, & modicum eorum tributum, cujus meminit Justinus lib. 2. c. 35 Tributum, utut leve, oneris semper rationem habet, non usura. Quando enim Mævius Sejo usuras solvit, quod hujus pecunia utatur, eam ipsam pecuniam, aliis alïs usibus impendendo, quæstum facere potest, quum nihil ex tributo, quod Victori principi, non viventi inter vectigales subditos, solvitur, redeat ad illos, qui solverunt. 2. Dicit, Vidi novique, qui quæve cum anicularum pecuniolas custodi-rent, &c. Non possum, quin exclamem cum Sexto Empirico adv. Mathematicos: τὰ ἀδάλεσχον ἰσπ καὶ γεωμμαλικῆς γεωλογίας πλῆσες. Si pannucia Baucis sic ineptiret, venia concedi posset ætati, quid vero facias tanto viro? An non omnis usura descendit ex contractu? An non ipse supra pag. 72. dixit: Qui ibat in creditum adpendendo centum aut mille libras æris, stipulabatur mercedem usufructus, &c. Nullum fœnus est gratuitum: quod leve quoque est, (ut modo vidimus) Suetonius gratuito opponit. Sim nostro J. V Doctori ridiculus JC. hoc tamen novi, quando mutuum distinguitur in gratuitum, &usurarium, semper implicari respectum ad contractum. Qui anicularum pecuniolis, quas custodiunt, quid adjiciunt, liberales agnosci debent, & forte simul vultures: sæpe captatio in quæstu fertilissimo, est, ut cum Plinio loquar ex Præf. lib. 14. Aliquis alius suspicari posset, Nostrum hominem, quia dicit, Vidi novique, Arruntii atque Aterii artes callere, quorum juxta Senecam lib. 4. de Benef. cap. 38. eadem, quæ dessignatorum & libitinariorum orum vota erant. non ego tamen. spero nescire il-la, quæ captatores sciunt. 3. Non attendit, Sene-cam loqui de fœneratore, & quidem tali, qui ad-modû elegater alicubi àPhilone Judæo βαρύπλαστος vocatur. At quis, qui modo novit fœneratorum ingenium, credat, talem hominem voluisse pecu-niam suam occupare usura haud millesima? Non subsistit Noster Senecæ interpres, pag. 82. ita de-inceps loquens: Quales sunt casus qui fingun-tur? nempe ex media vita & rebus plerumque obversantibus petiti, &c. Casum fingere, quem mos aut natura evenire non patitur, est inepti aut ingenio ludentis, &c. Quasi casum fingere & sub conditione statuere, una & eadem res sit, aut ubicunque particula Si habetur, ponatur conditio. Nihil hic adfirmatur aut negatur sub conditione, sed rogatur judicium de fa-ctis specie, quod quotidie occurrebat. Quam mul-ra hic iterum non occurrunt castiganda? 1. Mi-rum, quod qui Poëtas antiquos legit, & in ipsum Papinium Statium commentatus est, dicat omnes casus fingi ex media vita & rebus plerumque ob-versantibus? qui præ aliis hic videri volunt in-geniosi, sedulo operam dant, ne ex media vita, aut rebus plerumque obversantibus petiti sint. 2. Quis dixerit, omnes illos ineptos habendos esse, qui casum fingunt, quem mos aut natura evenire non re non patiatur? Quid de fabula dicemus, quæ apud viros quoque serios casus rationem sæpe habuit? Est ver o secundum Aristotelem de Poët.cap.6 τῆς πράξεως ὁ μῦθος μίμησις. Et, ne putet fabulas veri quid complecti, Pindarus Olymp: Od. 1. pronunciat, quod μῦθοι sint δεδαιδαλμένοι ψεύδεσι ποικίλοις, 3. Do lubens, particulam Si semper non arguere conditionem: quotiescunque vero illam arguit, conditio est dubia & incerta; nec vera aut certa evadit, nisi quatenus, illud, quod sub conditione dicitur, remota illa verum est. 4. Unde colliget,quod Romanus Sapiens,roget judicium de facti specie, quod quotidie occurrebat? Simile quid in Romanis Scriptoribus si invenerit, aures arrigemus. Confundere me quoque laborat, postquam pro sua modestia convitiatus esset.Si Centesima (inquit) nihil aliud est quam as usurarius annuus,& duodecim in centum, quid erit Millesima? Ex ipsius quidem explicatione longe maxima & iniquissima: nempe dua centesima. Quid enim mille nisi decies centena. At Seneca pro omnium levissima eam ponit. Quis nescit decies centena conficere mille, sed, an proptera ex meis principiis usura haud millesima conficere debet denas centesimas, quod similis sit terminatio? Nullus præter eum, qui cum Nostro Logicam ne quidem in pariete depictam viderit, ita instiinstituerit colligere? Sequuntur hæc pag. eadem, sive, pag. 83. Sit autem Chimæra, sit Centaurus, sit (quæ notior illi elegantia est) ens rationis: tamen monstra quoque commenticia, quæ nomina acceperunt, ob aliquam rationem acceperunt, etsi quandoque sit illa ignotior: saltem non Græci & Latini, ut vocabula illis darent, barbare sunt loquuti. Quid est στβυλλίαν, si hoc non sit? An non ætates, Latini sermonis ratione, distingui debent? Voces, quas elegantes Majorum barba putavit, posterior & cultior ætas ut scopulos vitavit, imo barbariei arguit. Eoque Fabius L. 1. c. 11. iis utendum non ait, quæ utique ab ultimis & jam obliteratis repetita sunt temporibus: qualia sunt toper, & antigerio, & exantlare, & prosapia, & Saliorum carmina, vix sacerdotibus suis satis intellecta, Vnciarium fœnus vetusta signatum nota est, & usque à xii. accersendum. Exposuimus illud juxta Romanæ rei statum, eoque, licet nobis securis esse minutiarum Grammaticarum; quarum ipsi Adversario, Grammatico licet, usque adeo non constat ratio, ut, (hoc & supra notare debuimus) coactus fuerit dicere, omne simile etiam dissimile est. Dein sollicitus de Senecæ salute, (quod cogitare debuisset à multis annis, ab eo manus abstinendo) ibid. dicit: Salvum igitur præstemus Senecæ Romanum os. Et præstabimus, si de nostra, imo omnium um fanorum, sententia admittetur dicta Cen-tesima. Quemadmodum igitur potuit pro le-visima nominare millesimam usuram? Nimi-rum, sicut centesima est, quoties in centum de-narios datur menstrua centesima pars sortis, ita millesima, ubi datur menstrua millesima pars sortis usura. Atque haec erit decima centesima. Ha forent usura uncia & semisciclici, paulo plus: videlicet in centum denarios as, & semis & as-sis decima: quia denarius sedecim assium. Quare bene observant Lipsius & Salmasius, non pos-se aliud esse quod intelligat Seneca, quam foenus unciarium: & ideo dicere illam usuram haud millesimam: habet enim paullo minus, nempe in centum denarios assem trientem: Gratulor, quod Cordubensi os Romanum tribuat. Eoque καὶ τὸ βίαιον hoc ipsum retorqueo. Quia ore Romano loquebatur Seneca, & ex illius praescripto, scribebat; sordes foeneratoris notaturus, eum sollicitum esse dicit de usura haud millesima, neutione facturus mentione foenoris Vnciarii: si (ut vult Adversarius) foenusRomae & levissimū fuisset, & inter foeneratores receptum. Cur enim castigati eloquii scriptor, incerta voce, & calculi dubii, (ex verbis praecedentibus patet) illud definivisset, quod, formula Quiritibus usitata, explicari poterat? Sed, quia foenus unciarium notum ex ipsis xii. Tabulis, quas pueri Romæ ut quotidianum carmen recitare sciebant, à fœnore levissimo tam longe remotum erat, atque singularis numerus a duodenario, meminisse voluit usuræ haud millesimæ. Non quod eà Romæ quisquam fœneraretur; ( hoc nunquam factum fuit, prout nunquam quoque in usu fuit fœnus Vnciarium, ex Grammaticis quasi Adversarii principiis intelligendum) sed,quod usurarum,usque ad minutias minimas, crudelis exactor fœnerator esset,quem Stoicus Romanus ut τὸν Δεινὰ notabat. Non dicit vero eum fœneratum fuisse Vsura haud millesima (hoc consentaneum non est ingenio fœneratorum, ternas quoque Centesimas stipulari solitorum) sed ob eam non solutam, clamasse. Accidere hoc potuit ratione ἀναλογισμῷ. Nihil donat, nihil remittit fœnerator, & vix millesimam usuram (licet nunquam stipuletur) Vsuris ad diem non solutis,exigere negligit. Apposite Philo Judæus lib. de Somniis per interpretem: ( Græcus Codex ad manum non est ) Potestne (inquit) inveniri tam avarus, aut crudelis, aut importunus fœnerator, ut quatuor pauciorsve drachmas fœnerari velit, quàm donare? & unicum illud vestimentum non verebitur accipere pignori? Forte dici posset, fœneratores præter usuras grandiores stipulari quoque consuevisse creditæ sortis, quando restituenda esset, additamentum exiguum, velut fœnusculum: quod dici posse accessionem crediti, nemo mo mirabitur, si modo vera sint, quæ Gronovius in Mantissa adversus Salmasium disputat pag. 108. & seqq. aut, si fœnusculum hoc non fuerit pars crediti, (minus hoc esse probabile, vindicaturus Salmasium, alio tempore ostendam) agnosci saltem debere usurarum ordinarium superpondium, fœneratoribus, quod laboranti succurrere dignati essent, solvi solitum. Huc mihi facere videtur singularis Plauti locus Pseud. i. 3. ubi Ballio Leno Calliodoro amatori hoc consilium dat: Amabas? invenires mutuum, Ad Danistam devenires; adderes fœnusculum: scil. usuris grandibus, quæ ordinario solvi solent ab iis, qui mutuabantur. Atque hoc videntur supra innuere Impp. in leg. 2. Cod. Theod. de Vsf. quando non solum meminerunt Centesimæ, quæ in stipulatum veniebat: sed hæc amplius verba addunt: Quidquid sub occasione necessitatis eruerit. Ob tale fœnusculum non solutum, licet vix millesimæ usuræ rationem haberet, indignari potuit avarus fœnerator, quem Seneca tangit. Sed nihil definio, sufficit evictum esse, quod usura vix millesima à fœnore unciario, (hoc, ut Adversarius explicat, Romæ ignotum fuit) toto cœlo distet. Postremo quod ὁ πάνυ Scaliger (qui circa fœnus Vnciarium cæteroquin favet) usuræ haud Millesimæ modum quoque definire voluerit, subducendo calculum, (in re plana Noster Assis sui comparationem omittere potuisset) erroneam interpretationem juvare nou poterit. Quot non Arithmeticorum rum calculi, extra calculum & cerebrum ipsorum mendaces sunt? Et tamen Noster pag. 84. & seq. in talibus offendit μέγ' ὀνειας. Ignoscendum homini Logicæ ignaro. Atque sic circa Senecam quoque confectum est. Finire possem, nisi Adversarius, Suffeni exemplo, applausum ambiret, se evehendo, & me vituperando. Hoc facere solent Aretalogi. Possem negligere, nisi homo dulci Fortuna ebrius, sibi ipsi (cujus oblitus est) offendendus esset. Eoque, qualis sibi videatur, videamus initio? Cum, ut Criticorum τῷ Alpha assurrexissem, sibi (est Trojano scil. ex sanguine Cæsar) quid decessurum putabat, si ego (aliud non ambiebam) Criticorum obscurissimus posthac haberer. Nam pag. 86. amplius deliberandum putat, an talem Titulum promerear. Ego, quod ad me, ex hac una solum Diatriba, ut quotquot digni Criticorum nomine vivunt, arbitrentur, rogo. Simul bonis libris testibus contendo, Joh. Fredericum Gronovium, fidem faciente hac sut Ἀνδξηγήσει, indignissimum esse augusto Critici elogio. Quod tam clarum reddam, atque cum meridie lucet. Crates (contra hunc testem quid excipiet?) apud Sextum Empiricum lib. adversf. Mathematicos pag. 16. ἔλεγε, ἀφέρειν τὸν κελλικὸν τῆς γραμματικῆς. καὶ τὸν μὲν κελλικὸν πάσης φησὶ δεῖ λογικῆς ἐπιστήμης ἐμπειρον εἶναι τὸν δὲ γραμματικὸν, ἁπλῶς γλωσσῶν ἐξηγητικόν, καὶ περσωδίας ἀποδοτικόν, καὶ τῶν τῶν τέτοις παρεμπλησίων εἰδήμονα: παρὰ κὴ εοικέναι ἐκεῖνον μὲν Αρχιτέκτονι, τὸν δὲ γραμ- ματικὸν ὑπηέτη. Crates dicebat Criticum dif- ferre à Grammatico. Et Criticum quidem di- cit oportere esse peritum omnis scientiæ Logicæ: Grammaticum autem esse tantum interpretem linguarum, & tradere accentus, & ea scire, quæ sunt his similia, & ideo illum quidem esse simi- lem Architecto, Grammaticum autem ministro. En! Critici nomine nemo dignus, nisi qui omnis scientiæ Logicæ fuerit peritus. Vnde & Marci- anus Capella (& eum bonum Authorem agnoscere debet) lib. 4. sic Dialecticam loquentem introducit: Quippe in ditione mea jureque constistunt sex normæ, quis constant cætera disciplinæ. Nam prima est de loquendo. Secunda de eloquendo. Tertia de proloquendo. Quarta de proloqui- orum summa. Quinta de judicando, quæ per- tinet ad judicationem poëtarum & carminum. Sexta, quæ dicenda Rhetoribus commodata est. Quis ultro jam, hominem hunc, omnis Dialecticæ non modo ignarum, sed & inimicum, Criticum a- gnoscat? Aut, quis eum ut Criticum commendare voluerit, qui & toties per imperitiam Dialecticæ, (supra patuit) sibi adversatur, & usquaque adeo à ratione est alienus, ut pag. 20. existimet se mihi convitium dicere, quod Dialecticum vocet? Dicet aliquis forte pro eo, tot authores emendavit, Statium, Livium, Senecam, & quos non alios? Fateor. Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis quoque manum admovit. Apud Doctissimum Vossium lib. 1. de Arte Gramm. cap. 6. ita lego: Peccari solet à sciolis & audaculis Criticis, qui dum sanis sæpe partibus medicinam facere volunt, vulnus faciunt Hujus furfuris Critici hoc ordine progrediuntur. Singulares aliquas voculas & locutiones, nomina quoque propria apud Authores observant; ea in Indicem redigunt. Sollicitantur postea variantes lectiones, quæ sæpe quoque multiplicantur; Vaticana, Medicæa, Regia Parisina, &c. Bibliothecis ad suffragium vocatis cum Codd. Mss. licet nunquam inspectis; & si aliqua ex iis vocula, aut locutioni, aut nomini proprio à se antea observato faveat; Authori, à cujus restitutione nomen æternum sperat, obtruditur: qui, si alibi non absimili modo videatur scripsisse, meus hic Criticus ultra hominem spirat, &, ut correxit, scribit, aliosque, ut imitentur, monet. Alias, ad præconceptam de re aliqua opinionem, pro qua quædam antiquorum Scriptorum testimonia militare videntur, aliorum Authorum loca obtorto collo trahuntur, & tam diu in equuleo torquentur, quam similem explicationem in speciem admiserint. Si perrexerint homines hi, Dialecticæ, & mihi, ut ejus Professori, maledicere, seseque Critico mangonio venditare, prolixo scripto æque solide hoc me evicturum spero, atque Vnciarium fœnus idem esse cum Centesima probavi. Interim non nego, fieri posse, ut aliquando veram lectio nem Scriptori alicui oforesDialecticæ Critici restituant. Sed hoc nomine haut magis sunt laudandi, quam a- leator qui in arte sua bonus est. Salmasius, assum- pto Simplicii Verini nomine, in Judicio de scripto Postumo Grotii, hunc, ut Criticum expendens p. 4. dicit: In Critica, quoniam & eam attigit, ut illis, qui alea ludunt, male aliquando res ca- dit, interdum & bene, prout fert fortuna ra- tio, ita huic contigit, non semper ευςόχως hunc ludum tentasse. Et tamen Adversarius somniat, me per se surgere voluisse, & gloriolam captasse, ut viderer acrior Philologicæ veritatis inquisi- tor. Quasi gloriam mereatur, qui aut muscas cum Domitiano confodit, aut erucas conterit? Hoc si laudi cessurum putassem, à pluribus annis affectum Adversariorum volumen, in quo forte ipse aliquan- do urramque paginam faciet, protrusissem. Acris veritatis inquisitor sum, cui quam diu ipse cede- re aut non vult, aut nescit, non modo ei malus, sed pessimus ero. Nec ideo illius sententia præva- lere debet, quod, ut sæpius inculcat, multo labore & diuturna diligentia omnia sua subegerit; (quan- quam hic non modo sibi adversatur, sed amplius ignorantiam doctrinæ de Oppositis prodit, quan- do pag. 86. contradictoria conciliare laborat) & quæ de re Nummaria atque Vsura, Scaliger, Sal-
units.tr: 3. Who would believe that these very people whom he mentions will be content with whatever small return? According to the Adversary himself, men of doubtful good faith are usually fellow citizens, and of the same sort. Let him hear himself. On page 72 he had already said: Whenever trust was thinner and money was hard to come by, the lender demanded a great deal, that is, he stipulated for it. 4. Who told him that such men are kept away from the approach of the powerful? The opposite is very true, and, alas, very many are found in this very Belgium who have amassed enormous wealth by borrowing money from poorer people, and even from their own maidservants, servants and clients, at a third of the principal in interest, and lending it to others at a half, or even at two-thirds. 5. I do not know why Julius Caesar is brought forward. In Suetonius, book 1, chapter 27, I read this: But to all those around him, and to a large part of the Senate, bound to him by gratuitous or light interest, and to others of the other orders, whether they were invited or came to him of their own accord, he gave a very generous largess. What follows from this? Julius bound some to him with light interest, so that this interest was hardly one per thousand, or the twelfth part of an ounce, as Accursius has it? Since in those times even three per cent was accepted, could Julius have bound some of the senators to himself and to his schemes by lending them money at two-thirds or a half? Today throughout Holland, in the name of the Illustrious Orders themselves, interest of a third is paid, and they reckon it light interest, since within only twenty-five years it used to be paid at a half. Our author goes on and plays the historian: Justin says that the Scythians, having conquered Asia, made it tributary, imposing a small tribute as a token of their rule rather than as a reward for victory. Does he think that private persons never did anything similar? But I have seen and know fathers, masters, mistresses, men and women, who, while they were in truth keeping the money of their children, slaves, maidservants, or of the poorer folk and old women, nevertheless obliged them in this way. But these are ἐμφυλίδες [idle chatter], and who would not be ashamed of such nonsense from Gronovius? I, for my part, am ashamed to have to examine these things and to call a spade a spade. 1. Why are the Scythians and their small tribute brought in here, which Justin mentions in book 2, chapter 35? A tribute, however light, always has the character of a burden, not of interest. For when Mævius pays interest to Sejus because he uses his money, he can make a profit by spending that very money on various purposes, whereas nothing from a tribute, which is paid to a victorious prince by subjects who are not living among tributaries, returns to those who paid it. 2. He says: I have seen and known men and women who were keeping the little sums of old women, and so on. I cannot help exclaiming with Sextus Empiricus against the Mathematicians: [ta adaleschon esti kai geōmmalikēs geologias plēsēs], that is, full of idle chatter and of earthy geology. If some old nurse talked such nonsense, indulgence could be granted to her age, but what can one do with a man of such stature? Does not all interest arise from a contract? Did he not himself say above, on page 72: He who went into a loan, paying out a hundred or a thousand pounds of bronze, stipulated a fee for the use of the money, and so on? No interest is gratuitous. Suetonius opposes gratuito to light, which, as we have just seen, is also light. I know that to our J.U.D. the jurist may seem ridiculous, but this at least I know: when a loan is divided into gratuitous and usurious, the reference to the contract is always involved. Those who add something to the little sums of old women which they keep ought to be recognised as generous, and perhaps at the same time as vultures. Often the seeking of gain in the most fertile profit is what it is, to speak with Pliny from the preface to book 14. Someone else might suspect that our man, because he says I have seen and known, understands the arts of Arruntius and Aterius, whose wishes, according to Seneca in book 4 of On Benefits, chapter 38, were the same as those of undertakers and funeral-men. I, however, do not think so; I hope he does not fail to know those things which seekers of legacies know. 3. He does not notice that Seneca is speaking of a moneylender, and indeed of the sort who is elegantly called barypl­astos [a heavy hand] somewhere by Philo the Jew. But who, knowing even a little of the mentality of moneylenders, would believe that such a man wished to invest his money at interest not even one per thousand? Our man, the interpreter of Seneca, does not stop there; on page 82 he goes on in this way: What sort of cases are imagined? Plainly those drawn from ordinary life and from things that usually happen, etc. To imagine a case which custom or nature does not allow to happen is the mark of a foolish or playful mind, etc. As if imagining a case and setting it up under a condition were one and the same thing, or wherever the particle "if" appears, a condition is laid down. Nothing here is asserted or denied under a condition; rather, a judgment is asked about a matter of fact that happened every day. How many things here again call for correction? 1. It is strange that he who reads the ancient poets, and has written a commentary on Papinius Statius himself, should say that all cases are imagined from ordinary life and from things that usually happen, when those who here want to appear more ingenious than others take great pains not to draw them from ordinary life, or from things that usually happen. 2. Who would say that all those who imagine a case which custom or nature does not allow to happen should be considered foolish? What shall we say of fable, which among serious men too has often taken account of imagined events? Indeed, according to Aristotle in the Poetics, chapter 6, τῆς πράξεως ὁ μῦθος μίμησις [the fable is an imitation of action]. And lest he think that fables contain any truth, Pindar in Olympian Ode 1 declares that μῦθοι are δεδαιδαλμένοι ψεύδεσι ποικίλοις [adorned with varied lies]. 3. I gladly grant that the particle if does not always indicate a condition; but whenever it does indicate one, the condition is doubtful and uncertain, and it becomes neither true nor certain, except insofar as what is said under the condition is true when that condition is removed. 4. From this he will conclude that the Roman sage asked a judgment about a matter of fact that happened every day? If he finds something similar in Roman writers, we shall prick up our ears. He is also trying to confuse me, after, in his modesty, he had hurled abuse. If the centesima, he says, is nothing other than an annual usurious as, and twelve in the hundred, what will the millesima be? By his own explanation it will be by far the greatest and most unjust, namely two centesimas. For what is a thousand but ten hundreds? Yet Seneca puts it down as the lightest of all. Who does not know that ten hundreds make a thousand? But is it for that reason, on my principles, that interest not even one per thousand must make ten centesimas, because the ending is similar? Would anyone except him who has never seen logic even painted on a wall infer in this way? The same page, or page 83, continues: But whether it is a Chimera, or a Centaur, or (what is more famous in his elegance) a being of reason, still the monstrous imaginary things which have received names have received them for some reason, even if that reason is sometimes less known; at least the Greeks and Romans did not speak barbarously in giving them names. What is στβυλλία [a stupidity], if this is not? Should not ages be distinguished by the rule of Latin speech? Words which the beard of our ancestors considered elegant, a later and more refined age avoided like rocks; indeed, it judges them barbarous. And so Fabius, in book 1, chapter 11, says that one should not use those that have been drawn from the most remote and now obsolete times: such as toper, antigerio, exantlare, prosapia, and the songs of the Salii, scarcely understood even by their own priests. The usurious loan of the ounce is marked with an ancient sign, and is to be traced back to the twelve tables. We have explained it according to the state of Roman affairs; and therefore, though we may be careless about grammatical trifles, the Adversary, who is a grammarian, has so little grasp of their logic that (as I ought to have noted here and above) he was forced to say: every similarity is also a dissimilarity. Then, anxious about Seneca's safety (which he ought to have considered many years ago, and refrained from laying hands on him), he says in the same place: Let us therefore preserve the Roman face of Seneca. And we shall preserve it if, in our opinion, or rather in the opinion of all sound men, the said centesima is admitted. How then could he have called the millesima the lightest interest? Clearly, just as the centesima is whenever the monthly hundredth part of the principal is given on a hundred denarii, so is the millesima when the monthly thousandth part of the principal is given as interest. And this will be the tenth of a centesima. These would make an interest of an ounce and a half of a semuncia, a little more: namely, a half as and a tenth of an as on a hundred denarii, because a denarius is sixteen asses. Hence Lipsius and Salmasius rightly observe that Seneca can mean nothing other than the interest of the ounce; and so he says that the interest is not even one per thousand, for it is a little less, namely a third of an as on a hundred denarii. I congratulate him on giving Seneca of Cordoba a Roman mouth. So I turn back on him this very thing, καὶ τὸ βίαιον [and the forcible]. For Seneca spoke with a Roman mouth, and wrote by its rule; wishing to brand the meanness of the moneylender, he says that he is anxious about interest not even one per thousand, and he would not mention ounce-interest at all, if (as the Adversary wishes) interest at Rome had been very light and accepted among moneylenders. For why would a writer of polished style, with an uncertain voice and a doubtful calculation (as is clear from the preceding words), have defined it in terms that could be explained by the formula used by the Quirites? But because ounce-interest was known from the very Twelve Tables, which boys at Rome knew how to recite as a daily song, and was so far removed from very light interest, and because the singular number was distant from the duodecimal, he chose to recall interest not even one per thousand. Not that anyone at Rome lent money at this rate (this never happened, just as ounce-interest was never in use, as is to be understood, as if from the principles of the Adversary himself, grammatically), but because the moneylender was a cruel exactor of interest, down to the smallest fractions, whom the Roman Stoic branded as a Dinas [a Dinas]. He does not say, however, that the moneylender was paid interest not even one per thousand (this does not agree with the nature of moneylenders, who were accustomed to stipulate even three per cent), but that he cried out because it was not paid. This could happen by ἀναλογισμός [reckoning]. A moneylender gives nothing and remits nothing, and when interest is not paid on the due day, he does not neglect to exact even one per thousand (though he never stipulates it). Philo the Jew, in his book On Dreams, speaks aptly, through an interpreter (the Greek text is not at hand): Can there be found (he says) so greedy, or cruel, or importunate a moneylender, as to wish to lend four or a few more drachmas rather than give them? And will he not hesitate to accept as a pledge that single garment? Perhaps it could be said that moneylenders were accustomed to stipulate, in addition to large interest, a small extra payment on the principal when it had to be repaid, as a little interest-on-interest; this may be called an addition to the loan, and no one will be surprised if what Gronovius argues in his Mantissa against Salmasius, pages 108 and following, is true. Or, if this little interest was not part of the loan (which is less probable; I shall show at another time, in vindicating Salmasius), it must at least be acknowledged that the ordinary surplus of interest was usually paid to moneylenders, because they deigned to help a debtor in trouble. A singular passage of Plautus seems to me to favour this, in Pseudolus 1.3, where the pimp Ballio gives this advice to Calidorus, the lover: You were in love? You would find a loan, you would come to the moneylender, you would add a little interest, namely at large rates, which are usually paid by those who borrow. And the emperors seem to hint at this above, in law 2 of the Theodosian Code, On Usury, when they mention not only the centesima which was stipulated, but add these further words: whatever he may extort on the occasion of necessity. A moneylender may be indignant at such an unpaid little interest, though it would hardly amount to one per thousand, and this is what Seneca touches on. But I define nothing; it is enough to have shown that interest of hardly one per thousand is worlds apart from ounce-interest (which, as the Adversary explains, was unknown at Rome). Lastly, that the most excellent Scaliger (who otherwise favours ounce-interest) wished also to define the measure of interest not even one per thousand, by calculating it (in a plain matter our man could have omitted the comparison with his own As), will not help an erroneous interpretation. How many of the calculations of arithmeticians are false, outside the calculation and their own brains? Yet our man, on pages 84 and following, stumbles into μέγ' ὀνειας [a great blunder] in such matters. One must pardon a man ignorant of logic. And so the business has been finished with Seneca too. I could stop here, were it not that the Adversary, following the example of Suffenus, seeks applause by praising himself and reviling me. This is what the boastful chatterers usually do. I could ignore it, were it not that the man, drunk on sweet Fortune, must be offended by himself, of whom he has forgotten. So let us see first what he thinks of himself. When I had risen, as it were, to the Alpha of the critics, he thought that (he is of Trojan, that is, of the blood of Caesar) he would lose something if I (I wanted nothing else) were henceforth regarded as the most obscure of critics. For on page 86 he thinks he must deliberate further whether he deserves such a title. As for me, I ask, from this single diatribe alone, whether all who live worthy of the name of critic judge this to be so. At the same time I contend, with good books as witnesses, that Johann Friedrich Gronovius, providing evidence by this very explanation, is most unworthy of the august praise of critic. I shall make this so clear that it shines as bright as noon. Crates (what will he object against this witness?), in Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians, page 16, said that the critic differs from the grammarian. And he says the critic must be experienced in every science of logic, while the grammarian is merely an interpreter of languages, who teaches accents and knows such things as are like these; and so the one seems like the architect, the other like the servant. Behold! No one is worthy of the name of critic unless he has been versed in every science of logic. Whence also Martianus Capella (whom he ought to acknowledge as a good author), in book 4, introduces Dialectic speaking in this way: For in my domain and under my law there stand six rules, of which the other disciplines consist. For the first is concerning speaking. The second concerning eloquent speaking. The third concerning pre-speaking. The fourth concerning the sum of pre-speaking. The fifth concerning judging, which pertains to the judgment of poets and poems. The sixth, which is to be spoken of, is suited to the rhetoricians. Who now, of his own accord, would acknowledge this man, ignorant not only of all Dialectic but hostile to it, as a critic? Or who would wish to commend as a critic him who, through lack of skill in Dialectic (as has appeared above), so often contradicts himself, and is so alien to reason that on page 20 he thinks he has uttered an insult against me when he calls me a dialectician? Perhaps someone will say in his defence that he has corrected so many authors: Statius, Livy, Seneca, and whom not? I admit it. He has also laid his hand on ecclesiastical writers. In the most learned Vossius, On the Art of Grammar, book 1, chapter 6, I read: There is a common fault among shallow and bold critics, who, while they often wish to apply medicine to sound parts, make a wound. These critics of chaff proceed in this order. They note certain single little words and locutions, and also proper names, in the authors; they bring them into an index. Then the variant readings are sought out, which are often multiplied as well: the Vatican, the Medicean, the Royal Parisian, and so on; the libraries are called to vote, with manuscripts, though never inspected. And if any of those little words, or locutions, or proper names previously noted by them favours the author whose restoration they hope will win them eternal fame, it is forced upon him. And if he seems to have written elsewhere in a not dissimilar way, my critic breathes more than a man, and, as he has corrected, writes, and advises others to imitate him. At other times, to a preconceived opinion about some matter, for which some testimonies of ancient writers seem to fight, passages of other authors are dragged by the neck, and tortured on the rack for so long, until they admit a similar explanation. If these men persist in reviling Dialectic and me, its professor, and in peddling themselves as a critic's hawkers, I hope that by a lengthy writing I shall prove this as solidly as I proved that ounce-interest is the same as the centesima. Meanwhile I do not deny that it may happen that critics sometimes restore the true reading of some writer through dialectical skill. But they are no more to be praised for this than a gambler who is good at his game. Salmasius, having assumed the name of Simplicius Verinus, in his Judgment on the posthumous writing of Grotius, weighing this man as a critic, says on page 4: In criticism, since he touched on it too, as with those who play at dice, things sometimes go badly and sometimes well, as fortune and reason bring it; so it has happened to him that he has not always tried this game successfully. And yet the Adversary dreams that I wished to rise by myself, and sought a little glory, so as to appear a keener inquirer into philological truth. As if he deserved glory who either slays flies with Domitian or crushes caterpillars? If I had thought this would be a credit, I would long since have pushed forward the Adversary's volume, in which perhaps he himself will make one side of a page. I am a sharp inquirer after truth, and as long as he either will not or does not know how to yield to it, I shall be not only bad to him but the worst. Nor should his opinion prevail on this ground, that, as he repeats very often, he has subdued all his material by great labour and long diligence (although here he not only contradicts himself, but further betrays his ignorance of the doctrine of Opposites, since on page 86 he struggles to reconcile contradictories); and those things which Scaliger, Salmasius, Budaeus, Hottomannus, Snellius, and others have written about money and usury, are too hastily made. Something might be conceded to his boastful voice if, to arrange his own matter, he had brought to bear the sharp judgment of Salmasius and a Dialectic acumen. And yet he so applauds himself that he opens his letter to the most illustrious man thus: Florus writes…

units.la: F masius, Budæus, Hottomannus, Snellius,& alii scripserunt, sint nimis festinata. Jactabundæ voci aliquid deferri posset, si,ad sua digerenda, peracre Salmasii judicium, & Dialecticum acumen attulisset. Et tamen usque adeo sibi plaudit, ut epistolam ad virum Illustrissimum sic ordiatur: Florus scribit Macedonas puduisse semel vinci, &c. & postea: Etsi enim in locis meis, sibi alienis, me imprudenter adortus facile succubuerit: tantum tamen tumultus excitavit & pulveris, ut dispici nequeat, penes utrum stet Verum & Victoria, nisi hoc tropæum erigam. Patior,ut hoc somnio se oblectet. Judicent, qui hæc legent, & mea cum suis contendere possunt. Tropæum, quod erexerit, fateor. sed se, hoc est, Grammatico ex disciplina Comitis de Clara Valle dignum. Ad illud primo pertinet vox etenim semel atque iterum eo judice redundans. Quid dixisset, si illam tam frequenter usurpassem, atque simili ratione,in uno quoque capite solet, Cælius Aurelianus, Medicus antiquus, ad hoc accuratus & nitidus. V. C. consulatur vel solum cap. 5. lib. 1. Tard. Paff. Secundo eodem refert jugeri: cur non & jugeres. Vtrumque juxta mea principia æque rectum, atque jugem. Tertio, collocare ad usuram: licet vetus Grammaticus ad Horat. Epod. 2. etiam dixerit ponere in usuram. Et quarto, quod hominem maxime asseaffecit, erratum Typographicum: As pro assem; as usurarius licet legisset num. 11. Unde, sui quoque sceptri mentione facta, temperare sibi non potuit, quin pro Grammatico candore & sapientia pag. 46. scriberet: Facile ferrem, non subtraxisset manum ferula PriscIani, priusquam ab eo didicisset, dicendum esse, certum assem. Dicite iô Paean! plausum date Gronovii discipuli! Atque ut Tropæum hoc penulati Hectoris sit magis conspicuum, Doctoris vestri verba ex pag. 62. præscribite: Dum nos hujus legis mentio propemodum a meta ad carceres revocat, repente advertit oculos aliud documentum, quanta, qui somnos nostros aucupatur,& quadrijugum verum per lancem & licium concipit, in scribendo aut vetvet cum vigilantia, aut cum veritate vigilet. Certe, si viveret Priscianus, hæc non intelligeret. ex Gellio licet sciamus, quid sit furtum per lancem & licium. Ac fortasse non intelligit ipse qui scripsit. dum morosè, Tullianæ elegantiæ & Liviano nitori Aborigenum jus & Saliorum hymnos intexit, Oedipo Lectore indiget. Insultat mihi ut Philosopho: si soloecismum quoque (quod pernego) commisisset, & ipse supra Grammaticam surrexisset, cogitasset illud Anastasii Sinaitæ: ὁ ἔχων νῦν ἐν τῇς νοήματι, παρεμφέρνει τῶν πολοιπῶν. & quod Chrysippus apud Plutarchum & Ellipses, & alia orationis flagitia Philosopho concedat; ἡ ν
units.tr: Salmasius, Budaeus, Hottomannus, Snellius, and others have written, are too hastily done.
