Some boastful word might be allowed if, in setting out his material, he had brought to bear Salmasius's keen judgement and dialectical acuteness. And yet he so applauds himself that he opens his letter to the illustrious man thus: Florus writes that the Macedonians were ashamed to be conquered once, etc. and afterwards: For although he has easily given way, having rashly attacked me on points foreign to him, yet he has stirred up so much dust and dust-cloud that it cannot be seen on which side Truth and Victory stand, unless I raise this trophy. I allow him to amuse himself with this dream. Let those who read these things judge, and let them compare mine with his. The trophy he has erected, I confess; but it is worthy of him, that is, of a grammarian trained in the school of the Count of Clara Valle. To the first point belongs the word etenim, which, in his judgement, recurs once and again. What would he have said if I had used it so often, and in a similar way as Caelius Aurelianus, an ancient physician who is accurate and polished in this respect, is accustomed to do in nearly every chapter? Let the learned reader consult at least chapter 5 of book 1 of the Tard. Paff. Secondly, to the same head he refers jugeri: why not & jugeres? Both are equally correct by my principles, just as jugem is. Thirdly, collocare ad usuram: although the old grammarian on Horace, Epode 2, also says ponere in usuram. And fourthly, which especially affected the man, a typographical error: As pro assem; as usurarius, although he had read it at number 11. Hence, having also mentioned his own sceptre, he could not restrain himself from writing on page 46, with grammatical candour and wisdom: I could easily bear it, had the hand of Priscian's ferula not been withdrawn before he had learned that it must be said certum assem. Sing, O Paean! Give applause, disciples of Gronovius! And that this trophy of the cloaked Hector may be more conspicuous, set forth the words of your Doctor from page 62: While the mention of this law almost recalls us from the goal to the starting-gates, suddenly the eyes notice another lesson, how great is the one who lies in wait for our sleep and conceives the fourfold theft by plate and licium; let him either be vigilant in writing with care, or let him be vigilant with truth. Certainly, if Priscian were alive, he would not understand these things. From Gellius we may learn what furtum per lancem et licium is. And perhaps he who wrote it does not understand it himself, since, while he laboriously weaves the Aborigines' law and the hymns of the Salii into Tullian elegance and Livian polish, he needs Oedipus as a reader. He mocks me as a philosopher: had he committed a solecism too (which I flatly deny), and had he himself risen above grammar, he would have considered that saying of Anastasius of Sinai: he who now has it in his thought, resembles the rest [ὁ ἔχων νῦν ἐν τῇ νοήματι, παρεμφέρει τῶν λοιπῶν]. And what Chrysippus, in Plutarch, concedes to the philosopher, ellipses and other faults of speech: yes, by Zeus, a solecism [ναὶ Δία σολοικισμός].

units.la: F

Δία σολοικισμός. Plinius secundus de quodam amico dicit: Eo ipso eum peccare, quod nihil peccaret. Vnde Longinus libel. π∊ρὶ ὕψους, quaedam ἀμαρτήματα εὐγενῆ agnoscit. Si ipsi quaedam in Stylo meo displiceant, norit mihi longe plura non probari in ipsius chartis, toties incudi reddi solitis. sed haec à scopo aliena sunt. Quando minax suum sceptrum intentat, viderit, quomodo solus posthac illius possessionem, ut Grammaticus, tutari queat. in eam jam olim Medici primores miti voluerunt, & adeo quidem ambitiose, ut volumina ingentia, à se edita, hoc titulo honestarint. Auctore Galen, τῶν κατὰ γένη lib. 5. ὁ μὲν ἥρως ἐν βιβλίον ἐποιήσατο τῆς τῶν Φαρμάκων συνθέσεως, ἐπιγεγραφόμενον φάρμακα. Cratippi φάρμακα citat idem Gal. l. 6. τῶν κατὰ τόπος. Sorani φάρμακα Aët. lib. 8. c. 44. Ne gloria hujus triumphi obliteretur, curabimus ne σφάλμα (factum licet jam sit) in iterata Exercitationum editione, quae jam adornatur, restituatur. Miror interim, quòd Noster hic edecumati eloquii superstitiosus observator, civitate Latina (aliae voces quum occurrerent) nomen Lombardi donaverit? Sed, cum alia ratione, prae imperitia Theologica & Juridica, honesto ordini obnunciare non posset, & tamen aliquibus, qui absque causa eundem oderunt, placere vellet; à nomine, apud vulgus invisio, invidiam provocari posse speravit. Ringitur pag. 86. quod aliquid in publipublicum emiserim, atque, nihil in posterum me scribere vellet, ne contingat quædam ex suis placitis examinari. Non ego equidem ambitiosus sum Scriptor, aut gloriam venor ex πολυγραφία. si aliquando aliquid prodeat, cui meum nomen est præscriptum, velim Lector, qui candorem non exuit, cogitet illud Plinii Junioris ad Arrianum: Edendum ex pluribus caussis: maxime, quod libelli, quos emisimis, dicuntur in manibus esse, quamvis jam gratiam novitatis exuerint, nisi tamen auribus nostris bibliopolæ blandiuntur. Arguor quoque passim πολυμαθίας. Si quis, novi illud Martialis: Quisquis ubique habitat, Maxime nusquam habitat. quod imitatus Tertullianus de Præscript. adv. Hæret. dicit: Ero itaque nusquam, dum ubique convenior. ut qualemcunque Theologiæ & Philosophiæ cognitionem indipisci possem, ex Veterum admonitione, putavi vacandum mihi esse Polymathiæ, quæ, ut mea, ad varias disciplinas pertinentia, publice leguntur, à quocunque discu-tiatior, in iis, si me prostitutum velit Adversarius, examinare tentet, & agat vel immodestissimè. Liquere postea poterit, hoccine auspicatò magis egerit, quàm propugnando contra meas rationes suam de fœnore Vnciario sententiam, solo Grammatico spiritu turgentem. Plura Ipsius errata atroci stylo confoderem, nisi hoc festinatum Schedium plus satis hominem occupaturum esset: salvam si velit existimaistimationem, tueatur sua, evertat mea. ut dixerit, audiet. Decretum enim paria paribus respondere. Interim Eleusis servat, quod ostensura sit rescriben-ti. Tertiò si somniet se vincere, tertiò vapulabit. Nam non modo διαχεῖν σιωπᾶν, sed publice quoque interest, veritatem astrui. Finirem, nisi Lentulo Auguri, ex Seneca mihi noto,antequam Ipse huic ungues injiceret, opponendus esset Rem-mius Palæmon Vicentinus, mulieris verna, idem-que Grammaticus, de quo Suetonius: Arrogantia (inquit) fuit tanta,ut Marcum Varronem por-cum appellaret, secum & natas & morituras lite-ras jactaret. nomen suum in Bucolicis non temere positum, sed præsagiente Virgilio, fore quandoque omnium poëtarum ac poëmatum Palæmonem ju-dicem. Gloriabatur etiam latrones quondam, sibi propter nominis celebritatem,parsisse. Qui-bus illustrandis singularis Sextì Empirici locus ser-vit, adductus quoque à Paschasio Grosippo, sive Caspare Scioppio Comite de Clara Valle, Epist.xiv. Pàrad. Literar. quem solum ex omnibus recentiori-bus Noster admiratur, & ducem quoque habuit in doctrina de Sestertio. Ita vero ibi Sextus per In-terpretem: Maxime (inquit) de artificio (N. B.) suo sibi placent seque magnificè jactant Gram-matici: eos autem semper insectantur, qui sunt aliis ornati disciplinis, quasi illi ne communem quidem Græcorum morem & consuetudinem novisnovissent: atque adeo (N. B.) si quando in disputatione premantur, sæpe non inveniunt aliam evadendi rationem ad abstrahendos eos, cum quibus disputant, quàm quod barbara sit ac soloœca eorum oratio. Videmus etiam Grammaticos, qui fere ne duo quidem verba dextre possunt contexere, velle unumquemque ex antiquis, qui dicendi facultate & Græci sermonis proprietate plurimum valuerunt, ut Thucydidem, Platonem, Demosthenem, tanquam Barbaros reprehendere. Noster ut tempestive sapiat, sequentia, in optimo libro occurrentia, meditetur. Intelligentia tua ne innititor. Abominationi est Jehova omnis altus animo. Eôque, superbis resistit, humilibus dat gratiam. Qui hæc legetis, arbitramini, nec præjudicium, quod forte circa Adversarium fovetis, transversos vos rapiat. Hieronymi verbum est ep. 69. ad Pammachium & Oceanum: Unumquodque non personarum, sed rerum pondere judicandum est. Quod Adversarius Mensa fœnebris Exercitoribus instituerit maledicere, & eorum Professionem arguere, fidem apud multos inveniet: &quòd ego eorum habear patronus, arguor injustitiæ & inscitiæ circa quæstionem, non tam Grammaticam quâ Historicam, quod meam sententiam in gratiam caussæ Trapeziticæ tutari videar. Frigidam dubio procul quoque Pythagoræ Pediani sectatores suffundent. dent. illi justi jam diu esse desierunt, quod rigidi summi Juris exactores circa alios magis, quam se esse praesumpserint. Non tamen moveor. Et, si haec praesumptio Lectores meos transversos rapuerit, ferre debeo. Quae pro Trapezitis aliàs scripsi, publice leguntur, nec eorum poenitet. Illi traducuntur, &c, cum illis ego. Sed, qui traducunt utrosque, tales sunt, ut nunquam vir bonus propterea commoveri voluerit. Ego jam diu concoxi illud Senecae: Male (inquit) de te loquuntur homines. Sed mali. Moverer, si judicio hoc facerent. nunc morbo faciunt, faciunt, quod solent. quibusdam enim canibus sic innatum est, ut non pro feritate, sed pro consuetudine latrent. Etiamsi Gronovius reip. vomicas existimet illos esse, quos Lombardos vocat: aliud tamen existimant supremae Patriae nostrae Potestates, Synodi, Classes, Consistoria, disciplinam admiserunt, utque veteres aviae sibi de pulmone revellerentur, permiserunt. Inde (rumpantur licet illia Codris) honesti Trapezitae alicubi in Consistoriis notati jam sunt, &c, ut confido, posthac inter eos & honestos mercatores nihil interesse, vulgus ipsum agnoscet. Opinio impedimentum profectus est. Mens modo erudiri velit, & rationes audire atque expendere; brevi valetudinario egredietur. Admisimus opinionem, & quare admiserimus, nescimus: exuere tamen nolumus, quia erubescimus discere bonam mentem. Patientes si modo Lectores mei fuerint, erint, & rationes ad Rationem exegerint, conse-quar quod ambio. Securus interim omnium sum,
units.tr: Pliny the Younger says of a certain friend: He sins by this very fact, that he sins in nothing. Hence Longinus, in his treatise On the Sublime, recognises certain noble faults [ἀμαρτήματα εὐγενῆ]. If some things in my style displease him, let him know that many more things in his own pages, which are so often hammered out and returned, do not please me. But these matters are foreign to the goal. When he threateningly brandishes his sceptre, let him see how, from now on, he alone can defend its possession as a grammarian. Long ago the chief physicians wished to make a claim to it, and so ambitiously that they honoured their huge volumes, published by themselves, with this title. Galen, in the fifth book of On the Kinds [τῶν κατὰ γένη], says: the hero made a book on the composition of drugs, entitled Drugs [φάρμακα]. The same Galen cites Crateuas's Drugs in book 6 of On Places [τῶν κατὰ τόπος]; Soranus's Drugs appears in Aëtius, book 8, chapter 44. Lest the glory of this triumph be obscured, I will take care that the slip (though it has already happened) is not restored in the repeated edition of my Exercitationes, which is now being prepared. Meanwhile I wonder that our man here, a superstitious observer of refined eloquence, gave the name Lombardi a Latin citizenship, though he might have used other words? But since he could not otherwise dismiss the honourable order because of his theological and juridical incompetence, and yet wished to please some who hate it without cause, he hoped to provoke odium by a name that is hated among the common people. At page 86 he rebukes me because I have published something in public, and because he says I wish to write nothing in future, lest some of my positions be examined. I am not, indeed, an ambitious writer, nor do I hunt glory from many writings. If ever something appears to which my name is affixed, I would have the reader, who has not lost his candour, think of Pliny the Younger's words to Arrianus: It must be put out for several reasons, chiefly because the little books we have published are said to be in people's hands, although they have already lost the grace of novelty, unless the booksellers flatter our ears. I am also charged, everywhere, with polymathy. Of Martial's line, whoever lives everywhere lives nowhere, Tertullian, imitating it in On Prescription against Heretics, says: I shall therefore be nowhere, while I am everywhere met. So that I might acquire some sort of knowledge of theology and philosophy, I thought, following the admonition of the ancients, that I must devote myself to polymathy, which, like mine, concerns various disciplines and is publicly read. Whoever wishes to examine me in these matters, if my adversary would put me forward, let him try, and let him act as immodestly as he likes. It will afterwards be clear whether he has begun more auspiciously by defending, against my arguments, his own opinion on the Unciarian usury, a view swollen with a purely grammatical spirit. I would stab his many errors with a fierce style, did not this hastily written Schedium occupy the man more than enough. If he wishes to keep his reputation safe, let him defend his own and overturn mine. Let him hear what he will say, for a decree is that like answers like. Meanwhile Eleusis keeps what it will show to the one who replies. If for a third time he dreams that he conquers, for a third time he will be beaten. For not only is silence [διαχεῖν σιωπᾶν] at issue, but it is also a public interest that the truth be established. I would finish, were it not necessary to set against Lentulus the augur, whom I know from Seneca, before he himself puts his claws on this matter, Remmius Palaemon of Vicenza, a slave of a woman and also a grammarian, of whom Suetonius says: His arrogance (he says) was so great that he called Marcus Varro a pig, and boasted that his literature would live and die with him. His name was not placed in the Bucolics by chance, but with Virgil foreseeing that Palaemon would one day be judge of all poets and poems. He also boasted that once robbers had spared him because of the celebrity of his name. A singular passage of Sextus Empiricus serves to illustrate these things, also cited by Pasquasius Grosippus, or Caspar Scioppius, Count of Clara Valle, Epistle 14 of the Paradoxical Letters, whom alone of all recent writers our man admires, and who has also been his guide in the doctrine of the sestertius. Thus Sextus, through his interpreter, says there: Grammarians (he says) are most pleased with their craft, and boast of themselves magnificently; but they always attack those who are adorned with other disciplines, as if they did not even know the common custom and usage of the Greeks, which they have newly ... ; and so (note well) if at any time they are pressed in a dispute, they often find no other way of escape to draw away those with whom they dispute, than that their speech is barbarous and solecistic. We also see grammarians, who can scarcely string together two words properly, wish to reprove, as barbarians, each of the ancients who were most powerful in the art of speaking and in the propriety of the Greek tongue, such as Thucydides, Plato, and Demosthenes. Let our man meditate on the following, from the best book, so that he may become wise in time: I do not lean on your understanding. Every proud man is an abomination to Jehovah; therefore he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. You who read these things, consider that a prejudice which you perhaps cherish about the adversary should not carry you off sideways. It is a saying of Jerome, in Letter 69 to Pammachius and Oceanus: each thing must be judged not by the weight of persons, but by the weight of the matter. That my adversary has undertaken to revile the Exercitors of the Usurers' Table and to attack their profession will find credence with many; and that I am thought their patron, I am charged with injustice and ignorance regarding a question which is not so much grammatical as historical, since I seem to defend my opinion for the sake of the banking cause. Doubtless the Pythagorean followers of Pedianus will also pour cold water on it. They have long since ceased to be just, because rigid exactors of the highest law presume to judge others more than themselves. I am not moved by this. And if this presumption carries my readers sideways, I must bear it. What I have elsewhere written for the bankers is read in public, and they do not regret it. They are traduced, and I with them. But those who traduce both are of such a sort that a good man should never be moved on their account. I have long since digested that saying of Seneca: Men speak ill of you (he says). But they are bad men. I would be moved if they did it with judgement; now they do it from sickness, and do what they are used to. For some dogs are so born that they bark not from ferocity but from habit. Even if Gronovius thinks that those whom he calls Lombards are abscesses of the commonwealth, yet our supreme national authorities, the synods, the classes, the consistories, have admitted discipline, and have permitted the old grannies to have their lungs plucked out. Hence (let Codrus burst with envy) honest bankers have now been noted in some consistories, and I am confident that hereafter the common people themselves will recognise that there is no difference between them and honest merchants. Opinion is an impediment to progress. If only the mind is willing to be instructed, and to hear and weigh arguments, it will soon leave its sickbed. I have admitted an opinion, and I do not know why I admitted it; yet we do not wish to shed it, because we are ashamed to learn a better mind. If my readers are and will be patient, and demand reasons at the bar of Reason, I shall attain what I desire. Meanwhile I am unconcerned about all men,

units.la: Quos mala stultitia, & quoscunque inscitia Excœcat. (vana
units.tr: Whom bad folly, and whatever ignorance, blinds. (vain

units.la: nam nemo est insanabilior illo, qui sibi sanus videri-ni. Gaudeat hactenus Adversarius juventutis præconcepta opinione, imo favore & applausu, apud eos, qui scruta emunt & æstimant, quia scrutarius laudavit: rationes meæ prævalebunt apud omnes illos, qui norunt (ut Ipse fateri compellitur) Visuras ad fata Reip. seu feliciora, seu infelicio-ra, se componere; & verba ex sensu Grammaticorum non esse explicanda, quando historia adversatur. Si dubitet, dignetur inspicere librum Belgicum, qui inscribitur: Noodige Verantwoor-dingh voor de Bancken van Leeninge, &c cujus Author est vir longe doctissimus, & a multis annis ab Incomparabili D. Salmasio æstimatus, Amplissimus & Consultiss. Dn. Justus Kriex, amicus plurimum colendus, superiori anno 1665. ascriptus τοις ἐν ἀγίοις. Ipse voluissem cum homine (quem hactenus æstimavi, & cujus omnia scripta diligentius excussi, ac forte quis alius mortalium) lenius egisse; sed fastu & præsumptæ suæ audaciæ imputet, quod stylum loliginis succo imbuerim. Non incidit in Cucullum Crucæi, aut in eum, qui se patiatur ab æquali contemni. Generosiores fumus (& tamen Christiani manemus) quàm ut hæc possimus concoquere, maxime cum illi nos lædant, qui publice histrioniam faciunt, &c, quibus perso-nam detrahi, reip. interest. Gratuletur interim si-bi, quod durius pro meritis non sit habitus. Idem si me astrum temperaret, tropæum erigerem. Et quidem triplex. Primo materiam suppeditarent putidæ contradictiones. Secundo aniles fabulæ. Tertio Grammatici coccysmi. Sed ambitiosus non sum: nec unquam, aut me, aut mea ostentare soleo. Patior, ut Noster sufflet, & sua per ora virum magnificè traducat. Alii, quæ inter nos controvertuntur, discutient. Exspecto ab eo responsum. Sed ipse interea simul exspectet Vindicias virorum summi Adr. Junii. Quibus an præscribere debeam titulum Ridiculi Sycophantæ, an Ridiculi Grammatici, adhuc ambigo. licet certo sciam Adrianum Junium non esse ridiculum Batavum, &c, per intolerandam calumniam,viro de rep. literaria meritissimo ridiculos errores objici à Gronovio, non Batavo. qui, ut spleni suo fibulas aliquantisper imponat, moneo. sane videtur cum quam petulantem habere. nam ego ipse pag. 87. lepidum caput ei videor. Ergo obleetet se leporibus, quos hic legit. Et,si in posterum melioribus, atque suo surcrcilio dignis recreari non velit, pueri Dinacii consilium audiat apud Plautum, æque meum atque suum, Stich. 2. 2. Age, quod placet. curre, ut lubet. cave, quemquam floccifeceris. Sed Ohe jam satis est! videor me expediisse. Viderit Gronovius,
units.tr: For no one is more incurable than the man who thinks himself sane. Let my opponent for now rejoice in the preconceived opinion of youth, and indeed in the favour and applause of those who buy and value junk, because a junk-dealer has praised him. My arguments will prevail with all those who know (as he himself is compelled to admit) that the Visurae shape themselves to the fortunes of the Republic, whether happier or more unhappy, and that words should not be explained by the sense the grammarians give them when history stands against it. If he doubts this, let him deign to look at the Dutch book entitled Noodige Verantwoordingh voor de Bancken van Leeninge, etc., whose author is a man far the most learned, and esteemed for many years by the incomparable Salmasius: the most distinguished and most learned Mr Justus Kriex, a friend deserving of the highest regard, enrolled among the saints [τοῖς ἐν ἁγίοις] in the year 1665. I would have preferred to deal more gently with the man, whom I have hitherto esteemed and whose writings I have examined more carefully than perhaps anyone else alive. But let him put it down to his own arrogance and presumptuous boldness that I have steeped my pen in cuttlefish ink. He has not fallen into the hood of Crucaeus, nor is he one who would suffer himself to be despised by an equal. We are too high-spirited (and yet we remain Christians) to swallow these things, especially since they injure us who publicly play the buffoon, and whose mask it is in the public interest to strip off. Meanwhile let him congratulate himself that he has not been treated more harshly than he deserves. If my star were so disposed, I would raise a trophy, and indeed a threefold one. First, putrid contradictions would supply the material; second, old wives' tales; third, the grammarians' jeers. But I am not ambitious, nor am I accustomed to display either myself or my own work. I allow our opponent to puff himself up and to parade his own man grandly on his lips. Others will examine the matters in dispute between us. I await his reply, but meanwhile let him also await the Vindiciae of the most eminent Adrian Junius. As to whether I should give them the title Ridiculous Sycophant or Ridiculous Grammarian, I am still undecided, although I know for certain that Adrian Junius is not a ridiculous Dutchman, etc. Through an intolerable calumny, ridiculous errors are imputed by Gronovius, who is not a Dutchman, to a man most deserving of the literary republic. I advise him, so that he may hold his spleen in check for a while, for he certainly seems to have a rather impudent spleen. For I myself, on p. 87, seem to him a witty fellow. So let him amuse himself with the witticisms he reads here. And if in future he is unwilling to be refreshed by better things, worthy of his own solemnity, let him hear the advice of the slave Dinacus in Plautus, which applies equally to me and to him (Stich. 2.2): Go on, do what pleases you; run as you like; beware of despising anyone. But enough, for heaven's sake! I seem to have disentangled myself. Let Gronovius see to it

units.la: Vgl. oben Seite 87. novius, utse pariter expediat. Securus sum minarum Æacidinarum, æque atque fulminis ê pelvj. Discutiantur interim hæc ab iis, quibus datum est sapere, ut confido: ἐχὶ περιπλοκὰς λόγων ἀθεγίσας εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ σοφοῖς, καὶ τοῖς Φαύλοις ἐνδιχ' ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ.
units.tr: See above, p. 87. Gronovius, so that he may likewise extricate himself. I am unconcerned by the threats of the Aeacidae, no more than by a thunderbolt from a basin. Let these matters be examined meanwhile by those to whom it has been granted to be wise, as I trust: I have not spoken in tangled arguments, but to the wise and to the foolish alike, as seems right to me [ἐχὶ περιπλοκὰς λόγων ἀθεγίσας εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ σοφοῖς, καὶ τοῖς Φαύλοις ἐνδιχ' ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ].

units.la: ERrata quædam & nostra, & styli, & operarum irrepsisse, disseri non audeo. Maximus ille Gronovius tertiam partem erratorum suorum in Syllabo non annotavit, & tamen ausus fuit, ex meis qualibuscunque Erratis, suum Tropæum erigere. quibus haut difficulter ignovisset, si tantum candoris haberet, quantum superbia. Ego nulla errata annotare volo, certus, mi benevole Lector, te tantum à Gronovio distare, quantum ille à Bona Mente. Festinanti & multis aliis distriƈto accidit, quod cuilibet accidere solet, & sæpe currenti evenit, quod ne eundo quidem evitari potest. Tu modo fave, & reliquos negligam. Simul vale, & alias adversus Gronovium Diatribas expeƈta.
units.tr: I do not dare to say that some errors have crept in, both of my own and of the printer's. That great Gronovius did not note a third of his own errors in the Syllabus, yet he dared to erect a trophy from my own errata, such as they are. He would have pardoned them without difficulty if he had as much candour as he has pride. I do not wish to note any errata, certain, kind reader, that you are as far from Gronovius as he is from good sense. What happens to a man in a hurry, or to one whose mind is pulled in many directions, happens to anyone, and what often happens to a runner cannot be avoided even by running. Only show your favour, and I will disregard the rest. Farewell, and look forward to other Diatribes against Gronovius.

units.la: SCriptorum lepidissimus Lucianus, in elegantissimo Dialogo, qui βίων περάσεις inscribitur, Chrysippum sic loquentem introducit: μόνῳ τὸ δανείζειν πρέπει ἂν τῷ σοφῷ. ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἴδιον ἀντῷ συλλογίζεσθαι, τὸ δανείζειν δὲ καὶ λογίζεσθαι τὰς τόκος, πλησίον εἶναι δοκεῖ τῷ συλλογίζεσθαι, μόνῳ ἂν ἐπὶ τῷ σπουδαίῳ καθάπερ ἐκεῖνο, καὶ τοῦτο. Solū sapientē fœnus exercere decet. Quandoquidem enim illius proprium est syllogismis concludere: Vsuras autem colligere,& fœnus computare, atq; syllogismis colligere, parum differre videntur; quemadmodum hoc soli studioso competit, ita quoq; illud, Stoicus, qui erat aurem mordaci lotus aceto, rationi in tota hac vita, circa hominis actiones primas deferendas esse, non modò didicerat ut homo, quem ratio à belluis distinguit: verum occasione quoque certorum negotiorum, quæ cum alijs ipsi intercesserant, homo homini quantum præstaret, suo forte malo expertus fuerat: atque, circumventus à mensarijs, (quorum ingenium contingit intendi à studio habendi) illorum, promptitudinem in calculo subducendo, & versu- tiam in mergendis ære alieno imperitioribus, & quidem specie æquitatis, perspexerat. Ad calcu- los qui sedet, ingenio valere debet, & artis syllo- gizandi peritus esse, quum ipsa Dialectica suum syl- logismum, qui φῶς τῆς ἀληθείας, quod ad no- men, Logisticæ debeat. Quisquis ergo Logicæ atque Arithmeticæ præsidio destitutus, Vsurarum dissici- les nodos solvere præsumit, æque temeritatis argui debet, atque, si solius scaphæ aut lembi præsidio, Oceanum trajicere, ac ad ultimos Indos, citra naufragium, navigare contenderet. Historia docere potest, quomodo illi, qui legum condendarum potestatem habent; ad suorum civium fortunas usu- ras exegerint, & Grammatica suppeditare vocabu- la, quorum quaque ætate usus fuerit in illis distin- guendis, juxta diversos temporis articulos: at, quan- do liquida non est historia, & de legum intellectu ambigitur, una ratio succurrere protest; nam scrupulose cavet, utfœnus tum civium opibus, tum temporı, leges vero, de illo latæ, etiamsi dubius sensus sit, quòd justæ esse præsumantur, ambobus respondeant. Legibus XII. Tabularum, (quæ à Ta- cito lib. 3. Annal. finis æqui juris, & à Livio lib. 3. Hist. fons omnis publici privatiq; juris vocan- tur) sanctum, ne quis unciario fœnore ampli- us exerceret, teste Tacito lib. 6. Annal. cap. 16. præter Tacitum, solus Livius unciarii fœnoris me- minit. cum vero nullus ex antiquis illius quantitatem explicuerit, jam diu viri docti quæsiverunt, quotæ assis usurarij parti, juxta quem usuræ apud Romanos distingui solent, respondeat. Quòdab uncia nomen habeat, multi putaverunt, æquivalere duodecimæ centesimæ parti, alij vero & Dialecti-ce & syllogismi usurarij peritiores, ipsi Centesi-mæ adæquant. His ego accedo, illis vero Grono-vius, cujus sententiam, cum jam anno 1657. oc-casione peculiaris Exercitationis de FoenoreTrape-zitico,modestissimè,imo antea veniam præfatus,ex-animassem, bonus vir adeo commotus fuit, ut ma-ledico libello anno 1662. rationes meas non tam examinaverit, quàm suas confirmaverit, per o-mnes paginas eadem chorda oberrando. Quod exististimatio mea laboraret, chartis à prælo adhuc madentibus serias Vindicias opposui, atque Suffe-no, qui nullum præter se æstimat, respondi, ut me-ritus erat. Mox varij rumores spargi coepetunt de altera Ἀνλεξηγήσεως, qua non modo jugulandus, sed & excoriandus cum Marsya essem, atque, ut pelli meæ tempestive metuerem, Auctor quibus-dam (quos sciebat mihi indicium facturos esse)Tra-ctatum suum, Manuscriptum adhuc (non nemo putabat laturum titulum Clavæ Herculis) often-dit, imo legendum exhibuit. Quod argumento-rum meorum certus essem, illorumq; pondus haut paucos, judicio præpollentes, atque inter illos Gro-novij quoque amicos & discipulos inclinassent, Æa-cidinas has minas contempsi, copiasque, quas in subsi-
units.tr: The most witty of writers, Lucian, in his most elegant dialogue, which is entitled The Sale of Lives, introduces Chrysippus speaking thus: [Only the wise man should lend money at interest. For since reasoning is peculiar to him, and lending money and calculating the interest seem closely akin to reasoning, this too belongs to the wise man alone, just as that does.] [μόνῳ τὸ δανείζειν πρέπει ἂν τῷ σοφῷ. ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἴδιον αὐτῷ συλλογίζεσθαι, τὸ δανείζειν δὲ καὶ λογίζεσθαι τοὺς τόκους, πλησίον εἶναι δοκεῖ τῷ συλλογίζεσθαι, μόνῳ ἂν ἐπὶ τῷ σπουδαίῳ καθάπερ ἐκεῖνο, καὶ τοῦτο.] The Stoic, who had his ear washed with sharp vinegar, had not only learned that in the whole of this life reason must be given precedence over the first human actions, as a man whom reason distinguishes from the beasts; he had also, by occasion of certain business dealings which he had entered into with others, learned by his own misfortune how far one man excels another. Circumvented by the moneylenders, whose nature is to be intent on getting money, he had observed their quickness in reckoning and their cunning in plunging the less experienced into debt, and that under the appearance of fairness. Whoever sits at the counting table must have a sharp mind and be skilled in the art of reasoning, since Dialectic itself, which is the light of truth, ought by its name to belong to Logistic. Whoever, therefore, lacking the aid of Logic and Arithmetic, presumes to untie the knotty problems of usury is no less to be charged with rashness than someone who should attempt to cross the Ocean in a mere skiff or small boat and sail to the furthest Indians without shipwreck. History can teach how those who hold the power of making laws have exacted interest from the fortunes of their citizens, and Grammar can supply the words whose usage in each age was used to distinguish them, according to the different periods of time. But when history is not clear and the sense of the laws is in doubt, reason alone can come to the rescue; for it carefully takes care that interest should correspond both to the resources of the citizens and to the times, and that laws passed concerning it, even if the sense is doubtful, are presumed to be just for both. By the Laws of the Twelve Tables (which Tacitus, Annals 3, calls the limit of fair right, and Livy, History 3, the source of all public and private right), it was forbidden for anyone to practise interest at the rate of one-twelfth, as Tacitus attests in Annals 6, chapter 16. Apart from Tacitus, only Livy mentions the unciary interest. But since none of the ancients has explained its amount, learned men have long sought to determine to what part of the as, by which interest among the Romans is usually reckoned, the unciary rate corresponds. Many have thought that, because it takes its name from the uncia, it equals the twelfth part of the hundredth; others, more skilled in Dialectic and in the reckoning of usury, equate it with the hundredth itself. I agree with these; but with Gronovius, whose opinion I had, in 1657, already examined on the occasion of a special exercise on banking interest, having first prefaced it very modestly, or rather with an apology, the good man was so stirred up that in an abusive little book of 1662 he did not so much examine my arguments as confirm his own, wandering through every page on the same string. Because my reputation was suffering, I opposed to him, with pages still wet from the press, a serious Vindiciae, and I answered Suffenus, who esteems no one but himself, as he deserved. Soon various rumours began to spread about a second Animadversio, in which I was to be not only throttled but flayed like Marsyas. And so that I should fear for my skin in good time, the author showed to certain persons (whom he knew would inform me) his treatise, still in manuscript, which some thought would bear the title The Club of Hercules, and even let it be read. Because I was confident in my arguments, and because I knew that their weight would impress not a few men of sound judgement, among them Gronovius' own friends and pupils, I despised these Aeacidan threats, and I kept reviewing from time to time the forces which I had stationed in reserve,

units.la: G subsidijs collocaram, subinde lustravi, edustum simul ac Hannibal aciem instruxisset. Sed, consultius huic visum festinare lente, & famā, quæ omnia in majus extollit, Grammaticarum rationum effusam fugam potius sistere, quam iterato prælij aleam experiri. Ego interim moræ impatiens, identidem ex omnibus, qui ex Hollandia redibant, scíscitari, quando prælo subducendus esset liber, non modo sententiæ de Vnciario fœnore, sed omnium meorum scriptorum (hoc Gronovio-μανέας apertis tibijs cecinerunt) exitio destinatus, εἰς φάος ἠλίοιο protrudendus esset. Hic unum, alius duo aut tria, quidam plura foliā a Typographo sibi ostensa esse, multis mensibus ante, quàm protrusus fuit, persuadere voluerunt. Credebam Lucam bovem uterum ferre; vel Phœbum Batavum, dubium adhuc esse pœnæ, quam irrogare vellet illi, qui secum in certamen literarium descendere ausus fuerat. quanquam amicus quidam affirmaret, montis partum exspectandum esse. nec hoc plane augurium fefellit; nisi, quòd vice ridiculi muris, natus fuerit erinaceus, spiculis maledicentiæ, non ferendi contemptus, & sycophantiæ undiquaque asper. Etenim, Ἀνθεξήγησις altera, Archilogium est Edictum, confutum ex meris sycophantijs & maledictis. Siquidem argumenta mea & responsiones non modo sycophanticè detorquentur, sed quaque etiam pagina multoties maledicitur. Crederes Professorem Leidensem cum Hecuba in canem conversum, itain me passim latrat. Inde prolixum hoc carmen: pag. 158. occurrit: Itaq; quum non nisi invidia, maledicentia, contumeliosus animus, & quosvis lacessendi ladendiq; libido, obrectatio & ingrata voluntas erga auctores suos, caca & praeceps temeritas, πολυπραγμοσύνη molestissima, frons pudoris expers, quaesitissima ὑπόκρισις, & per omnia fucata perpetuaq; vita histrionia, suspicax & maligna interpretatio innocentissimarum cujusq; actionum & cogitationum, & ex suspicionibus odium, eruditio ἐmπολαι, perfunctoria, vix ingenuo digna, & tamen omnia promittens, persuasio scientia & venditatio immodica & arrogantissima, gloriae insolentes ubiq; & verborum triumphi, ubi maxime & miserrime vitius tenctur, illecebra ad juventutem ab solidis ad inania convertendam, collegas refrigerandi calumniis, & quamvis amicos inter se committendi susurris artificium, avaritia speciem contempti quaestus induens, & quod recta via recusat, id duplum per pseudothyrum invitans quos & plures hujusmodi Furiarum stimulos additos habet atq; infixos, προσκαρτερης, πολυκαρδυας, ὑπαγκλίας, ὑποκολπίας, ἐνδομυχας; quum igitur, ut occepi dicere, non nisi haec ferales les species oculis ipsius obferrent, perpetuo laborat hoc morbo, in judicijs de aliorum persona faciendis, ut his attribuat, quae in se ipse invenit: nec certior est ratio deprehendendi hominem, quàm si aptes ei, quae pingit in illis, quos injuria insectatur: semper enim ab se formam & colorem sumit. Folia haec solummodo sunt, prae arboribus, quae pag. 133. cadunt, quâ audio: Theologorum Vomica, Jurisconsultorum carcinoma, Medicorum simia, Physicus in turpis & harengis & Maurorum genitura, Dialecticus sine Syllogismo, Philologus sine Grammatica, Rhetor Synecdochicus. Mirum, quod ex Asinaria sui Plauti (dubito an non plures hujus vernilis Poëtae versus memoriae mandaverit, quam Scripturae Sacrae textus) sequentia non addiderit: Edepol virtutes qui tuas nunc possit collaudare, (cisti, Sicut ego possim, quae domi duelli, male fenilla edepol pro merito nunc tuo memorari multa possint. Ubi fidentem fraudaveris, ubi hero infidelis fueris, Ubi verbis conceptis sciens libenter perjuraris, Ubi parietes perfoderis, in furto ubi sis prehensus,
units.tr: ...as Hannibal drew up his line of battle when he was about to set fire to his own camp. But it seemed to him wiser to hasten slowly, and to halt rather than risk another throw of the dice in battle, since rumour, which magnifies everything, had scattered the grammatical arguments in a rout. Meanwhile I, impatient of delay, kept asking everyone who returned from Holland when the book would be sent to the press, a book destined, not only on the subject of the unciary interest but of all my writings (as Gronovius, with bared shins, sang out like a madman), for destruction, and to be thrust out [into the light of the sun] [εἰς φάος ἠλίοιο]. One man said that a single sheet, another two or three, and some more, had been shown to them by the printer many months before it was published, and they tried to persuade me of this. I believed that Luca bore a calf, or that the Dutch Phoebus was still uncertain what punishment he would inflict upon the man who had dared to descend with him into a literary contest, although a certain friend declared that a mountain's birth was to be awaited. Nor did this augury quite deceive: except that, instead of a ridiculous mouse, a hedgehog was born, bristling with the quills of slander, intolerable contempt, and sycophancy on every side. For the second Animadversio is an edict of insult, compounded wholly of sycophancy and abuse. My arguments and replies are not only twisted sycophantically, but on almost every page I am slandered. You would think the Leiden professor had been turned into a dog along with Hecuba, so constantly does he bark at me. Hence this long poem: on page 158 there occurs: [And so, since nothing but envy, slander, a contumelious spirit, and the lust to provoke and injure anyone, detraction and an ungrateful will towards one's own authors, blind and headlong rashness, most troublesome curiosity, shameless brow, most studied hypocrisy, and a life everywhere painted over and a perpetual stage-play, suspicious and malignant interpretation of the most innocent actions and thoughts of anyone, and hatred arising from suspicions, learning which is a mere show, superficial, hardly worthy of a gentleman, yet promising everything, persuasion in place of knowledge, and immoderate and most arrogant self-advertisement, insolent pursuit of glory everywhere and triumphs of words, where vice is held most and most wretchedly, an allurement to turn the young from solid things to empty ones, the art of cooling colleagues with calumnies and setting even friends against one another with whispers, avarice wearing the appearance of contempt for gain, and inviting by a back door double what it refuses by the straight way; and he has many more such goads of the Furies added and fixed in him: [ever-persevering, many-hearted, sly, underhand, hidden in the bosom, inward-lurking]; since, then, as I began to say, nothing but these deadly forms are presented to his eyes, he constantly suffers from this disease in forming judgements of another's character, so that he attributes to others what he finds in himself. Nor is there a surer way of detecting a man than to apply to those whom he attacks with injury the features which he paints in them; for he always takes his own form and colour.] These are only leaves, as compared with the trees which fall on page 133, as I hear: [The vomit of theologians, the cancer of jurists, the ape of physicians, the physicist in the offspring of Turks and herrings and Moors, the dialectician without syllogism, the philologist without grammar, the orator who is all synecdoche.] It is strange that from the Asinaria of his Plautus (I doubt whether he has committed to memory more verses of this vulgar poet than texts of Holy Scripture) he did not add the following: "By Pollux, who could now praise your virtues, as I could, which at home are a war... by Pollux, many things could now be recalled, worthy of your deserts. Where you have cheated a trusting man, where you have been unfaithful to your master, where you have knowingly and gladly perjured yourself with words agreed upon, where you have bored through walls, where you were caught in theft,"

units.la: Ubi saepe caussam dixeris pendens adversus octo. Astutos audacis viros, valentis robore.
units.tr: Where you have often pleaded your case against eight, clever men of bold spirit and great strength.

units.la: Hac tamen vice me continebo, contentus hominis arrogantem & praefractam pertinaciam, adversus illa quae vera sunt, simul impudentissimam Sycophantiam in detorquendis & dissimulandis meis argumentis, publice ostendisse. Uterque, extra Belgium quoque noti sumus, aut, ut ipse dicit pag. 14.
units.tr: On this occasion, however, I will restrain myself, content to have publicly shown the arrogant and stubborn obstinacy of my opponent against what is true, and at the same time his most shameless sycophancy in twisting and concealing my arguments. We are both known even beyond Belgium, or, as he himself says on p. 14.

units.la: Nec adeo ignoramur uterq;. Quamvis hoc mihi prae illo peculiare fuerit, quod a prima ferme adolescentia, ex beneplacito Dei mei, aetatem transegi διαδοχης και αλιμιας, 2. Cor. 6. atque amplius, quam centies millies cum Davide exclamavi: Pf. 3. com. 2. 3. Jehova, quam multi sunt hostes mei; quam multi insurgunt contra me!
units.tr: Nor are we unknown to each other. Yet this has been peculiar to me compared with him: from almost my earliest youth, by the good pleasure of my God, I have passed my life through honour and dishonour [διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀτιμίας], 2 Cor. 6. And more than a hundred thousand times I have cried out with David: Ps. 3, vers. 2, 3: Jehovah, how many are my enemies! How many rise up against me!

units.la: Quam multi dicunt de anima mea, non est ulla salus ipsi in Deo plane! Gratias tamen immortales omnisicio & omnipotenti Deo debeo, quod huic misero homini, omniumque patronorum subsidio tam diu destituto, non modo fuerit Sol & scutum, sed amplius gratiam & gloriam dederit, Pf. 4. 12. Arrogantissimus mortalium, audet Dei partes sibi arrogare, & quasi καταδιογνώσης esset, ὑποκείμενος me arguere. Cui hoc unum solum oppono cum Jobo: In cœlis est testis meus, & conscius in excelsis. Job. 16. 19. atque dictum Apostoli Johannis, quod toties animum dimissum, atque præ adversariorum potentia & dolis parum quin fatiscentem, erexit: Si cor nostrum nos non condemnet, libertatem loquendi habemus apud Deum. 1. Joh. 3. 21. Si judex alienæ conscientiæ, contendat nihilominus, me in variis libris publicè prostantibus, multis modis argui, ac proinde se multo meliorem habendum esse hoc Æthiope, quòd bene audiat, &, à plurimis exquisitis præconijs efferatur; audiat Senecam ex Ep. 72. Nemo plus videtur æstimare virtutem, nemo magis illi esse devotus, quàm qui boni viri famam perdidit, ne conscientiam perderet. Calumnijs & convitijs, præmeditato studio ad modum centonis congestis, nihil reprono, memor dicti veteris scriptoris: ἥδιον ἁδὲν, ἁδὲ μασιχώτερον ἐςι, ἡ δυνασθαι λοιδορέμενον φέρειν. Unum tamen me pessime habet, quod à Vespertilione, & amatore moderatæ religionis, traducar Theologorum vomica. Deus novit, an non aliquis ex antiquis inimicis maledicum hoc carmen dictaverit. Persuasum illud est quibusdam Gronovij amicis, quod putent ipsius ingenium à tali scriptione abhorrere. quibusdam etiam affirmantibus, se legisse hanc Ἀνδεξήνησιν alteram, adhuc Manuscriptam, atque notasse minus fermentatam, quam typis exscripta legitur. Quanquam mea non refert, compositerit hæc Gronovius, an, alijs dictantibus, exceperit. Animus, odio & malevolentia æstuans, quoniam verum non videt, omnia credit, quæ in trivijs & circulis jactantur de illis, quibus male cupit: atque, ut est suspicax, suspicionibus, charitati licet adversentur, nihil falsi subesse putat. Digitum non verto, quòd ab hoc homine Theologorum Vomica traducor. Gratias Deo ingentes debeo, quod Christi Jesu cognitione Orthodoxa me donaverit, docueritque pendere à sola gratia; adeoque integrum servaverit à Photinianismo, Pelagianismo, & Papismo. Huic uni gratiæ acceptum refero (mihi relictus, in quæ non peccata unoquoque etiam momento incidere possum?) quod in professione Religionis me non exhibuerim Vertumnum, cum Papanis (quò favore illorum non exciderem) Missam frequentando, & Deum furfuraceum, in via publica forte obvium, cultu religiosæ adorationis venerando. Profiteor interim in Dei sanctissimi oculis me impurissimum, & præ alijs abominabilem peccatorem esse; atque æterno exitio destinandum fore, nisi charitas Dei superabundasset in Christo, qui semetipsum pro me tradidit, Gal. 2. 20. sanctus pro me peccatum, ut efficerer justitia Dei in eo, 2. Cor. 5. 21. Ego (qui novi me Philosophum & Christianum esse) omnibus hisce convitijs haut magis commoveor, atque Marpefia cautes. Au‑ctor vero fuerim homini meo, ad omnes occasiones rei faciendae nimium quàm attento, ad forum Oli‑torium & Piscatorium programma proponat, & invitet canes, ibi latrare solitas, in ludum suum Ora‑torium, cognoscent brevi, nullum hominem in to‑to Belgio vivere, per quem brevi aeque feliciter ad summum caninae loquentiae manuduci queant: ipsae quoque, quando sub tanto Praesidè declamaturae sunt, quomodo affectus concitari possint, exemplo suo, ingenuos adolescentes, expeditius docebunt, quam si centum millia passuum declamaverint. Nisi scirem formulam, quam antea exhibui, ab alijs dictatam esse, velut homo, à quo humani nihil alienum est, utramque forte buccam inflassem; &, existimationis meae (quod posteritatis quoque inter‑sit) publicas vindicias, ab aliquo tempore, instituissem. Adversarius à me non nisi Sycophanta audiet, quod nisi probaverim liquidò, ipse talis habear. Quàm probrosum vero sit Sycophantae nomen, & ipse quam sacer, atq; in societate hominum intole‑bilis, cognoscat ex Aristophanis Chremulo.
units.tr: Many say of my soul, there is no salvation for him in God at all! Yet I owe immortal thanks to the all-knowing and almighty God, who has not only been a sun and shield to this wretched man, so long left without the help of any patron, but has also given grace and glory, Ps. 84. 12. The most arrogant of mortals dares to claim for himself the part of God, and, as if he were a judge [καταδιογνώσης], presumes to accuse me as one under judgment [ὑποκείμενος]. To him I oppose only this, with Job: My witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high, Job 16. 19; and the saying of the Apostle John, which has raised up my spirit so often, when it was almost failing before the power and tricks of my adversaries: If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, 1 John 3. 21. If a judge of another's conscience should nonetheless insist that, because I am argued against in many ways in various books published in public, he must regard himself as far better than this Ethiopian, since he is well spoken of and extolled with many exquisite praises, let him hear Seneca, Ep. 72: No one seems to value virtue more, no one is more devoted to it, than he who has lost the reputation of a good man so as not to lose his conscience. I reproach no one for calumnies and abuse, gathered with deliberate care in the manner of a cento, mindful of the old writer's saying: it is more pleasant [ἥδιον] and more manly [ἀνδρικώτερον] to be able to bear being reviled. Yet one thing troubles me badly: that I am called the canker of theologians by a bat and lover of moderate religion. God knows whether some old enemy did not dictate this abusive verse. Some of Gronovius's friends are persuaded of this, since they think his talent shrinks from such writing; some even affirm that they have read this other Reply [Ἀνδεξήνησιν], still in manuscript, and noticed that it was less polished than what is read in print. Yet it makes no difference to me whether Gronovius composed these lines or wrote them down at others' dictation. A mind seething with hatred and ill will, since it does not see the truth, believes everything that is bandied about in the streets and circles concerning those whom it wishes ill; and, being suspicious, it thinks nothing false lies beneath suspicions, though they are contrary to charity. I do not mind being called the canker of theologians by this man. I owe immense thanks to God, who has given me the orthodox knowledge of Christ Jesus, taught me to depend on grace alone, and so kept me whole from Photinianism, Pelagianism and Papism. To this grace alone I attribute (for what sins might I not fall into at any moment, if left to myself?) that I have not played Vertumnus in my profession of religion, by frequenting Mass with the Papists (to win whose favour I would not fall away), nor worshipped with the religious adoration of worship a bran-god met by chance on a public road. Meanwhile I confess that in the eyes of the most holy God I am most impure, and more abominable than other sinners, and that I would be destined to eternal destruction, unless the love of God had abounded in Christ, who gave himself for me, Gal. 2. 20, holy one, made sin for me, that I might be made the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5. 21. I, who know that I am both a philosopher and a Christian, am no more moved by all these insults than a Marpessian crag. But I would advise my servant, who is far too attentive to every occasion for doing things, to set up a notice at the Oliterian and Fish markets, and invite the dogs that are wont to bark there to his oratorical school. They will soon learn that no man in all Belgium lives who could lead them so successfully to the height of canine eloquence. They too, when they are about to declaim under so great a president, will by their own example teach noble youths how emotions can be stirred more quickly than if they declaimed a hundred thousand paces. Unless I knew that the formula I put forward earlier had been dictated by others, I would perhaps, as a man to whom nothing human is alien, have blown out both cheeks; and from some time on I would have begun to vindicate my reputation publicly, as posterity too is concerned that I should. My adversary will hear nothing from me but "sycophant," which he will be taken to be himself unless I prove it clearly. How disgraceful the name of sycophant is, and how sacred he himself is, and how intolerable in human company, let him learn from Aristophanes' Chremylus.

units.la: II. Haec praefatus, ad rem ipsam me converto. Agere vero decrevi cum adversario bona fide, nec, exemplo illius, sycophanticè. Sub initium hujus secundae Ἀνἐξηγήσεως varios ad suffragium vocat auctores, qui de ratione supputandarum usurarum egerunt, atque inter illos, quosdam occurrere, qui meae opinioni de fœnore Vnciario faveant, infici‑as ire as ire non potest. Ne autem prosint, atque ego nihilominus vapulem, pag. 13. ita profatur: Hi ex-cusabiles, quia quàm multis,quamq; certis & perspicuis argumentis tam crassus error posset coargui, videre non potuerunt. At non tam parata venia homini, qui, cum pateret via pla-na & expedita, quam nos fecimus, jam bis ad eundem lapidem, ut habet proverbium, offen-dit, ut aliquid in nos injusta sua ac longa invi-dia collecta bilis evomeret. Resp. 1. Falsus est, quando perhibet bilem, & invidiam mihi dictasse Digressionem de foenore Vnciario, occurrentem in Exercitatione de Foenore Trapezitico. Non is erat Gronovius, in Schola Daventriensi mihi succidane-us in Professione Historiarum & Eloquentiæ,atque hoc tempore Professor Græcæ linguæ in Academia Lugduno-Batava, ut propter ipsum strabo fierem, iræ & odij caussas procul quoque habui. At, hoc hominis somnium est, quo, ut sese oblectet, facilè permitto, quicquid chartis illeverit, quoniam ipse admiratur, ab omnibus adorari & rotundum agno-sci cupit: eòque ferre non potest, ut aliquis sibi ob-loquatur. 2. Falsus pariter est, & non minus ar-rogantiam, quàm inanis gloriæ studium prodit, quando credere jubet, à se primitus in caussa usura-ria,viam planam & expeditam redditam fuisse. Au-ctoribus, per duodecim integras paginas laudatis, addidisset Carolum Sigonium, jam in priori Αὐ|ε‖ξη, ψὰσει γνται pag. 64. contra Pichenam (quem in eo citan-do dormitasse fateor) ad suffragium vocatum: atque huic iniuriam ab homine superbissimo fieri, lectori constitisset. Ita vero loquitur Sigonius lib. 2. de Antiquo Jure Civium Romanorum cap. 11. Vncia-riam usuram (inquit) si quis hoc fortasse requirat, dixerunt, respicientes Centesimam, quam maximam usuram aestimarunt: quae est, cum pars sortis Centesima singulis mensibus penditur, id est, cum quotannis duodeni pro centenis usurae nomine numerantur. Hanc vero quasi usurarum assem quendam esse voluerunt. unde aliae minores usurae, quasi assis partes, aut particulae fluxerunt; semis, cum dimidia pars centesimae in menses singulos solvitur; quadrans cum quarta; quincunx cum quinta; triens cum tertia; unciaria cum duodecima; semunciaria cum vigesima quarta. Haßenus Sigonius.
units.tr: II. Having said this by way of preface, I turn to the matter itself. I have decided to deal with my adversary in good faith, and not, after his example, sycophantically. At the beginning of this second Reply [Ἀνεξηγήσεως] he calls several authorities to vote, who have treated the method of calculating usury, and among them he says that some occur who favour my opinion on the uncial interest, which cannot be denied. Lest they help, and I nevertheless be beaten, he speaks thus on p. 13: These are excusable, because they could not see how such a gross error could be refuted by so many, so certain and clear arguments. But pardon is not so readily granted to a man who, although a plain and easy road lay open, which we have made, has already stumbled twice on the same stone, as the proverb says, so that he might vomit out against us a bile gathered from his unjust and long-standing envy. Reply 1. He is false when he claims that bile and envy dictated to me the Digression on uncial interest, which occurs in my Exercise on Banking Interest. Gronovius was not the man who succeeded me in the Daventer school in the professorship of History and Eloquence, and who is now professor of Greek at the Academy of Leiden, so that I should become cross-eyed on his account; I had no causes of anger or hatred even at a distance. But this is the dream of the man, by which, to amuse himself, I readily allow whatever he has daubed on paper, since he admires himself, wishes to be adored by all and recognised as a finished man; and he cannot bear that anyone should speak against him. 2. He is equally false, and betrays no less arrogance than a desire for empty glory, when he bids us believe that in the usury question the plain and easy road was first opened by himself. He would have added that Carolus Sigonius had already been called to vote in the earlier Reply, p. 64, against Pichena (whom I admit I nodded over when citing him), and it would have been clear to the reader that this wrong was done to him by a most arrogant man. Sigonius speaks thus in book 2 of On the Ancient Right of Roman Citizens, ch. 11: If perhaps anyone asks what the uncial interest is, he says, they called it so, looking to the centesimal rate, which they judged the greatest interest: that is, when a part of the principal is paid at one-hundredth each month, that is, when twelve are counted each year as interest on a hundred. They wanted this to be, as it were, a kind of unit of interest, from which other smaller rates flowed, as parts or fractions of the unit: the semis, when half of a hundredth is paid each month; the quadrans, with a quarter; the quincunx, with a fifth; the triens, with a third; the uncial, with a twelfth; the semuncial, with a twenty-fourth. So Sigonius.

units.la: III. Quae licet tam plana sint, ut a quovis, qui Latine scit, intelligi queant, nec Gronovius suam sententiam dilucidius propositerit, non tamen placere potuerunt viris, in ordine Jurisconsultorum primarijs. Non equidem Rittershusio, qui in consummatissimo Commentario ad legem xii. Tab. cap. 29. considerans foenus Vnciarium, a Decemviris definitum, Ad modum (inquit) foenoris quod attinet, in xii. tabulis definitum: permiserunt Decemviri, foenus unciarium, hoc est, usuram Centesimam. Eadem mens est Celeberrimo Dn. Jacobo Godofredo, cujus haec sunt verba in Indice ad xii. Tabulas: Fœnus unciari-um : quod unciam unam menstruam in assem pendit. Ne hic testis mihi faveat, Adversarius p. 135. ita cornicatur: Ambigue atq; obscure locutus est, fœnus unciarium definiendo, quod un-ciam unam menstruam in assem pendit. Neq; enim quem assem intelligat, explicuit, illumne nostri assem usurarium annuum, an assem centesimam menstruam, an deniq; assem sortem. Tertiæ sententiæ favisse Godofredum, nemo credi-derit, cui ipse modò notus fuerit, vel ex solis scrip-tis, diffusam non minus viri eruditionem, quàm limatum judicium arguentibus. Hanc si tuitus fuerit nescio quis Nicolaus Abrahamus, (jam pri-mitus eum nosse incipio) prolixo examine haud opus fuisset: quod tamen Gronovius instituit: (ut libelli sui paginæ multiplicarentur) nam sua absur-ditate semet jugulat. Quis enim credat inveniri homines, adeo improvide liberales, ut promiscue omnibus, à quibus rogantur, pecuniam mutuam dare velint, nec ullas usuras stipulari, sed solum-modo cavere, ut sors sibi duodenis æqualibus porti-onibus, & vicibus, restituatur. τὸν πύνυ Jacobum Godofredum, in animo habuisse assem centesimam menstruam, tum credam, quando Gronovius pro-baverit, duodecimam unciæ partem, ipsam unci-am esse, atque à Classicis Auctoribus ita vocari. Ve-rum, tum fuerit Rhetor Synecdochianus, quod mi-hi ut convitium applicat. IV. ProIV. Progredior ad vindicias argumentorum meorum. Vindicare vero primo convenit argumentum, desumptum à conditione non minus reip. Romanæ, quàm omnium illarum, in quibus, juxta regulam justitiæ, unquam contigit fœnus ordinari. In priori Ἀντεξηγήσει, Adversarius laboraverat quidem, multa ἀπεγσδιόυωσις admiscendo, illud de gradu dejicere: sed infelici conatu, ut fusius in Prioribus Vindicijs ostensum fuit. In hac altera Ἀνξεξη-γήσει crambem duntaxat recoquit, aut, si quid novi adferatur, homini prostituendo servit. Argumentum agnoscit tale fuisse, pag. 14. Ἀν. II. Quæcunq; resp. quum & populi & privatorum opibus floreret, admisit centesimas usuras, ea multo magis eadem tulit, quum esset inops. At Romana resp. quum publicis & privatorum opibus floreret, admisit usuras centesimas ordinarias. Dissimulando alia vulnera, responsionibus suis inflicta, sequentia pap. 15. ex illis repetit: Poterit fieri, ut aliqua resp. cum flore potentiæ & opibus acceperit vitia, quæ fœnus incitant: quibus vitijs quod vacaret inops & tenuis, nec instrumentum luxuriæ atque avaritiæ magno conducendum habebat. Idem multa privatorum exempla demonstrant, qui paupertatem egregie ac sine ære alieno tolerarunt: ut Valerius Poplicola, Menenius Agrippa, Men. Curjus, C. Fabricius, L. Æmilius Paullus, Tuberones, & alij. Hæc Noster, quæ, ad rem nihil
units.tr: III. Although these points are so plain that anyone who knows Latin can understand them, and Gronovius could not have stated his own view more clearly, they did not satisfy the leading jurists. Rittershusius did not accept them. In his very complete commentary on the Law of the Twelve Tables, chapter 29, considering the foenus unciarium defined by the Decemvirs, he says: As for the rate of interest, it is defined in the Twelve Tables: the Decemvirs permitted foenus unciarium, that is, the hundredth part as interest. Jacob Godefroy holds the same view, and his words in the index to the Twelve Tables are: Foenus unciarium: which pays one ounce a month on the as. So that this witness may not favour me, the Adversary, on page 135, crows as follows: He spoke ambiguously and obscurely when defining foenus unciarium as that which pays one ounce a month on the as. For he did not explain which as he means: whether our annual usurious as, or the monthly as of a hundredth, or finally the as of the principal. No one who knew Godefroy, even from his writings alone, would believe he favoured the third opinion, since those writings show a learning no less wide than a judgement that is refined. If some Nicolaus Abrahamus (whom I am only beginning to know) had defended this view, a lengthy examination would not have been needed. Gronovius nevertheless undertook one, to lengthen the pages of his little book, for his own absurdity destroys him. For who would believe there are people so rashly generous that they wish to lend money to everyone who asks, without demanding any interest, requiring only that the principal be repaid in equal instalments over twelve months? I would believe that the late Jacob Godefroy meant by the as the monthly hundredth only when Gronovius proved that the twelfth part of an ounce is the ounce itself and is so called by the Classical authors. But then he would be a Rhetor Synecdochianus, which he applies to me as an insult. IV. I proceed to defend my arguments. First I should defend the argument drawn from the condition of the Roman commonwealth, no less than that of all those states in which, by the rule of justice, interest was ever regulated. In his earlier Antexegesis, the Adversary did indeed labour to overthrow this point, mixing in a great deal of digression, but the attempt failed, as was shown at length in my earlier Vindiciae. In this second Antexegesis he merely reheats the old porridge, or, if he brings anything new, he serves it up in a disreputable way. He admits the argument was of this kind, on page 14: Any state which flourished with the wealth both of the people and of private persons admitted hundredth-part interest; it bore it all the more easily when it was poor. But the Roman state, when it flourished with public and private wealth, admitted ordinary hundredth-part interest. Passing over the other wounds my replies inflicted, he repeats the following from them on page 15: It may be that some state, with the flower of power and wealth, has acquired vices that incite usury, whereas a poor and needy state, lacking these vices, had no need of costly instruments of luxury and greed. Many examples of private persons also show this, who bore poverty nobly and without debt, such as Valerius Publicola, Menenius Agrippa, Manius Curius, Gaius Fabricius, Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the Tuberones, and others. Thus our author, who has nothing to do with the matter

units.la: nihil facere, jam antea ostendi: quum hic non quæratur, quid fieri possit, aut quid alibi factum fuerit; sed, quid Romæ accidisse, vero consentaneum videatur. Ne tamen Adversarius clamet, me ictum declinare, nec jam altera vice collato pede audere congredi; omnia hæc quàm presse examinabo, eaque, quæ præsidio esse putat, magis obesse ostendam. Initio vero notare convenit πρῶτον ψευδος, quod maximum Salmafium quoque transversum egit: fcil. Romanos, eo quoque tempore, quo à Decemviris leges xii. Tabularum ferebantur, admodum pauperes fuisse. Ita enim scribit in Præf. libri de Fœnore Trapezitico sol. 5. pag. 7. Nec mirum videri cuiquam debet, tam leve fœnus lege Duodecim tabularum fœneratoribus fuisse statutum. Præsertim, fi quis cogitet, statum Romanæ Reipublicæ, qualis illo in tempore fuit. Nec navigationibus, nec mercaturis erantediti. Solis inopibus foli divites fœnerabantur. &c. Mirum vero tantum virum tam turpiter lapsum fuisse. Veniam tamen meretur præ Gronovio, quod hic glorietur, fe per otium omnia spectantia ad hanc partem Historiæ Romanæ, præ omnibus mortalibus diligentissime enucleaffe. Ergone Romani, illo etiam tempore, quo LL. xii. Tabb. promulgabantur, pecuniæ inopes, &c, neq; navigationibus, neque mercaturæ dediti fuerint? Contrarium verum esse, adeo liquidò ostendam, atque meridie lucet: certe Polybius, scriptor gravissimus, &c πολλῶν ἀλλων. ἀλλων ἀνἀξι῾ lib. 3. cap. 22. & 23. testatur Romanos, mox ab ejectis Regibus, scil. Coss. Junio Bruto, & Marco Horatio, annis prius quam Xerxes in Græciam trajiceret, duodetriginta,sive, lx. ferme annis, ante latas leges xii. Tab. ex foedere cum Carthaginensibus, mercatura gratia adiisse Carthaginem, & regionem universam Africæ, cis Pulchrum Promontorium: atque, ne quis dubitet, ipsas foederis tabulas exhibet. Quid quod Ancus Marcius, quartus Romanorum Rex, referente Floro lib. i. cap. 4. Ostiam in ipso maris, fluminisq; confinio coloniam posuit, jam tum videlicet præsagiens animo futurum, ut totius mundi opes, & commeatus illo, veluti maritimo urbis hospitio, reciperentur. Nec falsus augur Ancus fuit: nam haut multo post fructum Roma percepit. Testis Halicarnassæus lib. 3. ἐν δὲ τῷ μεζαξὺ τῆ πολαμῷ καὶ τῆς Ἰταλάτης ἀγκῶνι, πόλιν ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐνιδρύσας, ἣν ἀπὸ τῆ συμβεβηκὸς ὠσίαν ὀνόματον, ὡς δ᾽ ἂν ἡμεῖς ἐπιμεν, Θύεσαν, ὁ μόνον ἡπειρωτῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἰταλατιῶν πατρεσκευάσε τὴν Ῥώμην γενέσθαι, καὶ τῶν διαπονήσων ἀγαθῶν ἐγένετο. Ubi inter flumen & mare prominens littus curvatur in cubiti speciem, oppidum Ancus munijt, quod ex re Ostiam appellavit: (Θύεσαν nos diceremus) effecit, ut Roma non mediterraneis tantum, sed etiam marimarinis hominibus patens, transmarina quoq; bona degustaret. Praeterea, contigit Romam ditari ex praeda Italica, atque exuvijs vicinarum urbium, partim expugnatarum, partim solo aequatarum. Signanter Florus occasione Tarquinij Prisci lib. 1. cap. 5. Duodecim namq; Tuscia populos (inquit) frequentibus armis subegit. Inde fasces, trabeas, curules, anuli, phaleras, paludamenta, praetextas; inde, quod aureo curru quatuor equis triumphatur; togas pictas, tunicas palmatas; omnia denique decora & insignia, quibus imperij dignitas eminet. Haec omnia, a Consulibus, qui in Regum jus & insignia successerunt, retenta, non potuerunt remp. & publice & privatim pauperem arguere. Ne dicam, Romanos, sub Romulo quoq; armillas aureas, in Sabinis vidisse, ut testis est Florus lib. 1. cap. 1. Atque, ne quis existimet nihil horum ad populum & Quirites, in communi consideratos, derivatum fuisse, sub Regibus etiam, si opulentus per Latium populus subactus esset, viritim argentum distribui consueverat. Patet ex Concione L. Junij Bruti apud Dionys. Halicarnassaeum lib. 6. ubi occasione regum, qui initio Romam habuerunt, haec disserit: κεραυνῷ... πολέμῳ μαχεῶν Σχέσεως τῆς πόλιν πάνυ εὐδαίμονος, ἔχον αὐτοῖς μηδενὶ κοινωνεῖσθαι τῶν λαφύρων· ἀλλ' αὐτοὶ καταςχεῖν, καὶ πάντας ὑπερβαλλέσθαι πλάτῳ βαςιλέων, ἐκ ἠξίωσαν·
units.tr: has nothing to do with it, as I have already shown earlier, since the question here is not what could happen or what has happened elsewhere, but what seems true to have happened at Rome. Yet lest the Adversary cry out that I am dodging the blow and do not dare to meet him again on equal footing, I will examine all these points closely and show that what he thinks is a help is rather a hindrance. First, it is worth noting a first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος], which greatly tripped up even the great Salmasius, namely that the Romans, at the time the laws of the Twelve Tables were enacted by the Decemvirs, were very poor. For he writes thus in the preface to his book on banking interest, page 7: Nor should it seem strange to anyone that so light an interest was set for moneylenders by the law of the Twelve Tables, especially if one considers the state of the Roman commonwealth at that time. Men were not given to navigation or trade. Only the poor borrowed, and only the rich lent. And so on. It is strange that so great a man fell so shamefully. Yet he deserves pardon compared with Gronovius, who boasts that by leisure he has explained more diligently than any mortal everything bearing on this part of Roman history. Were the Romans, then, even at the time the Twelve Tables were published, short of money, and not given to navigation or trade? I will show that the opposite is true, as clear as midday. Certainly Polybius, a most serious writer, and many others [πολλῶν ἄλλων], in book 3, chapters 22 and 23, testifies that the Romans, soon after the kings were expelled, namely in the consulship of Junius Brutus and Marcus Horatius, about forty-eight years before Xerxes crossed into Greece, or about sixty years before the Twelve Tables were enacted, went to Carthage and to the whole region of Africa on this side of the Fair Promontory for the sake of trade under a treaty with the Carthaginians. And lest anyone doubt it, he sets out the very tablets of the treaty. What of Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of the Romans? According to Florus, book 1, chapter 4, he founded a colony at Ostia, at the very meeting place of sea and river, clearly foreseeing in his mind that the wealth and supplies of the whole world would be received there, as at a maritime gateway to the city. Nor was Ancus a false prophet, for Rome reaped the fruit of it not long afterwards. Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a witness, book 3: where the land between the river and Italy's elbow curves out like a cubit, the king founded a town, which, from the circumstance, he called Ostia [Θύεσαν; we would say Ostia]. He made it so that Rome was open not only to inland but also to sea-borne men, and enjoyed the goods of overseas. Moreover, Rome grew rich from Italian plunder and the spoils of neighbouring cities, some taken by storm and some razed to the ground. Florus, speaking of Tarquin the Elder, book 1, chapter 5, says in particular: For he subdued twelve peoples of Etruria with frequent armies. Hence the fasces, the purple-bordered robes, the curule chairs, rings, horse trappings, military cloaks, and togas with purple borders; hence triumphs in a chariot of gold drawn by four horses; embroidered togas and palm-patterned tunics; in short, all the ornaments and insignia by which the dignity of empire stands out. These things were all retained by the consuls, who succeeded to the rights and insignia of the kings, and they could not prove the state, public or private, poor. Not to mention that the Romans, even under Romulus, saw golden armlets among the Sabines, as Florus testifies, book 1, chapter 1. And lest anyone think none of this affected the people and the Quirites considered as a community, even under the kings, when a wealthy people across Latium had been subdued, silver was customarily distributed to individuals. This is clear from the speech of Lucius Junius Brutus in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 6, where, on the occasion of the kings who first held Rome, he argues: [Greek text, garbled in the scan, speaking of war against a very prosperous city and of the spoils, which they did not share with the people but kept for themselves, and of wealth and riches far exceeding those of kings, which they thought fit to bring into the open, and to distribute among us all the benefit of the goods, apart from slaves, cattle and the rest of the property, which was large and fine, and to divide silver among men.] When they had stormed the very prosperous city of Suessa in a long war, and could have seized the booty, with no one in

units.la: ἀλλὰ Φέρεγνες, εἰς μέσον ἐθηκαν, ἁπασαν τὴν ὠφέλειαν ὡς ἀὐ ἡμᾶς χωρὶς ἀνδραποδων καὶ βο-σκημάτων, καὶ τῆς ἀλλης κ̣ήσεως, πολλῆς ἔσης καὶ καλῆς, ἀξγυρίς πένε μνας καὶ ἀνδρα διανειμα-θαι.Cum Sueffam urbe florentissimā longo bello expugnassent, potuissent q; prædam, nemine in partes ejus admisso, retinere sibi, & regum fi-eri ditissimi, noluerunt, malentes eam cedere vulgo militum: ita ut nobis præter mancipia & pecora, opesq; cateras multas & luculentas, viritim quinq; minas argenti tribuerentur. Eat nunc Gronovius, (qui mihi ignorantiam Historiæ Romanæ exprobrat) & inter suos discipulos de populi Romani paupertate declamet.
units.tr: "But the Pheregnes [Φέρεγνες] placed before the assembly all the advantage, as if apart from us, excluding slaves and cattle and other possessions, though these were many and fine, they had to distribute five minas of silver per man [ἀλλὰ Φέρεγνες, εἰς μέσον ἐθηκαν, ἁπασαν τὴν ὠφέλειαν ὡς ἀὐ ἡμᾶς χωρὶς ἀνδραπόδων καὶ βοσκημάτων, καὶ τῆς ἄλλης κτήσεως, πολλῆς οὔσης καὶ καλῆς, ἀργυρίου πέντε μνᾶς καὶ ἀνδρὶ διανεῖμαθαι]. When they had conquered the very prosperous city of Suessa after a long war, they could have kept the whole booty for themselves, admitting no one to a share, and become the richest of kings; but they refused, preferring to yield it to the common soldiers, so that to us, besides slaves, cattle and many other fine goods, five minas of silver were given apiece. Let Gronovius now go and hold forth on the poverty of the Roman people among his pupils, he who accuses me of ignorance of Roman history.

units.la: V. Ad quam probandam haud auspicato quoque advocat Valerios Poplicolas, Menenios Agrippas, Curios, Fabricios, &c. Eadem enim ratione inferas & Atheniensem & Thebanam remp. profundo paupertatis immersas fuisse, quòd in utraque similes heroës fuerint. Ita enim lib. 2. Var. Hist. cap. 43. per interpretem Ælianus: In summa egestate vitam traduxerunt Aristides Nicomacho satus, & Phocion Phocifilius, Epaminondas Polymatide genitus; Pelopidas Thebanus, Lamachus Atheniensis, Socrates filius Sophronisci, & Ephialtes Sophonida. At horum sc similium paupertas sancta, innocens, parvo contenta, privati fuit contemptrix, ut publici boni & ni & divitiarum ad alios potius, quàm ad se deri-vandarum foret propagatrix. Valerius Maximus lib. 4. cap. 4. postquam undecim exempla, viro-rum in rep. Romana illustrium, proposuisset, qui innoxiam paupertatem, absque querela fustinue-rant, sequentia,quæ admodum Pathetica, subjicit: Hæc igitur exempla respicere, his acquiescere so-latijs debemus, qui parvulos census nostros nun-quam querelis vacuos esse finimus. Nullum aut admodum parvi ponderis argentum, paucos ser-vos, septem jugera aridæ terræ, indigentia domi, publice impensa funera, inopes dotum filias; sed egregios consulatus, mirificas dictaturas, innu-merabiles triumphos cernimus. Quid ergo me-diam fortunam, quasi præcipuum generis humani malum, diuturnis convitijs laceramus? quæ ut non abundantibus, ita fidis uberibus Poplicolas, Ælios, Fabricios, Curios,Scipiones, Scauros, hisque paria robora virtutis aluit. Exurgamus poti-us animis, pecuniaeque aspectu debilitatos spiritus pristini temporis memoria recreemus: Namque per Romuli casam, perque veteris Capitolij humilia tecta, &æternos Vestæ focos, fictilibusque etiamnum vasis contentos juro; nullas divitias talium virorum paupertati posse præferri. Hæc Valerius. Omnes hi viri, ex Annalium, quâ Græcorum, quâ Romanorum memoria, non fuerunt paupetes absolute, (ut loquì amant Philosophi) quasi caruerint necessarijs πεϱὶ τὸν βίον (ijs fuf-
units.tr: V. To prove this point, he rashly calls upon Valerius Poplicola, Menenius Agrippa, Curius, Fabricius, and others. By the same reasoning one could infer that the Athenian and Theban commonwealths were sunk in deep poverty, because they too had heroes like these. For Aelian, through his translator, says in Varia Historia 2, chapter 43: "Aristides, son of Nicomachus, and Phocion, son of Phocus, Epaminondas, son of Polymnis, Pelopidas the Theban, Lamachus the Athenian, Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, and Ephialtes, son of Sophon, lived in the utmost want." But the poverty of these and similar men was holy, blameless and content with little; it despised private wealth and was rather the means of spreading public good and of deriving riches to others rather than to themselves. Valerius Maximus, Book 4, chapter 4, after setting out eleven examples of illustrious men in the Roman commonwealth who bore their blameless poverty without complaint, adds the following, which is very moving: "We ought therefore to look to these examples and find comfort in them, we who think our modest estates are never free from complaints. We see no silver, or almost none of any weight, few slaves, seven acres of dry land, want at home, funerals paid for by the state, daughters without dowries; yet we see splendid consulships, marvellous dictatorships, countless triumphs. Why then do we tear apart with long reproaches the middle fortune, as if it were the chief evil of the human race? It was that which, not with abundant but with faithful breasts, nursed Poplicola, Aelius, Fabricius, Curius, the Scipios, the Scauri, and men of equal strength of virtue. Let us rather rise up in spirit, and refresh our spirits, weakened by the sight of money, with the memory of former times. For I swear by Romulus's hut, by the humble roofs of the old Capitol, by the eternal hearths of Vesta, and by the earthen vessels with which they were still content, that no riches can be preferred to the poverty of such men." Thus Valerius. All these men, according to the record of the annals, whether Greek or Roman, were not poor "absolutely" (as the philosophers like to say), as if they lacked the necessities of life [πεϱὶ τὸν βίον]; (they had small fields which they tilled themselves). Rather they are considered poor because they did not abound in wealth, and neglected it when they could have increased it without difficulty.

units.la: H ficiebant exigua rura, quæ ipsi colebant) sed,pau-peres censentur, quòd opibus non abundaverint, neglexerintque eas,cum commodè quoque potu-issent augere.DePhocione Corn .Nepos. Fuit per-petuo pauper, quum ditissimus esse posset, pro-pter frequentes delatos honores, potestatesq; summas, quæ ei àpopulo dabantur. Inde & Cicero dixit Orat. Agraria altera : Luscinos, Calatinos, non solum honoribus populi, verum etiam patientia paupertatis, ornatos. Cum enim rem facere possent, exemplo aliorum, noluerunt. Hodiernum seculum non tam virtutum quoque sterile est, quin alicubi tales heroas exhibeat; quis tamen usque adeo elephanti corio est circumtectus, aut tantas à polypo molestias patitur, ut, inde concludat cum Gronovio, talia laudandæ paupertatis exempla, inopem remp. & egestatem populi arguere?
units.tr: Cornelius Nepos on Phocion: "He was always poor, though he could have been very rich, because of the frequent honours and the highest offices that were offered him by the people." Hence Cicero also said in his second Agrarian Oration: "The Luscini and the Calatini, adorned not only with the honours of the people but also with their patient endurance of poverty." For when they could have made their fortune, following the example of others, they refused. The present age is not so barren of virtue that it cannot show such heroes somewhere; yet who is so thick-skinned, or suffers such annoyances from the polyp, as to conclude with Gronovius that examples of such praiseworthy poverty indicate a needy commonwealth and the want of the people?

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Quòd vitia Romæ fœnus incitaverint, iterum recoquit.
