In priori responso uberius hoc expendere supersederam, ratus meum hominem sapientiorem redditum iri, per Martialem, cujus Epigramma proinde quoque adduxi pag. 65. Sed, cum antiquum obtineat, & sibi in stolido hoc commento placeat, omnia & pressius & distinctius exanimabo, simul quædam καὶ ἐπιλομὴν ex priori Ἀνʃεξηγήσει repetam: Nihil igitur (inquit) habet insani, putare Romanos inter fœnus non fuisse, isle tantum, dum circa matrem suam luctaban- tur, nec falces extra Italiam extenderant, quan- tum, postquam opes universi orbis corripuerunt. Nempe parvo contenti vivebant: aberat magnus nummi usus in commercia, aberat luxus: nemo tabulas, signa, toreumata emebat: nemo vetera negligebat, nova diruebat, alia aedificabat: nemo profundebat divitias, extrudendo mare & montibus coaequandis: nemo denique omnibus modis & summa libidine pecuniam trahebat, vexabat, ut in sua vitia disertus Catilina queritur apud Sallustium. Quid Romae in tantis divitijs publicis privatisque foenus reddidit immodicum? Ambitio candidatorum. Quid adegit homines ut iniquissimis conditionibus versuras facerent? Amor possessionum magno in aere alieno. Quid Romae usuras intendit? Redemptio scelerum, Sallustius: quiq; alienum as grande conflaverat, quo flagitium aut facinus redimeret. Quid Romae grandes reddidit usuras? Nequitia adolescentum, qui ut amicam redimerent, ab danista sumebant argentum in dies minasq; singulas nummis, ut est apud Plautum in Epidico: qui filij familias in mortem parentum Macedonijs se obligabant, ut apud Tacitum & Suetontum & juris conditores. Quod foenus magnum fecit? Aes alienum amplissimorum & nobilissimorum virorum: quum Caesar, antequam illum magistratum gereret, trecenties duodecies, quum Milo septingenties debe- ret. beret. Hac meus Gronovius, cujus errores, in his verbis (quæ jam antea examinari debuissent) occurrentes, si castigare velim omnes, πάρεργον ἔργα μᾶζον ἂν γένοιτό μοι Reliquis missis: pauca hæc duntaxat noto. 1. Ipsi ex Plutarchi elegantissimo libello περὶ τῆς μὴ δεῖν δανείζεσθαι, in priori Ἀνδεξηγήσει citat hæc: ἀδὲς γὰρ δανείζει πένητι. Nemo pecuniam credit pauperi. apud quem Plutarchum sequentia quoque offendas: τῆς ἀπόρως δὲ δανείζοντι, ἀλλὰ βουλομένοις ἐμ- πορίαν τινὰ ἑαυτοῖς κλᾶσθαι, καὶ μάτην ἀδύ- νατον καὶ βεβαιωτὴν ἄξιον. Egenis nec pecuniam credunt, (foeneratores scil.) sed iis, qui sibi copiam aliquam parare volunt, testemq; & sponsorem habent, esse se tales, quibus tuto mutuum committatur. Decoctoribus, hominibus ambitione excaecatis, luxuriosis, & insanas substructiones molientibus, nullus sapiens pecuniam suam credet, si omnibus fortunis excusi, destituantur non minus idoneo sponsore, quam hypotheca & pignore. Testis idem Plutarchus: ἡμεῖς δὲ τὴν ἀνάγκην ἀισχυνόμενοι καταδολλῶμεν ἑαυτὰς ὑποθήκας καὶ συμβολαίοις, δέον εἰς ἀνάγκην τάχεσιμα συσσαλεύσας καὶ συσπειρωθέντας, ἐκ τῶν ἀχρήστων καὶ πεπτωκότων καταχοπέντων ἢ πεφυλαγμένων, ἐλευθερίας ἀνδρὸς ἴσον ἰδεῦσθαι, καὶ πίκνωσις καὶ γυναῖκες. Nos, dum contentos esse nostris nostris rebus pudet, dandis pignoribus contra-stibusq; subeundis in servitutes nosmet damus,ubi par erat contraćtis ad utilia cupiditatibus,inutilia nos & ociosa concidere, aut divendere,itaq; nobis ac familiæ fanum libertatis extru-ere. Pignora siquidem aut fidejussorem dare de-bet, cujus apud fœnerarores dubia fides est. Fru-stra quoque adolescentes amatores sollicitantur.Quotquot ex argentarijs, vel micam sapientiæ un-quam habuerunt, ne quidem nummum sestertiumijs credere voluerunt. Alia ne sollicitem, testisesse potest Plauti Pseudolus, in quo Aćt. 1. sc. 3.Calliodorus Adolescens, & Ballio Leno, hos interse sermones miscent: CA. Nimis miser sum, nummum nusquam reperire argenti queo: Ita miser & amore pereo, & inopia argentaria. BA. Eme die caca hercle olivom, id vendito oculata die. Jam hercle vel ducentæ fieri possunt præsentes minæ. CA. Perij! annon tum lex meperdit quina vicenaria? Metuunt credere omnes. BA. Eadem est mihi lex, metuo credere.
units.tr: That the vices of Rome gave rise to usury, he cooks up again. In my earlier reply I had decided not to weigh this more fully, thinking that my opponent would be made wiser by Martial, whose epigram I therefore also cited on page 65. But since he keeps his old view and is pleased with this foolish invention, I shall examine everything more closely and distinctly, and at the same time repeat certain points from my earlier explanation. "Nothing, then," he says, "is more absurd than to suppose that the Romans had no usury, since they were struggling around their own mother and had not extended their sickles beyond Italy, until they seized the riches of the whole world. Indeed they lived content with little: there was no great use of coin in trade, no luxury; no one bought tablets, statues, or embossed work; no one neglected old things, pulled down new ones or built others; no one squandered his wealth by pushing out into the sea and levelling mountains; in short, no one by every means and with the greatest greed drew in money and harassed people, as the eloquent Catiline complains of his own vices in Sallust. What made usury so excessive at Rome amid such great public and private riches? The ambition of candidates. What drove men to make loans on the most unfair terms? The love of estates, with heavy debt. What increased usury at Rome? The redemption of crimes, as in Sallust: 'and he who had contracted a great debt in order to redeem some shameful or criminal act.' What made usury at Rome so great? The wantonness of young men, who, to redeem a mistress, took silver from a moneylender at a fixed sum a day for each mina, as in Plautus's Epidicus; the sons of families who pledged themselves to Macedo for their parents' deaths, as in Tacitus, Suetonius and the jurists. What made usury great? The debts of the most distinguished and noble men, since Caesar, before he held that office, owed 1,200,000,000 sesterces and Milo 700 million." Thus my Gronovius. If I wished to correct all his errors occurring in these words (which should have been examined before), it would become a greater task for me than the main business. Leaving the rest aside, I note only these few points. 1. He himself cites in his earlier Explanation, from Plutarch's elegant little treatise on not borrowing, these words: "No one lends money to a poor man." In the same Plutarch you will also find the following: "Usurers do not lend to the needy, but to those who wish to procure some resource for themselves, and have as witness and surety that they are such men to whom a loan may safely be entrusted." No wise man will lend his money to spendthrifts, men blinded by ambition, luxurious men, and men planning mad building projects, if they are cut off from all their resources and lack a surety no less reliable than a mortgage or a pledge. The same Plutarch is a witness: "We, ashamed of necessity, pledge ourselves with pledges and contracts, when it was necessary to gather and close ranks quickly, and to divide up what is useless and fallen, or guarded, and to make the freedom of a man and a woman equal..." Namely, when we are ashamed to be content with our own affairs, we hand ourselves over to servitude by giving pledges and entering into bonds, whereas we ought, having sought useful things with our desires, to cut away and sell off what is useless and idle, and so build a shrine of freedom for ourselves and our household. Indeed one who must give a pledge or surety, whose credit is doubtful with moneylenders, is also in need. Young lovers are vainly solicited too. As many moneylenders as have ever had even a crumb of wisdom would not wish to lend even a sestertius to them. To avoid dwelling on other examples, Plautus's Pseudolus can bear witness, where in Act 1, scene 3, the young man Callidorus and the pimp Ballio mix these words: CA. "I am too wretched; I cannot find any silver coin anywhere. So I am wretched, dying of love and of lack of silver." BA. "Buy oil by a blind day, and sell it by a seeing day! By Hercules, two hundred minas could now be had at once." CA. "Woe is me! Does not the law of 'five in twenty' destroy me? All fear to lend." BA. "The same law applies to me; I fear to lend."

units.la: Nec improbus ille, & improvidam juventutem circircumvenire solitus Macedo, (cui similis erat Horatij Fufidius, lib. 1. Serm. sat. 2. ) adolescentibus aliquid credebat, nisi in mortem paternam, Tacit. lib. 11. Annal. cap. 13. de Claudio Imp. Et lege lata sævitiam creditorum coërcuit, ne in mortem parentum pecunias filii familiarum fœnori darent. quo & facit colloquium Getæ & Demiphonis senis apud Terentium Phormione act. 2. sc. 11.
units.tr: Nor was that wicked Macedo, who used to prey on the heedless young (he was like Horace's Fufidius, Satire 2 of Book 1), lending anything to young men except against their fathers' deaths. Tacitus, Annals 11.13, on the Emperor Claudius: And by a passed law he restrained the cruelty of creditors, so that sons under paternal authority might not lend money at interest against the death of their parents. The conversation of Geta and the old man Demipho in Terence's Phormio, Act 2, scene 2, agrees with this.

units.la: GE. Non ratio, verum argentum deerat.
units.tr: GE. It was not reason that was lacking, but silver.

units.la: DE. sumeret.
units.tr: DE. He might take it.

units.la: Aliunde. GE. aliunde? nihil est dicto facilius.
units.tr: From elsewhere. GE. From elsewhere? Nothing is easier to say.

units.la: DE. Postremò, si malo, alio pacto, fœnore.
units.tr: DE. Lastly, if I must, by another arrangement, at interest.

units.la: GE. Hui! dixti pulchrè, siquidem quisquam adderet,
units.tr: GE. Hui! You have spoken well, if indeed anyone would add

units.la: Te vivo.
units.tr: While you are alive.

units.la: Adeoque, jam iteratò frustra sollicitantur, à Gronovio dissoluti nattæ, homines obæratì, importuni prensatores, adolescentes amatores, similesque, ut probet per talium vitia fœnus consuevisse intendi. Nullus unquam, cui modo sapientiæ gutta superfuit, dicet hæc vitia (quæ: mutuantes, mala nomina, aut esse, aut brevi fore arguunt) momenti plus contulisse ad intendendum fœnus, quàm assiduorum virtutes, & fidem, fallere nesciam. Contraxerit Maceponius Centesimis quoque, cum decoctore eodemque amatore adolescente, te, non tamen per clandestinum illum, & legibus adversantem contractum, usuræ in foro crescent.
units.tr: And so, now again in vain, Gronovius's ruined mistresses, debt-ridden men, importunate canvassers, young lovers and their like are brought forward, to prove that interest was usually raised through the vices of such people. No one who still has a drop of wisdom will say that these vices (which show that borrowers are either bad risks or soon will be) contributed more to raising interest than the virtues of diligent men and a faith that knows not how to deceive. Maceponius may have contracted at five per cent with a spendthrift who was also a young lover, but not for that reason, nor through that secret and law-breaking contract, do interest rates grow in the Forum.

units.la: 4. Incrementum illarum, potissimum pendet à ratione pecuniæ, cujus quò major aut minor copia fuerit, usuræ aut accrescunt, aut decrescunt. Lego quidem (citante quoque Gronovio) apud Ciceronem lib. 4. ad Att. ep. 15. Ardet ambitus : ση- μα δὲ τοι ἐρέω. fœnus ex triente Id. Quint. factum erat bessibus. at hoc non tam tribuendum est cœcæ ambitioni Candidatorum, quam partim inopiæ pecuniariæ, quæ erat apud argentarios, partim immodicæ horum liberalitati, qui cum grandem pecuniam inter tribus distribuere meditarentur, certatim argentum, quod in foro erat, sibi credi rogabant. 5. Alias ratione usuræ, quâ in foro Romano argentarij fœnerabantur, pendebat à conditione provinciarum, quibus, cum cogerentur vectigalia per ipsos Equites, & Provinciales Magistratus, fides multorum, in foro sæpe angusta notabatur, si metus subesset, parum argenti Romam deportatum iri. Inde Cicero dicit Orat. pro L. Manilia: Hæc fides, atq; hæc ratio pecuniarum, quæ Romæ, quæ in foro versatur, implicita est cum illis pecuniis Asiaticis. Item: Nam tum, cum in Asia res magnas permulti amiserunt, scimus Romæ solutione impedita, fide concidisse. Quorum autem fides concidit, ijsne quidem argentarij credere solent. Quicquid vero pecuniæ per avaritiam Provinciales Magistratus coegerant,
units.tr: 4. The rise of such interest depends chiefly on the state of the money supply: the greater or smaller the supply, the more interest rises or falls. I read (Gronovius also cites it) in Cicero, Letters to Atticus, Book 4, letter 15: Ambition is burning: I will tell you a sign [σῆμα δέ τοι ἐρέω]. Interest rose from a third; Quintus Fufidius had made it by bribery. But this should be attributed not so much to the blind ambition of the candidates as partly to the shortage of money among the bankers, and partly to the immoderate generosity of those who, intending to distribute a large sum among the tribes, eagerly asked that the money available in the Forum be lent to them. 5. At other times the rate of interest by which bankers lent money in the Roman Forum depended on the condition of the provinces. When the revenues were collected by the Equites themselves and the provincial magistrates, the credit of many men in the Forum was often seen to be strained, if there was fear that little money would be brought to Rome. Hence Cicero says in his speech for Lucius Manilius: This credit, and this state of money affairs, which is active in Rome and in the Forum, is bound up with those Asian funds. Likewise: For when many lost great sums in Asia, we know that at Rome, with payments blocked, credit collapsed. But those whose credit collapses are not normally trusted by bankers. Whatever money the provincial magistrates had squeezed out through greed,

units.la: Romæ fere fœnori per argentarios dabant. Non obscure colligere est ex eadem Ciceronis Oratione: Quid hunc hominem magnum, aut amplum de rep. cogitare, qui pecuniam ex ærario depromptam ad bellum administrandum, aut propter cupiditatum provincia magistratibus diviserit, aut propter avaritiam, Roma in quæstu reliquerit. 6. Atque sic argumentum meum probe vindicatum esse existimo, & iterum confectum, grandiores usuras solvi ordinario solere, si pecuniæ egestas esset, minores vero si abundaret. Licet interim (quod nunquam negavi, nec ad causam quoque nostram pertinet) usuras intendere aut remittere consueverit eorum fides, quibus fors credebatur, sive dubia, sive certa. Nam, cui non notum est illud Plauti ex Mostellaria, Act. 1. sc. 3.
units.tr: was mostly lent out at Rome at interest through the bankers. It is easy to gather this clearly from the same speech of Cicero: What great or lofty thoughts about the state could this man have, who either distributed among his provincial magistrates money taken from the treasury for conducting the war, to satisfy their desires, or, through greed, left it at Rome to be made a profit? 6. Thus I think my argument has been properly vindicated and again confirmed: that higher interest is usually paid when money is scarce, and lower when it is plentiful. Meanwhile it is allowed (which I never denied, nor does it bear on our case) that the credit of those to whom money was lent, whether doubtful or certain, has been wont to raise or lower interest. For who does not know that line of Plautus in the Mostellaria, Act 1, scene 3:

units.la: Ut fama est homini, exinde solet pecuniam invenire.
units.tr: As a man's reputation is, so he usually finds money.

units.la: Ego si bonam famam mihi servassso, sat ero dives.
units.tr: If I keep a good reputation for myself, I shall be rich enough.

units.la: VIII. Scripseram pag. 11. Cento credi debere in Rep. Romana, (fateor aliam me non intellexisse) cum egena & impotens adhuc esset, minimum usuras Centesimas per leges receptas fuisse; quod tanta Repubł. quam locupletata & potenti, jure probata fuerint.
units.tr: VIII. On page 11 I had written that in the Roman Republic, while it was still poor and weak, interest at five per cent was hardly allowed by law at all; I confess I did not understand otherwise. This was because the republic was so rich and powerful that it was rightly approved.

units.la: Gronovius, ut conconcoquere non potest, quòd addiderim hæc verba per leges; ita, postquam verba mea ad Syllogif- mi quasi formam redigiffet, sequelam negat pag. 16. nulla negationis reddita ratione, otiosa quip- pe sunt & homine futili digna, quæ subjicit verba:
units.tr: Gronovius, since he cannot digest my adding the words by law, after reducing my words to the form of a syllogism, denies the conclusion on page 16, giving no reason for the denial. Indeed, the words he adds are idle and worthy of a frivolous man:

units.la: Non id necessarium: potuerunt & non esse: potuerunt esse, (loquitur de Centesimis) non le- ge scripta, sed moribus introductâ, nulla le- ge vetante, quæ postea accesserit. Mirum ho- minis ingenium! per possibile laborat illud elude- re, quod & lege scripta & non scripta receptum su- isse probavi. Bonum interim factum! quod ta- le quid fieri potuisse concedat. Non propinavi ergo somnia, ut noster vates ante Endymionē,è La- tio monte redux, in priori sua Ἀνʃεξηγήσει, credu- lis discipulis persuadere laboraverat, At, quis non Doctoris juris exuvias ab hoc homine repetat, quòd legem, quam latam fuisse supponit, ad præterita quoque revocet? Vapulet Papiria, & simul noster J. V. D. Si in Juris Corpore æque versatus esset, atque in Justino, Petronio, & Statio Papinio, qui æra annuatim ei confecerunt, non ignorasset, quid decreverint Impp. Theodosius & Valentinia- nus leg. 7. Cod. de Legibus. Impp. in illa lege sic lo- quuntur: Leges & constitutiones futuris certum est dare formam negotijs, non ad facta præ- terita: nisi nominatim & de præterito tempo- re, & adhuc pendentibus negotijs, cautum sit.
units.tr: This is not necessary: they could have not existed; they could have existed (he is speaking of interest at five per cent) not by written law, but introduced by custom, with no law forbidding it, which came later. What a strange mind the man has! He labours to evade by "possible" what I have proved was received both by written and by unwritten law. Well done, anyway, for conceding that such a thing could have happened. I did not therefore serve up dreams, as our poet did before Endymion, returning from the Latin mountain, who in his earlier Explanation [Ἀνεξηγήσει] laboured to persuade his credulous disciples. But who would not strip this man of the trappings of a Doctor of Law, because he reaches back to past times with a law which he supposes was passed? Let Papirius be beaten, and our J.V.D. with him. If he had been as well versed in the Body of Law as in Justin, Petronius and Statius Papinius, who wrote the annual edicts for him, he would not have been ignorant of what the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian decreed in law 7 of the Code, On Laws. The emperors speak thus in that law: It is certainly right that laws and constitutions give form to future transactions, not to past acts, unless it is expressly provided for past time, and for transactions still pending.

units.la: Argumentum interim meum de statu non fuisse deturbatum, omnes agnoscent, qui supra Gronovium à judicij dexteritate commendari merentur. Adduxeram Batavicæ reip. exemplum, (quum ubique terrarum idem observari queat) ut ex illa Romanæ facies agnosceretur. Ut videar falsus fuisse, pag. 7. hæc friguttit: Nimia dissimilitudo est in exemplis, ob diversam illarum rerumpublicarum fortem. Batavi adflicti ac miseri, cum potentissimo hoste congressi, magna pecunia egebant, ad alendum mercenarium militem. Romani parvo contenti ac fortes, cum divitibus & male fortibus sine stipendio militabant. Deinde Batavi, postquam florent, nondum ad eam immoderationem luxus & corruptelarum pervenerunt, (& absit, ut eo perveniant) ad quem Roma florens cum magno fœnore. Resp. 1. Si ad penetralia Reip. Batavicæ æque penetrasset, atque Collegiorum prætextu ad imum fundum crumenæ studiosorum (illorum scil. qui creduli modo fuerint) penetrare jam diu novit, hæc sine rubore non legeret. Batavi auxiliarem militem, sub initium motuum Belgicorum, non mercenarium habuerunt, aut, si quem habuerint, alere potuerunt ære haut quaquam usurario. 2. Usuræ tamen ingentes illo tempore, nomine reip. quoque solutæ fuerunt, ne tributis egens populus gravaretur: maximè, quòd iniquior illorum lorum exactio per ducem Albanum, ipsos Pontificios à rege Hispaniarum alienos reddidisset.
units.tr: Meanwhile, all who deserve to be commended for judgement beyond Gronovius will acknowledge that my argument, that the state was not overthrown, stands. I had brought forward the example of the Dutch Republic (though the same can be observed everywhere on earth), so that the face of the Roman one might be recognised in it. In order to seem wrong, on page 7 he murmurs this: The examples are too unlike, because of the different fortunes of those republics. The Batavians, afflicted and wretched, when they met a most powerful enemy, were in great need of money to feed mercenary soldiers. The Romans, content with little and brave, fought without pay alongside the rich and the not very brave. Then the Batavians, since they flourished, have not yet come to that immoderation of luxury and corruption (and far be it that they should come to it) to which flourishing Rome came, with great interest. Answer: 1. If he had penetrated the inner workings of the Batavian Republic as thoroughly as he has long known how to penetrate, under the pretext of the colleges, to the bottom purse of students (namely those who are merely credulous), he would not read these things without blushing. At the beginning of the Belgic disturbances the Batavians had auxiliary soldiers, not mercenaries; or, if they had any mercenaries, they were able to pay them with money by no means lent at interest. 2. Yet enormous interest was paid at that time, even on behalf of the republic, so that the people, short of money for taxes, should not be burdened; especially since the harsher exaction under the Duke of Alva had made the Papists themselves alienated from the King of Spain.

units.la: 3. Usurae longe leviores fuissent, si pecuniae & fuisseт copia, & populi fiducia, detrectantis mutuum dare rectoribus reip. nutantis, atque nondum firmatae. 4. Quanquam in Historia Romana versatior deberet esse Gronovius, quàm in Biblijs, quorum ostendit hactenus se securiorem esse; in illa ipsa tamen, se hospitem esse, & lectorem, hactenus oscitantem, ostendit. Fingit rem Romanis fuisse, antequam militi stipendia solverentur, cum male fortibus. Sed, an tales haberi merentur Veientes, qui non modò fortiter Romanis restiterunt, sed bellum quoque inferre ausi fuerunt? Unus Florus audiatur lib. 1. cap. 12. Assidui verò anniversarij hostes ab Etruria Veientes, ac postea: Veientium quanta res fuerit, indicat decennis obsidio. Tunc primum hiematum sub pellibus. Taxata stipendio hiberna: Adactus miles sua sponte jurejurando, nisi capta urbe remearet. 5. Veij dum obsessi essent, stipendium solvi coeptum militi, quum, quinquaginta praeter propter annis ante, leges xii. Tabularum latae fuissent per Decemviros: at, quis praeter Gronovium, usque adeo ineptus, ut existimet omnes Romanos, quos ipse hactenus fingit fuisse pauperrimos, stipendio praeter opinionem solvendo fuisse pares: atque inopes pecuniae, tam levi foenore, (quantum ipse somniat fuisse unciarium) potuisse permovere homines, vix mediocriter divites, ut sibi pecuniam crederent? Certe in civitatibus, ubi viri, eminentiores quoque, mediocres solum divitias possident, & pauci pecunia affluentes occurrunt, illi ab his immodicis usuris exhauriuntur, quando mutua pecunia accipere coguntur. Si ambigat Gronovius, lustret Transfisulaniam ( in qua adhuc affines habet ) vicinamque Gelriam: aut, si longius libuerit exspatiari, invisat suos Chaucos. 6. Somnium est Gronovijs, omnes Romanos, ante latas LL XII. Tabularum, parvo fuisse contentos. Curios & Fabricios si adducat, ab Universali ad particulare argumentabitur. Æque, atque si aliquis concludere vellet, omnes, qui in Academijs docent, juventutem habere quaestui, atque extemporanea Collegia æstimare contra auream imaginem; Quoniam hoc fit in Belgio a duobus, tribusve. 7. Quod ipse circa Batavos abominatur, ego quoque abominarer, nisi vetarent experientia & conscientia. Roma florente quo non ruerunt Quirites: absorti in profundo luxuriæ? at, fuerunt hi pauci, Ganeones, aleones, gulones, sponsi Penelopes, discincti, insanientes Luculli, & similes. Sed det mihi gentem Gronovius, ubi, ab infima plebe sumpto initio, usque ad primores, & circa vestes, & circa magnificas aedes, & supellectilem, & mensam, & famulitium, & urbanas rusticasque delicias, speStacula quoque, usque adeo à modestiæ, sobrieta-tis, & continentiæ lineis recessum fuerit, atque in ipsa Batavia? Romanis luxuriantibus Sybaritas jun-gat Gronovius, atque delirantem amussim depre-hendet, si illos cum Batavis (in quibus exhiben-tur nobis Tyrij Ezech. cap. 27. atque utinam non eorum quoque plagæ!) voluerit componere. Nec tamen populator opum luxus apud Batavos usu-ras hactenus intendit, quòd pecuniæ abunde sit, eâque affluant illi quoque, qui in rep. obscuri ha-beri merentur. In statu ergo manet argumentum meum, nec cedit Gronovij λόγοις.
units.tr: 3. Interest would have been far lighter if there had been both an abundance of money and the confidence of the people, who were reluctant to lend to the rulers of a wavering and not yet settled republic. 4. Although Gronovius ought to be more versed in Roman history than in the Bible, in which he has so far shown himself the more secure, yet even in that history he shows himself a stranger and a reader who yawns. He invents that the Romans were paid their soldiers' wages before the badly brave were paid. But do the Veientes deserve to be considered such, who not only resisted the Romans bravely but also dared to make war on them? Let Florus alone be heard, Book 1, chapter 12: But the Veientes, enemies of Etruria who came back every year, and afterwards: How great a thing the Veientes were is shown by the ten-year siege. Then for the first time they wintered under tents. Winter quarters were assessed as pay. The soldier was bound by his own oath not to return unless the city was taken. 5. While the Veientes were still besieged, pay began to be given to the soldier, although about fifty years earlier the Laws of the Twelve Tables had been passed by the Decemvirs. But who, apart from Gronovius, is so foolish as to think that all the Romans, whom he himself imagines to have been very poor, could be equal to paying wages beyond expectation; and that men who were scarcely moderately well off, short of money, could have been induced by so light an interest (which he himself dreams was the unciarium) to lend their money to one another? Certainly in states where the more eminent men possess only moderate wealth, and few rich men are to be found, those men are drained by these excessive interest rates whenever they are forced to borrow money. If Gronovius is in doubt, let him survey Overijssel (where he still has relatives) and neighbouring Gelderland; or, if he wishes to range farther, let him visit his own Chauci. 6. It is a dream of Gronovius's that all Romans were content with little before the Laws of the Twelve Tables were passed. If he brings forward Curius and Fabricius, he will argue from the universal to the particular. It would be just as if someone wanted to conclude that all who teach in the academies regard young people as a source of profit, and value extempore colleges above the golden image, because this happens in Belgium with two or three men. 7. What he abominates among the Batavians I too would abominate, were it not forbidden by experience and conscience. When Rome flourished, into what depths of luxury did the Quirites not plunge? But these were few: debauchees, gamblers, gluttons, the suitors of Penelope, the dissolute, the raving Lucullus-types, and their like. But let Gronovius show me a people where, beginning with the lowest commons and reaching up to the chief men, in clothing, in magnificent houses, furniture, table, servants, urban and rustic delights, and even spectacles, there has been such a departure from the lines of modesty, sobriety and self-restraint, and this in Batavia itself. If Gronovius wishes to compare the Romans in their luxury with the Sybarites, he will catch the raving man exactly, if he wants to set them beside the Batavians (in whom we are shown the Tyrians of Ezekiel 27, and would that their plagues were not theirs too!). Nor yet has luxury, the plunderer of wealth, so far increased interest among the Batavians, because there is plenty of money, and it flows even to those who deserve to be considered obscure in the republic. My argument therefore stands in its condition, and does not yield to Gronovius's [λόγοις] arguments.

units.la: IX. Quàm appositè pag. 15. Vindiciarum, argumentando ex lcg. 26. §. 6. adduxerim Harme-nopylum, ut ostenderem, pei leges xii. Tabula-rum admissas fuisse usuras centesimas, quotquot sapiunt, dijudicent. Ne videar aliquid egisse, Gro-novius pag. 18. ita sciscit: Hæc vero quid ad cen-tesimam in omni fœnore? quid ad modum fœno-ris definitum lege xii. tabularum? Primum uter-que loquuntur de fœnore nautico, quod, quo tempore lex. xii. tabularum lata est, Romanis usu erat incognitum, quippe mare nondum expertis. Deinde uterque loquuntur de veteribus legibus, quibus excedere centesimam erat concessum. At lege xii. tabularum, si maxime in ea fœnus unci-arium sit centesima, concessum non erat, ut ea excederetur. Nec prodest hic capillum promitte-re & vaticinari, Tacito non exhiberi totum car-men men Legis, & forte in casibus quos tangit Impe- rator, per xii. tabulas, centesimas excedere licu- isse: quia, quod modo dicebam, nondum exer- cebant mare Romani. Denique neque Harmeno- polus VETERI JURE, sed τὸ πωλάιον. Hæc ad- versarius. Resp. 1. Fundamentum, quo hæc nitun- tur, est illud, quod Romani mare nondum exer- cerent, quo tempore Lex xii. Tabularum lata su- it: at falsum hoc est, & supra contrarium proba- tum fuit. 2. Non ego præcise ursi, per veteres Le- ges intelligendas esse Leges xii. Tabularum: Re- cognoscat adversarius, qui meretur Sycophanta haberi, mea verba: Scripseram pag. 15. Quid vetus jus, quid veteres leges, nisi, quæ Roma in cunis adhuc vagiente, vigebant, & præsenti pauperis reip. conditioni serviebant? Hactenus mihi sufficiebat, probasse, pro conditione Reip. sive florentis, sive afflictæ, usuras vel intendi, vel remitti. 3. At attendendo verba hæc: Veteribus legibus, quæ in d. l. 26. occurrunt, probabiliter intuli, pag. 16. respexisse Imperatorem Justinianum ad LL. xii Tabularum, quod passim audiant in jure Romano leges vetustæ, leges antiquæ, & lex antiqua. 4. Quam graphicus prævaricator sit, ostendit Gronovius, quando fingit Harmenopulum, per τὸ πωλάιον, aliud quid intellexisse, quam Duodecim, quasi vero, subintelligendo τὸ δίκαιον, æque hoc titulo non potuerit illas insignire, atque apud antiquos Latinos Jurisconsultos audiunt, jus antiquum, jus vetus, jus prisçum? 5. Nec vates sum, nec vatis filius, convenienter tamen intuli pag. 16. à Tacito totum legis carmen non fuisse exhibitum, quod de fœnore unciario loquebatur. Dignetur Lector ipsum Tacitum inspicere. Pag. 17. hominem proprio gladio jugulaveram, adductis longè meliori fide, quàm ipse agit, proprijs ipsius verbis, ex quibus cuivis liqueat, volentem nolentem Gronovium, coactum fuisse fateri, usuras aut majores, aut minores exsolvi, prout aut plus, aut minus pecuniæ inter cives alicujus rep. occurreret. Ne videatur, vapulasse, quàvis tergum oftreatum habeat, peponis cerebellum elabendi bellam ratiunculam ostendit. Ita autem loquitur pag. 18. & 19. Adscribit mea verba, & si quod magno ære conducere studuisset, non æque commodum testimonium se nancisci potuisse prædicat. Sunt autem ista: Fœnoris modus crescit minuiturve partim protempore proque modo pecuniæ, quæ inter homines versatur, partim pro fide illorum, qui mutuum petunt, &c. p. 72. Et gloriatur: Quid æque apposite pro statuminando meo argumento (circa quod adversarius frustra lacertos fatigavit) dici posset? Stuporem an malitiam appellem incredibilem? Ego narro, quid more plerumque fiat, quidque factum sit Romæ, sine lege & aliquando quando contra legem: ille centesimam vetustissi-ma Decemvirorum lege statutam, quod nunquam ei concessi, persuasum venit: & tamen testimo-nium illi praebui. Hæc iterum Adversarius. Resp. 1. Sed hactenus hoc solum inter nos controvertebatur, an non juxta remp. sive locupletio-rem, sive minus locupletem, usuræ aut grandes-cant, aut minuantur. Hoc negaverat in Ανεξηγησει priori pag. 6. ita scribens: At ego, quan-tum recordor de historia civitatum, quas olim hæc pestis corripuit, reperi, non perinde angustias familiares, quàm corruptos mores intendisse fœnus: non quo major apud omnes, atq; ipsius etiam reip. paupertas, apud alios pecunia, & quo major apud utrosq; opum sitis & ostentatio. Ut ostenderem hominem mendacem esse, utpote sibi contradicentem, bona fide exhibueram sua verba ex pag. 72. quæ cum ipse ausus fuerit imprudenter pro suis hoc loco iterum agnoscere, merito contra ipsum Deum atque homi-num fide inclamare possem, si idè Genius me regeret.
units.tr: IX. How aptly I adduced Harmenopulus on page 15 of the Vindiciae, arguing from law 26, §6, to show that under the laws of the Twelve Tables interest at one per cent was permitted, let all who have sense judge. Lest I seem to have achieved nothing, Gronovius on page 18 asks: "But what has this to do with the hundredth on every loan? What has it to do with the rate of interest fixed by the law of the Twelve Tables? First, both speak of maritime loans, which was unknown to the Romans at the time the law of the Twelve Tables was passed, since they had not yet tried the sea. Second, both speak of old laws, under which it was permitted to exceed the hundredth. But under the law of the Twelve Tables, even if the unciarian interest in it is one per cent, it was not permitted to exceed it. Nor does it help here to split hairs and prophesy that Tacitus did not give the whole text of the law, and that perhaps in the cases the Emperor touches on, under the Twelve Tables, it was permitted to exceed the hundredth, because, as I have just said, the Romans did not yet work the sea. Finally, Harmenopulus does not speak of the OLD LAW but of τὸ πωλάιον [the sale]." Thus the adversary. Reply: 1. The foundation on which these claims rest is that the Romans did not yet work the sea at the time the Law of the Twelve Tables was passed. But this is false, and the contrary was proved above. 2. I did not say precisely that by the old laws the Laws of the Twelve Tables were to be understood. Let the adversary, who deserves to be counted a sycophant, recognise my words. I had written on page 15: "What is the ancient law, what are the ancient laws, except those which were in force when Rome was still in swaddling clothes and served the present condition of the poor commonwealth?" Thus far it sufficed me to have proved that, according to the condition of the commonwealth, whether flourishing or afflicted, interest is either increased or remitted. 3. But attend to these words: "I have probably inferred, on page 16, that by the old laws which occur in the said law 26, the Emperor Justinian referred to the Laws of the Twelve Tables, because everywhere in Roman law one hears of 'old laws, ancient laws, and the ancient law'." 4. How much of a deceiving scribbler he is, Gronovius shows when he feigns that Harmenopulus by τὸ πωλάιον understood something other than the Twelve, as if, by understanding τὸ δίκαιον [the law], he could not equally have designated them by that title, just as among the ancient Latin jurists they speak of "ancient law, old law, primitive law"? 5. I am neither a prophet nor a prophet's son, yet I rightly inferred on page 16 that Tacitus did not give the whole text of the law, since it spoke of unciarian interest. Let the reader deign to look at Tacitus himself. On page 17 I had slain the man with his own sword, adducing, with far better faith than he himself shows, his own words, from which it is clear to anyone that Gronovius, willing or unwilling, was forced to confess that interest is paid either higher or lower according as more or less money is available among the citizens of a commonwealth. Lest he seem to have been beaten, although his back is bared, he shows a pretty little trick for scooping out the pumpkin's brain. "But he speaks thus on pages 18 and 19. He quotes my words and says that if he had wished to hire something at a great price, he could not have found a more convenient witness." These are the words: "The rate of interest rises or falls partly with the time and in proportion to the money circulating among men, partly with the credit of those who ask for a loan", and so on, p. 72. And he boasts: "What could be said so aptly to establish my argument (on which the adversary has vainly wearied his arms)?" Shall I call it stupidity or malice, incredible as it is? I relate what commonly happens and what has happened at Rome, without law and at times against law; he has persuaded himself that the hundredth rate was established by the most ancient law of the Decemvirs, which I never granted him, and yet I offered him testimony. "Again these things, says the Adversary." Reply: 1. But so far the only point in dispute between us was whether interest does not rise or fall according to whether the commonwealth is richer or less rich. This he had denied in his earlier Explanation, page 6, writing thus: "But I, as far as I remember from the histories of the states which this plague once seized, have found that the desire for usury was caused not so much by family straits as by corrupt morals: not because poverty is greater among all, even of the commonwealth itself, while money is held by others, but because the thirst and display of wealth is greater on both sides." To show that the man is a liar, since he contradicts himself, I had in good faith quoted his words from page 72. Since he has now dared, imprudently, to acknowledge them again here as his own, I could rightly cry out against him, appealing to the good faith of God and men, if my genius were guiding me.

units.la: Obtestor solummodo illos, qui hæc legent, prio-rem Gronovii Ανεξηγησιν inspicere dignentur & loca, quæ ut adversantia exhibui, inter se com-ponere diligenter. Quod si impetraverim, certò scio judicaturos, homini imprudentissimo nihil superesse præsidij, quam ut nomen profiteatur inter fanaticos Weigelianos, qui ut portentosam finxefinxerunt scholam Lucis, seu Spiritus Sancti; opposita Scholae tenebrarum, seu carnis; ita ulterius commenti fuerunt, juxta illius decreta; Duo contradictoria simul vera esse posse. 2. Generalia Gronovij verba frustra limitantur, nam in illis nulla Romae, aut Romanae reip. mentio occurrit. Ego vero argumentabar, à civitatibus, seu Rebuspublicis in communi consideratis ad Romanam. Inferendo, verosimile esse, Romae idem contigisse, quod in tot alijs civitatibus & olim & hodie obtinuit, & obtinet. 3. Frustra adDecemvirales LL. provocat, petit quippe principium, quòd agatur de earundem explicatione, dubiam significationem admittente illo vocabulo, quo usurae quantitas definita est. 4. Atque per unciarium foenus, cujus in XII. fit mentio, intelligendam esse Centesimam, ita probavi: Quod cum in alijs rebuspublicis, si pecuniae fuerit inopia, foenus intendi consueverit, non dubitare licere, quin hoc Romae quoque contigerit, observatumque fuerit, à prudentibus legislatoribus,
units.tr: I beg only those who read these things to deign to look at Gronovius's earlier Explanation and at the passages I set out as contradictory, and to compare them carefully with one another. If I obtain this, I know for certain that they will judge that this most imprudent man has no defence left except to profess his name among the Weigelian fanatics, who, having fabricated the portentous school of Light, or of the Holy Spirit, opposed to the school of darkness, or of the flesh, went on to devise, according to its decrees, that "two contradictory things can be true at the same time." 2. Gronovius's general words are vainly limited, for in them no mention of Rome or of the Roman commonwealth occurs. But I was arguing from states, or commonwealths considered in general, to the Roman one, inferring that it is probable that what happened, and still happens, in so many other states, both formerly and today, also happened at Rome. 3. He vainly appeals to the Decemviral laws; he begs the question, since the matter is their interpretation, the term by which the amount of interest was defined admitting a doubtful meaning. 4. That by the unciarian interest mentioned in the Twelve Tables the hundredth is to be understood, I proved thus: since in other commonwealths interest has customarily been increased when money was scarce, there is no doubt that this also happened at Rome, and was observed by prudent lawgivers,

units.la: XI. Ut ad incitas adversarium redigerem, adducto testimonio Dionis Cassij ex lib. 5. Hist. probaveram pag. 17. Vind. Romae quoque, pro modo pecuniae, aut abundantis, aut deficientis, usuras aut grandiores, aut minores solutas fuisse. Tantus Historicus ne faveat, pag. 19 sequentia verba conglobat: Sed sacra anchora est Dion, qui notavit, post Actiacum Octavij triumphum, τὰ δανεισματα ἀγαπητῶς ἐπὶ, δεχμῆ ὠφόπεσον ὀῦα, τότ' ἐπὶ τῷ τεμπμοεῖῳ αὐτῆς γεγενῆσθαι. Et ne hoc sine Thrafone transeat: Si aliud non haberem,solus hic locus Hectori no-ftro papiraceo æternum prostituendo sufficeret.
units.tr: XI. To drive the adversary into a corner, having adduced the testimony of Dio Cassius from book 5 of the History, I had proved on page 17 of the Vindiciae that at Rome too, according to the amount of money, whether abundant or lacking, interest was paid either higher or lower. So that the historian may not favour him, on page 19 he heaps up the following words: "But Dio is a sacred anchor, who noted that after Octavius's triumph at Actium, loans were eagerly [...] and that this happened at that time in the temple of..." [τὰ δανεισματα ἀγαπητῶς ἐπὶ, δεχμῆ ὠφόπεσον ὀῦα, τότ' ἐπὶ τῷ τεμπμοεῖῳ αὐτῆς γεγενῆσθαι]. And lest this pass without a flogging: "If I had nothing else, this one passage would suffice to prostitute our paper Hector for ever."

units.la: O te Bollane cerebri felicem, an infelicem dicam,fi quæ jactas, credis, quam simulas spem, habes! Ubi hic de jure? ubi de legibus, aut tabulis duodecim? Hæc ille. Resp. 1. O te, Sycophanta, frontis infelicem! Qui integrum Dionis locum non addu-xifti, è quo luce meridiana clarius patet, post triumphum Actiacum Octavij Augusti, tantum pecunia in urbem delatum fuisse, ut fœnus, quod antea denario pendebatur, ad trientem ejus reciderit? Hoc solum urgebam. 2. Hactenus inter nos controvertebatur, an pro ratione pecuniæ, cujus resp. aut est inops, aut qua abundat, usuræ vel augeantur, vel minuantur. Hoc Romæ quoque contigisse, cum ex Dione Cassio constet, hactenus pro me est confectum. 3. Frustra jus, leges, & duodecim tabulas Adversarius crepat, cum hactenus hoc inter nos controversum non fit. Deinceps disquirendum fuerit, an non Legislatores, occupati in ordinandis usuris juxta leges, attendere consueverint, quantum in civitate pecuniæ occurrat, aut saltem attendere debuerint: simul quoque fortunas civium. Unde scripseram:
units.tr: O you Bollanus of the brain, happy or unhappy shall I call you, if you believe what you boast and have what you pretend to hope! Where is the law here? Where are the laws, or the Twelve Tables? "So he." Reply: 1. O you sycophant, unhappy in your brazen face! You did not adduce the whole passage of Dio, from which it is clearer than midday light that after Octavius Augustus's triumph at Actium so much money was brought into the city that interest, which had earlier been paid at a denarius, fell to a third of that. This alone was what I was urging. 2. Thus far it was disputed between us whether, according to the amount of money in a commonwealth, whether it is poor or abounding, interest is either increased or diminished. That this also happened at Rome, since it is established from Dio Cassius, has so far been settled in my favour. 3. The adversary vainly rattles on about law, statutes and the Twelve Tables, since so far this has not been in dispute between us. Next it must be inquired whether legislators, occupied in regulating interest by law, have not customarily attended, or at least ought to have attended, to how much money there was in the state, and at the same time to the fortunes of the citizens. Whence I had written:

units.la: XII. pag. 13. Magistratus quàdo leges de fœnore ferunt, non modò conditione suorum civium attende-re, re solent, verum etiam ijs, qui pecunia sua usum, stipulando usuras, aliis concedere possunt, sic succurrunt, ut semper inveniantur, qui in illa mutua danda, nolint esse difficiles. Contra quae pag. 20. sic ferox adversarius insurgit: Primum, quae hic diversitas & differentia civium & illorum, qui pecuniae suae usum, stipulando usuras alijs concedere solerent? Nunquid igitur foenera-tores, non erant cives? immo civium optimi & praestantissimi. Deinde haec ut plurimum vera sunt de illis Magistratibus, qui jure suo parentibus & tranquillis praecipiunt, quid facere debeant: non in illis, qui rogant tantum, cum in populi potesta-te sit jubere legem, in quo pars multo maxima se foenore gravatam sentit. Eandem legem de uncia-rio foenore, quum a M. Duillio & L. Moenio, alte-ro & octogesimo anno, postquam tulerant eam decemviri, repeteretur, quod jam scilicet ejus ἡ λόγος δὲ ἀργύριος, haud laetam Patribus fuisse, scribit Livius lib. VII. cap. XVI. Cur haud laetam potissimum Patribus? quia in his erant maximi foeneratores, & quaestus iste minimus. Et quia haud laetam Patribus, intelligimus quàm di-ligenter observarint attenderintque hi legislatores, quod adversarius contendit. Hactenus Gronovius. Quoniam pag. 20. scripseram, laticlavios quoque & augusticlavios per foeneratores suam pecu-niam collocasse: ne valeat, pag. 22. sic intonat:
units.tr: XII. p. 13. When magistrates enact laws about interest, they are accustomed not only to attend to the condition of their citizens, but also to provide for those who can lend the use of their money to others at stipulated interest, so that there are always people found who are not unwilling to make such loans. Against this, at p. 20, my fierce adversary rises up thus: First, what is this difference and distinction between citizens and those who were accustomed to lend the use of their money to others at stipulated interest? Are moneylenders then not citizens? Indeed they are the best and most distinguished of citizens. Next, these things are for the most part true of those magistrates who by their own right prescribe to their parents and to the calm what they ought to do, not of those who merely ask, since it is in the power of the people to command the law, and in that case the greatest part feels itself burdened by interest. The same law on the unciarium foenus (twelve-per-cent interest), when M. Duillius and L. Moenius demanded it again in the eighty-second year after the decemvirs had passed it, was, as Livy writes in book VII, chapter XVI, already "and the matter of silver" [ἡ λόγος δὲ ἀργύριος], not pleasing to the Fathers. Why not pleasing, especially to the Fathers? Because among them were the greatest moneylenders, and that profit was very small. And from the phrase not pleasing to the Fathers we understand how diligently these legislators observed and attended to the matter, as my adversary contends. So far Gronovius. Since at p. 20 I had written that the laticlavii and augusticlavii also placed their money with moneylenders, in order to nullify this, at p. 22 he thunders thus:

units.la: Quibus verbis, ut & alibi, prodit se nescire, qui Romanis vocarentur Fœneratores. Imo ipsi Patres, ipsi nobiles, ipsi divites, ipsi boni viri in veteri historia, sunt & appellantur Fœneratores: non aliquod aliud genus hominum, quorum opera illi pecuniam suam collocarent. Erant quidem argentarij, mensarij, nummularij, penes quos depositas pecunias habebant: quibus & fœnerabantur aliquando; sed hic exiguus erat numerus præ multitudine illorum, qui per se ipsi fœnori darent. Hæc dictà pagina. Et quoniam homo meus, sibi in hac explicatione fœneratoris mirum quàm placet, instar cuculi eandem cantilenam recinit pag. 34. & 37. quando ita κοκκύζει: Aperit hic quoque, se ignorasse adhuc, quid essent in historia Romana fœneratores: & prorsus habuisse illos pro genere, his Lombardis, delicijs suis, simili. His namque solis, positam legem XII. tabularum ostendit, se opinari, verbis istis: si jure fœneratores, &c. Nunc singulis urbibus sufficit unus: at, Romæ sci-licet, ita frutificabat hæc tabes, tanta illorum multitudo fuit & gratia, ut essent materia discordiæ inter Patres & plebem. Fœneratores Romani, o bone, erant non alij quàm creditores, principes, nobiles, & optimi quique de plebe. Non tumultum fecit plebs propter pauculos, nescio quos nummularios, sed πενία πρὸς πλῆτον ἐξαπατᾶξε καὶ πατρανόμης πρὸς ἐπιφάνειαν, ut loquitur Dionyf. nyf. lib. 6. pauperum debitorum adversus nobiles & divites creditores, hoc est, fœneratores, erat motus. Pauci erant, qui per argentarios fœnera- bantur: pauci nummulârij: imo vix ulli illis tem- poribus, de quibus loquimur, quum nummus non effet argenteus: &, fi parum acciperent, qui ho- rum ministerio fœnerabantur, sibi habebant im- putandum, qui nihil acciperent, nisi contra legem. Hæc iterum χόχνυξ. Refp. I. Bonum factum, quod concedat paucos è locupletioribus Roma- nis per argentarios fœneratos fuisse. 2. Non in- vitus quoque concedo, quosdam è Patribus Con- scriptis, oblitos ordinis, atque legum, plura per fe- cula Romæ iniquo fœnore cives suos oppressisse, non tamen in propatulo, sed miras per artes, ut Tacitus loquitur lib. 6. Ann. cap. 16. Nam hic cogitare convenit, quod idemScriptor dicit eodem capite, Interea magna vis accusatorum in eos irrupit, qui pecunias fœnore auctitabant, ad- versum legem dictatoris Cæsaris, qua de modo addendi,,posfidendiq, intra Italiam cavetur; omissam olim, quia privato usui bonum publi- cum postponitur. Quis enim existimet,aliquem ex Patribus conscriptis, five per fe, five per procu- ratorem,fœnus contra leges exercere voluisse;quum jam olim Romæ verum fuerit, quod Cato dicit de R. R. sub initium: Majores nostri sic habuerunt, & ita in legibus posuerunt, furem dupli con- demna-
units.tr: By these words, as also elsewhere, he shows that he does not know who were called Fœneratores by the Romans. Indeed the Fathers themselves, the nobles themselves, the rich themselves, the good men themselves, in ancient history are and are called Fœneratores, not some other kind of men through whose work they placed their money. There were indeed bankers, money-changers and coin-dealers, with whom they had deposited their money, and by whom they were sometimes lent out at interest; but this number was small compared with the multitude of those who lent at interest themselves. Thus far the said page. And since my man is wonderfully pleased with this explanation of fœnerator, he repeats the same little song like a cuckoo at pp. 34 and 37, when he cuckoos thus [κοκκύζει]: Here too he reveals that he is still ignorant of what fœneratores were in Roman history, and that he has entirely regarded them as a kind, like his delights, the Lombards. For he shows that he thinks, from these words alone, that the law of the Twelve Tables, if the moneylenders (jure fœneratores), etc., applies only to them. Now one suffices for each city; but at Rome, of course, this sore flourished so much, and there was such a multitude and favour of them, that they were a cause of discord between the Fathers and the plebs. The Roman moneylenders, my good man, were none other than creditors, princes, nobles, and all the best men from the plebs. The plebs did not make a tumult on account of a few money-changers, I know not who, but, as Dionysius says in book 6, "poverty against wealth, and the fatherly against the appearance" [πενία πρὸς πλῆτον ἐξαπατᾶξε καὶ πατρανόμης πρὸς ἐπιφάνειαν], the movement was of poor debtors against noble and rich creditors, that is, fœneratores. Few were those who lent at interest through bankers, few the money-changers; indeed hardly any in those times of which we speak, when money was not yet silver; and if those who lent at interest through their agency received little, they had only themselves to blame, since they received nothing except against the law. Thus again the cuckoo [χόχνυξ]. Reply. First, a good point: he concedes that a few of the wealthier Romans lent at interest through bankers. Second, I also readily concede that some of the Conscript Fathers, forgetting their rank and the laws, oppressed their fellow citizens for many ages at Rome with unjust interest; yet not openly, but by wonderful arts, as Tacitus puts it in book 6 of the Annals, chapter 16. For here it is fitting to consider what the same writer says in the same chapter: Meanwhile a great force of accusers rushed in upon those who increased their money by interest, contrary to the law of the dictator Caesar, by which it is provided, within Italy, concerning the measure of adding and holding, a law long neglected, because the public good is postponed to private use. For who would suppose that any of the Conscript Fathers wished to practise usury contrary to the laws, whether in person or through an agent, since at Rome long ago it was true what Cato says at the beginning of his De Re Rustica: Our ancestors thought thus, and so they laid it down in the laws: that a thief is condemned to pay double, a moneylender fourfold.

units.la: 13 demnari, fœneratorem quadrupli, quanto pe-iorem civem existimaverint fœneratorem, quàm furem, hinc licet æstimare. Uni Catoni hoc tribuit Cicero lib. 2. de Off. sub finem: M. Cato olim interrogatus, nunquid fœnerari utile foret: Quid hominem, inquit, occidere? Putarim tamen rigidum veri antistitem Catonem, ita respondisse ex mente Majorum, quorum judicio plurimum deferebat. Quis vero in animum induxerit, Senatorij ordinis virum illud faẜtasse, quod omnium Quiritium judicio furto gravius habebatur? Nota ex Cicerone lib. 3. de LL. lex est, lata illis, qui Senatorio ordini accenseban-tur. Hic ordo vitio careto, cæteris specimen esto. 3. ὁ πάνυ Salmasius, abunde probavit, nomen τῆς δανειστῆς, ut & fœneratoris, in se μέσον, ut alijs quoque vocabulis accidit, in sequiorem significationem traductum fuisse. Eòque non est infamis fœnerator habendus, qui pro usu suæ pecuniæ, alijs mutuò datæ, justas duntaxat usuras (hoc est, eas, quæ legibus definitæ sunt) exigit, sed, qui legibus prævaricando plus exigit, quàm per illas permittitur. Hoc non licuisse Romæ Senatoribus citra infamiam, antehac contendi, atque etiamnum contendo: quibus nec licuisse fœnerari levioribus usuris, abunde probavi Vindic. Ser. pag. 20. Qui inter illos avari erant, exemplo & equitum, & aliorum, qui pecuniâ abundabant, pecuniam suam mensarijs credebant, atque cum illis contrahendo, fœne-
units.tr: 13 From this one may judge how much worse a citizen they considered a moneylender than a thief. Cicero attributes this to Cato alone in book 2 of De Officiis, near the end: When M. Cato was once asked whether it was profitable to lend at interest, "What," he said, "is it to kill a man?" Yet I would think that Cato, a rigid guardian of truth, answered thus in accordance with the mind of the ancestors, whose judgment he greatly valued. But who would have supposed that a man of the senatorial order would do what was regarded by the judgment of all Quirites as more serious than theft? Note from Cicero, book 3 of De Legibus, that there is a law passed for those who were counted in the senatorial order: Let this order be free of vice; let it be an example to the rest. 3. The most excellent Salmasius has amply proved that the name of the lender (δανειστής), like that of the moneylender fœnerator, was, as happens with other words too, in the middle sense [μέσον], transferred to a lower meaning. And so a moneylender is not to be held infamous who demands, for the use of his money lent to others, only just interest (that is, that which is defined by law), but he who, by transgressing the laws, demands more than is permitted by them. That this was not allowed to Roman senators without infamy I have contended before, and still contend; that they were not even allowed to lend at lower interest I have amply proved in my Vindiciae Serenae, p. 20. Those among them who were greedy, following the example of the knights and others who had plenty of money, entrusted their money to bankers, and by dealing with them lent at interest

units.la: Nota: text continues at the bottom, the last word "fœne-" is a catchword-like hyphenated line end. fœnerabantur. Facit huc lex 7. §. 2. ff. Depositi, ubi ita Ulpianus: Quoties foro cedunt nummularij, solet primo loco ratio haberi depositariorum, hoc est, eorum, qui depositas pecunias habuerunt, non quas fœnore apud nummularios, vel cum nummularus, vel per ipsos exercebant. Idem patebit ex Pauli Curculione, si quis aliquanto attentius instituerit expendere colloquium, quod intercessit inter Lyconem Trapezitam, atque Therapontigonum militem. Nec aliò referri potest querula Tranionis servi oratio Moftellaria act. 3. sc. 1.
units.tr: lent at interest. Ulpian's law in Digest 7, §2, De Depositi, bears on this, where he says thus: Whenever the money-changers withdraw from the forum, the account is usually first taken of the depositors, that is, of those who had money deposited, not of those who lent at interest with the money-changers or through them. The same will be clear from Plautus's Curculio, if anyone examines with some attention the conversation between the banker Lyco and the soldier Therapontigonus. Nor can the plaintive speech of Tranio the slave in the Mostellaria, act 3, scene 1, be referred to anything else:

units.la: Nunc Pol ego perij plane in perpetuum modum.
units.tr: Now, by Pollux, I am utterly ruined for ever.

units.la: Danista adest, qui dedit argentum fœnori, Qui amica est empta, quoq; opus in sumptum fuit.
units.tr: Here is a creditor who lent silver at interest, and the girl I bought as my mistress has also cost a great deal to keep.

units.la: Manifesta res est, nisi quod occurro prius, Ne hoc senex resciscat.
units.tr: It is a plain matter, unless I hurry to prevent it first, that the old man must not learn of this.

units.la: Ad quam orationem si diligenter Gronovius attendisset, pro imperio, quod præ stultitia Grammatica sibi arrogat, non compellasset me pag. 39. tali oratione: Excerpat locum: ego, unde patet, nec memini, nec reperio. Atqui patet ex ijs quæ adduxi? ideo enim à sene sibi metuunt, quod ejus pecuniâ, apud Danistam depositâ, amica & alia necessaria comparata essent. 4. Quòd plebs autem, aut verius, qui in plebe inopes agnoscebantur, tur, inviderent non modò fœneratoribus & equitibus, sed omnibus, qui censu prævalebant, fœneratores esse clamabant, si, quod crediderant, durius exactum venirent, debitores suos adducendo in nervum. Testis sit Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. 5. ubi agens de Latinorum legatis, qui Tarquinium Superbum reducere meditabantur, ita loquitur inter alia: τὸν πολιτικὸν Ἓς καὶ ἀφύλακτον ἐμπεχαιρῶνλο πόλεμον ἐξ αὐλῆς ἀναστῆσαι τῆς ῥώμης, ϕάσιν εισάγοντες τοῖς πένησι πρὸς εὐτόκιας, ἤδη δ' ὑπεκινεῖτο τὸ πολὺ τῆς δημοτικῆς μέρος, καὶ ἐνόει, μάλιστα δὲ τὸ ἀπρεγὸν μέρος καὶ ὑπὸ δανείων ἡναγκασμένον, μηκέτι τὰ κτήσεα τῷ κοινῷ Φερυπίζειν. ἃ γὰρ ἐμετρέχαλον ἐν τοῖς ἐ- ξεσίαις οἱ δανεί ζοντες, ἀλλ' εἰς δεσμὰς τὰ τῶν ὑπαχρέων ἀπῆγον σώματα καὶ ὥσπερ ἀγυρωνή- λοις ἕτως ἐχωνὸ. Conabantur vile & inexspectatum bellum in ipsa urbe concitare, irritatis contra divites pauperibus. jam enim magna pars plebis, præsertim egeni & oppressi fœnore, aliquantum commoti erant, ac pernicio-sas reip. cogitationes alebant, impotenter enim & immoderatè se gerebant fœneratores, & in nervum abducebant oberatorum corpora; quibus non aliter utebantur quàm emptitiis. Atque, hanc ipsam ob causam, populus potissimùm à Patribus recessit. Patet ex Sallustij libro primo Historiarū, ex quo insigne Fragmentum servavit Augustigustinus lib. 2. de Civit. Dei, cap. 18. in quo ita lego: Dein servili imperio Patres plebem exercere, de vita atq; tergo regio more consule-re, agro pellere, & cæteris ex partibus soli in imperio agere. Quibus sævitijs & maxime fœnoris onere oppressa plebs, cum assiduis bellis tributum simul & militiam toleraret, armata montem sacrum atq; Aventinum insedit. Si Gro-novium audiamus, & fœnus levissimum fuisse cogitemus, non tam hoc ipsum, quam sors & creditum tumultuantem plebem gravabat, inde & Titus Largius apud Halicarnassæum lib. 6. huic exprobrat, quod voluerit δὶ ἀεπαγῆς ὑπηεσίαν ἐκ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τῆς ἐπιθυμίας, per rapinas cupiditatibus suis de alieno satisfacere. atque idem Largius caussam seditionis ejusdem exponens, totam plebem are alieno demersam esse, pronunciat apud Liv. lib. 2. cap. 29. eoque non modo negabat, se fœnus exsoluturam esse, sed & creditū: atque, ut videretur hoc cum ratione facere, ingeminabat identidem quam duriter habita fuisset, non modò propter æs alienum à creditoribus suis; (inter quos, multos ex senatoribus & equitibus fuisse, non licet ambigere) sed ab ipso quoque Senatu, qui & tributum exigebat, & militare compelle-bat. signanter Florus lib. 1. cap. 13. Prima discor-dia ob impotentiam fœneratorum: quibus in terga quoq; serviliter sævientibus, in Sacrum monmontem plebs armata secessit. Aurelius Victor, ubi agit deMenenio Agrippa, nec fœnoris nec verberum meminit, sed duntaxat dicit: cum populus à Patribus secessisset, quòd tributum & militi-am non toleraret. Certo argumento, plebem non tam ingemuisse sub onere fœnoris, quàm æris alieni, contracti cum locupletioribus, à quibus durissimè exercebatur. 5. Ut probet, fœnus unciarium, utpote exile nimis, (at juxta υπόθεσιν in proprio cerebello cusam, eique ad modum characteris, qui deleri non potest, impressam) displicuisse senatorii ordinis viris, urget Livij verba lib. 7. cap. 16. locus, qui integre adducendus fuisset, ita habet: Haud æque Patribus lata insequenti anno C. Marcio, C. Mænio consulibus, de unciario fœnore à M. Duillio, L. Mænio tribunis plebis rogatio est perlata: & plebs aliquanto eam cupidius scivit, accepit. At, ô bone vir, senatum non offendit hæc rogatio de unciario fœnore, quasi hoc leve nimis effet, sed, quòd tribuni Plebis sibi potestatem arrogaffent definiendi usurarum modum. Plebs verò queri non sustinuit, (insigne licet onus agnoscendum fit unciarium fœnus, ex nostra sententia centesimæ æquale) quod per suos Magistratus usuras adeo grandes solvere compelleretur. Ideo signanter Scriptor addit, (quæ verba similiter Syccophanta expendere debuisset) quòd plebs rogationem eam aliquanto cupidius scive-rit. rit, acceperitq. Dicit cupidius, quia propter fœnoris unciarij magnitudinem antea Decemviris offensa, obliviscebatur hoc tempore querelarum suarum, quòd Tribuni plebis, æque atque Decem-viri,gnari, quantum usurarum pro præsenti statu reip. solvendum esset, legem in XII. Tabulis comparentem, peculiari Plebiscito confirmassent. 5. Quàm judicio destituatur,porro Adversarius ostendit;addens non fuisse Romæ in potestate Senatus,legě aliquam,æri incisam, publice proponere, nisi populus eandem jussisset. Quamdiu libera resp. fuit, libenter concedo : at, indignor, quod hoc applicet ad leges Romæ de fœnore latas. Certè nulla ratione favere potest præconceptæ ipsius opinioni,de fœnore unciario, LL. XII. Tabb. probato. Nam populus, ut ratas esse jussit XII. Tabularum LL. ita speciatim illam quoque probavit, quæ de fœnore Vnciario agebat. Liv. lib. 3. Cum ad rumores hominum, de unoquoq; legum capite edito, sa-tis correƈta viderentur, Centuriatis Comitijs decem Tabularum leges perlata sunt. Quod distinƈtius explicat Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. 10. Antiq. Rom. ita per interpretem loquens: Ubi leges scriptæ visæ sunt, satis bene habere, primùm coaƈto senatu, nemine amplius eas leges reprehendente, senatusconsultum de ipsis fecerunt. Deinde populo ad Comitia Centuriata convocato, Pontificibus, Auguribus,alijsque sacerdotibus præ-sentibus, &re divina ex eorum præscripto de mo-re re facta, centurias in suffragia miserunt. Leges autem plebiscito quoque confirmatas, & in æreis columnis incisas, in loco fori maximè conspicuo, ordine dispositas proposuerunt- Hactenus Dionysius. Eat nunc Gronovius, atque præsuppo-nendo, populum non probaturum fuisse illam in XII. Tabb. legem, quæ de fœnore unciario agebat, si hoc grande fœnus haberi debuisset; consensisse, in solutionem ejusdem fœnoris, cum a Tribunis plebiscito scisceretur, adeoque agnoscendum esse fœnusculum, quòd rogatio illa Patribus haut læta fuerit. Apagesis hominis præ pertinaci superbia delirantis nugas, quæ gerras Siculas multis ineptiarum momentis excedunt! 6. Non potuit verò hæc chartis illinere, nisi & calumniaretur; Lombardos (ad hos pertinent majorum quoque urbium in Hollandia magistratus) delicias meas vocando. Sed cur magis meæ deliciæ agnosci debent, quàm tot Theologorum, imo variarum Synodorum. Fateor, me ex primis, caussæ ipsorum patrocinatum fuisse in Belgio, quòd existimarem per summam iniquitatem injuria effici, quibusdam Theologis, opinionis præconceptæ nimium tenacibus. Cæteroquin, mihi cum illis nec feritur nec metitur, profiteorque, ex ordine illorum, me vix duos tresve vel de nomine nosse, &, cum uno duntaxat viro docto & bono (quales utinam patria multos haberet!) commercium literarum aliquando coluisse quod à longo quoq; tempore utrimq; intermissum sum atq; hic quoque superiori anno mortuus est.
units.tr: If Gronovius had attended to this speech carefully, he would not, with the arrogance that his grammatical folly claims for him, have addressed me on page 39 in these words: He excerpts the passage: I do not remember, and I cannot find, where it shows this. But does it not show it from the things I have adduced? They feared the old man because his money, deposited with the Danista, had been used to acquire a mistress and other necessities. 4. But the common people, or rather those recognised as poor among the plebs, resented not only the moneylenders and the knights but all who excelled in wealth, and they cried out that the moneylenders were at it again whenever they had exacted a debt more harshly than they had believed, bringing their debtors into bondage. Let Dionysius of Halicarnassus be the witness, in book 5, where, speaking of the envoys of the Latins who were plotting to restore Tarquin the Proud, he says among other things: [τὸν πολιτικὸν ... πόλεμον ἐξ αὐλῆς ἀναστῆσαι τῆς ῥώμης, ϕάσιν εισάγοντες τοῖς πένησι πρὸς εὐτόκιας, ἤδη δ' ὑπεκινεῖτο τὸ πολὺ τῆς δημοτικῆς μέρος, καὶ ἐνόει, μάλιστα δὲ τὸ ἀπρεγὸν μέρος καὶ ὑπὸ δανείων ἡναγκασμένον, μηκέτι τὰ κτήσεα τῷ κοινῷ Φερυπίζειν· ἃ γὰρ ἐμετρέχαλον ἐν τοῖς ἐξεσίαις οἱ δανείζοντες, ἀλλ' εἰς δεσμὰς τὰ τῶν ὑπαχρέων ἀπῆγον σώματα καὶ ὥσπερ ἀγυρωνήλοις ἕτως ἐχωνό]. Their Latin version runs: they tried to stir up a vile and unexpected war within the city itself, inciting the poor against the rich; for already a large part of the plebs, especially the needy and those oppressed by debt, had been somewhat roused, and they were nursing dangerous designs against the commonwealth, since the moneylenders behaved violently and immoderately and dragged the bodies of debtors into bondage, using them no differently than slaves bought for the market. And for this very reason, the people withdrew chiefly from the Patricians. This is clear from the first book of the Histories of Sallust, from which Augustine preserved a notable fragment in book 2 of the City of God, chapter 18, where I read: Then the Patricians began to rule the plebs with servile authority, to decide about their lives and backs in the manner of kings, to drive them from their land, and to act alone in power in all other respects. Oppressed by these cruelties, and above all by the burden of usury, while bearing both tribute and military service at the same time through constant wars, the plebs armed themselves and occupied the Sacred Mount and the Aventine. If we listen to Gronovius, and suppose that the interest was very light, it was not so much the interest itself as the principal and the loan that burdened the restless plebs. Hence Titus Largius, in Halicarnassensis book 6, reproaches him for wishing to satisfy his desires from another's property by plunder [δι' ἁρπαγῆς ὑπηρεσίαν ἐκ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τῆς ἐπιθυμίας]. And the same Largius, explaining the cause of the same sedition, declares in Livy, book 2, chapter 29, that the whole plebs was sunk in another's money; and he not only denied that he would pay the interest, but also the principal. And so that he might seem to act with reason, he repeatedly insisted how harshly he had been treated, not only on account of the debt to his creditors (among whom, that there were many senators and knights, no one may doubt), but also by the Senate itself, which both exacted tribute and compelled military service. Florus, book 1, chapter 13, is especially clear: The first discord arose from the power of the moneylenders, who raged like slave-masters against the backs of the debtors, and the armed plebs withdrew to the Sacred Mount. Aurelius Victor, where he treats of Menenius Agrippa, mentions neither interest nor blows, but says only: when the people had withdrawn from the Patricians, because they could not endure tribute and military service. This is a sure argument that the plebs groaned not so much under the burden of interest as under the debt contracted with the wealthier men, by whom they were treated most harshly. 5. Next, to prove that the uncial interest, as being too slight (but according to his hypothesis, forged in his own little brain and stamped on it like an indelible mark), displeased the men of the senatorial order, he presses the words of Livy, book 7, chapter 16. The passage, which ought to have been cited in full, reads thus: Not equally pleasing to the Patricians, in the following year, under the consuls Gaius Marcius and Gaius Maenius, a proposal concerning uncial interest was brought forward by the tribunes of the plebs Marcus Duillius and Lucius Maenius; and the plebs, somewhat more eagerly, voted for it and accepted it. But, my good man, this proposal about uncial interest did not offend the Senate as if it were too light, but because the tribunes of the plebs had arrogated to themselves the power of fixing the rate of interest. The plebs, however, did not endure complaining (although the uncial interest, by our reckoning equal to one per cent a month, is a notable burden to acknowledge) that they were compelled to pay such great interest through their own magistrates. Therefore the writer adds, pointedly (words which the sycophant ought likewise to have weighed), that the plebs voted for that proposal somewhat more eagerly, and accepted it. He says more eagerly because, offended before by the magnitude of the uncial interest under the Decemvirs, they now forgot their complaints, since the tribunes of the plebs, just as the Decemvirs, knowing how much interest was to be paid under the present state of the commonwealth, had confirmed by a special plebiscite the law appearing in the Twelve Tables. 5. How far he is destitute of judgement the adversary further shows, adding that at Rome it was not within the power of the Senate to publish publicly any law engraved in bronze unless the people had ordered it. As long as the commonwealth was free, I readily concede this; but I am indignant that he applies it to the laws concerning interest passed at Rome. Certainly he cannot by any reasoning favour his own preconceived opinion, which approves the uncial interest in the Laws of the Twelve Tables. For the people, as they ordered the laws of the Twelve Tables to be ratified, so also approved specifically that law which treated of uncial interest. Livy, book 3: When, from the rumours of men, each chapter of the laws had been published and seemed sufficiently corrected, the laws of the ten tables were passed by the Centuriate Assembly. Dionysius of Halicarnassus explains this more clearly in book 10 of the Roman Antiquities, speaking through an interpreter: When the written laws seemed sufficiently good, first, having convened the Senate, and no one any longer finding fault with those laws, they made a senatus consultum concerning them. Then, the people having been summoned to the Centuriate Assembly, with the Pontiffs, Augurs, and other priests present, and a sacred rite performed according to their prescription, they put the centuries to the vote. The laws, moreover, confirmed also by plebiscite and engraved on bronze columns, they set out arranged in order in the most conspicuous place of the forum. So far Dionysius. Let Gronovius now go on, and, presupposing that the people would not have approved that law in the Twelve Tables which treated of uncial interest, had this been meant to be a great interest; he agreed to the payment of that same interest when the tribunes decreed it by plebiscite, and so the small interest must be acknowledged, since that proposal was not pleasing to the Patricians. The absurd trifles of a man raving with stubborn pride, which outweigh the Sicilian cranes in a multitude of foolish points! 6. Nor could he have daubed these things on paper without also slandering the Lombards (to whom belong the magistrates of the greater cities in Holland as well), calling them my delights. But why should I be recognised as their delight more than so many theologians, indeed than various synods? I confess that I was among the first to defend their cause in Belgium, because I thought it a great injustice that some theologians, too tenacious of a preconceived opinion, should be injured. Otherwise I have no dealings or measures in common with them, and I declare that, of their order, I know barely two or three even by name; and that I once kept up a correspondence with only one learned and good man (would that our country had many such!), which has long since been interrupted on both sides, and he too died last year.

units.la: XIII. Quod solidè ostendissem p. 23. & 29. Livii locum ex lib. 7. qui ita habet: Etsi unciario fœnore levata usura erat, sorte ipsa oprimeban-tut inopes, nexumq; inibant; nulla ratione fave-re adversario, ipse, postquam convitiatus esset, pag. 27. hunc in modum fatur: Livius ipsa sorte posuit, Græcorum delicias secutus, quibus ἀῤῥος interdum est μόνῳ; velut, cum dicunt, ἀῤῥοι γὰρ ἡμᾶς ἐσμεν. Nec aliter Silius:
units.tr: XIII. Although I had shown solidly, at pp. 23 and 29, the passage of Livy from book 7 which reads: Although interest had been lightened to one twelfth, the poor were still crushed by the principal and entered into bondage, my opponent, who in no way favours his adversary's case, after abusing me, speaks thus at p. 27: Livy put ipsa sorte following the fondness of the Greeks, with whom ἀῤῥος [arrhos] sometimes means μόνῳ [monō], "only"; as when they say ἀῤῥοι γὰρ ἡμᾶς ἐσμεν [arroi gar hēmas esmen], "for we are ... alone". Silius does the same:

units.la: Ipsa quidem virtus sibimet pulcherrima mer-ces.
units.tr: Virtue itself is the fairest reward to itself.

units.la: Cogitandum, quum levata fœnore unciario es-set usura, id est, quum locupletiores non nisi unum annuum ex centenis percipere possent, iratos eos, subito & alieno debitorum tempore exegisse nomi-na (quod lege nulla erat vetitum) ut fundis potius mercandis, aut apud inquilinos & non cives socis-ve Italicos pecuniam suam majore fructu colloca-rent: ita in angustias adductos debitores, quum nec in arca quidquam nec versura solvendi copia esset, bonis exolutos & sorte intempestive restitu-enda obrutos. Sic solent auxilia reperta astu & malitia hominum, in perniciem vertere: & tale quid etiam Tiberio imperante accidit. Hoc igitur Li-vium dixisse accipient mentis compotes: Etsi ro-gatione Duillia perleves & tantum uncias centesi-marum sortis partium usuras pendebant, tamen vel solam & sine ullis usuris sortem solvendo, quod statim, vel ad brevem nimis diem, antequam tantum, quantum debebant, è fructibus suis aut operis refecissent, solutio instaret, evertebantur bonis, dein addictum corpus præbebant. Hæc Gronovius. Resp. 1. Usurpare merito mihi licet verba adversarij, quibus præter justam rationem meam responsionem elidere nititur pag. 48. Hoc verò garrire est, & nihil respondere. 2. Simus liberales & demus, ipsa forte idem esse, atque sola forte, non tamen evicerit, grave fuisse Romanis cum paupertate luctantibus, usuræ nomine ex centenis unum annuum solvere. 2. Oppresse-rint locupletiores egenam plebem sortem exigendo, hæc subsistitisset utcunque, si versuram facere potuissent. Libentissime centesimas usuras solvisset, suos modò agellos retinuisset. 3. Grandiori pecuniæ summæ solvendæ cum non sufficiant inopes, benivolos & minus difficiles creditores suos experiuntur; si ad diem usuras, grandiusculas quoque, solvant. Iudicet benivolus Lector, an non hic homo contra se ipsum sententiam dicat? Pro fœnore unciario, ex sua mente explicando, solicitaverat Tacitum, lib. 6. Annal. cap. 16. cujus locum cum expendissem circumspectè pag. 24. ipse, ut persuadeat nihil à me actum fuisse, pag. 24. & seq. verba multa effundit, nec tamen integrum Scriptoris locum exhibet, qui iterum adscribendus, ut pateat, quam dextre eum interpretetur Gronovius: vius: Sane vetus urbi fœnebre malum, & se-ditionum discordiarumq; creberrima caussa : eôq; cohibebatur antiquis quoq; & minus cor-ruptis moribus. Nam primò duodecim tabu-lis sanctum, ne quis unciario fœnore amplius ex-erceret, cum antea ex libidine locupletium a-gitaretur: dein rogatione Tribunicia ad sem-uncias redacta : postremò vetita versura, multisq; plebis scitis obviam itum fraudibus, quæ toties repressa, miras per artes rursum ob-oriebantur. Gronovius cum admodum urgeat voculam amplius, quæ in ipsa Lege occurrit,dicta pag. 28. sic loquitur: Etsi non plus uncia libra menstrua, una libra annua, solvebant in cen-tenas, tamen vel sola sorte obruebantur; o-stendit fœnus unciarium, genus usuræ perleve fuisse, & parum addens sorti. Resp. 1. Sed, si attendisset proxima Historici verba, mecum con-clusisset unciarium fœnus centesimæ æquivalere. Certè nemo præter Gronovium fuerit adeo de-mens ut credat, locupletes creditur os fuisse e-genæ plebi suam pecuniam, si unciarium fœnus, duodecima duntaxat centesimæ pars, ac proinde perleve fœnus fuisset? Locupletes avaros fuisse, ipse adversarius agnoscit. Tacitus addit,ante latas leges xii. Tabularum, fœnus ex libidine agitasse: credant ergo Judæus Apella atque Gronovius, il-los
units.tr: One should consider that, when interest had been lightened to one twelfth, that is, when the wealthier could receive only one year's interest out of every hundred, they were angered and suddenly called in their debts at a time not of their choosing (which no law forbade), so that they would rather invest their money in buying estates, or lend it at greater profit to tenants who were not citizens or Italian allies. Thus debtors were driven into straits: since there was neither money in the chest nor any means of borrowing to pay, they were stripped of their goods and crushed by the principal being demanded at an unseasonable time. So helpful inventions often turn to ruin through the cunning and malice of men, and something of the kind happened also under Tiberius.
