Let people of sound mind therefore understand that Livy meant this: "Although by the Duillian law interest was lightened and they paid only one twelfth of the principal, yet they were overthrown by their goods, even by the principal alone without any interest, when payment fell due immediately or within too short a day, before they had recovered from their produce or their work as much as they owed; then they gave up their bodies as bondsmen." Thus Gronovius. Reply 1. I may fairly use the words of my adversary, who, beyond all just reason, tries to evade my answer at p. 48: But this is mere chatter, and answers nothing. 2. Let us be generous and grant that ipsa forte is the same as sola forte; still it does not follow that it was burdensome for the Romans, who were struggling with poverty, to pay one year's interest out of every hundred as usury. 2. If the wealthier oppressed the needy plebs by demanding the principal, the matter would have stood somehow if they could have borrowed anew. They would most willingly have paid the hundredth as interest, if only they had kept their little fields. 3. Since the needy cannot find the larger sums to pay, they try their kindly and less difficult creditors, if they may pay the interest, however large, when due. Let the kindly reader judge whether this man is not pronouncing sentence against himself. To explain the interest of one twelfth in his own sense, he had called upon Tacitus, book 6 of the Annals, chapter 16. When I had weighed that passage carefully at p. 24, he himself, to persuade the reader that I had done nothing, pours forth many words at pp. 24 and following, and yet does not give the author's passage whole. It must be quoted again, so that it may be seen how skilfully Gronovius interprets it: Certainly usury was an old evil in the city, and the most frequent cause of seditions and discords; and it was restrained even in the older and less corrupt morals. For first, by the Twelve Tables it was sanctified that no one should exact more than one twelfth of interest, whereas before it had been driven by the caprice of the wealthy; then, by a Tribunician proposal, the rate was reduced to half that; lastly, borrowing again was forbidden, and many plebiscites were set against frauds, which, though often suppressed, kept breaking out again by wonderful arts. Since Gronovius presses hard on the little word amplius ("more"), which occurs in the Law itself and was discussed at p. 28, he speaks thus: Even if they did not pay more than one twelfth a month, or one pound a year, for every hundred, yet they were overwhelmed by the principal alone; this shows that interest of one twelfth was a very light kind of usury and added little to the principal. Reply 1. But had he attended to the Historian's next words, he would have concluded with me that unciarium fœnus is equal to the hundredth. Surely no one except Gronovius would be so mad as to believe that the wealthy lent their money to the needy plebs if the one-twelfth interest had been, as it were, merely the twelfth part of a hundredth, and therefore a very light usury? The adversary himself admits that the wealthy were greedy. Tacitus adds that before the laws of the Twelve Tables usury was driven by caprice. Let Judas Apella and Gronovius believe, then, that those men were willing to lend their money to men of doubtful credit at so small a rate of use?

units.la: os tantillo usum pecuniæ suæ hominibus dubiæ fidei credere voluisse? 2. Vrserat petulans adversarius, rationem ut redderem, cur Romæ fœnus omne abrogatum esset? Ego iterato inculcaveram postremaTaciti verba: Multisq; plebis scitis obviam itum fraudibus, &c. Quæ ne valeant, pag. 29. ita fatur: Tacitus hæc verba, quæ iste se iterum exhibere scribit, ponit, postquam jam vetitam versuram fuisse narraverat, & loquitur de eo, quod post illam vetitam tamen ad suam usq; ætatem factum sit, ut ea non possit accipi proprie fuisse caussa vetandi. Non igitur aliud significant ambo, (scil. Livius & Tacitus) quam, quod ne hoc quidem tam exiguum oneris usurarum plebs ferre posset, omne prohibitum fuisse. Resp. Prudenter, aut veriùs subdolé, si non nequiter factum à Gronovio, quòd totum Taciti locum non adduxerit. Nos bona fide illum repræsentavimus, atque ad quoscunque, qui hæc legent, provocamus, dignentur totum locum discutere, & prima verba, cum postremis conferre. Certe hæc verba: Sane Vetus urbi fœnebre malum, &c. quòd debeant componi cum ultimus, evincunt, Romæ omne fœnus abrogari debuisse, quòd fœneratores, ultra Sisyphum & Vlyssem fraudibus instructi, in ordinem redigi non possent.
units.tr: 2. My petulant adversary had demanded that I give a reason why all usury was abrogated at Rome. I had repeated again the last words of Tacitus: and many plebiscites were set against frauds, etc. To weaken this, he says at p. 29: Tacitus writes these words, which that man says he quotes again, after he had already narrated that lending at interest had been forbidden; and he speaks of what happened after that prohibition, even down to his own time, so that it cannot properly be taken as the cause of the prohibition. Therefore both writers (namely Livy and Tacitus) mean nothing other than that the plebs could not bear even this small burden of interest, and so all of it was forbidden. Reply: It was done prudently, or rather craftily, if not wickedly, by Gronovius, in that he did not quote the whole passage of Tacitus. We have presented it in good faith, and we appeal to whoever reads these pages to take the trouble to examine the whole passage and compare the first words with the last. Certainly the words Certainly usury was an old evil in the city, etc., when set alongside the final clause, prove that all usury ought to have been abrogated at Rome, since usurers, armed with frauds beyond Sisyphus and Ulysses, could not be brought into order.

units.la: XIV. Cum respondissem admodum apposite
units.tr: XIV. Since I had answered very aptly

units.la: pesite ad quaestionem ab homine meo propositam, cur, si unciarium foenus, centesimae respondere debeat, per sextantes, quadrantes, atque trientes inde non fuerit descensum: ipse pelves verborum profundit pag. 29. 30. & seqq. ut non modo mihi, sed & Lectori glaucoma procuret. Neque enim disputat ad lineas, sed glomerat quaestiunculas, quibus si responderem, me magis fatuum probarem, atque ipse est. Et tamen homo prae arrogantia phreneticus, attendendo majestatem sceptri Orbiliani, pag. 30. ita profatur: Quasi jus interrogandi non habuerim? Nihil responsione dignum occurrit, praeter illud, quod superba pertinacia dictavit. Unde pag. 31. contendit, viros laticlavios quoque, foenus non exercuisse per nummularios, sed, per dispensatores & procuratores suos. Quis vero medius terminus? Ciceroni, Livio, aliis faeneratores sunt ipsi locupletes. Qui mihi huic argumento similis esse videtur: Gronovius destinat collocare praegrandem pecuniae summam, cui cum multum adhuc adjiciendum sit, accedere debebunt, ex majoribus Hollandiae civitatibus plurimi novitij studiosi, qui, ut discant Justinum & Corn. Nepotem intelligere, non asses, sed unciales nummos argenti probae notae oblaturi sunt. Si attendatur exestimatio Ordinis Senatorij, & ea, quae jam antea diximus, luce meridiana clarius patebit, nullum in ordine amplissimo, usque adeo frontem perfricuisse, ut, per suos procuratores, usuras legibus vetitas, ex collocata pecunia exigere ausus fuerit, sed
units.tr: to the question my opponent raised, why, if an interest of one uncia should correspond to a hundredth, there was no descent from it through sextantes, quadrantes and trientes. He himself pours out a basin of words (pp. 29, 30 and following), so that he produces a cataract not only for me but also for the reader. For he does not argue in straight lines but heaps up little questions, and if I replied to them I would prove myself as foolish as he is. And yet the man, frenzied with arrogance and attending to the majesty of the Orbilian sceptre, speaks thus on p. 30: "As if I did not have the right to ask?" Nothing worthy of a reply occurs, except what his proud obstinacy dictated. Hence on p. 31 he contends that senators wearing the broad stripe also did not lend money through moneychangers, but through their stewards and agents. But what is the middle term? "For Cicero, Livy and others, the lenders are themselves wealthy men." He seems to me like someone who argues thus: Gronovius intends to place a very large sum of money, and much more still has to be added to it; very many eager young students from the greater cities of Holland will come forward, who, in order to learn to understand Justin and Cornelius Nepos, will offer not asses but uncial coins of silver of good standing. If the estimation of the Senatorial Order is considered, and what we have said before, it will be plainer than noonday light that no one in that most distinguished order was so brazen as to dare, through his agents, to exact interest forbidden by law from money he had placed out, but

units.la: K clanculum potiùs per nnmmularios, ut gratam Avaritiæ suæ victimam offerret,hoc peregisse. Quomodo constat, multos ex ipsis primoribus in Hollandia, iis,quos Adversarius per contemptum Lombardos vocat, pecuniam suam credere, ut grandiores usuras accipiant, dum ipsi (qui cæteroquin prohibere deberent) pecuniâ, atque fraudibus occulte illos instruunt, qui, ad LL. alias, juxta rationem compositas, severè exigendi forent. Nec tamen hi locupletes, atque simul purpurati hoc aperte agunt, per suos procuratores; sed insidiosè per alios: prout factum quoque fuisse Romæ à Senatorij ordinis viris, mihi quàm persuasum est. Ad locum vero Suetonij, ex vita Octavij adductum, atque cap. 39. hisce verbis comprehensum: Notavitque aliquos, quòd pecunias levioribus usuris mutuati, graviore fœnore collocassent: quod respondeteret, non invenit præter hoc; Qui hoc fecerunt, non nummularij erant, sed equites Romani. Concedo totum, ut ordinaria formula, in Scholis recepta,utar. Sed hoc probaverit, Equites hoc modo fœnus exeruisse, per suos procuratores, non vero per nummularios, (prout ego antea liquidò ostendi) & simul Tranquillo novam lucem attulerit. Quoniam putabam liquidam me ratione attulisse, cur locupletiores maluerint omni fœnore interdici, quàm leviori, & quod voto suo non satisfaceret, pecuniam suam argentarijs credere, pag. 32. & seq;multa verba profundit;quibus cũ nolim respondere, hominem meum in Hollandia viventem,tantum tum moneo, ut Amstelodamum abeat, atque inquirat, cur Dardanarij, imo & alij mercatores, sæpius recusarint quâ frumentum, quâ alias merces venum exponere, postquam superior Magistratus, ijs justum quoque pretium statuisset. Avaritia venenis malis imbuta, subdolè, si non possit plura converrere, audet quoque Dictatorium vultum induere, atque negare distractionem illarum mercium, quibus humana Societas vix carere potest, nullam aliam ob caussam, quàm quòd publica auctoritate justum pretium statutum fuerit, nec liceat pro arbitratu illud augere. Hæ artes perspectæ omnibus illis sunt, qui arcana mercaturę norunt. Nec earum ignari erant quâ Senatores quâ Equites Romani; (avarus diabolus semper fui similis fuit, ijsdemque artibus instructus) quibus quòd displicerent usuræ semisses, auctores fuerunt, omni ut fœnore interdiceretur; præsagiebant enim certò, tenuiores, qui absque fœnore agitare non poterant, legum repagula perrupturos esse, atque,ut subsidium paupertati domesticæ procurari posset, acturos esse cum argentarijs, qui omnes rogationes, quas populus sciverat, rumpere sciebant; atque, semper aliquam invenire rimam, ut in prioribus Vindicijs pag. 13. tũ prioris tum posterioris Edit. ex Plauti Curcul. act. 4. sc. 2. solidè probaveram. quod tamen adversarius subdolè dissimulavit, non âusus ferrum hoc arrodere.
units.tr: secretly, rather, through bankers, in order to offer this as a pleasing victim to his avarice. How do we know that many of the leading men in Holland, to those whom my opponent contemptuously calls Lombards, entrust their money so that they may receive larger interest, while they themselves (who ought otherwise to prohibit it) secretly supply these men with money and tricks, men who would otherwise be severely called to account under laws framed according to reason? Yet these wealthy men, who are also purple-clad, do not act openly through their own agents, but craftily through others; and I am persuaded that this was also done at Rome by men of the Senatorial order. As to the passage of Suetonius, quoted from the life of Octavius, chapter 39, comprehended in these words: "He noted that some, having borrowed money at lower interest, had lent it out at higher interest," he found nothing to answer except this: "Those who did this were not bankers, but Roman knights." I grant the whole of it, to use the ordinary formula received in the schools. But he would have to prove that the knights lent money in this way through their own agents, not through bankers (as I clearly showed before), and at the same time he would have brought new light to Tranquillus. Since I thought I had clearly shown the reason why the wealthier preferred that all interest be forbidden rather than a lighter rate, and why, since this did not satisfy their wish, they entrusted their money to money-changers, he at p. 32 and following pours out many words; to these I do not wish to reply, but I merely advise my man, who lives in Holland, to go to Amsterdam and inquire why the Dardanarii, and indeed other merchants, have often refused to sell grain or other goods, after the higher magistrate had fixed a just price for them. Avarice, imbued with baneful poisons, craftily, if it cannot sweep up more, dares also to put on a dictatorial face and to refuse the sale of those goods without which human society can scarcely live, for no other reason than that a just price has been fixed by public authority and it is not permitted to raise it at will. These tricks are known to all who understand the secrets of trade. Nor were the Roman senators or knights ignorant of them (avaricious devils were always alike and equipped with the same arts). When half-percent interest displeased them, they were the authors of a proposal that all interest be forbidden; for they foresaw clearly that the poorer folk, who could not carry on without interest, would break through the barriers of the laws, and that, in order to procure relief for domestic poverty, they would deal with the bankers, who "knew how to break all the enactments the people had passed," and who "always find some crack," as I had solidly proved in my earlier Vindiciae, p. 13 of both the earlier and later edition, from Plautus, Curculio, act 4, scene 2. Yet my opponent craftily dissembled this, not daring to gnaw at that iron.

units.la: XV. Sed imminet noster Hercules, vice ferulæ clava instructus, atque instar asini exuvijs leonis indu-ti, duti, pro imperio pag. 33. sic edicit: Atque ego duos auctores dabo, qui testatum faciant omnibus, hominem gnaviter ineptire. Hi erunt T. Livius & Appianus, ex quibus discimus hanc legem de non fenerando armis latam, quum post initum Samniticum bellum, qui Capua in hibernis erant relicti, conjurasent de illa urbe possidenda, interfectis incolis, & ubi sceleratum consilium prudentia C. Marcij Rutili consulis irritum fuit, metu quaestionis & poenarum, ingenti manu facta Romam armati contenderunt. His oppositus M. Valerius Corvus dictator cum justo exercitu, potius, quam civilem sanguinem misceri pateretur, & hanc, & alias indignas conditiones accepit, &c. Postea multa, quae ὐῖὐ ὐ, admisceť. Pag. vero 34. haec pergit ex Tripode suo depromere: Corvus veritus, ut suis militibus, magnam partem & ipsis are alieno gravatis, fides confiteret, senatui de omnibus per literas edocto auctor palam fuit novarum tabularum. Simul adducit locum Appiani, haut magis congruum, atque nani caleeus Herculi concinnus est: De suo insuper addit pag. 34. Tum & extortum, ne fenerari liceret. Legat Livij septimum extremum, &, quod de tertio Appiani superest in Excerptis Constantini Porphyrogeneta: ibi, quod ignorat, inveniet, & nullum locupletiorum & nummulariorum, quasi ranarum & murium, pugna locum. Resp. 1. O hominem impudentem, & fronte carentem! Extremae vero impudentiae indicium est, quod me ableget ad Livium & locum Appiani in ob-
units.tr: XV. But our Hercules looms over us, armed with a club instead of a rod, and clad in the skin of a lion like an ass; by his own authority, at p. 33, he decrees thus: "And I will give two authors who will make it plain to everyone that this man is foolishly clumsy. They will be T. Livy and Appian, from whom we learn that this law against lending at interest was passed under arms, when, after the Samnite war had begun, those who had been left in winter quarters at Capua conspired to seize that city, killing its inhabitants; and when their wicked plan was frustrated by the prudence of C. Marcius Rutilius, the consul, they, fearing inquiry and punishment, formed a great band under arms and marched on Rome." Opposed to them, M. Valerius Corvus, the dictator, with a lawful army, rather than suffer civil blood to be shed, accepted these and other unworthy conditions, etc. Afterwards he mixes in many things [...]. But at p. 34 he goes on to draw from his tripod the following: "Corvus, fearing that his soldiers, many of whom were burdened with debt, would fail in their pledges, openly advised the Senate, which had been informed of everything by letter, to enact new account-books." At the same time he adduces a passage of Appian, no more suitable, and it fits Hercules' boot as neatly as ... (a shoe). At p. 34 he adds on his own: "and it was wrung out so that it would not be permitted to lend at interest. Let him read the end of Livy's seventh book, and what remains of the third book of Appian in the Excerpts of Constantine Porphyrogenitus; there he will find what he does not know, and no place for a fight of the wealthy and the money-changers, like frogs and mice." Reply 1. O impudent man, without shame! But it is a sign of extreme impudence that he sends me away to Livy and to a passage of Appian, to be found in an obscure corner of a rare book.

units.la: obscuro angulo libri rarioris inveniendum. Provoco ad omnes, qui hec legent, dignentur Livium sub finem lib. 7. inspicere, & nihil, quod Adversario favere queat, invenient. Ipse Gronovius ostendit quoque, qua fide agat. si enim certus præsidij fuisset, equidem ipsa Auctorum verba adduxisset. 2. Concedo extortas fuisse Tabulas Novas: sed, pernego simul extortum fuisse, ne fœnerari liceret: Siquidem absque fœnore plebs licet onere æris alieni liberata, in futurum subsistere non potuisset. 3. Ubi dixi, aut scripsi, locupletiores cum nummularijs contendisse, seditiosos per latus nummulariorum locupletiorum fortunas petijsse, concedo; imo persuasum habeo: siquidem ignotum esse non poterat, Possidonios per argentarios pecuniam suam tenuioribus in fœnus dare. 4. At, quomodo hæc omnia faciunt ad evertendum illud, quod dixeram: locupletiores scil. & inter eos viros Amplissimos usos fuisse opera argentariorum, ut possent grandes usuras exigere? Pag. 34. more suo urget, ut indicem distincte locum Plauti in Mostellaria, ex quo pateat, locupletiores usos fuisse argentariorum opera in colligendis usuris ex pecunia, quam argentariis credidérant. At, cum ipse modo non adduxerit Livium, quo tamen ut tibicine niti videbatur; nolo quoque Plauti verba adducere. quæ ab omnibus & inveniri & legi possunt. Chartas ut conspurcaret, iterum contendit pag. 35. plebem non fuisse oppressam à fœneratoribus; sed, à locupletioribus ijsque nobilibus. At, rem actam agit, &, jam antea abundè respondi : judicet Le-ctor. Plebem verò per M. Valerium Corvum ære alieno solummodo exoneratam fuisse, testis est Aurel. Victor lib. de Vir. Illuftr. agens enim de Valerio, hæc habet: Hinc, cum ingens multitudo ære alieno oppressa, Capuam occupare tentaffet, & ducem sibi Quinctium necessitate compulsum fecisset, sublato ære alieno, seditionem compressit. Quæ pag. 36. mussitat de Manutio, plane aliena sunt, nec ad rem faciunt: ego pag. 36. libelli mei duntaxat innui, Manutium virum doctissimum, eandem, quam ego, de fœnore Vnciario fovisse sententiam: atque cum pag. 68. prioris Ἀνʼςξηγήσεως contentus fuerit dixisse: Nec Manutius rem, quam tractabat, intellexit, nec ille Manutium; ostendit hæc & similia fe congerere debuisse, ut colligeret ineptum, sed mole aliqua turgidum libellum, refponfionum solidarum quòd inops effet. Eòdem pertinent, quæ offendo eadem pag. Peccavi scil. quia censui unciarium & semunciarium fœnus Romæ grande onus fuisse. Non hoc dixi in universum, sed pro tempore & loco. Recognoscat ergo sua verba ex pag. 25. prioris sui Responsi: Petit exemplum ullius nationis, quæ adeo & argenti fuerit inops & usurarum impatiens, ut accipere fortem sub conditione restitu-endæ cum additamento annuo centesimæ partis recusaverit. Quærit quod habet, leges videlicet, quæ ostendunt plebem Romanam, hoc quoque, quod ille levissimum censet, grave duxisse. Quis Argus, hic sive loci, sive temporis mentionem fieri videt?
units.tr: I call on all who read these things to deign to examine Livy near the end of book 7, and they will find nothing that could favour my opponent. Gronovius himself also shows what faith he keeps; for if he had had a sure support, I would indeed have quoted the very words of the authors. 2. I grant that the New Tables were forced through; but I flatly deny that interest was at the same time extorted so that lending at interest would not be permitted. For if the plebs, freed from the burden of debt, could not have continued without interest in future. 3. Where I said or wrote that the wealthier contended with the money-changers, and that the seditious sought the fortunes of the wealthy by the side of the money-changers, I grant it; indeed I am convinced of it, since it could not be unknown that the Possidonii lent their money to the poorer through bankers. 4. But how do all these things help to overturn what I had said: namely that the wealthier, and among them the most distinguished men, used the services of bankers so that they could exact large interest? At p. 34 he urges, in his usual manner, that I should point out distinctly a passage of Plautus in the Mostellaria, from which it would appear that the wealthier used the services of bankers in collecting interest from money they had lent to bankers. But since he himself has not now quoted Livy, on which he seemed to lean as on a crutch, I am unwilling to quote Plautus's words either, which can be found and read by everyone. In order to foul the pages again, he contends at p. 35 that the plebs was not oppressed by the usurers, but by the wealthier and by nobles. But he is doing the thing over again, and I have already answered this fully: let the reader judge. That the plebs was relieved of debt only by Marcus Valerius Corvus is attested by Aurelius Victor, in his book on Illustrious Men; for speaking of Valerius, he says: "Hence, when a huge multitude oppressed by debt had tried to seize Capua, and had compelled Quinctius, against his will, to be their leader, he quelled the sedition by cancelling the debt." What he mutters at p. 36 about Manutius is entirely foreign and has nothing to do with the matter. At p. 36 I only hinted at my little book, that Manutius, a most learned man, held the same opinion as I did about unciary interest; and since at p. 68 of the earlier Explanation he was content to say: "Manutius did not understand the matter he was treating, nor did that man understand Manutius," he shows that he ought to have piled up these and similar things in order to produce a foolish but somewhat bloated little book, because he lacked solid replies. To the same point belong the things which I find again at the same page: "I erred, namely because I thought that unciary and semiunciary interest was a great burden at Rome. I did not say this in general, but for the time and place." Let him therefore recall his own words from p. 25 of his earlier Reply: "He seeks an example of any nation which was so short of silver and so impatient of usury that it refused to receive principal on the condition of repaying it with the addition of a yearly hundredth part. He asks what he has, namely the laws, which show that the Roman plebs considered this, which he thinks the lightest, to be a heavy burden." What Argus sees any mention here of place or time?

units.la: XVI. Pag. ead. sive 36. accedit ad considerationem novarum tabularum: atque initio, pro sua scil. ingenuitate & modestia, contendit me non intellexisse „quid tabulæ novæ essent, quòd dixissem, eas proponi consuevisse abillis, qui eodem ingenio erant praediti, quo Catilina: ipse scil. pag. 37: probaturus Romæ palam plebem eas sæpe petiisse à Senatu & Nobilibus: sed, quando ipse addit hæc verba, ante adductum Dionysii Halicarnassæi locum ex lib. 6. Quæ (scil. plebs) recedebat in montem sacrum; probat se esse misellum atque infelicem disputatorem, qui suo se gladio jugulat. Plebs enim in montem Sacrum discedens, seditiosam sese esse probavit. Audiat vel solum Florum lib. 1. cap. 23, alterà jam vice, ut testem laudandum, Prima discordia ob impotentiam fœneratorum: quibus interga quoque serviliter sævientibus, in Sacrum montem plebs armata secessit: ægreque, nec nisi Tribunos impetrasset, Menenij Agrippæ facundi & sapientis viri auctoritate, revocata est: Haut magis eum juvant Solon Atheniensis pag. 38. Theocles & Thrasonides Corinthij, Praxis Mitylenæus, pag. 39. & Agis Spartanus Lycurgo dignissimus pag. 40. & seq. Ex ipso enim illorum facto nihil aliud elicueris, quàm fuisse viros prudentes, qui in tempore voluerint plebem à consilijs, in seditionem prorumpere solitis, avertere, quacunque, eâque variâ ratione succurrendo ejusdem egestati. Verum siquidem est, quod dicit Antiphon Orat. 5. ita per Interpretem loquens: Pauperibus nova moliri confert. (τοῖς (τὰς ἀτυχίας νεωτερίζειν συμφέρει) Ex mutati-onibus enim miseriam suam mutare meditantur. Atque huc faciunt quoque Sallustij verba, quae ipse inauspicato pro se adducit, pag. 47. Saepe majores nostri, (inquit) miseriti plebis Romanae, decretis suis inopiae ejus opitulati sunt: ac novissime, memoria nostra, propter magnitudinem aeris alieni, volentibus omnibus bonis, argentum aere solutum est. Providebant enim viri prudentissimi, plebem, extrema inopia laborantem, gravia Reip. consilia inituram esse. Obstupesco vero ad hominis impudentiam, quod pag. 42. de Heracleotis ausus fuerit adducere locum Justini, illius scil. Justini, qui more Ascensiano explicatus, tantum lucri hactenus homini meo apportavit. Adscribam integrum Justini locum, quem mutilum Ipse adduxit. Occurrit ille lib. 16. Passi sunt (inquit) inter pluxima mala, etiam tyrannidem: siquidem cum plebs etiam novas tabulas, & divisionem agrorum divitum impotenter flagitaret, diu re in senatu tractata, cum exitus rei non inveniretur: ad postremum adversus plebem nimio otio lascivientem, auxilia a Timotheo Atheniensium duce, mox ab Epaminonda Thebanorum petivere. Utrisque negantibus, ad Clearchum, quem ipsi in exilium egerant, decurrunt. An non aperte hic locus pro me facit? Equidem manifesto evincit, plebem otio lascivientem, & novas res molientem, flagitasse novas tabulas (a Catilina quoque promissas) & divisionem agrorum divitum: quae Liv. lib. 32. pronunciat esse duas faces novantibus tibus res, ad plebem in Optimates accendendam? Ea tamen Gronovij cæcitas, dubium risu an miseri-cordia digna, ut hunc locum pro se adducere ausit. Nec Rhetores, Quintilianus, & Curius Fortunatianus, pag. ead. sive 42. adducti, succurrere possunt: proponunt enim casus, sive veros sive fictos, qui occasione tabularum novarum, Legum confultis proponi potuerint. Ergo confectum quoque est circa novas tabulas: quas cum à Cicerone quoque reprehensas fuisse pag. 27. innuissem, ipse, postquam multa inutilia verba profudisset, pag. 43. hæc subjicit; Cicero reprehendit novas tabulas? Et, quis non reprehendat, si potest alia ratione concordiæ consuli, & as alienum tolli? Quid factum sit, non quid utilius factu fuerit, quæritur. Sed, quod factum fuit, Cicerone teste, injustum censendum, & raro fieri solet, nisi turbata republica, atque ab illis, quibus idem cum Catilina Genius est.
units.tr: XVI. On page 36 of the same work (or 36 in the same edition) he takes up the question of the new account books (tabulae novae). At the start, out of his usual candour and modesty, he claims that I did not understand "what the new account books were", because I said that they were usually proposed by men endowed with the same character as Catiline. He himself, on page 37, sets out to prove that the plebs at Rome openly often asked the Senate and the nobles for them. But when he adds these words, before quoting Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 6, which (that is, the plebs) withdrew to the Sacred Mount, he shows himself to be a wretched and unlucky debater who cuts his own throat with his own sword. For the plebs, when they withdrew to the Sacred Mount, proved themselves seditious. Let him hear, if only from Florus, book 1, chapter 23, cited now for a second time as a witness worth quoting: The first discord arose from the power of the moneylenders, who raged slavishly even against the men's bodies; the plebs, armed, seceded to the Sacred Mount, and they were won back only with difficulty, and not until they had obtained tribunes, by the authority of Menenius Agrippa, an eloquent and wise man. Nor does Solon of Athens, on page 38, help him any more, nor Theocles and Thrasonides of Corinth, nor Praxis of Mitylene on page 39, nor Agis the Spartan, most worthy of Lycurgus, on page 40 and following. For from their deeds you can draw nothing except that they were prudent men who, in good time, wanted to turn the plebs away from the counsels they were accustomed to rush into sedition over, and to relieve their poverty by whatever varied means were available. It is true, as Antiphon says in Oration 5, speaking through an interpreter: It is in the interest of the poor to make revolutions. (τοῖς (τὰς ἀτυχίας νεωτερίζειν συμφέρει)) For by revolutions they plan to change their misery. And the words of Sallust, which he unluckily adduces against himself on page 47, also serve this point: Often, our ancestors (he says), out of pity for the Roman plebs, came to the aid of its want by their decrees; and most recently, in our memory, because of the great size of the debt, with all good men willing, the silver was paid off in bronze. For the most prudent men foresaw that the plebs, labouring under extreme want, would take up serious measures against the commonwealth. But I am astonished at the man's impudence, that on page 42 he dared to cite a passage of Justin, that Justin, namely, who, explained in the Ascensian manner, has so far brought my opponent so much gain. I shall set out the whole passage of Justin, which he cited mutilated. It occurs in book 16: They suffered (he says) among very many evils, even a tyranny; for when the plebs, not only demanding new account books but also the division of the rich men's lands, kept clamouring without restraint, and the matter had been long discussed in the senate without any outcome being found, at last, against the plebs running wild in excessive idleness, they sought aid, first from Timotheus, the Athenian general, then from Epaminondas of the Thebans. When both refused, they ran to Clearchus, whom they themselves had driven into exile. Does not this passage plainly favour me? Indeed it clearly proves that the plebs, wantoning in idleness and plotting revolution, demanded new account books (also promised by Catiline) and the division of the rich men's lands, which Livy, book 32, declares to be two torches for kindling the Optimates against the plebs, to those who would make changes in affairs. Yet such is Gronovius's blindness, worthy of laughter or of pity, that he dared to cite this passage in his own favour. Nor can the rhetoricians Quintilian and Curius Fortunatianus, cited on page 42, come to his aid: they propose cases, real or invented, which could have arisen from the new account books for the consultation of lawyers. So the matter of the new account books has also been settled. When I had hinted that they were condemned by Cicero too, on page 27, he himself, after pouring out many useless words, adds on page 43: Does Cicero condemn new account books? And who would not condemn them, if concord can be secured and the debt removed by some other means? What was done is asked, not what would have been more useful to do. But what was done, according to Cicero's testimony, must be judged unjust, and it usually happens only when the commonwealth is thrown into confusion, and by those for whom the same genius as Catiline's prevails.

units.la: XVII. Proximè pag. 43. & seqq. me laborat arguere ignorantiæ, quasi nescivërim, quid significet decidere besse vel quadrante. Verba hominis ambitiosi, qui hisce & similibus delitijs pasci solet, mea fide, hoc est bona, (cum Gronoviana, in exscriben-dis tum meis tum aliorum verbis sæpe deprehendatur pessima) primùm adducam: Dixi (inquit) secundò, hanc interrogationem adversarij confutari numero illarum civitatum, quæ besse aut quadrante deciderunt. Ad hoc ille: Quid ad rem? earum rectores, quantum oneris pro pecunia usu civibus suis imponi posset, prudenter attenderunt: Roma idem ,, idem factum jam dixi. Putavit nimirum besse aut quadrante decidere, esse, legem ferre, ut usura non sint justa, nisi quadrantes, aut besses: ut quum Roma ex unciario semunciarium foenus factum est, (quod ille contendit esse a centesimis ad semisses reductum:) & hanc prudentiam laudat magistratuum æstimantium, quid pro usu pecunia civibus imponen-dum sit. Sed discat, (NB.) decidere besse, Latine dici, ita cum creditore transfigere, ut sine ullis usuris, ne forte quidem integra, pro tota summa crediti recipiat duas ejus tertias. &c. Hactenus attentum me exhibui Auditore atque discipulum. Audiat porro superciliosus Doctor, me duodecennem scivisse, quid esset decidere cum creditore. Ipse, loco minervalis, vicissim ex me discat, non saltem decidi posse cum creditore juxta fortem, verum usuras quoq;, quae in stipulatum venerunt, atq; de quarum quantitate merito arbitratur Magistratus, si contingat innocuum debitorem, haut sua culpa, succumbere. Hanc decisionem secundum usuras respexi, quod existimarem, adversarium, eandem in animo habuisse, atque propius pertinet ad illud, quod inter nos controvertebatur. Nec per auctores, quos adducit, ignorantia mea probari poterit. Incipio a Paterculo, e quo haec verba exhibet: Valerius Flaccus auctor legis, qua creditoribus quadrantem solvi jusserat. Expendas initio, mi Lector, Gronovianam fidem, quam modo ut pessimam notavi, in citando Paterculo. Verba apud auctorem lib. 2. cap. 23. ita habent: In hu-jus jus locum suffectus Valerius Flaccus, TURPISSIMÆ legis auctor, quâ creditoribus quadrantem solvi jusserat: cujus facti merita eum pœna intra biennium consecuta est. Quòd augurarétur, illud turpissimæ, sibi adversari; Vir scil. bonus, & ingenuus scil. disputator Gronovius, subdolè, si non malitiosè, cum sequentibus verbis omisit. Velleium sibi verò adversari, & me ab ignorantia vindicare, discat ex τῷ παἰν Dn. Boeclero, (hic mihi ἀντιξι@ ἀνοῖν ξευνοβίων) qui in Indice ad Velleium, explicaturus verbum Quadrantis, sequentia habet: Id est, quartam partem, ita ut tres (crediti an usura NB) partes perirent creditori, quarta deberetur. Est hoc genus novarum tabularum. Quare Velleius turpissimam (NB) vocat hanc legem Valeriam, quippe quæ & manifestam haberet iniquitatem, & seditioso potius turbulentoque esset consilio à trib. pl. lata, quàm summæ ac inexsuperabili necessitati publicæ data. Jactet jam Gronovius pag. 44. inveniri populos, apud quos creditores coacti fuerint, fortem absque usuris recipere magna parte imminutam? Hoc equidem non dicit Paterculus: atque si alicubi hoc factum fuerit, pronunciat turpissimum esse, quod Noster homo, qui & Christianus atque Ecclesiæ filius censeri gestit, justum & pium esse censet. Qua fide Paterculum adduxit, eadem citat Suetonium: ut pateat Lectori, quàm veteratorie egerit, prius locū exhibebo, ut ab ipso pag. 45. exscriptus est. Julius (inquit) decrevit, ut debitores creditoribus satisfacerent per æstimationem possessionū &c. qua conconditione quarta pars fere crediti deperibat, teste Suetonio. Integer vero locus, adversans multoti- es Nostro homini, ita habet: De pecunijs mutuis, disiecta novarum tabularum exspectatione, qua exe- bro movebatur, decrevit tandem, ut debitores credi- toribus satisfacerent, per aestimationem possessionum, quanti quaeque ante civile bellum comparatae sent, de- ducto summa aeris alieni, si quid usurae nomine nume- ratum aut perscriptum fuisset: qua conditione quar- ta pars fere crediti deperibat. Mi DEus! quid mor- talibus non suadet superba pertinacia! Hic homo in propatulo, atque coram toto orbe, destinato consilio, iterato est falsarius, nullam aliam ob causam, quam, ne videatur impegisse, atque vere me ignorantia arguisse. Miseret me viri: verba interim Suetonij examine digna sunt. I. Quod Caesar Julius, Poplicola licet, & cui multi Marij inerant, disiecerit exspectationem novarum tabularum, atque, decreverit, ut debitores creditoribus satisfacerent: summam earundem tabularum injustiti- am arguit: simul Noster homo prostituitur, qui us- que adeo prolixe, pro earundem aequitate, digla- diatus fuit. II. Quoniam decisio cum creditori- bus facta fuit, usurarum quoque ratione habita, confirmatur mea sententia; atque, usuras plebi Ro- manae prae forte graves fuisse, manifesto patet. III. Ignorantia intoleranda Gronovij pellucet, qui hinc cognoscere potest, cum creditoribus decidi aeque secundum usuras (& quidem saepius) atque secundum sortem. Criticam impudentiam, in supplendo, juxta suum caput, sed cerebri vacuum, Festi loco, deinceps patefacerem, nisi destinarem alteri operi, quo, cum bono Deo, aliquando ostendam, ipsum esse furfuraceum Criticum, ( ut ut à se hoc amoliri moliatur, pag. 159. ) tam infallibiliter, ut jam demonstravi multoties, eum Cirminis Falsi reum esse, quam maculam nullo lixivio, aut quaesito fuco, unquam abstergere poterit.
units.tr: XVII. Next, on page 43 and following, he labours to charge me with ignorance, as if I did not know what to settle by a besse or a quadrans means. I shall first cite, in good faith, that is, honestly (since Gronovius's good faith is often found in the worst form when he copies my words or those of others), the words of this ambitious man, who is wont to feed on such trifles: I said (he says) secondly that this question of my opponent is refuted by the number of those cities which settled by a besse or a quadrans. To this he replies: What has that to do with it? Their magistrates prudently considered how much burden could be laid on their citizens in return for the use of money; I have already said that Rome did the same. He evidently thought that to settle by a besse or a quadrans means to pass a law that interest is not lawful unless it is a quadrans or a besse, as when at Rome interest was reduced from the unciary rate to the semuncial (which he insists was a reduction from one percent a month to half percent), and he praises this prudence of magistrates in judging how much should be laid on citizens for the use of money. But let him learn (mark this) that to settle a besse in Latin means to come to terms with a creditor so that, without any interest, he receives for the whole sum of the debt two thirds of it, and so on. Thus far I have shown myself an attentive listener and pupil. Let the supercilious Doctor hear further that I knew at the age of twelve what it was to settle with a creditor. He himself, instead of a school fee, may in turn learn from me that a settlement can be made with a creditor not only on the principal but also on the interest that has been stipulated, and on whose amount the magistrate rightly decides if an innocent debtor, through no fault of his own, happens to fail. I had this settlement on interest in mind, because I thought my opponent had the same in mind, and it bears more closely on the point then in dispute between us. Nor can my ignorance be proved from the authors he cites. I begin with Paterculus, from whom he sets out these words: Valerius Flaccus, the author of the law by which creditors were ordered to be paid a quadrans. Consider first, my dear reader, the Gronovian good faith, which I just now called the worst, in citing Paterculus. The words in the author, book 2, chapter 23, read thus: In his place was appointed Valerius Flaccus, the author of a most DISGRACEFUL law, by which creditors were ordered to be paid a quadrans; for this deed the punishment came upon him within two years. Since he foresaw that the word disgraceful was against him, the good man and honest disputant Gronovius slyly, if not maliciously, omitted it along with the following words. That Velleius is not against me but for me, and that I am cleared of ignorance, he may learn from the very learned Dn. Boeclerus (who is to me a [...] adversary), who, in the index to Velleius, explaining the word quadrans, has the following: That is, a fourth part, so that the creditor would lose three parts (of the principal or of the interest, NB) and receive a fourth. This is the kind of new account book. Therefore Velleius calls this Valerian law most disgraceful (NB), since it both had manifest injustice and was passed by the tribunes of the plebs with a seditious and turbulent purpose, rather than being granted under the highest and unavoidable necessity of the state. Let Gronovius now boast, on page 44, that peoples are found among whom creditors were compelled to receive the principal without interest, greatly reduced. Paterculus does not say this at all; and if it has happened anywhere, he pronounces it most disgraceful, which our man, who eagerly wishes to be counted a Christian and a son of the Church, judges just and pious. In the same faithless way in which he cited Paterculus he cites Suetonius, so that it may be plain to the reader how craftily he has acted; I shall first give the passage as he copied it on page 45. Julius (he says) decreed that debtors should satisfy creditors by an assessment of their possessions, etc., on which condition about a quarter of the debt was lost, according to Suetonius. But the whole passage, which is very much against our man, reads thus: Concerning loans, after the hope of new account books, which was stirred up by the tribunes, had been dashed, he decreed at last that debtors should satisfy creditors by an assessment of their estates, at what each had been bought for before the civil war, the sum of the debt being deducted, if anything had been paid or entered in writing as interest; on which condition about a quarter of the debt was lost. My God! What will not proud obstinacy persuade mortals to do! This man, in full view and before the whole world, has with settled purpose falsified the text a second time, for no other reason than not to seem to have been mistaken, and to have truly charged me with ignorance. I pity the man. Meanwhile the words of Suetonius deserve examination. I. That Julius Caesar, though a Poplicola and having many Marians within him, dashed the expectation of new account books, and decreed that debtors should satisfy creditors: this shows the injustice of those same account books; at the same time our man is exposed, who has so long and so wordily babbled in praise of their fairness. II. Since the settlement with creditors was made with interest also taken into account, my opinion is confirmed; and it is plain that interest was too heavy a burden on the Roman plebs. III. The intolerable ignorance of Gronovius shines through, for he can learn from this that settlement with creditors was made as much according to interest (and indeed more often) as according to principal. I would expose the critic's impudence in supplying words, according to his own head, which is empty of brains, like a Festus, further on, did I not reserve it for another work, in which, with God's good help, I shall one day show that he is a bran-brained critic (however much he tries to ward this off from himself, p. 159), and so infallibly, as I have already shown many times, that he is guilty of the crime of Cirminius's falsehood, a stain which no lye and no sought-after dye will ever wash away.

units.la: XVIII. Male cum haberet hominem, sibi non constantem in examinandis meis argumentis, solisque suis principijs inhaerentem, quod dixissem pag. 27. Roma praerogativam non fuisse debitoris, cujus fortunas tristis aliquis casus perdiderat, prae debitore: Verba mea instar Penthei, pag. 45: & duabus sequentibus pagg. discerpit, juxta fidem Gronovianam, cujus ut Sathanicae jam manifestus est, & quidem, nullam aliam ob causam, quam ut appareret suffecisse λόγοις hautquaquam in hac causa profuturis. Injurius essem in meas horas, melius collocandas, si premerem Adversarij vestigia, & chartas innocuas commacularem. Lector mea duntaxat relegat, hic iterum exhibita, attendatque ad Senecae locum ( quem adductum fuisse Sisyphus dissimulat ) occurrentem lib. 7. de Benef. cap. 16. Per saltum deinde transit, ad enervandas vindicias testij mei argumenti. Quae, ad examinandas illas, prolixe adferuntur, sunt ejusdem notae, hoc est, Gronovianae verborum pelves, quas si exonerare meditarer, homini ineptissimo similem me exhiberem. Argumenti mei nervus firmatus matus magis est, quàm ut hac ratione infirmari possit. Aliquid videri posset pro se adduxisse, quando dicit pag. 49. Dixi gratuitorum nullam esse necessitatem: nec qui octo condonat, illaudatum ef- se, etsi non undecim condonarit, quum nihil condo- nare compellatur. Sed, hæc propterea concidunt, imo collabuntur; quòd, optimi Principes revoca- re potuissent duodecim Tabulas, si fœnus unciari- um ex mente Adversarij intelligendum fuisset. Su- bodorabatur Noster, hoc objici posse, eòque tem- pestivè sese munire voluit: atque, dicta pag. 49. dicit: Caput illud XII. tabularum ante tot secula exoleverat. Et pag. 51. Antoninus nono, Alexan- der decimo seculo populi Romani vivebant: quum Lex XII. tabularum trunco, non frondibus umbram efficeret: nec tamen sola, sed vix colebatur. Ho- mo cluit IC. & audit I. V. D. cœterum prodit se in ipsis Institutionibus Justiniani Principis, qui & An- tonino & Alexandro multo fuit posterior, admo- dum peregrinum esse. Ille cum suo Triboniano, quoties non provocat ad XII. illas quoque inter- pretando: alios Textus ne adducam, inspiciantur duntaxat init. & §. 1. Tit. de Legit. agnat. tutela. Atque hanc ob caussam Imp. Justinianus novum quoque jus condens, vetus illi attemperare perpe- tuò fere laboravit, prout V. C. ipse manifestò in- nuit Leg. un. Cod. de Cad. toll. §. 9. quod frustra fuisset, si venerandæ illæ LL. quòd vellet Grono- vius, plane à pluribus seculis abrogatæ & quasi se- pultæ fuissent. Vult haberi antiquitatis promus con-
units.tr: XVIII. He had a hard time with a man who is not consistent in examining my arguments and clings only to his own principles, when I wrote at p. 27: Rome did not give a creditor precedence over a debtor whose fortunes some sad accident had ruined. He tears my words to pieces, like Pentheus at p. 45 and the two following pages, following the Gronovian creed, of which he is now plainly a Satanic adherent, and for no other reason than to show that mere words were enough, though they would never help in this matter. I would be wasting my hours, which are better spent elsewhere, if I trod in my opponent's footsteps and dirtied innocent paper. Let my reader go back to what I have quoted here again, and note the passage of Seneca (which Sisyphus conceals that I quoted), in book 7 of On Benefits, chapter 16. He then skips ahead to weaken the defence of my witness's argument. The arguments he sets out at length to examine these are of the same kind, that is, Gronovian bowls of words, and if I tried to empty them I would look like a most inept man. The sinew of my argument is too firmly set to be weakened in this way. He might seem to have offered something in his favour when he says at p. 49: I said there is no necessity for gratuities; nor is one who remits eight not to be praised, though he did not remit eleven, since he is not compelled to remit anything at all. But this falls apart, indeed collapses, because the best princes could have revoked the Twelve Tables if the interest of an uncia were to be understood in my opponent's sense. Our man suspected that this might be objected, and wanted to fortify himself in time: and at the page cited he says: That chapter of the Twelve Tables had fallen into disuse so many centuries before. And at p. 51: Antoninus in the ninth and Alexander in the tenth century lived under the Roman people, when the Law of the Twelve Tables cast its shade with a trunk rather than with leaves, and yet it was not cultivated alone, but was barely tended. The man plays the jurist and poses as a teacher of law, but he betrays himself as quite a stranger in the very Institutes of the Emperor Justinian, who was much later than both Antoninus and Alexander. That emperor, with his Tribonian, whenever he does not appeal to those Twelve Tables, even while interpreting them, let me not cite other texts, but let them look at the beginning and §. 1 of the title On Agnatic Guardianship. And for this reason Emperor Justinian, when he too was making new law, laboured almost constantly to adapt it to the old, as our author himself clearly hinted in Leg. un. Cod. de Cad. toll. §. 9, which would have been pointless if those venerable laws had, as Gronovius wishes, been wholly abrogated and buried for many centuries. He wants to be held a storehouse of antiquity, so why does he not heed the Emperor declaring in §. 1 of the Institutes on Testamentary Wills: Nothing of antiquity is to be wholly ignored. I refer my jurist to the Institutes, for in those very books he is quite ignorant.

units.la: . condus, cur ergo non audit Imp. pronunciantem §. 1. Inst. de Test. Ord. Nihil antiquitatis penitus ignorandum esse. Relego studio meum J. V. D. ad Institura: nam in illis ipsis per quam rudis est.
units.tr: . [Nothing of antiquity is to be wholly ignored.] I refer my jurist to the Institutes, for in those very books he is quite ignorant.

units.la: XIX. Redit deinde ad locum Dionis, de quo jam antea contendimus; sed, ut antiquum obtinea-at; atque more solito verba det. Existimationem suam potius vindicasset ab anilis fabellæ censura, quam institui pag. 29. Cæterum non quivit κοκκυζειν, quin & vellicaret mea verba, omitten-do illa, in quibus cardo rei præ cæteris vertebatur. Urget quod verbum περιτρεψιν pag. 36. Verterim usque ad: quum tamen adducto textu Græco atque secutus versionem Leunclavij pag. 18. illud reddiderim prius: quanquam fateor voculas has usque ad occurrere in argumento, quod ipse inte-grum meis verbis proponere debuisset. Addit pag. 54. Nihil apud Dionem neque de lege, neque de jure video: sed ex eo moribus receptam fuisse (centesimam scil.) intelligo, ita ut momentis variaret. Sed, unde ipse probabit, centesimam usurarum maximam ante Actiacum triumphum moribus solum-modo receptam fuisse? Quum Dioni propositum fuerit exponere fructus triumphi Augustæi, & quantum effectum fuerit illata ingenti pecuniæ summa, quousque fœnus imminutum fuerit, osten-dit: si rationem habuisset fœnoris, ut solet exer-ceri ex libidine argentariorum, aliorumque, qui illis pecunias suas credere solebant, nihil dixisset: nam per ganeones, decoctores, similesque homi-nes? nes, æque omni tempore satisfieri poterat libidini hominum avarorum: at, hoc singulare fuit, quod usura maxima, sive Centesima, ( cui respondet fœnus unciarium ) legibus scil. permissa, usque adeò diminuta fuerit./ Vivit meus homo in Hollandia: ergo consideret rationem fœnoris, nomine Reip. solvi soliti ante pacem cum Rege Hispaniarum initam, illiusque diminutionem & reductionem: quæ equidem non debet expendi juxta illud quod moribus receptum, sed illud, quod legibus permissum erat: applicentur hæc ad Dionem, & omnia salva erunt.
units.tr: XIX. He then returns to the passage of Dio, about which we have already argued; but, to keep his old view, he plays his usual tricks with words. He would have done better to rescue his reputation from the charge of an old wives' tale than to attack what I set out at p. 29. Besides, he could not keep from cackling, and he even picked at my words, leaving out those in which the hinge of the matter turned more than any others. He presses the word περιτρεψιν at p. 36, which I rendered up to, although with the Greek text quoted, and following Leunclavius' version at p. 18, I rendered it before. I admit that the little words up to do occur in the argument, which he should have set out whole in my words. He adds at p. 54: I see nothing in Dio about law or right, but I understand that from that time the (hundredth, that is) rate was received by custom, so that it varied with the circumstances. But how will he prove that the highest rate of a hundredth had been received only by custom before the triumph at Actium? Since Dio intended to set out the proceeds of Augustus' triumph, and how much was done when such a huge sum of money was brought in, and how far the interest was reduced, he shows that if he had taken account of interest as it is usually charged by the greed of bankers and others who used to lend their money to them, he would have said nothing: for the greed of covetous men could equally be satisfied at all times through spendthrifts, bankrupts and similar people; but this was singular, that the highest rate of interest, or the hundredth (to which the fenus unciarium corresponds), which was permitted by law, was so greatly reduced. My man lives in Holland, so let him consider the rate of interest which was customarily paid in the name of the Republic before the peace made with the King of Spain, and its reduction and restoration. These are indeed not to be weighed according to what was received by custom, but according to what was permitted by law. Apply these points to Dio, and all will be safe.

units.la: XX. Argumentum desumptum ab eo, quod Ciceroni Ciliciæ Proconsuli obvenerat, distrahit, & vellicat multis modis, & quidem adeo prolixè, ut paginas ferme octo compleat. Nec ego modo vapulo, sed, pagina quoque 56. Manutius & Bosius, at, quanti Viri! pariter imprudentiæ arguuntur. Præterea fateri cogitur pag. 57. me auctorem habere Ausonium. Popmam, à quo hos carbones pro thesauro suffuratus sim: ut mecum vir doctus traducatur. Quod dixissem ne liceret dare accipere pecuniam in versuram, pag. 57. arguor, quòd locutus sim bene barbare. At, si cogitasset, me verbum versura in eadem significatione accepisse, quam Cuiacius ei aptat, ( cui nec parcere scivit pag. 162. & seq. ) clementiorem equidem sese præbuisset. Cicero ne faveat, verba ipsius mutat. Quod videret probari posse, Salaminios in duas syngraphas consensisse, atque huc sequentia Ciceronis verba, quæ lib. 6.Epist ad Act. ep. 2. occurrunt, pertine-re: Salaminios adduxi, ut totum nomen Scaptio vellent solvere, sed centesimis, ductis à proxima quidem syngrapha, nec perpetuis sed renovatis quotanuis: proinde illius verba, 'proxima quidem syngrapha, sibi adversari: nullo MS. Cod. favente, audacter substituit: à proxima die syngraphæ: simul, aliquantum tribuit conjecturæ Manutii, cui placuerat legendum esse, à prima quidem syngrapha, atque voculam primam ita interpretatur, ut debeat hunc sensum habere, ab initio syngraphæ. qui certè est maximè inconveniens. Si ergo duæ Syngraphæ admittantur, nullum in verbis meis contradictionss vestigium admitti poterit, quam-vis pag. 56. ita me incessit: Vide quâ imprudentiâ homo contraria loquatur. Præcedenti pagina scripsit, Salaminios per imprudentiam quaternas promisisse: hic tantum singulas. Ut evictum jam est, duas syngraphas admittendas esse, ita hæc immunia manent à contradictione; quòd oppositio non instituatur ad idem, ut vulgò in Scholis loquuntur. Quæ ipse pag. 60. de Salaminiis, eorumque syngrapha garrit, meis evertendis non sufficiunt; nituntur enim conjecturis magis, quam mea. Si evicerit, per consuetudinem solam, non verò per legem Gabiniam, centesimas usuras in provinciis receptas fuisse, everterit meum argumentum, quod hoc fuit, atque in statu adhuc permanet. Scripseram: Quæ verò iniquitas fuisset,
units.tr: XX. He takes apart the argument drawn from what fell to Cicero as Proconsul of Cilicia, and picks at it in many ways, and at such length that he fills almost eight pages. Nor am I the only one who is beaten: at p. 56 Manutius and Bosius, and what great men they are! are likewise charged with imprudence. Besides, at p. 57 he is forced to admit that I have Ausonius as my authority, and Popma, from whom I stole these embers as if they were treasure, so that a learned man may be dragged across with me. At p. 57 I am charged, because I said that it was not lawful to give and receive money on loan, with having spoken very barbarously. But if he had considered that I took the word versura in the same sense that Cuiacius applies to it (on whom he did not know how to spare himself at p. 162 ff.), he would have shown himself rather more lenient. Cicero is not on his side, so he changes Cicero's words. To show that it could be proved that the Salaminians had agreed to two syngraphae, and that the following words of Cicero, which occur in book 6, letter 2 to Atticus, pertain to this: I brought the Salaminians to the point of wanting to pay the whole debt as Scaptius' claim, but at a hundredth, reckoned from the nearest syngrapha, and not as a perpetual but as a renewed charge each year. Therefore his words, the nearest syngrapha, which work against him, he boldly replaces, with no manuscript in his favour, by from the nearest day of the syngrapha; at the same time he gives a good deal to the conjecture of Manutius, who had preferred reading from the first syngrapha, and he interprets the word first so that it must have this sense, from the beginning of the syngrapha, which is certainly most inappropriate. If, then, two syngraphae are admitted, no trace of contradiction can be found in my words, although at p. 56 he attacks me thus: See with what imprudence the man says contrary things. In the preceding page he wrote that the Salaminians had promised four times through imprudence; here only once. As it has now been proved that two syngraphae must be admitted, so these words remain free from contradiction, because the opposition is not set up with respect to the same thing, as they commonly say in the Schools. What he chatters about the Salaminians and their syngrapha at p. 60 is not enough to overturn mine; for it rests more on conjectures than on mine. If he proves that centesimal usury was received in the provinces by custom only, and not by the Gabinian law, he will overturn my argument, which was this, and which stands as it is. I had written: What injustice would it have been

units.la: L ſ Si Romae per leges XII. Tabularum, daodecima solum centesima pars maxima usura fuisset, & tamen promiscue omnibus, lege quoque lata, centesimis in provinciis fenerari licuisset. Quibus exarmandis neutiquam sufficiunt sequentes adversarij Λόγοι: Tabulis duodecim cavebatur civibus & tradebatur jus Quiritium: hi erant provinciales, Tabularum duodecim hoc caput tunc temporis ne in civibus quidem valebat, quippe quod statim a primo ortu irritum fuerit. Praterea in Gracia & Asia semper maiores usura viguerunt, etiam inter ipsos incolas, quam Romae. Quae ipse pag. 59, non tam in omnes formas vertit, quam in equuleo detorquet, ut valeant a proxima quidem syngrapha; quae ambitiosum hominis animum usque adeo vexarunt, ut ultro fateatur, illa Scabis aliquid habere. Videantur porro, quae ego habeo prioris Dissertationis pag. 37. & seqq. quorum robur dissimulat Adversarius, contentus quaedam, quae ad rem minime faciebant, sed occasionem large garriendi tribuebant, perstrinxisse.
units.tr: [If at Rome, under the laws of the Twelve Tables, the highest interest had been only the twelfth part of a hundredth, and yet it had been lawful for everyone alike, even by a law passed for the purpose, to lend at a hundredth in the provinces.] The following arguments of my opponent are in no way sufficient to disarm this: By the Twelve Tables provision was made for citizens, and the right of the Quirites was granted; these were provincials. This chapter of the Twelve Tables was not in force even among citizens at that time, since it was void from its very first origin. Besides, in Greece and Asia higher usury always flourished, even among the inhabitants themselves, than at Rome. What he himself at p. 59 does not so much turn into every shape as stretch on the rack, so that they may stand from the nearest syngrapha; these things have so troubled the ambitious man's mind that he freely admits they smack of the scab. Let them also see what I have in the earlier Dissertation at p. 37 ff., whose strength my opponent conceals, being content to have touched on certain things that did not bear on the matter at all, but gave him occasion to chatter freely.

units.la: XXI. Pag. 63. & pluribus sequentibus, occupatur adhuc circa Plebiscitum Genucium, ordinans quasi foenus, & modum, qui excederent, puniens, adducit quoque pag. 65. non sine sarcasmo Grammatico locum Appiani, in quo tamen neque Genucii, neque XII. Tabularum mentio occurrit: interea ipsi hoc est principium, immotae quasi veritatis, juxta Legem XII. Tabularum, centesimam [illegible, ~10 letters]nam (cui secundum nos unciarium respondet) non fuisse usuram maximam. Rogo Lectorem, priorem meum Tractatum adire dignetur, atque expendere illa, quæ pag. 44. & aliquot sequentibus occurrunt. Me cum jam diu distædeat impudentiæ Gronovianæ, nec dementis otii, inter tot occupationes, afflicta quoque valetudine, exi-stam; non decrevi singula dicta mea recoquere, atque ineptiis hominis ultra respondere. Quod certè aliud non foret, quàm futilissimis quisquiliis honorem habere, quibus non aliter quàm silentio & contemptu respondendum est. Et hæc causa est, quare transiliam interjacentes paginas, usque ad pag. 73. quâ, ostentando se Dialecticum esse, arrodit argumentum nostrum, Achillæi cæteroquin roboris, quod pag. 43. super. Tract. & subsequentibus, proponitur. Itaque tu
units.tr: XXI. On page 63 and many following pages he still labours over the Genucian plebiscite, which he takes to set a kind of interest rate and to punish those who exceeded it. On page 65 he also cites, not without sarcasm toward the grammarian, a passage of Appian in which no mention of Genucius or of the Twelve Tables occurs. Meanwhile he takes it as the principle of an almost unshakeable truth that, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, the centesima [illegible] nam (which by our reckoning corresponds to the uncia) was not the highest rate of interest. I ask the reader to be good enough to consult my earlier treatise and weigh what appears on page 44 and some following pages. Since I have long been weary of Gronovian impudence, and since, amid so many occupations and with my health also impaired, I have no leisure for mad trifling, I have decided not to rework each of my statements one by one or to answer this man's silliness at further length. That would be nothing other than giving honour to the most worthless rubbish, which can be answered only with silence and contempt. This is also why I skip the intervening pages, up to page 73, where, showing off as a dialectician, he gnaws at our argument, which is otherwise of Achillean strength and is set out on page 43 of the earlier treatise and those following it. So you, herald:

units.la: Exurge praeco, fac populo audientiam.
units.tr: Stand up, herald, and make the people give attention.

units.la: Ego interea togam compono. Dum ille meus homo pag d. seu 73. ita proloquitur:
units.tr: Meanwhile I put on my toga. While that man of mine, on page 73 or thereabouts, speaks thus:

units.la: Quid dabit hic tanto dignum promissor hiatu? Lex XII. tabularum fœneratorem, (hæc mea verba fuerunt) qui fœnus unciarium excederet, condemnat quadrupli. Centesimam ultra si quis aliquid eruerit, Theodosius condemnat quadrupli. Ergo centesima est fœnus unciarium. Ad quæ ita Nosier: Sed scit ex lege artis hac figura non colligi adfirmatè. An igitur sic mavult: Quadrupli fœneratorem condemnant duodecim Tabulæ, qui excesserit cesserit fænus unciarium. Quadrupli condemnat Theodosius, qui excesserit Centesimâ. Ergo ,Centesima est fœnus unciarium. Sed & hoc οὐσφισμα est: nec nescit, opinor, sic colligi debere: Ergo quidam, qui excessisset usuram legibus permissam, eodem modo puniebatur à Theodosio, quo in Duodecim tabulis. Quæ verò fit illa usura legibus permissa: nihil sic definitum est. An denique sic statum ad præliandum componit: Quicunque legem XII. tabularum respexit in poena fœnoris illegitimi, is eandem etiam respexit in fœnore puniendo. At Theodosius respexit legem XII. Tabularum in poena fœnoris illegitimi. Ergo & eandem respexit in modo. Hactenus meus homo. Hæc verò ad rem faciunt tam belle, quàm Buttubata Nævii, aut Brececex Aristophanis. Quod didicerit Syllogismos Sophisticos, sive fallaces contexere, ego vim argumenti mei, sequenti, eoque legitimo, complector: Quicunque feneratur, ultra quàm lege definitum, ille juxta leges XII. Tabularum punitur quadrupli. Sed qui amplius feneratur, quàm Centesima, ille feneratur ultra quàm lege definitum: Ergo, qui feneratur amplius quàm Centesimâ, juxta L. XII. Tabularum punitur quadrupli. Unde ulterius infero, pariter eum, qui olim ultra fœnus Unciarium fœnerando procederet, tantundem exigere potuisse, atque Centesima complectebatur: obnoxium verò fuisse pœnæ quadrupli, æque atque illum, qui centesimam excedebat.
units.tr: What will this promiser deliver, worthy of so great a gaping? The Law of the Twelve Tables (these were my words) condemns a moneylender who exceeds the uncia rate to a fourfold penalty. If anyone has extracted more than the centesima, Theodosius condemns him to a fourfold penalty. Therefore the centesima is the uncia rate. To which our man replies as follows: But he knows, by the rules of his art, that this figure does not allow a conclusion to be drawn affirmatively. Would he therefore prefer it put like this: the Twelve Tables condemn to a fourfold penalty the moneylender who exceeded the uncia rate; Theodosius condemns to a fourfold penalty the one who exceeded the centesima; therefore the centesima is the uncia rate? But this too is a fallacy, and I think he does not fail to see that the conclusion should be drawn thus: therefore someone who exceeded the interest permitted by law was punished by Theodosius in the same way as under the Twelve Tables. But what that permitted rate of interest was is nowhere defined. Or finally, he sets up his battle line thus: whoever had regard to the Law of the Twelve Tables in the penalty for illegal interest also had regard to it in the manner of punishing interest. But Theodosius had regard to the Law of the Twelve Tables in the penalty for illegal interest. Therefore he had regard to it also in the manner. So far my man. These points bear on the matter as prettily as the Buttubata of Naevius or the Brececex of Aristophanes. Let him learn to weave sophistical, or fallacious, syllogisms; I grasp the force of my argument in the following, and legitimate, form: Whoever lends at interest beyond what the law defines is punished by fourfold penalty under the Law of the Twelve Tables. But whoever lends at more than the centesima lends beyond what the law defines. Therefore whoever lends at more than the centesima is punished by fourfold penalty under the Law of the Twelve Tables. From this I further infer that whoever formerly lent beyond the uncia rate could likewise demand as much as the centesima comprised, and was liable to the fourfold penalty just as much as the one who exceeded the centesima.

units.la: Sequens enim axioma invictae veritatis est, &, quod nullus quoque mortalium negare potest; Ubi in eodem genere delicti eadem poena irrogatur, delicta aut nomine aut accidentibus differentia, essentialiter eadem censeri debent: Quomodo juxta Cornelium Legem gladio feritur, qui sive veneno, sive fame, sive gladio, sive, quocunque alio telo, hominem occiderit, quoniam homicida censetur. Ita foenerator aequè est, qui ultra centesimam, atque ultra foenus unciarium foeneratur. Noster quidem injicit modi mentionem, at distinguere debuisset, inter modum juxta quantitatem, & modum juxta qualitatem. In delictis, secundum Legem Corneliam jam enumeratis, occurrit aequalitas secundum qualitatem; atque in poenae irrogatione semper quantitas respicitur, licet qualitas (manente tamen eadem poena) intensionem aut remissionem procurate possit, suadentibus illud circumstantiis, quas ad qualitatem consuevisse referri, in confesso est. Dicet, Theodosium non meminisse LL. XII. Tabularum, sed simpliciter Juris, per quod etiam jus recentius intelligi possit. At, cum in cod. Theodof. l. 1. Fin. regundorum, jus XII. Tabb. jus vetus, & l. un. de Usuris, jus priscum vocetur: In Lege vero alibi allegata simpliciter, propter excellentiam Jus audiat. Quomodo & Ausonius ferme συγχεῖν; in Gripho de Ternario numero:
units.tr: For the following axiom is an unconquered truth, and one that no mortal can deny: Where the same penalty is imposed for offences of the same kind, offences that differ in name or in accidents ought to be regarded as essentially the same. Thus under the Cornelian law he who kills a man is struck with the sword whether he did it with poison, hunger, a sword, or any other weapon, since he is considered a murderer. So the moneylender is equally guilty whether he lends beyond the centesima or beyond the uncia rate. Our man indeed raises the matter of mode, but he ought to have distinguished between mode according to quantity and mode according to quality. In the offences already listed under the Cornelian law, equality is according to quality; but in the imposition of a penalty, quantity is always regarded, although quality (the penalty remaining the same) can bring about greater or lesser severity, as the circumstances, which are commonly referred to quality, make clear. He will say that Theodosius did not mention the Laws of the Twelve Tables but simply the law, by which more recent law also may be understood. But since in the Theodosian Code, in the title on boundaries, the Twelve Tables are called the old law, and in the single law on usury the ancient law, while in the law cited elsewhere it is simply called the law on account of its excellence, the same usage applies. Ausonius too almost confuses the two, in the Gryphus on the number three:

units.la: Jus triplex, tabula quod ter sanxere quaterna: Sacrum, Privatum, populi, commune quod ufq; est.
units.tr: Threefold is the law, which the four-fold tablet sanctioned three times: sacred, private, of the people, and what is common to all.

units.la: XXII. Dein pag. 80. prolixè, quæsita occasione, iterum disserit de Grammatices præstantia, quam in universum nunquam, sed morosam & tetricam illam, quæ omni prudentia destituitur & cujus Gronovius cultor est, argui: de quallibus Grammaticis Augustinus lib. 1. Confess. cap. 12. testatur, quod vela pendeant in vestibulo Scholarum Grammaticarum, sed, illa non pandere honorem secreti, quam tegumentum [?]rroris. Pag. 88. probaturus omnes Romæ, usque ad pueros, assem in minimas sui partes potuisse deducere, sequentem ex Horatio locum adducit:
units.tr: XXII. Then on page 80, at length, having found an occasion, he again discourses on the excellence of grammar. Grammar is never to be blamed as such; what is to be blamed is that sullen and crabbed grammar which lacks all prudence and of which Gronovius is a devotee. Augustine, in book 1 of the Confessions, chapter 12, testifies about grammarians of this sort, that the sails hang in the vestibule of the grammar schools, but do not open up the honour of the secret, which is a covering of error. On page 88, wishing to prove that all in Rome, even boys, could divide the as into its smallest parts, he quotes the following passage from Horace:

units.la: Romani pueri, longis rationibus assem Discunt in partes centum diducere. Dicat Filius Albini, si de quinque remota est Uncia, quid superest? poterit dixisse triens. eu. Rem poteris servare tuam. redit uncia, quid sit? Semis.
units.tr: Roman boys learn by long calculations to divide the as into a hundred parts. Let the son of Albinus say: if an ounce is taken away from five-twelfths, what remains? He will have answered "a third." Good! You will be able to keep your property. An ounce comes back; what is it? A half.

units.la: Quod argumentum est simile huic: Gronovius, qui admodum infensus est ordini illorum, quos ipse per contemptum Lombardos vocat, non novit rationem calculi apud mensam recepti: Ergo, neque noverit; Vela sua Grammatica expandere & diducere? Horatius loquitur de Albini, & similium fœneratorum filiis, qui à primis annis talibus præceptis instruebantur, quorum subsidio commodè fœneratoriæ artis exercitio vacare possent. fent: quam rationem calculum subducendi & af- fem in minutissimas partes diducendi, quum vul- gus Quiritium ignoraret, contingebat multoties decipi. Dein pag. 94. meaeris Campani sono ex- plodere laborat, ita proloquens: Putes audire: O- mnis clocca cloccabilis, in clockerio clockerando clo- cas cloccative facit cloccabiliter clockerantes; Qui- bus nihil aliud repono, quàm illud Paulinum, di- cendo, quòd homo meus fit χαλκὸς ἠχῶν, ἢ κύμ- βαλον ἀλαλάζον, 1. Cor. 13. v. 1. Gravius est, quod occurrit pag. 96; qua enim verecundia est nostrer homo, quòd soricis innutritus fit, salutât me Anum dialectici, cum ipse, honos auribus ha- beatur, vix ejusdem merda sit. Quòd forte alicubi profestus fuissem, me esse proletarium ex Dei be- nedictione, atque proinde non sufficere omnige- nis libris emendis, eadem pag. traducor columbu- lus Dioneus. At, tali elogio convenientius po- tuisset condecorare, suum amicum, & quondam meum fallacem Collegam, si non proditorem; cujus Adonidis horti, ancillae eo evocari solitae, uxor cum studiosis eosdem quotidie, ante meridi- em quoque invisens, Groningae apud multos in re- centi sunt memoria. At, ulterius me contineo, nam cum mortuis non nisi larvae luctantur.
units.tr: This argument is like the following: Gronovius, who is very hostile to the order of those whom he himself contemptuously calls Lombards, does not know the method of calculation accepted at the banker's table; therefore he does not know how to spread out and unfold his grammatical sails? Horace is speaking of the sons of Albinus and of similar moneylenders, who from their earliest years were trained in such precepts, so that they could conveniently devote themselves to the practice of the moneylending trade. Since the common people of the Quirites did not know the method of calculating and of dividing the as into the smallest parts, it often happened that they were deceived. Then on page 94 he labours to explode the sound of my Campanian [phrase], speaking thus: you would think you heard: All clucking clucker, clucking in a clucking-place, you cluck and make cluckers cluck cluckably. To which I reply nothing other than that saying of Paul's, that my man is sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, 1 Cor. 13:1. More serious is what occurs on page 96. For with what shame is our man, who was reared by a mouse, when he greets me as the anus of the dialectician, whereas he himself, to whom honour is paid by the ears, is scarcely more than the same thing's dung. Because I once happened to be called, by God's blessing, a proletarian, and therefore not able to buy books of every kind, on the same page I am called the Dionean little dove. But he could more fittingly have adorned with such praise his own friend, and my former deceitful colleague, if not betrayer, whose Adonis gardens, to which maids were accustomed to be summoned, his wife visited daily with students, even before noon, and many at Groningen remember this in recent times. But I hold myself back further, for with the dead only ghosts wrestle.

units.la: XXIII. Paulatim devenimus ad vexatum Plinij locum, qui occurrit lib. 10. Ep. 62. quae circa illum annotaverim, ex prioribus vindiciis cognoscan- tur: sepositis vero ronchis nostri Suffeni, qui à pag. 100. per plures sequentes extenduntur, attendi duntaxat velim quæ à me scripta sunt, & componi cum iis, quæ plenis pelvibus inanium verborum & sarcasmorum, profundit. Antea improbabat conjecturam Magni Salmasij, pro duodenis assibus, substituentis usuris assibus, nunc vero eandem probat, quò jactare posset (videtur pag. 112.) juxta modestiam sibi vernaculam, se invenisse vera, adhuc ab omnibus frustra quæsita, usurarum assium incunabula. at hunc Thrasonismum pessimè homini Φιλαυτῷ modò cessurum esse, spondeo: antea verba ejus exhibeo, prout occurrunt pag. 111. Usuras centesimas dixerunt usuras asses, quia qui centesimas usuras promiserat, menstruos dabat asses in centenos asses, vel menstruas libras in centenas libras. Una erat differentia inter assem & libram ex instituto Servij Tullij, quòd as signatus habebatur cum partibus suis, &c. Libra etiam dicebatur de non signato æne. &c. qui centesimas usuras promiserat; menstruos dabat asses in centenos asses. pag: 112. Invaluit, ut potius dicerent usuras asses, quam usuras libras, quia in signato & pecunia hujus nuncupationis erat. pag. 113. Assibus ut plurimum ibant in creditum, quibus emebant, vendebant & pretia omnium rerum æstimabant. pag. 109. Romani assem considerarunt, non ut nummum, sed ut divisorem centesimæ. Resp. 1. Cur prius ergo usque adeo tumultuatus fuit, tantumque pulveris concitavit? Mea erat sententia, semperque manebit. nebit, Plinium signlficare Imp. Trajano, non potuisse se consulere egestati publicæ, nisi promissa creditoribus usura centesima ; contenderamque assem pro uncia sumi, & duodenos asses anno quoque conficere centesimam, & consequenter juxta Plinium, συνεκδοχικῶς assem menstruum considerari divisorem Centesimæ, ad annum Romanum relatæ, cujus proprie divisor erat uncia. Nolebat hoc antea admittere, at, nunc volens nolens cogitur, quia expedire se non poterat. Imo non me solum sic statuisse profitetur, sed Matthæum Hostum quoque, virum scriptis celeberrimum, & quondam per quinquaginta tres annos magnum ornamentum illius Academiæ, in qua per Dei gratiam jam vivo. Verba Hosti ab adversario ipso exhibita pag. 108. hæc sunt: Duodenos asses in annum pro plena centesima usura posuit : est enim centesima usura velut as : quod ut in mensem uncia, quæ assis duodecima pars est, ita in annum duodeni asses nummi, velut integer as, ut a quibus compleatur, cedant de centum assibus : fuit itaque hæc centesima usura annua, scilicet duodeni asses, ut unus as quoque mense datus, usura menstrua. Ita veritas invitos & reluctantes subigere quoque potest! Cur maledicus homo pariter fassus non fuit, Hostum mihi esse ὁμόψηφον, atque, idem per usuram unciam, & fœnus unciarium intelligere: Certè tom. 1. de re Nummaria, pag. 164. hæc occurrunt: Ab uncia est unciaria usura: quæ Centesima fima est Ciceroni, unciarium fœnus. Tacito & Livio: qua centesimam fortis partem singulis mensi-bus capit, & centesimo mense fortem æquat. Resp.2.
