Concedo, apud Scriptores illibatam Romani elo-quii elegantiam exhibentes, assem æris signati, sive nummi rationem habere: Sed, unde proba-verit lepidum nostrum caput cum Salmasio,quem in posteriori Exegesi sequitur, atque, cujus partes defendendas suscepit, in usu fuisse hanc loquendi formulam, ut usura asses significarent usuras cen-tesimas? quàm diu auctoritatem Veterum non ad-ducit, quæ Salmasij quâ ipsius conjecturæ tantun-dem deferemus, atque anus febricitantis somnio 3. As receptus veluti nummus in quemque mensem, ut annuatim conficiat usuram Centesimam, quò-nam referri poterit,nisi ad Centesimam assis hujus usurarii regulam? Centesimo enim mense, nomine usurarum, centenarius numerus assium num-morum debuerit solutus esse. Quæ centesima quatenus distribuitur juxta menses singulos, annuatim duodenos effagitat asses, à sorte centum assium nummorum: qui duodeni asses, relati ad assem libram, secundum quam mensuræ, usuræ, & hereditates æstimari atque dividi solent,quoque mense,quid aliud, quam unciam exhibere possunt? Uncia verò mensrua, juxta annum, qui duodenos mensēs completi censetur, non potest non centesimæ usuræ æquivalere. 4. Quocunque adversarius se verterit, aliud, quod respondeat, non inveniet,
units.tr: XXIII. We have gradually come to the troublesome passage of Pliny, which occurs in Book 10, Letter 62. My remarks on it may be learned from my earlier Vindiciae. I ask only that, setting aside the brambles of our friend Suffenus, which run on through many pages from p. 100 onward, my own writings be considered and compared with his, which pour forth brimming basins of empty words and sarcasm. Previously he disapproved of the conjecture of the great Salmasius, which substitutes usuris assibus for duodenis assibus. Now, however, he approves it, so that he may boast (he appears to do so on p. 112), in his native modesty, that he has discovered the true origin of the interest in asses, a thing sought in vain by everyone until now. But I promise that this boasting will very badly suit this self-admiring man. First I set out his words as they occur on p. 111: They called interest at a hundred per cent "interest in asses", because the man who had promised interest at a hundred per cent paid monthly asses at a hundred asses, or monthly pounds at a hundred pounds. There was one difference between the as and the pound, according to the institution of Servius Tullius, in that the as was regarded as stamped, with its parts, etc. The pound was also called the unstamped bronze, etc. He who had promised interest at a hundred per cent paid monthly asses at a hundred asses. P. 112: It prevailed that they should say interest in asses rather than interest in pounds, because the money of this name was stamped. P. 113: Asses for the most part went into credit, with which they bought, sold, and valued the prices of all things. P. 109: The Romans regarded the as not as a coin but as the divisor of the hundredth. Reply 1. Why, then, did he first make such a fuss and raise such a cloud of dust? My view was and always will be that Pliny was signifying to the Emperor Trajan that he could not provide for the public need unless interest at a hundredth were promised to the creditors. I contended that the as was taken as the twelfth part (the uncia), that twelve asses each year make the hundredth, and consequently, according to Pliny, by synecdoche, the monthly as is regarded as the divisor of the hundredth, referred to the Roman year, whose proper divisor was the uncia. He was unwilling to admit this before, but now, willy-nilly, he is compelled to, because he could not get out of it. Indeed, he does not merely profess that he himself thought this, but also Matthaeus Hostus, a man famous for his writings, who was for fifty-three years a great ornament of that Academy in which, by God's grace, I now live. The words of Hostus, quoted by the adversary himself on p. 108, are these: He set twelve asses a year for the full hundredth interest: for the hundredth interest is as it were the as; and as the uncia, which is the twelfth part of the as, is per month, so twelve asses per year, as the whole as, so that by them it may be completed, are taken from the hundred asses. This hundredth interest was therefore annual, namely twelve asses, so that one as was given each month as monthly interest. Thus truth can also compel the unwilling and the reluctant! Why did this slanderous man not likewise admit that Hostus agrees with me, and that both understand by the interest of an uncia the uncial interest? Certainly in the first volume of De re Nummaria, p. 164, these occur: From the uncia comes the uncial interest, which is the hundredth for Cicero, uncial interest. For Tacitus and Livy: which takes the hundredth part of the principal each month, and in the hundredth month equals the principal. Reply 2. I grant that among writers who display the unimpaired elegance of Roman eloquence, the as has the sense of stamped bronze or coin. But from what source has our witty head, with Salmasius, whom he follows in his second Exegesis and whose parts he undertook to defend, proved that this manner of speaking was in use, so that interest in asses meant the hundredth interest? As long as he does not bring forward the authority of the ancients, we shall grant as much to Salmasius's conjecture as to the dream of a feverish old woman. 3. The as, received as a coin for each month, so that it makes up the hundredth interest annually: to what can this be referred, unless to the rule of the hundredth of this usurious as? For in the hundredth month, under the name of interest, a hundred stamped coins ought to have been paid. This hundredth, insofar as it is distributed over the individual months, demands annually twelve asses from the principal of a hundred coins. These twelve asses, referred to the as-pound, by which measures, interests and inheritances are usually valued and divided, what else can they give each month except an uncia? And the monthly uncia, according to the year, which is considered to be completed by twelve months, cannot fail to equal the hundredth interest. 4. Wherever the adversary turns, he will find no other answer than to repeat his arguments, as he has already done in both of his Exegeses. But arguments are not solved in this way, nor is the opponent satisfied. Rather, with words that will profit nothing (such as occur on p. 106, and which he ought to have set before his private audience of acorn-eaters), he merely stains harmless paper.

units.la: Nota: fragments of the neighbouring page at right are cut off and not transcribed. veniet, quàm ut sua argumenta repetat ; quod jam fecit in utraque sua Exegesi ; hac vero ratione non solvuntur argumenta, aut adversario satisfit; sed λόγοις, nihil profuturis (quales scil. pag. 106. occurrunt, quosque suis βαλλνοφάγοις audito- ribus privatis apponere debuisset) duntaxat chartæ innoxiæ maculantur. 4. Ipse fatetur, quod suam & Salmafij conjecturam de usuris assibus,per alterum idoneum testem probare non possit,eòque pag. 114. in antecessum mihi sic occurrit: Hic rursus, ut qui locis obscuris aut ignotis deprehensi omnia tuta timent, ille ignarus, quid probatione indigeat, quid fine teste recipiatur, poscet auctores. (modò hoc feci) Ego vero nullum alium auctorem illi, quàm rerum evidentiam dabo: quam quisquis non capit, ei consilium dandum est, ut illos bonos libros evolvat, quibus tantopere nosier offenditur. Secum verò ante omnia ambitiosus & Campano supercilio tumidus scriptor in concordiam redeat, pag. 95. ita mihi petulanter insultaverat, urgenti usum loquendi: Ubi autem usus ille loquendi? Duo sunt auctores omnes, qui faciunt mentionem fœnoris unciarii: quid sit, neuter exponit? contra omnem loquendi usum explicat nosier: & tamen crepat usum loquendi. Cur mihi auctoribus tribus munito, (Scævolam JC. Livio & Tacito adjicias) atque rationibus pluribus instructo, (in quibus Gronovius hactenus genuinum fregit) non licuit ad usum loquendi provocare, dum sola conconjectura, eaque irrationali, adversarius nititur ? Ita revera
units.tr: Note: fragments of the neighbouring page at right are cut off and not transcribed. Let me say, once more, that he confesses he cannot prove by another suitable witness his own and Salmasius's conjecture about interest in asses. So on p. 114 he anticipates me thus: Here again, like one who, when caught in obscure or unknown places, fears everything as unsafe, he who is ignorant of what needs proof and what may be accepted without a witness will ask for authorities. (Well, I have done this.) But I shall give him no other authority than the evidence of the matter itself: whoever does not grasp this must be advised to read through those good books by which our man is so greatly offended. Let this ambitious writer, swollen with a Campanian haughtiness, first of all come to terms with himself. On p. 95 he had insolently insulted me, pressing the usage of speech: But where is that usage of speech? There are only two authors who mention uncial interest: what it is, neither explains. Against all usage of speech our man explains it, and yet he boasts of usage of speech. Why, when I was armed with three authorities (you may add Scaevola the jurist, Livy and Tacitus) and furnished with many arguments (in which Gronovius has hitherto broken the genuine reading), was I not permitted to appeal to usage of speech, while my adversary relies on a mere conjecture, and an irrational one? Indeed,

units.la: Frigida depugnant calidis, humentia siccis,
units.tr: Cold things fight with hot, moist with dry,

units.la: Mollia cum duris, sine pondere habentia pondus. Quemadmodum per calumniam mihi Gronovius pag. 105. exprobrat. Interea idem jus deberet esse Accij quod Titij.
units.tr: Soft with hard, things lacking weight with things having weight. Just as Gronovius, by slander, reproaches me on p. 105. Meanwhile the same right ought to belong to Accius as to Titius.

units.la: XXIII. Alicubi in prioribus Vindiciis, auctori, identidem bonos suos auctores jactanti,voveram, in libro optimo, qui solus Θεόπνευστος, esset versatior, quam in Statio Papinio, Justino, Plauto, Petronio, Livio, Seneca, &c. quod cum conquere non posset, pudendum τῆς αὐθεόπτου Emblema Lectori suo exhibet, hisce verbis pag. 114. patrocinando bonis suis libris, quibus mallet immori, quam Sacrosanctis Bibliis: At illi (inquit) non desinunt boni esse, quod omnibus bonis melior est ὁ Θεόπνευστος. Est enim in suo ordine bonum, quod NB. ad summum bonum non patet aut pertinet. & qui ista tanquam adversantia statuit, ostendit se malum dialecticum, nec perdidicit doctrinam de oppositis, ut illi sua verba reddam. Ergo, mi Athee, aliquid bonum esse potest, quod a Deo non pendeat, nec ad eum pertineat ? At, quid dicit Apostolus Jacobus, Epist. Cath. cap. 1. verf. 17. πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθή, καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον ἄνωθέν ἐστι, καταβαῖνον ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν φώτων. Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum num est superne, descendens a Patre luminum. Atque, quicquid bonum est, ad Deum referendum esse, hinc claret, quòd cum Ipse solus bonus sit, Matth. 19. 17. Omnia quoque propter se Ipsum fecerit, Prov. 16.4. Certè Cicero, præ homine meo, majori reverentia de Deo loquitur Orat. pro Rosc. Amer. quando ita fatur: Commoda,quibus utimur; lucem, quâ fruimur; Spiritum, quem ducimus; à Deo nobis dari & impartiri videmus: atque, hoc referendum esse ad ipsos bonos auctores Gronovii, idem Philosophus docet lib. 1. de Nat. Deor. Nemo (inquit) magnus, sine aliquo afflatu divino unquam fuit. Cæterum Gronovius lucelli Scholasti (neque enim alio loco privatæ ipsi- ut lectiones haberi debent) nimium quàm avidus, securus est Scripturæ, atque, tantus natu, nondum prima elementa Catechetica intelligit: præterea Ciceronem, aliosque ejusdem farinæ auctores, juxta suum, (sed verveceum) judicium bonos, consuevit legere non ut melior reddatur, attendendo sententias ad Theologiam & jus naturale pertinentes; sed, ut supra Theatrum Grammaticum, famæ Criticæ Trophæum erigere possit.
units.tr: XXIII. Somewhere in my earlier Vindiciae, when the author kept boasting of his good authorities, I had vowed that in the one excellent book, which alone is theopneustos [θεόπνευστος], he would be more practised than in Statius Papinius, Justin, Plautus, Petronius, Livy, Seneca, and so on. Since he could not complain of this, he presents to his reader the shameful emblem of self-seeing [τῆς αὐθεόπτου], in these words on p. 114, defending his good books, by which he would rather die than by the most sacred Bible: But those books, he says, do not cease to be good, because theopneustos [ὁ Θεόπνευστος] is better than all good things. For a thing is good in its own order, which NB. does not extend to or pertain to the highest good; and he who sets these up as opposed shows that he is a bad dialectician, and has not learned the doctrine of opposites, to give his words back to him. So, my dear atheist, can there be something good which does not depend on God, nor pertain to Him? But what does the Apostle James say, Catholic Epistle, chapter 1, verse 17? Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. [πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθή, καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον ἄνωθέν ἐστι, καταβαῖνον ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν φώτων.] That whatever is good must be referred to God is clear from the fact that, since He alone is good (Matt. 19.17), He has also made all things for Himself (Prov. 16.4). Certainly Cicero, before my man, speaks of God with greater reverence in his speech for Roscius of Ameria, when he says: The blessings we enjoy, the light in which we live, the breath we draw, we see as given and bestowed on us by God. That this must be referred to the good authors of Gronovius themselves, the same philosopher teaches in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods: No one, he says, has ever been great without some divine inspiration. Moreover, Gronovius, too greedy for a little profit from a schoolboy (for these readings ought to be had not in some other place but in private ones), is careless of Scripture, and, though so old, does not yet understand the first elements of catechetical teaching. Besides, Cicero and other authors of the same stamp, according to his own (but asinine) judgement, he is accustomed to read as good authors, not so that he may become better by attending to the sentiments which pertain to theology and natural law, but so that, beyond the Grammatical Theatre, he may raise a trophy to his critical fame.

units.la: XXIV. Quæ de Denario, quondam decem, postea duodecim assibus valente, dixeram; non merebantur exfibilari à Gronovio. Nam inde effectum, ut in aliis, ita circa usuram unciam, aut fœnus unciarium, usum loquendi magis attendi debere, quàm Grammaticorum regulas, rigidasque susupercilii Critici rationes. Quod ipse juxta me- cum,expugnatus à veritate, fatetur: pag. 115. ita ptoloquendo : Justa volumina condi possunt in omnibus linguis vocabulorum ,quorum significatio ab origine ita deflexerit, ut, vel contractior vel amplior, aliquando & prorsus alia & omnino contraria reddita fuerit : quod ita ne fieret, intercesssisse Grammaticem, aut, se invita fieri, obtestatâ Deum hominumque fidem , nullis unquam nunciis accepi. Quo ingenio hic homo fit, mi Lector , attende? In toto hoc scripto, pro, fœnore Unciario, ex suis principiis explicando, nullis aliis armis, quàm Grammaticis, digladiatur: Interim mihi detrahere studet, quòd, attendendo conditionem temporum atque rerumpublicarum , ostenderim , frementibus licet Grammaticis, quos ipse hic submovet, fœnus unciarium Centesimæ adæquari debere ? Deinde , pag. 116. dissimulando ea, quæ de ἀναξονισμῶ dixeram , arguit me quòd Licinnium eum vocaverim, ( secutus fui fidem Dionis Cassij lib. 54.) qui in Veteri Epigrammate Licinus vocatur. Certè , mihi oppido adhuc puero, notum fuit hoc ipsum Epigramma , quod Vetus Persij Scholiastes nobis servavit, varronique tribuit, atque ita habet :
units.tr: XXIV. What I had said about the denarius, once worth ten asses and later twelve, did not deserve to be hissed at by Gronovius. For it follows that, in other cases as well as in the matter of the uncia, or unciary interest, the actual usage of speech ought to be attended to rather than the rules of the grammarians and the stern arguments of the critic with his frowning brow. He himself, overcome by the truth, admits this along with me, p. 115, speaking thus: Just volumes could be written in all languages about words whose meaning has so departed from its origin that it has become now narrower or broader, sometimes altogether other and wholly contrary. That this should not happen, grammar has not intervened; or, if it has happened against its will, I have never received any report of it, calling God and the faith of men to witness. What sort of mind this man has, my dear reader, do you notice? In this whole writing, in explaining the unciary interest from his own principles, he fights with no weapons but grammatical ones. Meanwhile he strives to detract from me because, attending to the condition of the times and of the commonwealths, I showed that the unciary interest ought to be equated with the centesima, even though the grammarians, whom he here dismisses, rage? Then, p. 116, passing over what I had said about anaxonismos, he argues that I called him Licinnius (I followed Dio Cassius, book 54), who is called Licinus in an old epigram. Certainly, when I was still quite a boy, this very epigram was known to me, the one the old scholiast of Persius preserved for us and attributed to Varro, and it reads thus:

units.la: Marmoreo Licinus tumulo jacet, at Cato parvo,
units.tr: Licinus lies in a marble tomb, but Cato in a small one,

units.la: Pompejus nullo, credimus esse Deos ?
units.tr: Pompey in none. Do we believe there are gods?

units.la: At, unde Gronovius probaverit, Dionis Licinnium eundem esse, cum Licino, pro quo ipse stat ? Aut, quare nobis non licebit dicere poëtam propter me-trum scripsisse Licinum, pro Licinnio? Eadem Salaminijs consuli posset, ut centesima perpetuò fœnore ducerentur. at λόγοις ipsius verbo non re-spondeo, cùm sint
units.tr: But from where would Gronovius have proved that Dio's Licinnius is the same as Licinus, for whom he himself stands? Or why should it not be permitted for us to say that the poet wrote Licinus for Licinnius because of the meter? The same could be said of the Salaminii, that centesimas were always reckoned as interest. But I do not answer his words [λόγοις], since they are

units.la: Inopes rerum, nugaque canora.
units.tr: empty of substance, and a resounding trifle.

units.la: Duntaxat Lectorem meumrogo, Epistolam illam defæcata à præjudiciis mente legere dignetur, & qualis paraphrastes iniquissimus meus adversarius haberi debeat, patebit. Postea, per plures pagi-nas nempe usque ad 127. insignes inmugis tragædi-as agit, ut mihi invito persuadeat, Centesimam ipsam hactenus debuisse agnoscere assem u-surarium pro explicatione usuræ unciæ, aut fœno-ris unciarii: atque, cum videret àse mihi hoc af-fingi, pag. 117, pro imperio ita me juxtimque Lectorem suum affatur: Det age vel nunc definitionem aut descriptionem qualemcunque Centesimæ usuræ, in quam non intret anni aut annui mentio: credam illum non fecisse, quod totiès fecit. Quæ vero iniquitas est, si hæc non sit? Priores vindiciæ altera jam vice typis exscriptæ, satis exhibent mentem meam, quam sibi mortalium iniquissimus, omnia, quæ à me dicta fuerunt, dissimulando, exponi jubet. Parebo, sed hac duntaxat vice, quoniam veritas latebras non quærit. Ergo juxta mea principia: Centesima est usura maxima, quæ cum cencentesimo mense forti adæquaretur, Romæ, relata ad Numæ Pompilii annum, quoque mense singulas un- cias, annuatim verò duodenas exhibebat. Quum verò hæ unciæ, ratione anni Romani, qui respon- debat quod ad primam divisionem, unciis veri af- fis libræ, quoque mense juxta consuetudinem solvi deberent, factum fuit, ut eadem hæc usura unciaria diceretur. Quòd verò Centesima à me considerata fuerit ut as usurarius, (passim hoc in- nui) non debet absolute considerari, sed secun- dum annum Romanum, cujus ratione habita, quoq; mense Centesima singulas uncias exhibet, quæ du- odecies juxta anni Romani menses multiplicatæ, ipsam Centesimam absolvunt. Adeo, ut Cente- sima, alio modo nequeat considerari As usurari- us, quàm in ordine ad eundem annum : Pariter nec uncia usura, juxta nostra principia, debeat re- ferri ad assem libram, sed ad Centesimam relatam ad annum Romanum duodenis mensibus constan- tem. Atque, ut maxima hæc usura, totum af- fem libram exhauriens, non potest secundum no- men suum commodè explicari, nisi interveniente anno Romano duodenis mensibus constante; ita convenienter, cœterum synecdoche simul in par- tes sollicitata, Centesimâ usuram æquivalere fœ- nori unciario statuimus: quatenus, ipsa ad annum Romanum relata, singulis mensibus singulas un- cias assis librae exigit. Hæc quàm dilucide in u- troque Scripto exposueram, &c., quasi nihil egifsem atque me similem Apollini τῷ λοξίῳ exhi-buissem, Gronovius mihi altera jam vice insultat. Mentem hanc meam fuisse, ipse volens nolens profiteri cogitur pag. 129. ubi ita more suo, sive maledicè loquitur: Hæc sententia hujus velut à Caco eructati fumi, diversam esse rationem uncia-rum, & reliquarum usurarum: quippe uncias unci-is anni solutas, (hoc verissimum est) nullas autem sextantibus aut trientibus anni. Atque hoc adRo-manorum mores, neque ulterius referendum esse pariter ex principiis meis patet: frustraque est ad-versarius, quando me mecum vult committere quod scripserim, aliter potuisse convenire inter eos qui contractum usurarium inibant, quàm ut quo-que mense usuræ solverentur. Dato enim, illa solutas fuisse singulis anni quadrantibus, (quod circa usuras Centesimas quoque, eminenter qua-ita dictas, per contractum fieri potuit) ratio ta-men haberi debuit anni partium, adeo ut anni qua-drante, sive tribus mensibus elapsis solvi debuerint ternæ unciæ. Quum per contractum non potue-rit mutari modus usurarum, quoque mense exsol-vi solitarum, sed tantùm consuli debitori, quòd minùs illi molestum esset anni quadrantibus, quàm quoque mense usuras exhibere. At duo-bus præterea argumentis instructus est, quibus hanc sententiam de gradu præcipitare conatur. d. pag. 129. sequentia offendo: Hoc speciem haberet in unciario: sed quid fiet semunciario accepto prosemissibus usuris ? fi omnino quoque mense solvebant, nunquam etiam solvebant, semuncia vel semissé (eadem enim hæc illi) anni: & sic in semunciario fœnore, eadem ratio cessat, quæ in sextantibus, &c. De suo affingit, quod juxta mea principia, dilucidè mentem meam exponentia, æquivalere debeant semuncia anni atque semissis. Panicus verò metus est, quo corripitur pro fœnore semunciario, æquivalente quasi semissibus usuris. Nam usura centesima ad annum Romanum relata, juxta illa, quæ modo dixi, æque semunciarii fœnoris, imo usurarum sextantium, &c. reddere rationem possum, atque illi, qui varias usurarum differentias, juxta assem libram considerare assolent. Attendamus quoque alterum argumentum, quod sequentibus verbis pag. 130. proponit: Deinde quòd uncia usura solvantur unciis anni, sive unoquoque mense, est commune accidens omnium usurarum, non fœnoris unciarii proprium: & propterea unciarum usurarum naturam invertere, aut differentem ab aliis, quod ad originem nominis ac significationis, reddere non potest. At hoc frivolum est, & ad rem nequicquam facit. Qui cum Gronovio sentiunt usuram centesimam omnium maximam, Romæ fuisse, non possunt eandem secundum assem libram explicare, nisi hunc comparaverint cum anno Romano: cur pariter ergo mihi non licuerit, Centesimam ad eundem annum relatam, distribuere propter duodenos anni Romani menses, per totidem uncias? XXV. Quòd XXV. Quòd hominem præsidentem pro meritis notassem, persuasum vellet Lectori, (sed judicio destituto) hæc non sibi soli, sed ipsi Salmasio quoque dicta fuisse, cujus tamen ne quidem memineram, atque à quo se diversum sentire aperte professus fuerat. Eòque, unicum hunc meum hominem respexi, nec conjectura assequi poteram, eum in postremo hoc Tractatu Salmasio accessu-rum esse. Si ipse putet hæc Salmasio quoque competere, per me judicio suo frui poterit: atque, de Salmasio idem exi-stimabo, quod ipse alibi Grotio applicat. Quò majori, inquit, nominis famâ suffarcinati sunt, qui curas suas publicant: eo majore cum pernicie reip. Literariæ peccant, si quando ipsis, ut peccent, usu venit.
units.tr: I only ask my reader to deign to read that letter with a mind cleansed of prejudice, and it will be plain what kind of paraphrast my most unjust adversary ought to be considered. Afterwards, through many pages, namely up to 127, he performs remarkable tragedies, so as to persuade me against my will that the centesima itself should hitherto have been acknowledged as the usurious as, for the explanation of the usury of the uncia or unciary interest. And since he saw that this was being fastened on me, at p. 117 he addresses me and his reader imperiously thus: Come now, give even now some definition or description of centesimal usury in which no mention of the year or of yearly interest enters. I will believe he did not do what he has done so often. What injustice is this, if it is not? My earlier defence, already printed a second time, sufficiently sets forth my mind, which this most unjust of mortals, by passing over everything I said, orders to be expounded. I will obey, but on this occasion only, since truth does not seek hiding places. So, according to my principles: The centesima is the greatest usury, which, when reckoned at the hundredth month, would equal the principal. At Rome, referred to the year of Numa Pompilius, it paid one uncia each month, and twelve uncias yearly. Since these unciae, by the reckoning of the Roman year, which corresponded to the first division of the as into unciae, were to be paid each month according to custom, it came about that this same usury was called unciary. But that I considered the centesima as an as of usury (I have hinted at this throughout) ought not to be considered absolutely, but according to the Roman year, in view of which the centesima pays one uncia each month, and these, multiplied twelve times according to the months of the Roman year, complete the centesima itself. So the centesima can be considered as an as of usury in no other way than in relation to that same year. Likewise, according to our principles, the uncia of usury ought not to be referred to the pound of the as, but to the centesima referred to the Roman year, which consists of twelve months. And just as this greatest usury, exhausting the whole as of the pound, cannot be explained suitably according to its name unless the Roman year of twelve months intervenes, so, suitably, with the synecdoche also applied to the parts, we have established that the centesima is equivalent to the unciary interest, inasmuch as, referred to the Roman year, it demands a single uncia of the pound of the as each month. How clearly I had set this out in both writings, &c., as if I had done nothing and had shown myself like Apollo the Loxias, Gronovius again insults me. He is compelled, whether he likes it or not, to confess that this was my meaning, where he speaks in his usual fashion, abusively, at p. 129: This opinion of his is like smoke belched out by Cacus: that the reckoning of the unciae and of the other usuries is different, since unciae are indeed paid in the unciae of the year (this is most true), but not in the sextantes or trientes of the year. And from this it is equally clear, from my principles, that the Roman custom is not to be referred further; and the adversary is wrong when he wishes to quarrel with me over what I wrote, that those who entered into a usurious contract could have agreed otherwise than that the usury be paid each month. For granting that they were paid at each quarter of the year (which, in the case of the centesimal usuries, also called eminently so, could be done by contract), still the reckoning of the parts of the year ought to have been kept, so that three uncias were to be paid at the quarter of the year, that is, after three months had elapsed. For the mode of the usuries, which used to be paid each month, could not be changed by contract, but only consulted for the debtor, so that it would be less burdensome to him to pay the usuries at quarters of the year than each month. But he is armed with two further arguments, by which he tries to overthrow this opinion from its standing. At the same page, 129, I encounter the following: This would have some appearance in the case of the unciary interest; but what will happen with the semunciary interest received at half-uncia? If they paid it every month, they never paid the half-uncia or semis of the year (for it is the same for him), and so in semunciary interest the same reasoning fails which applies to the sextantes, &c. He adds from his own invention that, according to my principles, which set out my meaning clearly, the semuncia ought to be equivalent to the half of the year and to the semis. But the fear with which he is seized over the semunciary interest, as if it were equivalent to semis-usuries, is a groundless one. For the centesima, referred to the Roman year, according to what I have just said, can give an account of the semunciary interest, indeed of the sextantal usuries, &c., just as well as those who are accustomed to consider the various differences of usuries according to the pound of the as. Let us also consider the other argument, which he sets forth at p. 130 in the following words: Further, that unciary usuries are paid in the unciae of the year, that is, every month, is a common accident of all usuries, not a property of unciary interest; and therefore it cannot invert the nature of unciary usuries, or make them different from others as regards the origin of the name and its meaning. But this is frivolous, and comes to nothing for the matter. Those who agree with Gronovius that the centesima was the greatest of all usuries at Rome cannot explain it according to the pound of the as unless they have compared it with the Roman year. Why, then, should it not likewise be permitted to me to distribute the centesima, referred to that same year, into as many unciae as there are months in the Roman year, twelve? XXV. That I had noted this man, as he deserved, he would have the reader believe (though without judgement) was said not only of himself but of Salmasius too; yet I had not even remembered him, and he had openly professed that he thought otherwise than Salmasius. Therefore I had regard to this one man alone, nor could I by conjecture reach the point that he would approach Salmasius in this last treatise. If he himself thinks these things apply to Salmasius too, he may enjoy his own judgement through me; and about Salmasius I will think the same as he elsewhere applies to Grotius: The more they are stuffed with the fame of a great name who publish their cares, the greater the harm they do to the republic of letters when it happens to them to err.

units.la: XXVI. Hisce expeditis, lepidus meus Suffe-nus, ut se efferre posset, Grammaticæ suæ (quam non potueram non antea notare) Mosen ipsum patronum sollicitat, atque juxta dispositionem Cerebelli sui ita profari audet pag. 132. Quanquam valde malignus est iste voluntatis alienæ interpres, volo tamen, si Grammaticum est, quicquid literatum, & ex interiore censu ac mundo eruditionis petitum: ut Mosen primum σοφὸν fuisse τὸν γραμματικὸν, id est, docte scribendi arte discat: τῆς Ἰσδαίοις παραδόσεως, ut, ex Eupolemo refert Clemens: ut Eratosthenis solertia in omni genere literarum, Grammatici nomine addito significavit antiquitas: & ad tantum opus aliquid conferre mea scripta, magnificum duco. Volo etiam, si Grammaticam est, quicquid non discrepat à praeceptis recte loquendi; quicquid non est ὑποσόλοι-κὸν aut βαρβαρίζωνον: &, qui vel hoc assequatur, eum cur poeniteat, quantum profecerit, nihil esse causse censeo. Resp. 1. Adeste ergo omnes, qui vestrum merum Imperium (quod caeteroquin ludi puerilis parietes non egreditur, ) ferulâ, Orbilii illo tremendo sceptro, metiri soletis: at ne oblivisicamini, manum cavam assibus repletam, in sinum viri, scil. ab avaritia alieni, Gronovii profundere: is vos Mosi adaequabit, ut posthac supra ipsos Pastores Ecclesiae incedere debeatis.
units.tr: XXVI. With these matters settled, my charming Suffenus, in order to puff himself up, calls on Moses himself as his patron for his Grammar (which I could not help noticing earlier). Following the plan of his little brain, he dares to speak thus on p. 132: Although that interpreter of another's will is very ill-natured, I nevertheless want, if whatever is literary and drawn from the inner treasury and world of learning is grammar, that Moses first learn to have been a σοφός, that is, a man skilled in the art of writing well, [τὸν γραμματικόν] in the tradition of the Jews, as Clement reports from Eupolemus; just as antiquity used the title Grammarian, with the addition of his name, to signify Eratosthenes' skill in every kind of literature; and I think it a fine thing to add something of my writings to so great a work. I also want, if it is grammar, whatever does not depart from the rules of correct speech, whatever is not solecistic or barbarous; and I think there is no reason for anyone who reaches even this to regret how far he has advanced. Reply 1. Come then, all of you who are accustomed to measure your petty empire (which otherwise does not go beyond the walls of a boys' school) with a rod, with that dread sceptre of Orbilius; but do not forget to pour out your cupped hand full of coins into the lap of a man, namely one free from avarice, Gronovius. He will make you equal to Moses, so that from now on you ought to walk above the very ministers of the Church.

units.la: 2. Aures quoque arrigite omnes in Academia Lugduno-Batava studiosi, modo Gronovii discipuli fueritis: atque incedite posthac supra veteranos Theologiae studiosos, quum juxta Doctorem vestrum Mosi Aaron cedere debuerit.
units.tr: 2. Prick up your ears too, all you students at the Academy of Leiden, provided you have been pupils of Gronovius; and from now on walk above the veteran students of theology, since, according to your teacher, Aaron ought to yield to Moses.

units.la: 3. Sed Mosen hunc Grammaticum, aliquanto presfius excutere debeo; ut homo meus frontem recuperet, quae diu ipsi periit. Adducere & examinare convenit ipsa Clementis verba, quae occurunt lib. 1. Strom. Εὐπόλεμος δὲ ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ βασιλέων, τὸν Μωυσῆ φησι πρῶτον συφὸν γενέσθαι, καὶ γραμματικὴν πρῶτον τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις παραδοῦναι, καὶ πρὸς Ἰουδαίων Φοίνικας παραλαβεῖν. Eupolemus autem in libro de Judaeorum regibus, dicit, Mosen primum fuisse sapientem, & grammatimaticam primum tradidisse Judæis, & Phœnices accepisse à Judæis, Græcos autem à Phœnicibus. Quis verò Genius Gronovio suggessit τὴν γραμματικὴν esse artem docte scribendi? Eupolemus hoc dunta-xat innuere vult, Mosen primum literarum inven-torem fuisse. Sed, an omnes illi, qui literas in-venerunt, Grammatici tales agnoscendi sunt, qua-lis Gronovius salutatur? Non possum quin insi-gnem Taciti locum adducam, qui occurrit lib. 11. Ann. cap. 14. Primi (inquit) per figuras animali-um Ægyptii sensus mentis effingebant; & anti-quissima monimenta memoriæ humanæ impressa sa-xis cernuntur; & literarum semet inventores per-hibent: inde Phœnicas, quia mari præpollebant, in-tulisse Græciæ, gloriamque adeptos, tanquam repe-rerint, quae acceperant. Quippe fama est, Cadmum classe Phœnicum vectum, rudibus adhuc Græcorum populis artis hujus auctorem fuisse. Quidam Cecro-pem Athenien sem, vel Linum Thebanum, & tempo-ribus Trojanis Palam edem Argivum memorant, sex-decim literarum formas: mox alios, ac præcipuum Simonidem caeteras reperisse. At in Italia Etrusci ab Corinthio Damarato, Aborigenes Arcade ab Evandro didicerunt, & forma literis Latinis, quae veterrimis Græcorum. Sed nobis quoque paucae primum fuere: deinde additae sunt. Quo exem-plo Claudius tres litteras adjecit, quae usu, impe-ritante eo, post obliteratae. Volui integrum lo-cum adscribere, ut meus adversarius, minime scil. ambitiosus, prænobili Grammaticorum genti, posthac, tot Reges & Principes ex Annalium memoria inserat. Cum verò Claudius Imperator, judicio titulum Grammatici, non tamen Gronoviani, affectasse videatur, suaserim, ut hic illius Imaginem in Museo statuat, addito elogio matris Antoniæ, quæ stultiorem filio suo Claudio nemi-nem fuisse censebat. 4. Pari ratione Phrygiones, imo, & Domini sartores, quotquot occurrunt, Mo-sen patronum suum esse clament, docuit enim eos, qui in exilio Israelitico hanc artem exercebant, qua ratione conficiendæ essent Aaronis vestes; nominatim Betzaleelem (Exod. 36.) qua-li artificio vela tabernaculo destinata, ordinari o-pereque Phrygiano pingi deberent. 5. Nec pudeat posthac Actæonis fraterculos, quòd cornua objiciantur: nam cornutam Moßs faciem fuisse, aperte indicat Vulgata Versio Latina, Exod. cap. 34. verf. 29. cui non dubito, quin meus homo plus deferat, quàm ulli alii Versioni Latinæ, propter Styli scil. elegantiam. Usque adeo verò ad animum revocat, quòd Grammaticum eum vocaverim, ut pag. 133. hoc convitiorum emblemate conspurcari debeam: Theologorum vomica, Juris consultorum carcinoma, Medicorum simia, Physicus in Turfis & harengis, & Maurorum genitura, Philologus sine Grammatica, Rhetor Synecdochicus. At, quid aliud facit, quam si mulier, olera aut pisces vendere solita, uxorem illius (quam honestam stam coeteroquin esse puto) meretricem vocasset ; ipse vicissim pro vindiciis honoris, convicIantem; scrophaum,veneficam,trivenefi cam , incendiariam &c. agnoscendam esse proclamaret : Quis qualisque sim publicè constat, nec movere me possunt hæc & similia convitia. Scio cui crediderim : Ideo-que non timebo in die malâ, Prov. 3, 25. nec per-cellar repentino timore, Prov. 1, 33. Sed absque terrore requiescam, Jer. 17. 8. Plura non addo, quòd ad hæc & similia jam antea responderim. Fero, ut Gronovius titulo Grammatici sese oblec-tet, eoque nomine sufflet. Ego hactenus ma-neo Socraticus, barbatus enim ille magister, teste Athenæo lib. 12. dicere solet, tria esse mala: Gram-maticum, pauperta tem , & malam uxorem.
units.tr: 3. But I must examine this grammarian Moses a little more closely, so that my man may recover the face he has long lost. It is fitting to bring forward and weigh Clement's own words, which occur in book 1 of the Stromata: Εὐπόλεμος δὲ ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ βασιλέων, τὸν Μωυσῆ φησι πρῶτον σοφὸν γενέσθαι, καὶ γραμματικὴν πρῶτον τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις παραδοῦναι, καὶ πρὸς Ἰουδαίων Φοίνικας παραλαβεῖν. [Eupolemus, however, in his book on the kings of the Jews, says that Moses first became wise and first handed grammar down to the Jews, and that the Phoenicians received it from the Jews.] Yet what genius suggested to Gronovius that grammar is the art of writing well? Eupolemus means only that Moses was the first inventor of letters. But are all those who invented letters to be acknowledged as grammarians of the kind Gronovius is greeted as? I cannot refrain from citing the notable passage of Tacitus, which occurs in book 11 of the Annals, chapter 14: The Egyptians (he says) first expressed the sense of the mind by figures of animals; and the most ancient monuments of human memory are seen carved in stone; and they claim to be the inventors of letters: from them the Phoenicians, because they excelled at sea, brought letters to Greece, and gained glory as if they had discovered what they had received. Indeed, the story goes that Cadmus, sailing with a Phoenician fleet, was the author of this art among the Greek peoples, still rude. Some name Cecrops of Athens, or Linus of Thebes, and in the Trojan period Palamedes the Argive, as inventors of the sixteen forms of letters; then others, and above all Simonides, are said to have discovered the rest. But in Italy the Etruscans learned them from the Corinthian Demaratus, and the Aborigines the Arcadians from Evander, and the letter forms were like those of the most ancient Greeks. But for us too there were at first few, and then more were added. By this example Claudius added three letters, which after his reign fell out of use. I wished to quote the whole passage, so that my opponent, who is by no means ambitious, may later insert in the most noble race of grammarians so many kings and princes from the memory of the annals. But since the Emperor Claudius seems to have aspired to the title of grammarian, though not of Gronovius's kind, I would advise that he set up an image of Claudius in his museum, with the inscription of his mother Antonia, who thought no one more stupid than her son Claudius. 4. In the same way the Phrygians, and indeed all the tailors of the Lord whoever they are, cry out that Moses is their patron; for he taught those who practised this art in the Israelite exile how the garments of Aaron were to be made; and by name Bezaleel (Exod. 36.), by what skill the veils destined for the tabernacle were to be ordered and painted in Phrygian work. 5. Let the little brothers of Actaeon not be ashamed from now on, though horns are thrown at them; for the Latin Vulgate version clearly indicates that Moses' face was horned, Exod. ch. 34, verse 29; I do not doubt that my man values it more than any other Latin version, on account of its elegance of style. Indeed he so much keeps in mind that I called him a grammarian that, on p. 133, I must be defiled with this emblem of abuse: The festering sore of theologians, the cancer of jurists, the ape of physicians, a physicist of turfs and herrings, and a Moor's offspring, a philologist without grammar, a rhetorician of synecdoche. But what else does he do than if a woman who is accustomed to sell vegetables or fish were to call a man's wife (whom I otherwise think respectable) a whore, and he in turn, in defence of his honour, scolding her, should proclaim that she must be recognised as a sow, a poisoner, a three-times poisoner, an incendiary, etc. What and what sort of man I am is publicly known, and these and similar insults cannot move me. I know in whom I have believed: therefore I will not be afraid of evil day, Prov. 3:25, nor be struck with sudden fear, Prov. 1:33. But I shall rest without terror, Jer. 17:8. I add no more, since I have already replied to these and similar things. I permit Gronovius to delight in the title of grammarian and to puff himself up with that name. As for me, I remain a Socratic so far; for that bearded master, as Athenaeus reports in book 12, used to say that there are three evils: a grammarian, poverty, and a bad wife.

units.la: XXVII. Omissis sexcentis ratiunculaꝛū quisquiliis, quas per plures paginas accumulat, pag. 138. ufq; ad pag. 145. accedit ad legem 48. ff. de administr. & periculo tutor. meisque verbis accilis, & instar Penthei discerptis, respondet more Gronoviano, hoc est, sycophantice, seu mala fide. Interim, quod ipse dissimulat, notandum est, veteres tu-tissimum censuisse, si omnes suas fortunas habe-rent in præsenti pecunia. Si ipse, qui habetur Juris Utriusque Doctor, in lectione Pandectarum Versatior fuisset, non ignorasset Celsum in lege, si Chorus 79. §. 1. ff. de Legat. 111. perhibere Proculum solitum referre, audivissese, rusticos se-nes ita dicentes, pecuniam sine peculio fragilem ef-se: se: peculium illud vocantes, quod præsidii caussa se-poneretur. Cui consonum est, quod Constanti-nus Imp. in pecunia,veteres omne robur parrimo-niorum posuisse testatur, leg. 22. Cod. de Admi-nist: Tutor. Verba legis ita habent: Ipsius pecuniæ (in qua robur omne patrimoniorum veteres posue-runt) fœnerandi usus vix diuturnus, vix continuus & stabilis est. Unde jam patet, cur testator cen-turio, noluerit pupillorum suorum nummos dispergi, qui semper cum usuris ordinarijs, minimum centesimis, à trapezita locuplete, atque boni no-minis, repeti poterant. Hæc circa legem d. an-notasse sufficit, nec reliqua, quæ conglobat ad-versarius, merentur responsionem.
units.tr: XXVII. Passing over the six hundred trifles of little arguments which he piles up over several pages, from p. 138 to p. 145, he comes to the law 48, Digest, on the administration and risk of guardians, and, having snatched my words and torn them apart like Pentheus, he replies in the Gronovian manner, that is, slanderously, or in bad faith. Meanwhile, what he himself conceals must be noted: the ancients judged it safest if they held all their fortunes in ready money. If he himself, who is held to be a Doctor of Both Laws, had been more versed in reading the Pandects, he would not have been unaware that Celsus, in the law Si chorus 79, §1, Digest, on legacies III, reports that Proculus used to relate that he had heard old country people saying that money without a reserve fund is fragile: they called that reserve fund a peculium, which is set aside for protection. Consonant with this is what the Emperor Constantine testifies about money, that the ancients placed all the strength of patrimonies in it, law 22, Code, on the administration of guardians. The words of the law are: The use of lending that money itself (in which the ancients placed all the strength of patrimonies) is scarcely lasting, scarcely continuous and stable. Whence it is now clear why the centurion testator did not want his wards' coins scattered, which could always be recovered with the usual interest, at least one per cent, from a rich and reputable banker. It is enough to have noted these things about the law mentioned; the rest which my opponent heaps together does not deserve a reply.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Pro Senecæ quoq; usura millesima,ut æ-quivaleat ipsius unciariæ,paginæ complures replen-tur: ad quas si responderem, & injurius in meam valetudinem, & otium essem. Contendantur so-lummodo eum meis, atque, nihil solidi illis in-esse liquebit. Interim, qui tam prolixè & ope-rosè illis, quæ à me dicta sunt, respondere nititur, oblivisci ur bulgæ anicularum suarum, nec semet liberat hac suspicione, quasi instar hæredipetarum, aut testamentis illarum insidietur, aut levibus usu-ris pecuniam ab iis accipere solitus sit, ut majori-bus occupet. Altum quoque apud eum silenti-um de Classibus avarorum, deseritque hanc senten-tiam, extra eos, qui in summa cavea sedebant, nullos avaros inveniri, quum certum sit, eos po-tissi. tisfimum pertinere ad Orchestram, atque Quatu- ordecim. Ne dicam inveniri quoque in ipso Re- gum, atque Excelsorum Principum ordine.
units.tr: Several pages are also filled with Seneca's usury at one per thousand, so that it equals his uncial rate. If I were to answer these, I would be doing an injury to my own health and wasting my leisure. I will only set them against my own arguments, and it will be clear that they contain nothing solid. Meanwhile, the man who strives so long and laboriously to answer what I have said forgets his gang of old women. He does not free himself from the suspicion that, like a legacy hunter, he lies in wait for their wills, or that he is accustomed to take money from them at light interest so as to seize larger sums. He also keeps a deep silence about the seating classes of the avaricious, and abandons his position that the only misers are those who sat in the top tier. It is certain that they belong chiefly to the orchestra and the fourteen rows. Not to mention that they are also found in the very order of kings and the highest princes.

units.la: XXIX. Hactenus, sepositis Gronovianis nugamen- tis, responsione planè indignis, sufficiat mea argu- menta vindicasse. Cæterum, quibus hactenus placuit arbitrari de controversia, quæ mihi cum homine intercedit, faverunt quidem (inter illos occurrunt plures ex honoratioribus ejusdem ami- cis) rationibus meis; interim optarunt sibi often- di Grammaticum antiquum, qui mihi esset ὁμό- ψηφος. Verū, quot non difficilia quà in Græcis qua Latinis auctoribus occurrunt, quasi ἅπαξ λεγόμενα; quæ solis virorum eruditorum sagaci- bus conjecturis illustrata, nullius, sive antiqui Scholiastæ, sive Grammatici suffragio adjuvantur. Quod aliud non possim, interim exhibeo locum Porphyrionis, cujus hæc verba, cæterum admo- dum mendosa, occurrunt in Comment. ad Ho- ratium, lib. 2. Sat. 3. quando occasione horum ver- borum poëtæ, sive, ad vers. 69. Scribæ decem Ne- rio; Ita commentatur: Avaros tangit. Sensus est. Pecuniam à fœneratore acceptam lege duo- decim tabularum, quas Nerio instituit, & aliis centum Perillius Cicuta amarissimus consignato- res furabitur. Hactenus Porphyrion. Quæ ita in ordinem redigo, salvo aliorum judicio: Sensus est, Pecuniam à fœneratore acceptam lege duodecim Tabularum, quam Nerio instituit ex aliis centum (scil. nummis) Perillius Cicuta amarisi- mus, per consignatores (eos scil. qui una cum aliis sigillis suis syngraphas munire solent) furabitur. Quum vero Flaccus decem pro duodecim (quod versum ingredi non poterat) posuerit; atque Porphyrion dicat expresse illos decem (revera duodecim in stipulatum venisse juxta Legem XII.) videor hinc colligere per fœnus unciarium, cujus meminit Lex XII. Tabularum, intelligi debere usuram centesimam. Cæterum ultra conjectu- ras hæc æstimari non cupio.
units.tr: XXIX. Thus far, setting aside Gronovius's trifles, which are wholly unworthy of an answer, it is enough to have defended my arguments. As for the others, who up to now have been pleased to form an opinion on the controversy between me and this man, they have indeed favoured my reasons (among them are several of the more distinguished friends of the same man). Yet they wished for an ancient grammarian who would be ὁμόψηφος [of the same vote] with me. But how many difficult passages occur in both Greek and Latin authors, as if they were ἅπαξ λεγόμενα [said only once], which, though illustrated by the keen conjectures of learned men alone, are supported by the authority of no ancient scholiast or grammarian. Since I cannot do otherwise, I here present a passage of Porphyrion, whose words, though very corrupt, occur in his commentary on Horace, Satire 2.3, where the poet's words give occasion for comment on verse 69, "the ten scribes of Nerius." He comments: "He touches on misers. The meaning is this: Perillius Cicuta, most bitter of men, will steal money received from a moneylender under the law of the Twelve Tables, which Nerius instituted, and will steal another hundred from the sealers." Thus far Porphyrion. I reduce these words into order, saving the judgement of others: "The meaning is this: the money received from a moneylender under the law of the Twelve Tables, which Nerius instituted, Perillius Cicuta, most bitter of men, will steal from the other hundred (that is, coins) through the sealers (that is, those who usually secure contracts with their own seals along with others)." Since Flaccus put "ten" for "twelve" (which could not enter the verse), and since Porphyrion expressly says that those ten (in fact twelve came into the stipulation according to Law XII), I seem to gather from this that by the unciary interest, which the Law of the Twelve Tables mentions, one should understand the hundredth part as interest. Yet I do not wish these things to be judged beyond conjecture.

units.la: XXIX. Postremò expugnanda mihi est Gronovii ἀκεφάλις, quam ipse judicio Mathematico-Architectonico, sed simul Grammatico statuit: & quâ ipse se solum defensurum esse, confidit, quòd eâ concluserit meos barbarismos, solœcos, & solœcismos, tanquam jure belli Grammatici captivos. Rationem, cur præ petulantia hoc egerit, hanc reddit pag. 150. Orationis (inquit) reprehendendæ, perinde ut omnis hujus litis, ab ipsius procacitate (mendacium, hominem ambitiosissimum urebat, quòd à me erroris convictus esset) initium est factum. Postquam illam quoque legem certaminis accipit & se inferiorem videt (mendacium alterum; herbam nunquam porrexi, nec porrigam) tropæum id Grammaticum est. Ego verò ita sentio, (nos poma natamus) qui se Philologicæ veritatis quæsitorem, qui de Criticorum familia, quamquamvis obscurissimum profiteatur ; qui ad ma-teriam ex antiquitate Romana petitam lectu & arbitratu suo disputet, (hoc ab ipso factum) atque in ea plus alijs vidisse confidat ; (conferantur scri-pta, & in iis rationes) qui eloquentiae doctoris personam ultro ambierit, fuscepepit, gesserit ; (tertium mendacium : admodum juvenis citra ullum ambitum, à Nobilissimo & Ampliff. Magistra-tu Daventriensi ad Professionem Historiarum & Eloquentiae vocatus fui: ipse verò memoriam su-am excutiat, quae dictabit cum Groningam discederem, per duos Professores, aut verius gane-ones, quotidie-frementibus uxoribus, omnia diver-soria & gurgustia perreptare solitos, hoc procura-tum fuisse, ut meus successor esset,) qui se oratio-nem pectere scire jactitet; ei sermonem duntaxat Latinum, ut nunc haberi potest, praestandum, eumque turpiter discedere, si tropaeum erigi de se Grammaticum injuria queratur: Euge! probe! Hae scil. sunt rationes ; propter quas ad ferulam Gronovii vocari debui. At, qui usque adeo acer mei, & styli mei censor est, eum aestimo intra peritiam vulgarium Grammaticorum, quibus solemne est ea obelo configere, quae optimis auctoribus sunt usitata. Gustum dedisse suffecerit. Quis penulatorum Doctorum non asserit, voces sequentes numerum unitatis non excedere. Ros-rores tamen apud Virgilium & Horatium legimus; roribus, apud Columellam & Plinium. SOBO-LES. LES. Et tamen Columella dixit: nova soboles, FUGA, cū tamen apud Tacitū fugas offendamus. GLORIA, quum ipse Cicero scripserit fugas & exilia. SOLUM, licet idem scripserit; sola terrarum omnia. Sexcenta similia liceret adferre, nisi pauca hæc, speciminis duntaxat loco allata, suf-ficerent; gronoviusque, postea miserrimè vapu-laturus, talium non tam grammaticorum, quàm grammatistarum numerum auctpurus esset. Ipse vero priusquam ad decretorium hunc stylum ac-cessisset, inquirere debuisset, quo impetu, arre-pto Calamo chartis aliquid inarare consueve-rim. Quod de se Erasmus in libro, qui inscribi-tur Ciceronianus, testatur, idem de me, testibus laudatis omnibus, qui propius me norunt, adfir-mare possum. Varia Batavorum eruditissimi hæc sunt: Quid Erasmus Roterodamus? abjicit ac præcipitat omnia, nec parit, sed abortit, interdum justum volumen scribit, stans pede in uno, nec un-quam imperare potest animo suo, ut vel semel rele-gat, quod scripsit. nec aliud quàm scribit, cum post diutinam lectionem demum ad calamum fit venien-dum, & raro. Si clamet, stylum tamen sæpius eum vertere debere, qui Criticus haberi cupit, &c, ab elegantia Latini sermonis commendari; Re-spondebo: Interim hominem meum manere in tribu grammatistarum, atque tam similem esse grammatistæ Porcello, ut non ovum ovo magis. De hoc lepida hæc narratio occurrit, apud Senecam Suaf. 2. ubi cum Cornelii Severi illud de militibus Romanis laudasset:
units.tr: XXIX. Lastly, I must attack Gronovius's headless [ἀκεφάλις] attack, which he judges by a mathematico-architectonic standard, but at the same time a grammatical one. He is confident that he alone will defend it, because by it he has concluded that my barbarisms, solecisms and solecisms are captives, as it were, by the right of grammatical war. He gives the reason why he has done this out of impudence, in these words on page 150: "The censure of my speech, just as the whole of this quarrel, began from his own pertness (a lie: the most ambitious man was burning because he had been convicted of error by me). After he also accepts that law of the contest and sees himself as the inferior (a second lie: I have never held out the herb, nor will I), that is a grammatical trophy. For my part I think (we are swimming among apples) that he who professes to be a seeker of philological truth, who belongs to the family of critics, though he is most obscure, who debates a subject drawn from Roman antiquity as he pleases (this was done by him), and who is confident he has seen more in it than others (let the writings be compared, and the reasons in them), who has willingly sought, undertaken and held the persona of a teacher of eloquence, who boasts that he knows how to dress a speech, should be required to produce only Latin speech as it can now be had, and should depart shamefully if he complains of injury because a grammatical trophy has been raised over him. Bravo! Well done! These, then, are the reasons for which I had to be summoned to Gronovius's ferule. But since he is so sharp a censor of me and my style, I judge him to be within the skill of common grammarians, who are accustomed to mark with an obelus those things which are in use among the best authors. It will be enough to give a taste. Who among learned grammarians does not assert that the following words do not exceed the number of the singular? Yet we read rores in Virgil and Horace, and roribus in Columella and Pliny. SOBOLES. And yet Columella said: nova soboles. FUGA, and yet in Tacitus we find fugas. GLORIA, when Cicero himself wrote fugas & exilia. SOLUM, although he wrote the same: sola terrarum omnia. I could bring six hundred similar examples, were these few, offered only as a sample, not enough; and Gronovius, who was afterwards to be most wretchedly thrashed, would be increasing the number not so much of grammarians as of schoolboys. But before he came to this decisive style, he ought to have inquired with what impetus I am accustomed to scribble something on paper once I have taken up the pen. What Erasmus, in his book entitled Ciceronianus, attests about himself, I can affirm about myself too, with all the witnesses I have named, who know me more closely. These are the very learned Dutchman's words: What of Erasmus of Rotterdam? He throws away and dashes down everything, nor does he bring forth, but miscarries; sometimes he writes a substantial volume standing on one foot, and he can never bring his mind to read over once what he has written. He does nothing but write, and that only after long reading, and at last must go to the pen, and rarely. If he cries out that anyone who wishes to be considered a critic ought to turn his style over more often, and that he is recommended by the elegance of Latin speech, I shall reply: in the meantime, my man remains in the tribe of schoolboys, and is as like a schoolboy as one egg is like another. About this there is a witty story in Seneca's Suasoriae 2, where, having praised Cornelius Severus's line about the Roman soldiers:

units.la: stratique per herbam,
units.tr: Strewn across the grass,

units.la: Hic meus est, dixere dies.
units.tr: "This day, they said, is mine."

units.la: Illud (inquit) Porcellus grammaticus arguebat in hoc versu tanquam solœcismum, quòd cum plures induxisset, diceret, Hic meus est dies, non, Hic dies est nostep: Et in ea sententia optima, accusabat id quod erat optimum: Nam quasi proverbii loco est: Hic dies meus est. Et, cum ad sensum retuleris, ne grammaticorum quidem calumnia habebit locum, dixerunt enim non omnes simul, sed singuli ex his, Hic meus est dies. Ultra hunc Porcellum, æstimandum non esse Gronovium, per varia exempla proximè patebit. Nam exemplo ejusdem, dum porcino illo rostro, inscriptis aliorum, nominatim meis, quærit illud, quo porci valde delectantur, sed, adversus quod, omnes qui sapiunt, nares suas munire solent, ut ut ringatur, invenit vel rosam, vel violam. Fidem faciènt sequentia.
units.tr: Porcellus the grammarian (he says) objected to this line as a solecism, because, having introduced several speakers, the poet wrote "Hic meus est dies" ("This day is mine") and not "Hic dies est noster" ("This day is ours"). And in that excellent sentiment he found fault with what was most excellent. For it is almost a proverb: "Hic dies meus est" ("This day is mine"). And when you refer it to the sense, not even the grammarians' calumny will have any place, for they did not all say it together, but each of them singly said "Hic meus est dies." That Gronovius is not to be valued above this Porcellus will shortly be made plain through various examples. For by his own example, while with that piggish snout he searches through the writings of others, especially my own, for that thing which pigs delight in greatly, but against which all who are wise are accustomed to guard their nostrils, however much he roots about, he finds either a rose or a violet. The following will give proof of this.

units.la: XXX. Ergo initio pag. 150. & seq. iterum exagitat, quod etenim in oratione mea redundarit. nec acquiescere potuit, quod testem pro me adduxisset Cælium Aurelianum, tersi eloquii ac nitidi styli medicum. Sed, ut à Cœlio usurpatum fuit etenim, à me pariter. si cum judicio antiquos auctores legisset, sciviset etenim, non semper causalem esse particulam. Quanquam se gerit pro dictadictatore reip. literariæ, omnes tamen opes Latinæ linguæ exploratas non habet. nec scivit, dum hæc scriberet, etenim ad continuandam orationem sæpe adhiberi. Audiat Horatium Tursellinum, in aureo Opusculo de particulis Latinæ Orationis, qui pag. 78. ex ultima recensione Cl. Thomasii sic loquitur: Utramque enim & etenim continuat interdum orationem. Cic. 4. Verr. Attendite etenim diligenter. Idem Verr. 4. Etenim rem totam breviter cognoscite. Abeat jam scurra grammaticus, & Ciceroni ipsi inclementer dicat! Simul, mi Porcelle, habet hæc prima tua censura. Nec juvare potest lepidum porcellum, tam belle grunnientem, Diomedis definitio de Solœcismo, huic enim oppono auctoritatem Augustini lib. 2. de Doctr. Christiana cap. 13. Solœcismus (inquit) qui dicitur, nihil aliud est, quàm cum verba non eâ lege sibi coaptantur, quâ coaptaverunt, qui, priores nobis, non sine auctoritate aliqua locuti sunt. Item: Barbarismus, quid aliud est, nisi verbum non ex litera, vel sono enunciatum, quo ab eis, qui Latinè ante nos locuti sunt, enunciari solet.
units.tr: XXX. Therefore, at the beginning of page 150 and following, he again attacks the fact that etenim appeared in my speech, nor could he be content that I had cited as a witness Caelius Aurelianus, a physician of polished eloquence and elegant style. But just as etenim was used by Caelius, so it was used by me as well; had he read the ancient authors with judgement, he would have known that etenim is not always a causal particle. Although he plays the dictator of the literary commonwealth, he does not have all the resources of the Latin language explored, nor did he know, while writing this, that etenim is often used to continue a discourse. Let him listen to Horatius Tursellinus, in his golden little work on the particles of Latin speech, who on page 78, in the latest edition by the late Thomasius, speaks thus: "Etenim and utramque sometimes continue the discourse. Cicero, Verrines 4: Attendite etenim diligenter [For pay close attention]. The same in Verrines 4: Etenim rem totam breviter cognoscite [For learn the whole matter briefly]." Let the grammarian buffoon now depart, and let him unkindly speak against Cicero himself! At the same time, my dear Porcellus, this is your first censure. Nor can Diomedes' definition of solecism help the little piglet, so charmingly grunting, for against it I set the authority of Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 13: "What is called a solecism is nothing other than when words are fitted together by a rule other than that by which those who spoke before us, not without some authority, fitted them together. Likewise: what else is a barbarism than a word pronounced not according to the letter or the sound by which those who spoke Latin before us are accustomed to pronounce it?"

units.la: XXX. Antea pag. 103. objecerat mihi, quòd sed pro enim accepissem. At, audiat Buchnerum ex Thesauro Eruditionis Scholasticæ in Vocula sed. Caussalis est, & pro nam poni videtur in istis. Cicero lib. 3. de Finib. Sedulò faciam. Sed fortuna fortes: quare conare quæso. Mart. lib. 10. Ep. 18.
units.tr: XXX. Earlier, on p. 103, he had objected to me that I had taken sed for enim. But let him hear Buchner, in the Thesaurus Eruditionis Scholasticae, under the particle sed. It is causal, and it seems to be used for nam in such passages. Cicero, De Finibus book 3: Sedulò faciam. Sed fortuna fortes: quare conare quæso. I will do it diligently. For fortune favours the brave; so, I beg you, make the attempt. Martial, book 10, epigram 18.

units.la: Ignota toga est: Sed datur petenti Rupta proxima vestis è cathedra.
units.tr: Ignota toga est: Sed datur petenti Rupta proxima vestis è cathedra. The toga is unknown to him; but to the one who asks, a torn garment is given from the nearest chair.

units.la: Hoc habet secundò Porcorum magna propago. Pa-ri felicitate in priori Exegesi arguerat me, quòd unde pro quare usurpassem. Audiat verò eundem Buchnerum. Apud quem sequentia offendo: Aliquando & pro quare, cur ponitur. Flor. lib. 3. cap. 12. Unde enim P. R. agros flagitaret, nisi per famem. pag. 153. valde ππεφατεραγωδίει, quòd dixerim ponere, vel collocare ad usuras. Cum tamen fateatur, auctores, qui apud eũ Clasici sunt, habere: Ponere infænus, dare infænus, &c. at, cur mihi non licuit pari jure dicere, collocare in usuram: Quàm multa apud Scriptores non occurrunt singularia? Cum Hieronymus in Chronico dixisset. XVIII. ætatis gerere annum. Scaliger in Animadv. pag. 128. Ed. altera hæc subjicit: Gerere annum ætatis (inquit) an alius præter Hieronymum dixerit, equidem non memini.
units.tr: This is the second brood of pigs. In the earlier Exegesis he had charged me with using unde for quare. But let him hear Buchner again, where I find the following: Aliquando & pro quare, cur ponitur. Flor. book 3, ch. 12: Unde enim P. R. agros flagitaret, nisi per famem. For whence would the Roman people demand fields, if not through famine? On p. 153 he is greatly over-tragic [ππεφατεραγωδίει] because I said ponere or collocare ad usuras (to put out at interest). Yet he admits that the authors who are classical in his own estimation have ponere infænus, dare infænus, and so on. Why, then, was I not allowed by the same right to say collocare in usuram? How many singular usages do not occur among the writers? Jerome, in the Chronicle, had written XVIII. ætatis gerere annum, to bear a year of eighteen years of age. Scaliger, in his Animadversions, p. 128, second edition, adds this: Gerere annum ætatis (he says), whether anyone other than Jerome has said it, I certainly do not remember.

units.la: Quod non monerem, nisi essent, qui Hieronymum ponerent inter eos, qui Latinissimè loquuntur. Mi lutosa sus, hoc habet jam quarta vice. Dato vero, me minus Latinè locutum fuisse (quod factum nunquam probabitur) Noster, si modò mica humanitatis in eo superfuisset, cogitare debuisset illud Augustini lib. 9. Confess. cap. 6. Non ideo verum (inquit) quia impolitè enunciatur: nec ideo falsum, quia splendidus sermo est: sed perinde esse sapientiam & stultitiam: sicut sunt cibi utiles & inutiinutiles: verbis autem ornatis & inornatis, sicut vasis urbanis & rusticanis utrosque cibos posse mi- niftrari. Haec Augustinus. Sed interim pergit Porcellista , atque barbarismos meos indicare & exagitare instituit: bidental sc. contrecta- vi quod suis pro eis usurparim,& vice versa: quasi verò hoc familiare non fuerit primae notae scriptoribus Romanis, qui ipsa florente Roma scripserunt, atque adeo ipsi Cornelio Nepoti. Videatur Buchnerus in thesauro, Bangius in Observ. Philolog. part. 2. p. 952. Ne dicam de Budaeo in Commentar. Graeca Ling. & Laurentio Valla in peculiari libello hac de re. Sed tanta est porci hujus impuritas, ut gemmas aliorum, in me, tanquam οχύβαλα notet: Arguor graviter, quod assertionem pro sententia, discursum pro scripto usurparim, quod non fecisset, modo cogitasset illud Diomedis Grammat. lib. 1. Pari passu morum ac Literarum cucurrit licentia. Et perinde ut alii mores, ita alius prisci extitit sermo: postera aetas veluti disciplinam pristini seculi, ita & sermonem fastidire coepit. At ita fieri debuit ab homine confidentissimo, quo elogio nostri dilectissimus CaspárScioppius, condecoratur ab AgateGronoviano Tanaquilo Fabro in Not. ad Phaedrum. p. 63. Quis unquam inclementer dixit Africano Jurisc. apud quem tamen utramque paginam faciunt multae dictiones, ab aliis scriptoribus Romanis nunquam usurpatae. Speciatim haec; Indifferenter, ex abundanti, abusive, transfigurare, caussa lucrativa, derisorium, sufficienter, &c.
units.tr: I would not mention this, were there not people who put Jerome among those who speak most elegant Latin. O muddy sow, this is now the fourth time. But granting that I spoke less than elegant Latin (which will never be proved), our friend, if there had been any crumb of civility in him, ought to have considered that saying of Augustine, book 9 of the Confessions, ch. 6: Not therefore true, he says, because it is badly expressed; nor therefore false, because the speech is splendid; but wisdom and folly are alike, as foods are useful and useless; and with ornate or unornate words, as with urbane or rustic vessels, both kinds of food can be served. Thus Augustine. But meanwhile the little pig keeps on, and sets about pointing out and harrying my barbarisms: as if he had touched something accursed, I used suis for eis and vice versa. As though this were not a common practice among the Roman writers of the first rank, who wrote while Rome was flourishing, and indeed among Cornelius Nepos himself! See Buchner in the Thesaurus, and Bang in Observationes Philologicae, part 2, p. 952. I say nothing of Budé in his Commentaries on the Greek language, or of Lorenzo Valla in a separate little book on this subject. But so great is the filthiness of this pig that he brands the jewels of others, as it were [ὀχύβαλα], upon me. I am gravely accused of using assertio for sententia and discursus for scriptum. He would not have done so, had he considered that saying of Diomedes the grammarian, book 1: Licence in customs and in letters ran on side by side. And just as other customs arose, so another kind of speech arose from ancient times; later ages, as if they had begun to despise the discipline of the former age, began to despise its speech too. But this was bound to happen from a man of the utmost self-confidence, a title with which our dearest Caspar Scioppius is honoured by Tanaquil Faber, of the Gronovius circle, in his notes on Phaedrus, p. 63. Who ever said unkindly that the jurist Africanus was unrefined? Yet in him two whole pages are made up of many words never used by other Roman writers. Specifically these: indifferenter, ex abundanti, abusive, transfigurare, causa lucrativa, derisorium, sufficienter, and so on.

units.la: Porro secundum hunc eundem calumniatorem profundere pelves non est Latinum, sed effundere est descendum, si tanto Pythagoræ credimus. At cur Cicero ergò dicit: omnes profudi ingenii vires atque animi mei? Eodem loco habendum, quod non admittat procurare famam pro acquirere famam, cum tamen Tibullus dixerit:
units.tr: Further, according to this same slanderer, profundere pelves is not Latin, but effundere must be used, if we believe so great a Pythagoras. But then why does Cicero say, omnes profudi ingenii vires atque animi mei? In the same category must be placed his refusal to admit procurare famam for acquirere famam, although Tibullus has written:

units.la: Ipse procuravi, ne possent sæva nocere omnia.
units.tr: Ipse procuravi, ne possent sæva nocere omnia. I myself took care that all cruel things should not be able to harm.

units.la: Non placet quoque noltro Aristarcho exhara, quod dixerim aliquid deducere prolixè, pro multis de aliqua re agere. cum eodem sensu à me hoc dictū fit, atq; Virg. Eccl. 6. deductum carmen dixit. Nam volui innuere, me simplici oratione prolixius aliquid exposuisse. Nec est quod turbet verbum coincidere, quod respondet Græcorum τὸ συμπίπτειν, ut ipse Vossius fatetur lib. 1. cap. 23. de Vitiis Latin. Sermon. Illud ratione, potuisset quoq; intactum reliquisse & cogitasse illud August. Ep. 49. Sermoni humano verba nova, vel minus usitata, moderatè ac decenter adspersa, splendorem attulerunt.
units.tr: Nor does our Aristarchus approve of the word exhara, or of my saying aliquid deducere prolixè for to treat a matter at length, though Virgil, in Eclogue 6, used deductum carmen in the same sense. For I meant to hint that I had set forth something somewhat more fully in plain prose. Nor should the word coincidere trouble anyone; it corresponds to the Greek τὸ συμπίπτειν [to sympiptein], as Vossius himself admits in book 1, ch. 23, of his De Vitiis Latini Sermonis. He could reasonably have left that alone, and considered that saying of Augustine, Ep. 49: New or less usual words, moderately and fittingly scattered through human speech, have brought splendour.

units.la: Deinde locutiones quoq; Syntacticas, sed, per calumniam invadit. Explicet initio, quo jure Cicero dixerit. Orat. 5. in Verrem. hanc rem sibi præsidio fuerant futuram, & illud Plauti Amph. a. 1. f. 1. Nunc vero mihi in mentem fuit. Vel, ut redundans, non arguisset, si observasset à me pro etiam accipi, sicut sæpe apud Ciceronem, spectatim in Orat. pro Leg. Manil. quando dicit: Cum jam populus Rom. suam auctoritatem vel contra omnes, qui dii sentiunt, posse defendi. defendere. Æqve innocuum est illud tamdiu quam, nec necessum substituere donec. Nam æque sic loqui potui, quam Cic. in Tusc. dicit: Corpus tam diu gaudet, dum sentit voluptatem. Nec est quod arrodat mutare pecuniam, pro mutuo dare. Cum sciat Plautum ita locutum fuisse. Si dicat lectionem vulgarem sibi non placere, ad alios, quibus non displicet, provocabo. Interea videatur Vossius de Vit. Lat. Ser p. 157. Quod si maneat sudes in oculis hominis malevoli, componat illud Lucretii in lib. 3.
units.tr: Next he attacks my syntactic idioms too, but by calumny. Let him first explain by what right Cicero said, in the fifth Verrine, hanc rem sibi præsidio fuerant futuram, and Plautus, Amphitruo act 1, scene 1: Nunc vero mihi in mentem fuit. Or, if it is redundant, he would not have found fault had he observed that I took it as even, as Cicero often does, especially in the Oration for the Manilian Law, where he says: Cum jam populus Rom. suam auctoritatem vel contra omnes, qui dii sentiunt, posse defendi. Equally harmless is tamdiu quam; there is no need to substitute donec. For I could speak in the same way as Cicero does in the Tusculans: Corpus tam diu gaudet, dum sentit voluptatem. Nor is there reason for him to gnaw at mutare pecuniam for mutuo dare (to lend money), since he knows that Plautus spoke so. If he says that the common reading does not please him, I shall appeal to others to whom it does not displease. Meanwhile see Vossius, De Vitiis Latini Sermonis, p. 157. But if the stake stays stuck in the eyes of this malicious man, let him compare that line of Lucretius, book 3:

units.la: Quod bene si videant animo distinguere sequantur.
units.tr: Quod bene si videant animo distinguere, sequantur. Which, if they see clearly how to distinguish in the mind, let them follow.

units.la: Dissolvent animi magno se angore metuque.
units.tr: Dissolvent animi magno se angore metuque. They dissolve themselves in great anguish and fear of mind.

units.la: At, nae ego fatuus sum, quod singulis hominis ineptiis respondeam? Et tamen audet mihi Pethaurus destinare, cujus vice, ego, jam morti vicinus, à Deo meo praestolor angelorum comitatum, à quo anima mea devehatur in sinum coelestis Patris. Longè majori jure, Grammatico homini, ex Porcelli gente destinavere porcum, ut eo duce tendat Anticyras, & postquam Lares placaverit, eum quoque immolet. Si forte inanæ illud cerebellum, ineptiis Grammaticis & solo Porcello dignis, liberari possit. Si alicui hæc duriora videantur, cogitet illud vetus dictum: Quamvis non praestat, ne exigat modestiam, & Sophoclæum illud: ἐγὼ ἀνδρὶ συγγνώμην Κλέων Φλαῦρα, συμβαλεῖν ἔχω ἐπηκαδ Huic ego igne sco viro, Qui probra cum audit, probra probris regerit.
units.tr: But, indeed, am I a fool to answer each of this man's silly remarks? And yet Pethaurus presumes to appoint me, when, now near to death, I await from my God the company of angels, by whom my soul is to be carried into the bosom of the heavenly Father. With far greater right, they have appointed a pig of the Porcellus family as guide for this grammarian, to lead him to Anticyra, and, once he has appeased the Lares, to sacrifice him too, should perhaps that empty little brain be freed of grammatical trifles fit only for a little pig. If these things seem too harsh to anyone, let him consider the old saying, Although it is not fitting, let it not demand modesty, and that Sophoclean line: [ἐγὼ ἀνδρὶ συγγνώμην Κλέων Φλαῦρα, συμβαλεῖν ἔχω ἐπηκαδ] I forgive this man, who, when he hears insults, returns insults with insults.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.
